pts: Composition \(g\circ f\) applies \(f\) first, then \(g\); order matters, so composition is not commutative.
Composition of functions is associative: \(h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f\), proven by checking both sides give \(h(g(f(x)))\) for every \(x\in A\).
For an arbitrary set \(A\) there are no interesting functions from \(A\) to itself unless operations such as addition and multiplication are defined on \(A\).
defs: Composition of functions
For \(f:A\to B\) and \(g:B\to C\), the composite \(g\circ f:A\to C\) is defined by \((g\circ f)(x)=g(f(x))\): apply \(f\) first, then \(g\).
tips: Composition \(g\circ f\) means apply \(f\) first; reversing the order usually gives a different result or is not even defined.
Associativity proofs must show equality for every element \(x\) in the domain, not just one example.
rq: Why is composition associative even though it is not commutative?
Both bracketings apply \(f\), then \(g\), then \(h\) in the same order, so both give \(h(g(f(x)))\); commutativity would require swapping the order of application, which changes results.
Why can't we define a function like \(x\mapsto 3x+1\) on the set \(A=\{\text{apple},\text{blue},\diamond\}\)?
Because multiplication by 3 and addition of 1 are not defined on \(A\); the rule needs operations that the set does not have.

notes.t: Identity Function
pts: The identity function on a set A sends every element to itself and is the only function definable without any prior knowledge.
Composing any function with the identity (on either side) returns the original function, so id acts like 1 or 0 under composition.
Identity functions on different sets have different domains/codomains, so id_A and id_B are different functions even with the same rule.
The composition property f ∘ h = f and h ∘ g = g force h to equal id_A, so the identity is characterised by this property.
defs: Identity function
For a set A, the identity function id_A : A → A is defined by id_A(x) = x for all x ∈ A; it is also written 1_A, or simply id when A is clear.
eqs: x = element of A (no unit); A = set (domain and codomain)
f = function A → B; id_A = identity on A
f = function A → B; id_B = identity on B
tips: Do not treat id_A and id_B as the same function just because they share the rule x ↦ x; check the domain and codomain.
Be careful with composition order: f ∘ id_A is defined only when the codomain of id_A matches the domain of f, and the result is still f.
rq: Why are id_A and id_B considered different functions even though they have the same rule x ↦ x?
Because a function is defined by its domain, codomain and rule together; id_A : A → A and id_B : B → B have different domains and codomains.
Why does composing with the identity leave f unchanged, and why is this analogous to adding 0 or multiplying by 1?
Because id maps each input to itself, so f(id(x)) = f(x); like x + 0 = x and x·1 = x, the identity does nothing in the operation.
What would it mean if some h satisfied f ∘ h = f and h ∘ g = g for all such f, g?
Such an h must be the identity, id_A, since the identity is the unique element that leaves all compositions unchanged.

notes.t: Invertible functions
pts: A function f is invertible if some function g composed with f (in either order) gives the identity map on the relevant set.
Invertibility requires both compositions to be identities: g∘f = id_A and f∘g = id_B.
To verify an inverse, it suffices to check both composites equal x for the given functions; the order of computation can be chosen freely.
defs: Invertible function
A function f: A → B is invertible if there exists a function g: B → A such that g∘f = id_A and f∘g = id_B.
eqs: x ∈ A (domain element); y ∈ B (codomain element); f = forward function; g = candidate inverse; id = identity map (dimensionless)
x ∈ ℝ (dimensionless); g(x) = inverse function value
tips: Check both g(f(x)) = x and f(g(x)) = x; verifying only one composition is incomplete.
Be careful with the domain and codomain: the inverse must map B back to A, not just satisfy the identity formally.
rq: Why must both g∘f and f∘g be checked, rather than just one of them?
One composition being the identity only shows f is injective (or g is a left inverse); the other is needed to guarantee g is also a two-sided inverse, i.e. f is onto with g as its inverse on B.
For f(x)=3x+1, why does computing f(g(x)) give the same result as computing g(f(x))?
Both compositions equal x because g undoes the operations of f in reverse order: subtracting 1 then dividing by 3 cancels multiplying by 3 then adding 1.

notes.t: Inverse functions and bijectivity
pts: If a function has an inverse, that inverse is unique (proved by composing with both candidate inverses and using associativity).
An invertible function f: A → B has inverse f⁻¹: B → A satisfying both f⁻¹∘f = id_A and f∘f⁻¹ = id_B.
The notation f⁻¹ is suggestive only; the composition symbol ∘ is not multiplication, so f⁻¹ is not 1/f.
A function is invertible exactly when it is bijective: a bijection supplies the unique pairing used to define the inverse, and an inverse forces injectivity and surjectivity.
defs: Inverse function f⁻¹
For an invertible f: A → B, the unique function f⁻¹: B → A with f⁻¹∘f = id_A and f∘f⁻¹ = id_B.
eqs: f = function A → B (dimensionless map); f⁻¹ = inverse function B → A; id_A, id_B = identity maps on A and B
tips: Do not treat f⁻¹ as 1/f: the ∘ operation is composition, not multiplication.
Check both compositions f⁻¹∘f = id_A and f∘f⁻¹ = id_B when verifying an inverse.
rq: Why must an invertible function be bijective?
Injectivity follows because applying f⁻¹ to f(x)=f(x′) gives x=x′; surjectivity follows because every b equals f(f⁻¹(b)), so every b is hit.
Why is the inverse unique?
If h and g are both inverses, g = id_A∘g = (h∘f)∘g = h∘(f∘g) = h∘id_B = h.

notes.t: Computing Inverses of Functions
pts: A bijective function has an inverse; to find it, write y = f(x), solve for x, then express x as f⁻¹(y).
Bijectivity guarantees an inverse exists, but you may still need to work out what the inverse actually is.
The method works for functions between subsets of ℝ, but you must pick y in the codomain and check the domain to discard spurious solutions.
Finally, rename the variable y as x to write the inverse in the usual form f⁻¹(x).
defs: Inverse function f⁻¹
For a bijection f: A → B, the inverse f⁻¹: B → A is the function sending each y ∈ B to the unique x ∈ A with f(x) = y.
Bijection
A function that is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto); only bijections have inverse functions.
eqs: x = input variable (dimensionless in this example); f⁻¹ = inverse function
tips: When restricting to subsets of ℝ, choose y only from the codomain and discard solutions outside the domain.
Remember to rename y to x at the end, and do not confuse f⁻¹(x) with 1/f(x).
rq: Why does the procedure of solving y = f(x) for x produce the inverse only when f is bijective?
Solving for x gives a unique value for each y only if each y corresponds to exactly one x; injectivity ensures uniqueness and surjectivity ensures every y in the codomain has a preimage.
Why must we rename y as x at the end?
By convention the independent variable is written x, so f⁻¹(y) is rewritten as f⁻¹(x) without changing the function.

notes.t: Restricting domains to obtain inverses
pts: A non-invertible function can become invertible after restricting its domain and codomain so it is a bijection; the inverse depends on that restriction.
For f(x)=x²+1 on x≥0 with codomain ≥1, solving y=x²+1 gives x=√(y−1), discarding the negative root because x≥0.
Always verify an inverse by checking both compositions f(f⁻¹(y))=y and f⁻¹(f(x))=x.
Restricting to x≤0 instead gives a different inverse g⁻¹(y)=−√(y−1), so the same formula can yield different inverses.
Without restriction, h(x)=x²+1 is not invertible, so h⁻¹ does not exist; f⁻¹ and g⁻¹ are only inverses on subsets of the domain.
defs: Bijection
A function that is both injective (one-to-one) and surjective (onto); only bijections have a genuine inverse function.
eqs: Inverse of f(x)=x²+1 on x≥0 with codomain y≥1
y = output in ℝ≥1 (dimensionless); f⁻¹(y) = input x ≥ 0 (dimensionless)
y = output in ℝ≥1 (dimensionless); g⁻¹(y) = input x ≤ 0 (dimensionless)
tips: Always state the restricted domain and codomain; the inverse formula (e.g. +√ vs −√) depends on them, so an answer without them is incomplete.
Do not write h⁻¹ for a non-bijective function; instead say the inverse exists only on a restricted subset, such as f⁻¹ or g⁻¹.
rq: Why must we discard the negative square root when finding f⁻¹ for f defined on ℝ≥0?
Because the domain of f is x≥0, so the inverse's outputs must lie in ℝ≥0; the negative root would be outside the domain of f.
Why does h(x)=x²+1 on ℝ have no inverse, even though its formula can be solved for x?
Because h is not injective (x and −x give the same output), so solving gives two values and there is no unique inverse function.
What if we restricted the codomain of f differently, say to ℝ≥5?
The output y would be constrained to y≥5, but the inverse formula √(y−1) still applies; the restriction changes which outputs are valid, not the algebra.

notes.t: Computing inverses by plotting (mirror images in y = x)
pts: The graph of an inverse function is the mirror image of the original graph in the line y = x.
Plotting y = f⁻¹(x) is the same as plotting f(y) = x with x and y roles flipped, which is why the reflection holds.
Plotting is less rigorous than algebraic computation, but a good guess can be checked quickly against the graph.
Examples shown: y = x² and y = √x; y = 3x + 1 and y = (x − 1)/3 are mutual inverses.
defs: Inverse function f⁻¹
A function that reverses f, so that f⁻¹(f(x)) = x and f(f⁻¹(x)) = x; its graph is the reflection of the graph of f in the line y = x.
eqs: Equation defining the inverse graph (reflection of y = f(x))
x, y = dimensionless real variables (roles swapped relative to y = f(x))
tips: Graphical checking is a verification aid, not a rigorous derivation of an inverse; still compute algebraically in exams.
Check the domain/range restriction when reflecting, e.g. y = x² on x ≥ 0 is needed for √x to be its inverse.
rq: Why does swapping x and y in y = f(x) give the graph of the inverse, and what geometric transformation does this correspond to?
Swapping x and y gives x = f(y), i.e. y = f⁻¹(x); swapping coordinates reflects every point (a,b) to (b,a), which is reflection in the line y = x.
Using the example y = 3x + 1, how can you check a guessed inverse graphically?
Plot the guessed inverse y = (x − 1)/3 and check it is the mirror image of y = 3x + 1 in y = x, e.g. the point (0,1) maps to (1,0).

units.name: 07 Symmetries of Functions
units.ov: This material classifies functions by symmetry: even functions (\( f(-x)=f(x) \), mirror symmetry in the y-axis), odd functions (\( f(-x)=-f(x) \), half-turn symmetry about the origin) and periodic functions (\( f(t+T)=f(t) \)). Parity rules for sums, products and compositions, the even/odd decomposition and the integral shortcuts over \([-a,a]\) all follow from the same substitution \(x\to -x\). Periodicity brings in period, frequency, angular frequency and wavenumber, which connect to oscillations such as the pendulum.
must: Definitions: even \( f(-x)=f(x) \), odd \( f(-x)=-f(x) \), for ALL x in a domain symmetric about 0; one counterexample disproves either.
Integral shortcuts over \([-a,a]\): even gives \( 2\int_0^a f\,dx \), odd gives \( 0 \). These hold only for symmetric limits.
Standard examples: even are \(x^{2n}\), \(|x|\), \(\cos x\), \(\cosh x\), \(e^{-x^2}\); odd are \(x^{2n+1}\), \(\sin x\), \(\tan x\), \(\sinh x\), \(\tanh x\), \(\mathrm{sgn}\,x\), \(\sqrt[3]{x}\).
Parity algebra: even+even=even, odd+odd=odd, even×even=even, odd×odd=even, even×odd=odd.
Composition: if f is even then \( g\circ f \) is even for any g; \( f\circ g \) need not be. Do not confuse \( f\cdot g \) with \( f\circ g \).
Decomposition: \( f_e=\tfrac12[f(x)+f(-x)] \), \( f_o=\tfrac12[f(x)-f(-x)] \), \( f=f_e+f_o \). Most functions are neither even nor odd (e.g. \(x^2+x\), \(x^3+2x^2\)).
Periodicity: \( f(t+T)=f(t) \) for all t, and the period is the smallest such T. Any multiple of T also works. Example: the fractional part (sawtooth) has period 1.
\( \nu=1/T \), \( \omega=2\pi\nu=2\pi/T \), and wavenumber \( k=2\pi/\lambda \) (spatial analogue); know the units (Hz, rad/s, rad/m).
Pendulum: \( T=2\pi\sqrt{L/g} \) (formula cut off in the notes, so verify it), independent of the bob's mass. Clock hands have periods 12 h, 60 min and 60 s.
Signed integral versus geometric area: an odd function's integral over \([-a,a]\) is zero but its area is not. The symmetry trick fails for \([0,a]\) or \([-a,2a]\).
conn: Parity algebra plus the integral shortcuts: classify the integrand as even×odd, odd×odd and so on, then decide whether to double the integral or set it to zero.
Even/odd decomposition plus integration: for a general f, \( \int_{-a}^a f=2\int_0^a f_e \), because the odd part integrates to zero.
Periodicity plus parity: \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) are periodic with \(T=2\pi/\omega\) and have opposite parity, which links to the later Fourier-style splitting.
The even/odd split parallels the symmetric/antisymmetric split of a matrix, \( A_s=\tfrac12(A+A^T) \) and \( A_a=\tfrac12(A-A^T) \).
exq: Classify each of \(x^3\cos x\), \(x^2+x\), \(\sin x+\tan x\), \(e^{-x^2}\sin x\) and \(|x|\,x\) as even, odd or neither, with a proof via \(x\to -x\).
Evaluate \( \int_{-2}^{2}(x^3+3x^2+\sin x)\,dx \) using symmetry, stating which terms vanish and which are doubled.
Find the even and odd parts of \( f(x)=e^x \) and verify that \( f_e \) is even, \( f_o \) is odd and \( f_e+f_o=f \).
Prove that if f is even and g is arbitrary then \( g\circ f \) is even, and give a counterexample showing \( f\circ g \) need not be even.
A signal has period T = 0.02 s. Find its frequency and angular frequency. Then find the wavenumber of a wave of wavelength 0.5 m, and the period of a pendulum of length 1 m.

notes.t: Even Functions (symmetry about the y-axis)
pts: Reflecting \( y=f(x) \) in the \( y \)-axis gives \( y=f(-x) \), because swapping \( x \) with \( -x \) reflects the inputs through 0.
If a function equals its own reflection in the \( y \)-axis, it has mirror symmetry about \( x=0 \), which is the defining feature of an even function.
The example \( f(x)=x^2 \) is even: its plot is unchanged by reflection in the \( y \)-axis.
Even symmetry is a condition on all inputs, not just some of them.
defs: Even function

A function \( f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} \) is even if \( f(-x)=f(x) \) for all \( x\in\mathbb{R} \). Its graph is symmetric about the \( y \)-axis. The definition extends to domains \( [-a,a] \) or \( (-a,a) \), and more generally to any sets \( A,B \) where \( -x\in A \) whenever \( x\in A \).
eqs: \( f \) = function; \( x \) = input (dimensionless in this context)
tips: Check the condition for all \( x \) in the domain, not just a few sample values; a single counterexample disproves evenness.
For domains like \( [-a,a] \), the domain must be symmetric about 0 for the condition \( f(-x)=f(x) \) to make sense.
rq: Why does replacing \( x \) with \( -x \) produce a reflection in the \( y \)-axis rather than the \( x \)-axis?

Changing the sign of the input reflects the inputs through 0 (the origin in x). This moves each point's x-coordinate to its mirror image across \( x=0 \), which is the \( y \)-axis, while the output values stay the same.
If \( f(-x)=f(x) \) holds only for \( x\in(0,1) \), can we conclude \( f \) is even?
No. Evenness requires the identity for all \( x \) in the domain (or the symmetric domain), so checking a subset is not sufficient.

notes.t: Even and odd functions: definition and integral symmetry
pts: A function is even when f(−x) = f(x) for every x in its domain; this must be checked for all x, not just a few values.
A cubic such as x³ fails the even test: f(−1) = −1 ≠ 1 = f(1), so it is not even.
For an even function, the integral over [−a, a] equals twice the integral over [0, a], which saves work when finding areas under curves.
Powers x^{2n} with integer n, |x|, cos x, cosh x and e^{−x²} are all even; x⁵, x and sin x are not.
defs: Even function
A function f: ℝ → ℝ is even if f(−x) = f(x) for all x ∈ ℝ, so its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
eqs: Integral of an even function over a symmetric interval
a = positive real limit (dimensionless here); f = even function; x = real variable
tips: Check evenness over the whole domain; testing one or two points like f(0) or f(1) is not enough to prove a function is even.
Remember the doubling rule applies only to even functions and symmetric limits [−a, a]; using it for odd functions gives the wrong answer.
rq: Why does the doubling rule for integrals only work when f is even, and what goes wrong for an odd function?

Evenness makes the areas on [−a,0] and [0,a] equal by reflection in the y-axis; for an odd function the areas are negatives of each other, so the integral over [−a,a] is 0 rather than twice the half-integral.
Why is f(x) = x² + x⁴ even while f(x) = x³ + 2x² is not?
Every term of x² + x⁴ has an even power, so substituting −x leaves it unchanged; x³ + 2x² contains an odd power x³, which changes sign, so f(−x) ≠ f(x).

notes.t: Even functions: graphs and symmetry about the y-axis
pts: Even functions are symmetric about the y-axis: the graph to the left of the axis is a mirror image of the graph to the right.
Examples shown include polynomials with even powers, the absolute value, cosine, hyperbolic cosine and a Gaussian-type exponential, all of which look identical on either side of x = 0.
Even functions with a minimum at the origin (x², x⁴, |x|) are non-negative, while cos x oscillates and eˣ² peaks at x = 0.
defs: Even function
A function f satisfying f(−x) = f(x) for all x in its domain; its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
eqs: x = input variable (dimensionless or unit of the domain); f = function value
x = input variable; y = output value (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse even functions (symmetric about the y-axis) with odd functions (symmetric about the origin); test by substituting −x.
Even functions are not necessarily positive or with a minimum at zero; cos x and e^(−x²) show that symmetry alone says nothing about sign or shape.
rq: Why does the graph of y = |x| look like a 'V' yet still count as even?
Because |−x| = |x| for every x, so the values on the left of the y-axis mirror those on the right, giving symmetry about the y-axis.
How can you tell from a graph alone whether a function is even?
Check whether folding the paper along the y-axis makes the two halves of the curve coincide.

notes.t: Even functions: closure under sums, products and composition
pts: The sum of two even functions is even, since each term's sign is unchanged when x is replaced by −x.
The pointwise product of two even functions is even, because f(−x)g(−x) = f(x)g(x).
If f is even and g is any function, then g∘f is even, because the inner function f(−x) = f(x) first removes the sign change.
Composition order matters: the product result holds for f·g, not for f∘g.
Odd functions are introduced as those whose reflection in the y-axis equals their reflection in the x-axis, i.e. y = −f(x).
defs: Even function
A function f: ℝ → ℝ is even if f(−x) = f(x) for all x ∈ ℝ; its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
Odd function
A function f is odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for all x ∈ ℝ; its graph is symmetric under reflection through the origin.
eqs: f, g = even functions (dimensionless here); x = input variable
f, g = even functions; x = input variable
f = original function; y = output of reflected graph
tips: Do not confuse f·g (pointwise product) with f∘g (composition): the closure result is proved for f·g and for g∘f with f even, not for f∘g in general.
Check the condition carefully: Lemma 7.1.13 requires only the inner function f to be even; the outer function g can be arbitrary.
rq: Why does composing an even function on the inside, g∘f, always give an even result, regardless of g?
Because (g∘f)(−x) = g(f(−x)) = g(f(x)) = (g∘f)(x); the evenness of f is used before g is applied, so g's behaviour does not matter.
Why is f∘g not guaranteed to be even when f and g are even?
Because the composition's symmetry depends on the outer function; if the outer function is not symmetric, (f∘g)(−x) = f(g(x)) need not equal f(g(x)) in general with the symmetric property being lost.
What does the reflection in the x-axis do to the sign of the function values?
It multiplies every value by −1, so a point above the x-axis moves below it and vice versa, giving y = −f(x).

notes.t: Odd functions and symmetry in integrals
pts: An odd function satisfies f(−x) = −f(x), so its graph is symmetric about the origin.
Integrating an odd function over a symmetric interval [−a, a] gives zero, since the areas on either side cancel.
Symmetry lets you evaluate some definite integrals instantly without computing an antiderivative.
Powers x^(2n+1) with integer n, sin x, tan x and cube roots of x are all odd functions.
defs: Odd function
A function f: ℝ → ℝ is odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for all x ∈ ℝ.
eqs: Integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval
a = positive real limit (dimensionless or in the units of x); f = odd function; A = area between 0 and a (units of f·x)
tips: Symmetry gives zero only over a symmetric interval [−a, a]; it does not apply to ranges like [0, a] or [−a, 2a].
Check the oddness condition f(−x) = −f(x) explicitly; a product of an even and an odd function is odd, but a product of two odd functions is even.
rq: Why does the area from −a to 0 equal −A when f is odd, rather than simply +A?
Because f(−x) = −f(x) makes the function values on the negative side the negatives of those on the positive side, so the area lies below the x-axis and is counted as −A.
Why can you conclude ∫_{-1}^{1} x² sin x dx = 0 without computing an antiderivative?
x² sin x is odd (even times odd), and the interval [−1, 1] is symmetric about 0, so the integral vanishes.

notes.t: Even and odd functions: areas under symmetric curves
pts: For an even function, the area from −a to a is twice the area from 0 to a, because the two halves mirror each other across the y-axis.
For an odd function, the two halves of the area from −a to a are equal in size but opposite in sign, so the signed total integral is zero.
Area below the x-axis counts as negative in an integral, which is why odd functions give a total of zero over a symmetric interval.
Symmetry can reduce the work needed to evaluate integrals, especially for odd functions where the answer often vanishes.
defs: Even function
A function f satisfying f(−x) = f(x) for all x in its domain; its graph is symmetric about the y-axis.
Odd function
A function f satisfying f(−x) = −f(x) for all x in its domain; its graph is symmetric about the origin.
Signed area
The integral of a function over an interval, where regions above the x-axis contribute positively and regions below contribute negatively.
eqs: Integral of an even function over a symmetric interval
f = even function; a = limit of integration (dimensionless or in the units of x); x = variable of integration
Integral of an odd function over a symmetric interval
f = odd function; a = limit of integration; x = variable of integration
tips: Only use the symmetry shortcut when the interval is symmetric about zero; ∫ from −a to b with a ≠ b does not simplify this way.
Do not confuse 'area' with 'signed integral': an odd function's integral over a symmetric interval is zero, but the geometric area is not.
rq: Why does the integral of x³ from −a to a equal zero even though the area on each side is clearly non-zero?
The left-hand area lies below the x-axis, so it is counted as negative; it cancels the equal positive area on the right, giving A + (−A) = 0.
How could you use symmetry to evaluate ∫ from −2 to 2 of x² dx quickly?
Since x² is even, the integral equals 2∫ from 0 to 2 of x² dx = 2·(8/3) = 16/3.
Is the sign function sgn x odd, even, or neither, and what does this imply for its integral over [−a, a]?
It is odd (sgn(−x) = −sgn x), so its integral over [−a, a] is zero.

notes.t: Odd functions: graphical symmetry (plots of odd functions)
pts: An odd function is symmetric about the origin: the graph is unchanged by a half-turn (rotation by 180°) about (0,0), so f(−x) = −f(x).
Examples shown include y = x, y = x³, cube root, sin x, tan x, sinh x, tanh x and sgn x; each passes through the origin when defined there.
Odd-function graphs look the same after reflection in the y-axis and then in the x-axis, which is the origin-symmetry test read off a plot.
Odd functions can have jumps or be unbounded (tan x, sgn x) yet keep point symmetry about the origin wherever they are defined.
defs: Odd function
A function f is odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for every x in its domain; its graph is symmetric about the origin.
eqs: x = input variable (dimensionless unless stated); f = function value
tips: Do not confuse odd (origin symmetry) with even (y-axis symmetry); a function can be neither, e.g. y = x² + x.
Check the domain: symmetry f(−x) = −f(x) only needs to hold for x and −x both in the domain.
rq: Why does y = tan x show point symmetry about the origin even though its graph has vertical asymptotes?
Because tan(−x) = −tan x for every x where it is defined, so each branch is mirrored through (0,0) with the asymptotes mirrored too.
How can you tell from a graph alone that y = x³ is odd rather than even?
Rotating the graph 180° about the origin leaves it unchanged, whereas an even function would be unchanged by reflection in the y-axis.

notes.t: Even and odd functions: combining odd functions
pts: Odd functions satisfy f(−x) = −f(x); checking this definition (or plotting) identifies odd functions, e.g. x⁵, x³+x⁵, x, sin x + tan x, and the zero function.
The sum of two odd functions is again odd, since (f+g)(−x) = −f(x) − g(x) = −(f+g)(x).
The product of two odd functions is even, because the two minus signs cancel: (f·g)(−x) = [−f(x)][−g(x)] = (f·g)(x).
Combining odd functions does not always give an odd function; the product rule produces an even function, so the type of the result must be checked each time.
defs: Odd function
A function f: ℝ → ℝ is odd if f(−x) = −f(x) for all x ∈ ℝ.
Even function
A function f: ℝ → ℝ is even if f(−x) = f(x) for all x ∈ ℝ.
eqs: f, g = functions ℝ → ℝ; x = real input (dimensionless)
f, g = functions ℝ → ℝ; x = real input (dimensionless)
tips: Do not assume a combination keeps the parity of its parts: the product of two odd functions is even, not odd.
Check odd/even by substituting −x and simplifying; a function such as x³+2x² is neither odd nor even.
rq: Why must the product of two odd functions be even rather than odd?
Evaluating at −x gives [−f(x)][−g(x)] = f(x)g(x), so the product satisfies the even condition; the two sign changes cancel.
Why does the sum of two odd functions stay odd?
(f+g)(−x) = −f(x) − g(x) = −(f+g)(x), so the odd condition is preserved under addition.

notes.t: Odd and even parts of a function
pts: Every function ℝ→ℝ splits into an even part plus an odd part, which is the key reason even/odd functions are useful, especially for integrals.
The even part is half the sum of f(x) and f(−x); the odd part is half their difference, so the two parts add back to f.
Showing f_o is odd (or even) requires substituting −x into the defined expression and comparing with the original, using f(−(−x)) = f(x).
The proof of evenness of f_e is left as an exercise (Problem 7.1.35), mirroring the odd-part check.
Most functions are neither even nor odd, so the decomposition is needed in general.
defs: Even part of f
f_e(x) = ½[f(x) + f(−x)], which satisfies f_e(−x) = f_e(x).
Odd part of f
f_o(x) = ½[f(x) − f(−x)], which satisfies f_o(−x) = −f_o(x).
eqs: f = original function; x = real input (dimensionless here); f_e = even part
f = original function; x = real input; f_o = odd part
f = original function; f_e = even part; f_o = odd part
tips: The notation f_e and f_o is not standard; always define it before using it in an answer.
Remember f(−(−x)) = f(x) when substituting −x into an expression, otherwise signs are lost.
rq: Why does subtracting f(−x) from f(x) produce an odd function rather than an even one?
Replacing x by −x flips the sign of the difference: f_o(−x) = ½[f(−x) − f(x)] = −f_o(x), so it is odd.
If f is already even, what are its even and odd parts?
f_e = f and f_o = 0, since f(−x) = f(x) makes the odd part vanish.

notes.t: Periodic Functions (sawtooth/fractional part example, definition of period)
pts: The fractional part function repeats every time 1 is added to the input, so it is periodic with period 1.
A function is periodic if shifting its input by a fixed T leaves the output unchanged for all t.
The period is defined as the smallest T satisfying the periodicity condition, not just any such T.
Any even or odd decomposition of a function, and similarly any matrix, splits into symmetric and antisymmetric parts.
defs: Periodic function
A function f: ℝ → B is periodic if there exists some T ∈ ℝ such that f(t+T) = f(t) for all t ∈ ℝ; the smallest such T is the period.
Fractional part function
The function giving the part of x after the decimal point, e.g. f(3.14) = 0.14; it is periodic with period 1 (sawtooth shape).
eqs: f = function; t = input variable (dimensionless); T = period (same units as t)
f_e = even part of f; x = input variable
f_o = odd part of f; x = input variable
Symmetric and antisymmetric parts of a matrix
A = square matrix; A_s = symmetric part; A_a = antisymmetric part; A^T = transpose
tips: Periodicity requires f(t+T)=f(t) for ALL t; checking only a few points is not enough, and any multiple of the period also works, so take the smallest.
A function that is a sum of even and odd functions is not itself even or odd; use the even/odd parts formulas to split it.
rq: Why does the fractional part function f(x+1)=f(x) make its period exactly 1 rather than 2 or 0.5?
Period 1 is the smallest positive T for which shifting by T leaves the output unchanged; shifting by 0.5 changes e.g. f(0)=0 to f(0.5)=0.5, so 0.5 fails, and any multiple of 1 works.
Why is x² + x³ neither even nor odd, even though x² and x³ individually are?
Even and odd properties require f(−x)=f(x) or f(−x)=−f(x) for all x across the whole function; the sum gives f(−x)=x²−x³, which is neither f(x) nor −f(x).

notes.t: Periodic functions: period, frequency, angular frequency and wavenumber
pts: Frequency is the reciprocal of the period: it counts repetitions per unit time.
Angular frequency \( \omega \) is used for circular/trigonometric motion, related to frequency by a factor \(2\pi\).
Wavenumber \(k\) is the spatial equivalent of angular frequency, with period \(\lambda\) in space.
Clock hands give periodic functions: the hour hand has period 12 h, minute hand 60 min, second hand 60 s.
A pendulum's angle is periodic, and its period does not depend on the mass of the bob.
defs: Frequency
The number of times a periodic function repeats per unit time; equal to the reciprocal of the period.
tips: Do not confuse the symbol \(\nu\) (frequency) with \(f\), which the notes reserve for functions.
Angular frequency \(\omega\) is in rad/s, while frequency \(\nu\) is in Hz (s\(^{-1}\)); remember the \(2\pi\) factor when converting.
rq: Why does the hour hand have period 12 h rather than 24 h?
The hand's position repeats every 12 hours (and no sooner) on a clock face, so the smallest repeating interval is 12 h.
Why is the pendulum's period independent of its mass?
The mass cancels out of the equation of motion, since gravitational force and inertia are both proportional to mass; the period depends only on L and g.
Why introduce \(\omega\) and \(k\) instead of just using \(\nu\) and \(\lambda\)?
They absorb the factor \(2\pi\) that appears in circular and trigonometric formulas, simplifying expressions.

notes.t: Periodic functions and the small-angle pendulum
pts: A function with period T repeats its values every T, so it is fully determined by one period.
The small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ θ underlies the pendulum result and holds only for small θ in radians (up to about 0.2 rad).
sin and cos have period 2π, while tan has half that period, π, because adding π flips the signs of both sin and cos.
Trigonometric functions are the most common periodic functions, and Fourier analysis relies on periodicity.
defs: Periodic function
A function f with period T satisfies f(t) = f(t + kT) for all integers k, so it repeats over and over with period T.
eqs: f = function; t = independent variable; T = period (s or unit of t); k = integer
θ = angle from vertical (rad); valid for small θ
x = angle (rad); π = period of tan
tips: The small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ θ is only valid with θ in radians and for small angles (about 0.2 rad or less); using degrees invalidates it.
Do not confuse the period of tan (π) with that of sin and cos (2π).
rq: Why is it enough to know a periodic function's behaviour over one period?
Because the function simply repeats: f(t) = f(t + kT), so every later or earlier value equals a value within one period.
Why does tan have period π while sin and cos have period 2π?
Shifting x by π gives sin(x+π) = sin x and cos(x+π) = −cos x; the two minus signs cancel in the ratio, so tan repeats after π.
What happens to the accuracy of the pendulum result if θ is 0.5 rad?
The approximation sin θ ≈ θ becomes poor, so the result is no longer reliable; it is valid only for small θ in radians.

notes.t: Periodic functions and the period of sin
pts: A function is periodic with period T if shifting the input by T returns the same output, for every input.
The sine graph repeats its shape exactly every 2π: the points x₁ and x₁+2π, and x₂ and x₂+2π, give identical heights.
Any starting point x works: the repetition holds wherever we start on the axis, so the pattern is the same over every interval of length 2π.
defs: Periodic function
A function f is periodic with period T > 0 if f(x + T) = f(x) for all x in its domain; T is the smallest such positive value when one exists.
tips: The period of sin is 2π (radians), not 360; check the angle unit used in the question.
The period is the smallest positive T; any integer multiple of 2π is also a period, so state the smallest one.
rq: Why does the graph of sin repeat even though the points x₁ and x₂ are at different locations?
Because the periodicity condition sin(x+2π)=sin(x) holds for every x, so the pattern repeats wherever you start; the starting location does not matter.

units.name: 08 Least Squares Regression
units.ov: This material introduces linear least squares regression: fitting y = mx + c to noisy paired data by minimising the sum of squared residuals, which is the maximum likelihood estimate under independent, normal, constant-variance errors. It gives the formulae for m and c from the means and deviation sums, then applies them to a V–I circuit experiment to extract resistance R and EMF. Fit quality is judged with r², and the units and sign conventions need careful handling.
must: Gradient: \( m = \frac{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2} \), with numerator and denominator computed separately
Intercept: \( c = \bar{y} - m\bar{x} \), so the best-fit line always passes through \( (\bar{x},\bar{y}) \)
Residual \( \varepsilon_i = y_i - f(x_i) \); least squares minimises \( \sum \varepsilon_i^2 \), not \( \sum \varepsilon_i \), because signed errors cancel
Why squares are used: no sign cancellation, they distinguish error sets that absolute errors cannot, they are computationally efficient, and they give the maximum likelihood estimate
Assumptions behind least squares: errors independent, normally distributed with mean 0 and constant variance; other methods may suit other data
Circuit application: \( \mathcal{E} = V + IR \) rearranges to \( V = -RI + \mathcal{E} \), so V is y, I is x, gradient \( = -R \) and intercept \( = \mathcal{E} \)
Worked result: \( V = -0.172 I + 1.57 \); \( R = -m \) (keep the minus sign) and \( \mathcal{E} = \bar{V} - R\bar{I} \)
Units: with I in mA and V in V the slope is in kΩ, so convert mA to A before quoting R in Ω

Goodness of fit: \( r^2 = 1 - \frac{\sum (y_i-\hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum (y_i-\bar{y})^2} \) is dimensionless and close to 1 for a good fit, but a high r² does not mean the true parameters are recovered, especially with few points
Do not force a line through just two points; use all n points, and use a computer for the sums when n is above about 10
conn: Residuals and the sum of squares link to the r² formula: the numerator of r² is exactly the minimised least squares error

The means link the slope and intercept formulae, because c uses \( \bar{y} \) and \( \bar{x} \) and the fitted line passes through the centroid; in the circuit case \( \mathcal{E} = \bar{V} - R\bar{I} \)
Physical law to regression: rearrange the law into straight-line form first, then read the physical quantities from the gradient and intercept, watching signs and units
Statistical assumptions (normal, constant-variance errors) justify least squares as the maximum likelihood estimate and explain why few noisy points give estimates that differ from the true values
exq: Five (I, V) readings are given with I in mA. Compute \( \bar{I} \), \( \bar{V} \), the slope by the deviation formula, then the internal resistance R in Ω and the EMF in V. Quote the line of best fit.

Show that summing raw errors can be near zero for a poor fit. For two given error sets, compute \( \sum|\varepsilon_i| \) and \( \sum\varepsilon_i^2 \) and explain which criterion distinguishes them and why.
Given 4 data points, fit y = mx + c by hand, then calculate the residuals and r², and comment on the fit quality.
State the assumptions under which least squares is the maximum likelihood estimate. Explain why a high r² from only 5 points does not guarantee accurate R and \( \mathcal{E} \).
Rearrange \( \mathcal{E} = V + IR \) into straight-line form, identify the gradient and intercept, and explain why the fitted slope of \( -0.172 \) V/mA gives R = 172 Ω rather than 0.172 Ω.

notes.t: Least Squares Regression: motivation and formal setup
pts: Real measured data with a linear relationship y = mx + c contains errors, so points only approximately lie on a line.
Least squares regression estimates the gradient m and intercept c from measurements alone, giving the line of best fit.
'Best' line here means the maximum likelihood estimate: given one coordinate, the point on the line is most likely to be close to the other measured coordinate.
Data is given as n pairs (x_i, y_i) for i = 1,…,n, which is the starting point for the formulae.
Hand calculation is only sensible for a few points; for more than about 10 points use a computer for the sums.
defs: Line of best fit (least squares)
The straight line y = mx + c that, under mild assumptions, is the maximum likelihood estimate of the linear relationship between paired data, obtained by minimising the squared errors.
Maximum likelihood estimate
The parameter values that make the observed data most probable under the assumed model; here, the line that gives the best chance of predicting one variable from the other.
eqs: Formal data set of n paired observations
x_i = independent (measured) value of the i-th point; y_i = dependent (measured) value of the i-th point; n = number of data points (dimensionless)
tips: Do not assume the data lies exactly on y = mx + c; the equation holds only approximately because of measurement error.
Remember the regression is hand-calculated only for small data sets; for larger sets the sums should be done by computer.
rq: Why can't we simply read m and c off a graph of noisy measurements as precisely as we can from exact data?
Measurement error means the points do not lie exactly on the line, so there is no single exact line; least squares gives a principled estimate of m and c.
What does 'maximum likelihood' add over simply drawing a line by eye?
It gives a unique, objective line defined by a statistical criterion, rather than an subjective guess.

notes.t: Linear least squares regression: formulae for slope m and intercept c
pts: Data are assumed to follow a straight line y = mx + c, but real data points only lie near the line, not exactly on it.
Compute the means of x and y first, then use them in the formulae for m and c.
Compute the numerator and denominator of m separately, then take their ratio.
The method is called least squares because the loss minimised is the sum of squared errors.
Regression is a general term for methods that find equations fitting a set of data.
defs: Linear least squares regression
A method of fitting a straight line y = mx + c to data by choosing m and c to minimise the sum of squared errors between the data and the line.
eqs: Gradient m of the least squares line
m = gradient of fitted line (dimensionless if x,y share units; units of y/x); x_i, y_i = data values; \bar{x}, \bar{y} = sample means; n = number of data points
\bar{x} = mean of x (same unit as x); x_i = data values; n = number of points
\bar{y} = mean of y (same unit as y); y_i = data values; n = number of points
Intercept c of the least squares line
c = y-intercept (same unit as y); m = gradient; \bar{x}, \bar{y} = sample means
tips: Do not confuse the sample means \(\bar{x}\), \(\bar{y}\) with the individual data values x_i, y_i when writing the formulae.
Ensure the numerator sum uses (x_i − \bar{x})(y_i − \bar{y}) and the denominator uses the squared (x_i − \bar{x})^2, not the product of raw values.
rq: Why must the means \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\) be computed before m?
Because the formula for m uses deviations from the means (x_i − \bar{x}) and (y_i − \bar{y}), and the formula for c uses \bar{y} and \bar{x} directly.
Why is the method called 'least squares' rather than just minimising the error?
Raw errors can be positive or negative and cancel out, so the loss is defined as the sum of squared errors, which is always non-negative and minimised to find m and c.
Why does the line pass through the point (\(\bar{x}\), \(\bar{y}\))?
Substituting x = \bar{x} into c = \bar{y} − m\bar{x} gives y = m\bar{x} + c = \bar{y}, so the fitted line passes through the mean point.

notes.t: Least squares: the formal statement of the error measure
pts: Summing raw errors lets positive and negative errors cancel, so a small total can hide large errors.
Squaring each error removes the sign problem and is the preferred measure of total error.
Sum of squares gives the maximum likelihood estimate when errors are independent, normally distributed with mean 0 and constant variance.
Sum of absolute errors cannot always distinguish between error sets, whereas sum of squares can (e.g. 82.29 vs 50.29).
Least squares is computationally efficient, which matters for large data sets.
defs: Error (residual)
The difference between the observed value and the value predicted by the model at data point i: ε_i = y_i − f(x_i).
eqs: Sum of raw errors (naive total error, flawed because of signs)
ε = total error (same units as y); ε_i = error at data point i (units of y); n = number of data points
Sum of squared errors (least squares criterion)
ε_i = error at data point i (units of y); n = number of data points; result has units of y²
tips: Do not confuse the signed sum Σε_i (which can cancel to near zero) with the sum of squares Σε_i²; use squares when measuring total error.
Fitting a line exactly through two points ignores the remaining data, so it usually gives large errors elsewhere; minimise over all points.
rq: Why can the plain sum of errors give a misleadingly small total even when individual errors are large?
Positive and negative errors cancel each other, so the total can be near zero (e.g. errors 1.2, 0.9, −1.7, −0.8, 0.5 give total 0.1).
Why is the sum of squares preferred over the sum of absolute values?
It is the maximum likelihood estimate under independent normally distributed errors with mean 0 and constant variance, and it is easier and faster to compute.

notes.t: Least squares fit of EMF and resistance from a circuit experiment
pts: Least squares is one method among others; the best method depends on the data and the assumptions you can make about it.
Least squares assumes errors are unrelated and the average error size (variance) is constant.
Rearrange the circuit law into straight-line form so that V is the y variable and I the x variable; the gradient is −R and the y-intercept is the EMF.
The sample means of I and V are found by summing the data and dividing by n = 5.
defs: EMF (ℰ)
The electromotive force of the battery, equal to the y-intercept of the V versus I line.
eqs: \(V\) = voltage (V) as y; \(I\) = current (A) as x; gradient \(-R\) (Ω); intercept \(\mathcal{E}\) (V)
\(\bar{I}\) = mean current (mA); \(I_i\) = i-th current reading (mA); \(n\) = number of data points
\(\bar{V}\) = mean voltage (V); \(V_i\) = i-th voltage reading (V); \(n\) = number of data points
tips: Units: the current is given in mA but must be converted to A before computing R in ohms.
The mean of I and V must be computed as sums divided by n, not by the number of sums or by a wrong count of data points.
rq: Why is V chosen as the y variable rather than I, given that either choice is possible?
Because the algebra is slightly easier; rearranging gives V = −RI + ℰ directly in the form y = mx + c.
If the fitted gradient is −R, how would you obtain the resistance from the fit, and what sign should it have?
Take R as the negative of the gradient; a positive resistance means the fitted gradient is negative.

notes.t: Least-squares slope for resistance from V–I line of best fit
pts: The slope m of the best-fit line gives the resistance R, with a minus sign: R = −m.
The numerator is the sum of products of deviations of I and V from their means; the denominator is the sum of squared deviations of I.
The EMF is the intercept: ℰ = V̄ − R Ī, using the mean values of V and I.
The fitted line is V = −0.172I + 1.57, so the data show a negative slope consistent with Ohm's-law-type behaviour for a source with internal resistance.
The data in this example are simulated (fake), built from an assumed relationship plus noise.
defs: Line of best fit (least squares)
The straight line minimising the sum of squared vertical deviations of the data from the line, whose slope and intercept are computed from sums of deviations about the means.
eqs: R = resistance (Ω); I_i = current (A or mA); V_i = voltage (V); \bar I, \bar V = sample means (same units)
ℰ = EMF (V); \bar V = mean voltage (V); R = resistance (Ω); \bar I = mean current (A)
tips: Watch units: mA and V give a slope in V/mA = kΩ, not Ω; convert carefully.
Don't forget the minus sign when taking R from the slope; a negative R is unphysical.
rq: Why does the slope come out negative, and why do we write R = −m?
Voltage falls as current rises in the circuit (V = ℰ − RI), so the fitted slope m is negative; since R is positive, R = −m.
Why must we use mA and the stated unit relation when reading R?
Current is in mA and voltage in V, so the slope is in V/mA = kΩ; converting with 1 Ω = 1 V A⁻¹ gives R = 0.172 kΩ = 172 Ω.

notes.t: Least squares regression: fit quality and the r² value
pts: Least squares gives the best estimate of the true parameters from the data, not the exact true values; with few data points the estimates can differ noticeably from the true values.
The quality of a linear fit is judged by the coefficient of determination r²; values close to 1 indicate a good fit.
The example data was synthetic: true values were chosen and normally distributed random errors were added, so it is not real data.
defs: r² value (coefficient of determination)
A measure of how well a regression line fits the data, between 0 and 1; the closer to 1, the better the fit.
eqs: r² = goodness-of-fit measure (dimensionless); y_i = observed value; ŷ_i = fitted value from the regression; ȳ = mean of observed values
tips: Do not confuse a high r² (good fit) with exact recovery of the true parameter values; estimates from few data points can still be off.
r² is dimensionless and lies between 0 and 1 for a least squares linear fit; don't quote it as a percentage without converting.
rq: Why might the least squares slope differ from the true slope even though the fit looks very good?
Least squares gives the best estimate from the noisy data, not the true parameter; with only five points random errors have a large effect, so the estimate can deviate from the true value.
If r² = 0.993, what does this tell you, and does it guarantee the parameters are exactly correct?
The line explains about 99.3% of the variation in the data, so the fit is very good; however, a high r² does not guarantee the estimated parameters equal the true values.

units.name: 09 Polynomials
units.ov: This module defines polynomials over a ring A (Z, Q, R, C), their degree, and how they are evaluated and factorised. Factorisation depends on the coefficient ring: irreducibles over R are linear terms and quadratics with negative discriminant, while over C everything splits into linear factors. Polynomial long division, modelled on integer division with remainder, is the main computational tool and leads to roots and factorisation.
must: A polynomial is a finite sum \(\sum_{r=0}^{n} a_r x^r\) with non-negative integer powers only; \(1/x\), \(\sqrt{x}\), \(\sin x\) and \(e^x\) are not polynomials, and infinite Taylor series are power series.
Degree is the largest power of x with a nonzero coefficient, so \(0x^5+3x^2\) has degree 2; the names are constant, linear, quadratic, cubic, quartic and quintic.
Factorisability depends on the coefficient ring: \(x^2-2\) is irreducible over Q but equals \((x-\sqrt2)(x+\sqrt2)\) over R, so always state the ring.
A quadratic \(ax^2+bx+c\) factorises over R iff \(\Delta=b^2-4ac\ge0\). Then \(x^2+bx+c=(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)\), after taking out a to make it monic.

Over C (algebraically closed, by the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra) every degree-n polynomial is \(C(x-\alpha_1)\cdots(x-\alpha_n)\); over R the irreducibles are linear and quadratics with \(\Delta<0\).
Polynomial division: \(f(x)=g(x)q(x)+r(x)\) with \(\deg r<\deg g\) (or \(r=0\)); q and r are unique. A linear divisor gives a constant remainder.
Long division method: include zero-coefficient terms, divide leading terms, multiply back, subtract (change every sign), bring down, and repeat. Example: \(5x^3+4x-2=(x+1)(5x^2-5x+9)-11\).
A root satisfies \(f(\alpha)=0\), and then \(f(x)=(x-\alpha)\,q(x)\) with \(\deg q=\deg f-1\). Repeating this gives the full factorisation.
Z, Q, R and C are UFDs, so Z[x], Q[x], R[x] and C[x] are too: factorisation into irreducibles is unique up to order and units (units are ±1 in Z, any nonzero element in Q, R, C).
A polynomial defines a function by evaluation, \(f(t)=\sum a_r t^r\). Check any factorisation or division by expanding and comparing.
conn: Roots, factors and division: f(α)=0 means the remainder on dividing by \((x-\alpha)\) is zero. Long division then reduces the degree, and repeating it gives a complete factorisation.
Discriminant, ring and irreducibility: the sign of \(b^2-4ac\) decides whether a quadratic splits over R, and it always splits over C with complex-conjugate roots.
Integer division and polynomial division: both use the same a = bq + r structure, with degree replacing size. This links to UFD ideas and to prime and irreducible factorisation.
Taylor series and polynomials: sin x and e^x are approximated by truncated polynomials, but the full series are power series, not polynomials.
exq: Divide \(2x^4-3x^2+x-5\) by \(x-2\) using long division (remember the 0x^3 term). State the quotient and remainder, and verify by expansion.
Given that \(x=1\) is a root of \(x^3-2x^2-5x+6\), factorise it completely over R and list all roots.
Factorise \(x^4-16\) over Q, over R and over C. In each case state which factors are irreducible and why.
For \(2x^2+bx+8\), find the values of b for which the polynomial factorises over R. Then factorise it when b = 10.

State the degree of \(0x^5+3x^2-1\). Explain why \(\sqrt{x}+1\) and the Taylor series of \(e^x\) are not polynomials. Then write \(7x^4+7x^3-21x^2-7x-14\) in the form 7(x−1)(x+2)(x²−1), or check that this form is correct.

notes.t: Polynomials: definition, coefficients and degree
pts: A polynomial is the simplest kind of function, and Taylor series let us approximate most other functions by polynomials, so understanding polynomials helps understand many functions.
Polynomials with coefficients in a ring A are built from powers of x combined by addition and multiplication by coefficients.
The degree is the largest index n with a nonzero coefficient, not simply the highest power written.
A is required to be a ring so that addition, subtraction and multiplication are defined and obey the usual algebra rules; examples are Z, Q, R.
Every element of A is a polynomial of degree 0 (taking n = 0 in the formula).
defs: Polynomial with coefficients in A
An expression in x of the form a_0 + a_1 x + ... + a_n x^n = sum_{r=0}^{n} a_r x^r with each a_r in A.
Coefficients
The elements a_i in A appearing in front of the powers of x in a polynomial.
Degree
The largest n for which the coefficient a_n is nonzero.
A[x]
The set of all polynomials with coefficients in A in the variable x.
eqs: General polynomial of degree n in x with coefficients in A
a_0 + a_1 x + a_2 x^2 + \cdots + a_n x^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} a_r x^r
a_r = coefficients in A (dimensionless, element of the ring); x = the variable; n = degree (integer, non-negative); r = summation index
tips: Degree depends on nonzero coefficients: 0x^5 + 3x^2 has degree 2, not 5.
Do not confuse the variable x with an element of A; a constant polynomial has n = 0 only if its constant coefficient is nonzero.
rq: Why must the leading coefficient a_n be nonzero when we define the degree, and what happens to the degree if a_n = 0?
Because the degree is defined as the largest n with a_n ≠ 0; if a_n = 0 the term vanishes and the true degree is smaller, so the written power is not the degree.
Why does the definition require A to be a ring rather than any set?
The polynomial operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication by coefficients) must always be defined and satisfy the algebra rules, which is what a ring guarantees.

notes.t: Polynomials over Z, Q, R and non-polynomial functions
pts: A polynomial over a set (ℤ, ℚ or ℝ) has coefficients from that set; the sets nest, so ℤ[x] ⊆ ℚ[x] ⊆ ℝ[x].
The variable is a placeholder and can be renamed; using y instead of x gives A[y].
Polynomials may only contain non-negative integer powers of the variable; expressions with 1/x or sin x or eˣ are not polynomials.
Infinite series such as the Taylor series of sin x and eˣ are not polynomials, since a polynomial has finitely many terms; they are generalised as power series.
defs: Polynomial over a set A
An expression of the form a_n xⁿ + … + a_1 x + a_0 with all coefficients a_i in A and n a non-negative integer; the set of all such expressions is written A[x].
Power series
A generalisation of a polynomial allowing infinitely many terms, e.g. the Taylor series of sin x or eˣ; it is not a polynomial.
eqs: Taylor series of sin x (not a polynomial)
x = real variable (dimensionless when used as an argument of sin)
Taylor series of eˣ (not a polynomial)
tips: Do not classify 1/x or √x type terms as polynomial terms: only non-negative integer powers qualify.
Infinite series like sin x and eˣ look like polynomials but are not; a polynomial has a finite degree.
rq: Why is 3x + 1/x not a polynomial in x, even though it has only 'nice' terms?
Because 1/x = x⁻¹ has a negative power of x, and polynomials only allow non-negative integer powers.
Why does ℤ[x] ⊆ ℚ[x] ⊆ ℝ[x] hold?
Every integer is a rational number and every rational is a real number, so a polynomial with integer coefficients is also one with rational or real coefficients.

notes.t: Polynomials: degree, naming and polynomial functions
pts: The degree of a polynomial in x is the largest power of x that appears with nonzero coefficient.
Degree 0, 1, 2, 3 polynomials are called constant, linear, quadratic and cubic; degree 4 and 5 are quartic and quintic, beyond which people simply say 'degree n'.
The focus is mainly on polynomials of degree 3 or below, since higher-degree polynomials over ℝ can be written in terms of degree 2 or lower.
Every polynomial defines a function from A to A by evaluating it at t; the notes do not usually distinguish the polynomial from its function.
defs: Degree of a polynomial
The largest power of x which appears in the polynomial (with non-zero coefficient); e.g. deg(ax²+bx+c)=2.
Polynomial function
Every polynomial \sum_{r=0}^{n} a_r x^r in A[x] defines a function f: A→A given by f(t)=\sum_{r=0}^{n} a_r t^r; this is called evaluating the polynomial at t∈A.
Constant polynomial
A polynomial of degree 0, of the form a, which does not depend on x.
Linear polynomial
A polynomial of degree 1, of the form ax+b, whose graph y=ax+b is a straight line.
eqs: a_r = coefficient of x^r (dimensionless in A); t = value at which the polynomial is evaluated (element of A); n = degree (integer)
tips: Degree counts the largest power of x with nonzero coefficient; a term with zero coefficient does not raise the degree.
Don't confuse the polynomial with the function it defines unless the context requires it; for engineering this distinction is almost never important.
rq: Why is deg(a)=0 for a nonzero constant a, even though no x appears?
Because a = a x⁰, so the largest power of x present is x⁰, giving degree 0.
Why are higher-degree polynomials over ℝ less important for engineering than degree 2 or lower?
Bigger numbers are harder to handle, and over ℝ higher-degree polynomials can be rewritten in terms of polynomials of degree 2 or lower.

notes.t: Polynomials: evaluating and factorising over different coefficient rings
pts: A polynomial over a ring defines a function by substituting values for the variable.
Checking a factorisation is easy: expand the product and compare with the original polynomial.
Whether a polynomial factorises depends on which coefficients are allowed.
A factorisation uses non-constant polynomials whose coefficients lie in the same ring A.
x² − 2 is irreducible over ℚ but factorises over ℝ using √2.
defs: Factorisation
A factorisation of a polynomial over A is a way of writing it as a product of polynomials (other than constant polynomials), all of which lie in A[x].
eqs: Evaluating a polynomial function at a point
t = input variable (dimensionless); f(t) = value of the function at t
tips: Factorisability is not a property of the polynomial alone: x² − 2 is irreducible over ℚ but factorises over ℝ, so always state the coefficient ring.
Do not count constant factors as part of a factorisation; the definition requires non-constant polynomial factors.
rq: Why can x² − 2 be factorised over ℝ but not over ℚ?
Its roots ±√2 are irrational, so the linear factors need irrational coefficients, which are only in ℝ, not ℤ or ℚ.
How can you verify that a claimed factorisation of a polynomial is correct?
Expand the product of the factors and check it returns the original polynomial.

notes.t: Irreducible polynomials and factorising over ℝ
pts: An irreducible polynomial over A cannot be factorised further, analogous to a prime number; reducibility depends on which coefficients are allowed.
A quadratic factorises over ℝ if and only if its discriminant is non-negative (it has real roots).
Any quadratic with a ≠ 1 can have the constant a factored out, leaving a monic quadratic.
Over ℝ, the only irreducible polynomials are constants and linear terms with leading coefficient 1, so every real polynomial factors into these.
The number 1 is not treated as a prime/factor, so 1·17 is not counted as a factorisation of 17.
defs: Irreducible (over A)
A polynomial which cannot be further factorised over A is irreducible over A; a polynomial that is not irreducible is reducible.
Leading term
The leading term of a polynomial is the coefficient of its highest degree term.
eqs: Factorisation of a quadratic with real roots α, β
x = variable (dimensionless); α, β = roots; b, c = coefficients
Δ = discriminant (dimensionless); a, b, c = coefficients
a = leading coefficient (dimensionless); b, c = coefficients
tips: Reducibility depends on the coefficient field: x² − 2 is irreducible over ℚ but reducible over ℝ; always state the field.
Do not count the factor 1 or a constant multiple as a separate factorisation when stating factorisations uniquely.
rq: Why is 1 not considered a prime, and why does the same reasoning apply to polynomials like 1·(x+1)?
Allowing 1 as a factor would make factorisations non-unique (1·17, 1·1·17 both valid), so 1 (and constants/units) are excluded from being counted as factors.
Why can a real quadratic with negative discriminant not be factorised over ℝ?
Factorisation into linear real factors (x−α)(x−β) requires real roots; Δ < 0 gives complex roots, so it is irreducible over ℝ.

notes.t: Factorising polynomials over ℂ and unique factorisation domains
pts: Over ℂ every non-constant polynomial factorises completely into linear factors, because the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra guarantees roots, so there are no irreducible quadratics.
Over ℂ, any polynomial of degree n factorises as a constant times n linear terms with leading coefficient 1.
Factorising polynomials into irreducibles is analogous to factorising integers into primes; ℤ and ℤ[x] are both unique factorisation domains.
Over ℚ, factorisations are not unique: 17 can be written in infinitely many ways as a product of two smaller numbers, so UFD property depends on the ring used.
Example: 7x⁴+7x³−21x²−7x−14 = 7(x−1)(x+2)(x²−1), showing constant, linear and irreducible quadratic factors.
defs: Algebraically closed
A field in which every non-constant polynomial has a root; equivalently every polynomial factorises into linear factors. ℂ is algebraically closed.
Unique factorisation domain (UFD)
A ring in which every element can be written as a product of irreducible elements in exactly one way, up to order and units.
eqs: Factorisation of a polynomial over ℂ
C = leading constant (dimensionless, C ∈ ℂ); α_i = roots of the polynomial (dimensionless, α_i ∈ ℂ); n = degree (dimensionless); x = variable
tips: Do not assume a quadratic is irreducible over ℂ; over ℂ every quadratic has roots and splits.
Remember that uniqueness of factorisation is only meaningful up to units and the field/ring in use; over ℚ a number like 17 has infinitely many factorisations.
rq: Why can a quadratic such as x²−1 be irreducible over ℚ or ℤ but not over ℂ?
Over ℂ the Fundamental Theorem of Algebra gives roots, so x²−1 = (x−1)(x+1) splits into linear factors; irreducibility depends on the field.
Why does the uniqueness of factorisation fail over ℚ for the number 17?
Because units such as rationals (e.g. 2/3, 3/2) can be moved between factors, giving infinitely many factorisations, unlike over ℤ where units are only ±1.

notes.t: Factorisation uniqueness over Q, R, C and polynomial division
pts: Factorisations in ℚ and ℝ are unique only up to units; multiplying by x·(1/x) gives no genuinely new factorisation.
ℤ, ℚ, ℝ and ℂ are UFDs, hence so are ℤ[x], ℚ[x], ℝ[x] and ℂ[x].
Division with remainder in ℤ: a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b, giving unique q and r.
Dividing polynomials need not give a polynomial, since the quotient can contain a 1/x term.
defs: Unit
An element x of a ring whose inverse 1/x also lies in that ring; in ℤ the only units are ±1, while in ℚ or ℝ every nonzero element is a unit.
UFD (unique factorisation domain)
A ring in which every non-zero, non-unit element factorises into irreducibles, uniquely up to units and order of factors.
eqs: a = dividend (dimensionless); b = divisor; q = quotient; r = remainder (all integers)
tips: Do not count factorisations differing by units (e.g. multiplying by x·1/x) as distinct in ℚ or ℝ.
In ℤ units are only ±1, so the uniqueness argument differs from ℚ or ℝ.
rq: Why does 17 have infinitely many factorisations in ℚ but we still call ℚ a UFD?
Because each extra factorisation differs only by multiplying by a unit x·(1/x), which is ignored under uniqueness up to units.
Why is 13/5 not allowed in ℤ but division with remainder still works?
Division with remainder writes 13 = 5·2 + 3, keeping the quotient in ℤ and the remainder smaller than the divisor.

notes.t: Polynomial division with remainder
pts: Polynomial division writes f(x) as g(x)q(x) + r(x), with the remainder's degree strictly less than that of the divisor g(x).
Degree plays the role that size plays for integers: the remainder is bounded by degree, not magnitude.
Integer division is the model: find the largest multiple of the divisor not exceeding the dividend, then solve for the remainder.
Polynomial division repeats the step, each time lowering the degree by 1, until the remainder degree is below deg g(x).
Working with rational functions (terms like 1/x) is allowed where integer-style division would otherwise need fractions.
defs: Degree of a polynomial
The highest power of x with non-zero coefficient; deg r(x) ≥ 0 always, since degree cannot be negative.
Quotient q(x) and remainder r(x)
In f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), q(x) is the quotient and r(x) the remainder, with deg r(x) < deg g(x).
eqs: f(x) = dividend polynomial (dimensionless); g(x) = divisor; q(x) = quotient; r(x) = remainder, with deg r(x) < deg g(x)
x = variable; quotient q(x) = 3x + 2; remainder r(x) = −1
tips: Remember that the remainder must have degree strictly less than the divisor, not merely be smaller in value.
Do not confuse deg r(x) ≥ 0 with a requirement that the remainder be positive; the remainder may be a negative constant such as −1.
rq: Why is the degree of the remainder, rather than its size, the right thing to bound in polynomial division?
Polynomials have no natural ordering by magnitude; degree gives a well-defined notion of size that guarantees the division process terminates after finitely many steps.
In integer division of 13 by 5, why is q = 2 and not q = 3?
5·3 = 15 exceeds 13, so 2 is the largest multiple of 5 that is still less than or equal to 13, leaving a non-negative remainder 3.

notes.t: Polynomial division (long division of polynomials by a linear factor)
pts: To divide f(x) by g(x), we can only subtract or add multiples of g(x), so each step chooses a multiple of g(x) to match the leading term of the remaining polynomial.
Whatever cannot be matched as a multiple of the denominator is left as the remainder r(x), with degree less than deg g(x).
For a linear divisor g(x), the remainder is a constant, since its degree must be 0.
Standard layout: write all powers of x including zero coefficients, then repeatedly divide leading terms, multiply back, subtract and bring down.
defs: Polynomial division algorithm
For polynomials f(x) and g(x) ≠ 0, there exist unique q(x) and r(x) with f(x) = g(x)q(x) + r(x), where deg r(x) < deg g(x) or r(x) = 0.
eqs: f(x) = dividend polynomial; g(x) = divisor polynomial; q(x) = quotient polynomial; r(x) = remainder polynomial (degree less than deg g(x))
tips: Forgetting to include zero-coefficient terms (like 0x^2) misaligns columns and produces wrong subtractions.
Sign errors when subtracting: remember to change the signs of every term of the multiplied line before combining.
rq: Why can we only subtract multiples of x+1 when reducing f(x), and what does this force about the remainder?
Because the quotient must be multiplied by g(x) to be subtracted; any leftover term not expressible as a multiple of x+1 becomes the remainder.
Why must the remainder be a constant when dividing by x+1?
Since deg g(x) = 1, the remainder must have degree less than 1, i.e. degree 0, so it is a constant with no x term.
Why do we insert 0x^2 in 5x^3 + 0x^2 + 4x - 2 before dividing?
So that the columns of powers align during subtraction and no term is accidentally skipped.

notes.t: Polynomial long division and factorising polynomials
pts: Long division of polynomials repeats the steps: divide leading terms, multiply back by the divisor, subtract, and bring down the next terms until the remainder has lower degree than the divisor.
The division result can be written as dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, with the remainder of lower degree than the divisor.
If α₁ is a root of f(x), then f(x) factorises as (x − α₁) multiplied by a polynomial of lower degree.
Repeating the factorisation gives f(x) as a product of linear factors (x − αᵢ) times a remaining polynomial f_k(x).
defs: Root of a polynomial
A value α such that f(α) = 0.
Quotient q(x) and remainder r(x)
In dividing f(x) by (x + 1), q(x) is the polynomial read off the top line and r(x) is the constant left at the bottom, so f(x) = (x+1)q(x) + r(x).
eqs: α₁ = root of f; f₁(x) = polynomial of degree less than deg f
tips: Include zero coefficients (e.g. 0x²) when setting out long division, or terms will be misaligned.
Check the remainder's degree is less than the divisor's; a final term like −11 with divisor x+1 is a constant, which is correct.
rq: Why must the remainder have lower degree than the divisor?
Otherwise another step of long division could subtract a further multiple of the divisor, so the process would not have finished.
Why does a root α give a factor (x − α)?
Because f(α)=0, dividing f(x) by (x−α) leaves remainder f(α)=0, so (x−α) divides f(x) exactly.

notes.t: Factorising polynomials using roots and polynomial division
pts: Find a root α (a value where the polynomial vanishes) by trying simple values such as 1, −1, 2, −2.
Divide f(x) by (x − α); since (x − α) is a factor there is no remainder, and the quotient is the next polynomial to factorise.
Repeat the root-and-divide process on the quotient until you reach a polynomial with no roots.
When a quadratic remains, check its discriminant: if negative stop, if non-negative factorise it fully.
A non-zero remainder signals an arithmetic error or that α is not actually a root.
defs: Irreducible polynomial
A polynomial f_k(x) that cannot be factored further (over the relevant field, e.g. real numbers), so the factorisation process stops.
eqs: Factorisation after removing root 1 from f(x)
x = variable; f_1(x) = quotient polynomial of degree at most 3 (dimensionless)
Full factorisation of the example quartic
tips: Only test simple candidates like ±1, ±2 first; verify f(α)=0 by substitution before dividing.
When dividing, keep track of signs of all coefficients (e.g. the −20x and +48 terms) to avoid errors in the quotient.
rq: Why must the remainder be zero when you divide by x − α for a genuine root α?
Because if α is a root, f(α)=0, and by the remainder theorem the remainder of dividing by (x − α) equals f(α)=0, so (x − α) is an exact factor.
What should you do if you find a remainder after dividing by x − α?
Recheck the arithmetic of the division, and check that α really is a root (i.e. f(α)=0); a non-zero remainder means α is not a root.

notes.t: Quadratic formula, roots and overall scale factor of a polynomial
pts: The quadratic formula gives the roots of ax²+bx+c=0; here it yields x = −2 and x = 4.
Roots alone only determine a polynomial up to an overall scale factor, which must be added manually.
A check by expanding the factored form shows that (x+2)(x−4) alone is not the full polynomial, since it lacks the leading factor 2.
Factored form of a polynomial with known roots and leading coefficient is f(x)=a(x−r₁)(x−r₂)…, where a is the leading coefficient.
defs: Root of a polynomial
A value of x for which the polynomial f(x) equals zero; it corresponds to a factor (x − r) of f(x).
Overall scale factor
The constant multiplying the product of linear factors in a factored polynomial; it is not determined by the roots alone.
eqs: x = root (dimensionless); a, b, c = coefficients of ax²+bx+c (dimensionless)
Factored form of the cubic/quartic polynomial with scale factor
f(x) = polynomial value (dimensionless); x = independent variable (dimensionless); 2 = overall scale factor (dimensionless)
tips: Forgetting the leading coefficient when writing a polynomial from its roots; always multiply by the scale factor.
Sign errors when reading roots: a factor (x+2) has root x = −2, not +2.
rq: Why does the factored form (x+2)(x−4) not match the original quadratic even though its roots are correct?
Because roots only fix the linear factors; the overall leading coefficient (here 2) must be multiplied in, giving 2(x+2)(x−4) = 2x² − 4x − 8.
How would you find the constant multiplying the factors if you only knew the roots and one value f(x₀)?
Write f(x)=a∏(x−rᵢ), substitute x₀ and solve f(x₀)=a∏(x₀−rᵢ) for a.

units.name: 10 Rational Functions
units.ov: A rational function is a ratio of two real polynomials, \(F(x)=f(x)/g(x)\), defined on \(\mathbb{R}\) minus the roots of \(g\) (the poles). Partial fractions rewrites it as a polynomial part plus simple strictly proper fractions with linear or irreducible quadratic denominators. The steps are: check the degrees, divide if improper, factorise \(g\), choose the correct form for each factor, find the constants, and recombine to check. This makes rational functions easier to plot and integrate.
must: Definition and domain: \(F(x)=f(x)/g(x)\) on \(\mathbb{R}\setminus\{\text{roots of } g\}\). The roots of \(g\) are the poles, and the domain must always be stated.

Strictly proper means \(\deg f<\deg g\). Improper means \(\deg f\ge\deg g\), and then a polynomial part \(A(x)\) is needed. The notes' wording 'proper when \(\deg f\le\deg g\)' is loose and conflicts with the p128 definition. Treat the decomposition terms as strictly proper.
If \(\deg f\ge\deg g\), do polynomial division first. Example: \(5x^3+2x-1=(x^2-1)(5x)+(7x-1)\), so \(F=5x+\frac{7x-1}{(x+1)(x-1)}\).
Fully factorise the denominator before setting up the decomposition.
Each distinct linear factor \((x-a)\) gives \(\frac{A}{x-a}\) with a constant numerator.
Cover-up (substitution) method: put \(x=a\), a root of a factor, to get its constant quickly. Example: \(\frac{7x-1}{(x+1)(x-1)}=\frac{4}{x+1}+\frac{3}{x-1}\).
An irreducible quadratic factor such as \(x^2+1\) gives \(\frac{Bx+C}{x^2+1}\), a linear numerator. Find the constants by equating coefficients.

A repeated factor \((x-a)^n\) needs one fraction for each power \(1\) to \(n\), e.g. \(\frac{B}{x-1}+\frac{C}{(x-1)^2}\). Substitution only gives the highest-power coefficient directly; the rest need coefficient matching or another value of \(x\).
Always recombine the fractions to check you recover the original and to catch sign errors. Check example: \(\frac{17}{x-2}-\frac{17}{x-1}-\frac{12}{(x-1)^2}=\frac{5x+7}{(x-2)(x-1)^2}\).
Mixed strategy: use substitution for the easy constants, then equate coefficients or pick extra values of \(x\) for the rest.
conn: Polynomial division and partial fractions: the remainder from long division is the strictly proper numerator that gets decomposed. Skipping the division makes every constant wrong.
Factorisation and root-finding determine the poles and the form of the decomposition. A quadratic with negative discriminant is irreducible and so needs \(Bx+C\).
Substitution and coefficient matching are combined for repeated or quadratic factors. Substitution gives some constants, then matching powers of \(x\) gives the rest.
Partial fractions are the preparation for integrating and plotting rational functions. Each term integrates to a log, an arctan or a power, and the poles give the vertical asymptotes.
exq: State the domain and the poles of \(F(x)=\frac{5x^3+2x-1}{x^2-1}\). Then use polynomial division and partial fractions to show \(F(x)=5x+\frac{4}{x+1}+\frac{3}{x-1}\).
Decompose \(\frac{5x+7}{(x-2)(x-1)^2}\) into partial fractions. Show why the form needs both \((x-1)\) and \((x-1)^2\) terms, find the constants, and verify by recombining.
Write the correct partial fraction form (without solving) for \(\frac{x^3+1}{(x-2)(x^2+1)}\). Say whether it is improper, and find the constants \(A,B,C\) once any polynomial part is removed.
Classify each as strictly proper or improper: \(\frac{x^2}{x^2-1}\), \(\frac{3x-2}{x^3+x}\), \(\frac{x^4}{x+1}\). Explain what you would do first in each case before decomposing.
A student writes \(\frac{3x+1}{(x-1)^2(x+2)}=\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+2}\). Explain the error, give the correct form, and find all the constants.

notes.t: Rational Functions
pts: Dividing one polynomial by another gives a rational function, not necessarily a polynomial; rational functions are the next simplest class after polynomials.
Partial fractions decomposition writes a rational function as a sum of simpler fractions, useful for plotting and integrating.
The domain must exclude the roots of the denominator g, since division by zero is undefined there.
Roots of the denominator g are called the poles of the rational function.
defs: Rational function
For polynomials f(x) and g(x) with real coefficients, the rational function is F(x) = f(x)/g(x), defined on ℝ excluding the roots of g.
Poles
The roots of the denominator polynomial g(x) of a rational function; these are the points excluded from the domain.
eqs: f(x), g(x) = real polynomials; x = real input (dimensionless unless modelling a physical quantity)
tips: Forgetting to exclude the roots of the denominator from the domain; always state the domain as ℝ minus the roots of g.
Assuming a quotient of polynomials is always a polynomial; division generally produces a rational function instead.
rq: Why must the roots of g be removed from the domain of a rational function?
Because at those inputs g(x) = 0, so the function would divide by zero and be undefined.
Why is partial fractions decomposition useful for integration?
A general quotient of polynomials is hard to integrate, but the simpler fractions produced by decomposition are much easier to integrate term by term.

notes.t: Partial Fractions
pts: A rational function f(x)/g(x) is strictly proper when deg f < deg g, and proper when deg f ≤ deg g; if the numerator's degree is larger it is improper.
Any improper rational function can be split into a polynomial part plus a sum of strictly proper fractions, which is the goal of partial fractions.
The first step is always to fully factorise the denominator before setting up the decomposition.
Each linear factor of the denominator gives its own fraction term with a constant numerator, and the decomposition has a polynomial term A(x) when the function is improper.
defs: Strictly proper rational function
A rational function f(x)/g(x) in which the degree of the numerator f is strictly less than the degree of the denominator g.
Improper rational function
A rational function f(x)/g(x) in which the degree of the numerator f is greater than the degree of the denominator g.
Partial fractions decomposition
A way of writing a rational function as a sum of strictly proper rational functions whose denominators have degree 1 or 2.
eqs: Partial fraction form of an improper rational function with two linear factors
F(x) = rational function; A(x) = polynomial part; B, C = constants (dimensionless in this example); x = variable
tips: Check whether the function is improper (deg numerator > deg denominator) before decomposing; an improper function needs a polynomial term A(x) added.
Do not confuse 'proper' (deg f ≤ deg g) with 'strictly proper' (deg f < deg g); the decomposition terms must be strictly proper.
rq: Why must the denominator be fully factorised before choosing the form of the partial fraction decomposition?
Because each distinct linear factor (and each repeated or quadratic factor) determines which fraction terms appear, so the correct form cannot be written until the factors are known.
