Why is 5/2 split as 2 + 1/2 but the same idea applies to rational functions with a polynomial part A(x)?
Writing 5/2 = 2 + 1/2 separates an improper fraction into a whole-number part and a proper part; likewise an improper rational function has a polynomial part A(x) and a proper remainder.

notes.t: Partial fractions: polynomial division, finding unknown coefficients, irreducible quadrati
pts: If the numerator degree is not less than the denominator degree, first divide to get a polynomial part A(x) plus a proper fraction.
Proper-fraction numerators over linear factors are constants, found by substituting values of x that make factors vanish.
Always recombine the partial fractions to check you recover the original fraction.
With an irreducible quadratic factor, its partial fraction numerator must be a linear polynomial, not a constant.
defs: Proper fraction
A rational function whose numerator degree is strictly less than its denominator degree.
eqs: Partial fraction decomposition of F(x) over (x+1)(x-1)
x = independent variable (dimensionless); F(x) = the rational function being decomposed
Polynomial division identity for the numerator
tips: Do polynomial division first if the degree of the numerator is at least the degree of the denominator, otherwise the partial fraction constants will be wrong.
Always recombine the partial fractions and check you recover the original expression to catch sign errors.
rq: Why can we set x = 1 to find C directly, rather than expanding and comparing coefficients?
At x = 1 the factor (x−1) becomes zero, so the B term vanishes and the equation reduces to 2C = 6, giving C = 3 immediately.
Why must the numerator over an irreducible quadratic be linear rather than constant?
Because the quadratic has degree 2, the numerator must have degree less than 2 to keep the fraction proper, so a linear polynomial Ax + B is needed.

notes.t: Partial fractions: irreducible quadratic and repeated linear factors
pts: For an irreducible quadratic factor in the denominator, the numerator of its fraction is a degree-1 polynomial Bx + C, not a constant.
A repeated linear factor (x − a)^n needs a separate fraction for each power 1 through n, not just one fraction.
Set x to a root of a linear factor to find its coefficient quickly; equate coefficients when no real root makes a factor vanish (e.g. x² + 1).
When a root is used for a repeated factor, only one of the repeated factors cancels, so other unknowns must be found by equating coefficients.
Check the final decomposition is consistent by recombining; the coefficients obtained gave F(x) = 17/(x−2) − 17/(x−1) − 12/(x−1)².
defs: Partial fraction decomposition
Writing a proper rational function as a sum of simpler fractions whose denominators are the factors of the original denominator (linear, irreducible quadratic, or powers of these).
eqs: Partial fractions for an irreducible quadratic factor and a linear factor
A, B, C = constants (dimensionless); x = independent variable
Partial fractions with a repeated linear factor
A, B, C = constants; x = independent variable
tips: Do not use only one fraction for a repeated factor; include every power from 1 up to the multiplicity.
When substituting a root into a repeated factor, remember only one factor cancels, so the remaining coefficient needs coefficient matching, not just substitution.
rq: Why must the numerator over x² + 1 be Bx + C rather than a constant?
Because the fraction must be proper: the numerator degree must be less than the denominator degree (2), so degree 1 is the most general allowed form.
Why is a term (x − 1) alone insufficient for the factor (x − 1)² in the denominator?
Repeated factors need one fraction for each power up to the multiplicity, so both 1/(x−1) and 1/(x−1)² are required to represent the function fully.
Why can't we find the coefficient of x² + 1 by substituting a real value?
x² + 1 has no real roots, so no real x makes it vanish; coefficients must instead be found by equating coefficients of powers of x.

units.name: eng1063-block-1-key-formulae
units.ov: This block collects the core algebra, geometry and trigonometry tools for first-year engineering maths: index laws, the modulus, quadratics, binomial expansion, lines and conics, number bases, error propagation, and trig/hyperbolic/wave functions. These ideas link because they are used together to manipulate expressions, describe curves and waves, and quantify uncertainty in calculated results.
must: Quadratic formula: \(x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}\) for \(a\neq0\); the discriminant \(b^2-4ac\) decides the number of real roots
Binomial theorem: \((a+b)^n=\sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}a^kb^{n-k}\) with \(\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\)
Circle \((x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2\) and ellipse \(\frac{(x-a)^2}{r^2}+\frac{(y-b)^2}{s^2}=1\): read off the centre and semi-axes (denominators are \(r^2, s^2\), so take square roots)
Hyperbola \(\frac{(x-a)^2}{r^2}-\frac{(y-b)^2}{s^2}=1\): the minus sign gives two branches
Error propagation: absolute errors add for sums; relative errors add for products, \(\varepsilon_{ab}=ab\left(\frac{\varepsilon_a}{a}+\frac{\varepsilon_b}{b}\right)\)
Travelling wave \(y=A\cos(kx-\omega t)\) with \(k=2\pi/\lambda\), \(\omega=2\pi f\); keep angles in radians
Modulus: \(|x|=x\) if \(x\ge0\), \(-x\) if \(x<0\) (the minus sign alone does not mean negative)
Line \(y=mx+c\) (gradient m, y-intercept c) and point–gradient form; the same line family
Polar angle: \(\theta=\arctan(y/x)\) is only valid for \(x,y>0\), so correct for other quadrants; also \(\sin 2x=2\sin x\cos x\), \(\cosh x=\tfrac12(e^x+e^{-x})\), \(\sinh x=\tfrac12(e^x-e^{-x})\)
conn: Completing the square on a general quadratic in x and y converts it to circle/ellipse/hyperbola standard form, giving centre and semi-axes
Binomial expansion with small errors or small terms gives first-order error estimates, e.g. \((a+\varepsilon)^n\approx a^n+na^{n-1}\varepsilon\), linking to error propagation for powers
Wave \(y=A\cos(kx-\omega t)\) needs radian conversion, \(\omega=2\pi f\), \(k=2\pi/\lambda\), and trig identities, with errors in f or λ propagating to ω and k
Index laws underpin logs and the exponential definitions of cosh/sinh, while the modulus appears when solving inequalities and quadratics
exq: Expand \((2x-3)^5\) using the binomial theorem and state the coefficient of \(x^3\).
Rewrite \(x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0\) in standard form, identify the shape, centre and radius, then find where it meets the line \(y=x\).
A rectangle has sides \(a=12.0\pm0.1\) m and \(b=5.0\pm0.2\) m. Find the area and its absolute and relative error.
A wave has \(f=50\) Hz and \(\lambda=0.8\) m with \(A=0.02\) m. Find \(\omega\) and \(k\), write \(y(x,t)\), and find \(y\) at \(x=0.1\) m, \(t=0.01\) s.
Convert the point \((-3,4)\) to polar form, explaining the quadrant correction, and solve \(|2x-1|=5\).

notes.t: Engineering Mathematics 1 – Key Formulae (indices, modulus, quadratics, factorials, binomi
pts: Index laws let you combine powers of the same base by adding or subtracting exponents, and define negative and fractional powers.
The modulus returns the non-negative value of x: x itself if x is non-negative, otherwise −x.
The quadratic formula gives both roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 when a ≠ 0.
The binomial coefficient counts ways to choose k items from n and is used in the binomial theorem.
A line can be written in gradient–intercept form or point–gradient form; both describe the same family of lines.
defs: Factorial
n! is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n, with n! = 1·2·…·(n−1)·n.
Gradient (slope) m
The ratio of vertical change to horizontal change along a straight line.
y-intercept c
The y-coordinate where the line crosses the y-axis (x = 0).
Centre and radius of a circle
A circle (x−a)² + (y−b)² = r² has centre (a, b) and radius r, the constant distance from centre to every point on the circle.
Semi-axes of an ellipse
In (x−a)²/r² + (y−b)²/s² = 1, r is the x-radius and s is the y-radius (semi-axes) about centre (a, b).
eqs: Index laws (product, negative and fractional powers)
a, b, c = coefficients (dimensionless); x = unknown (dimensionless)
n, k = non-negative integers with k ≤ n (dimensionless)
a, b = terms (dimensionless); n = non-negative integer power
x, y = coordinates (m, if lengths); m = gradient; c = y-intercept (same units as y)
x, y = coordinates; a, b = centre coordinates; r = radius (same units as x, y)
tips: Watch the sign when using the modulus: |x| = −x only applies when x < 0, not whenever a minus sign appears.
In the ellipse equation, r and s are the semi-axes, not the squares; r² and s² appear in the denominators, so take square roots carefully to find the radii.
rq: Why does a^{0} = 1 follow from the index laws rather than being a convention?
Since a^{m}a^{n} = a^{m+n}, taking n = 0 gives a^{m}·a^{0} = a^{m}, so a^{0} must equal 1 (for a ≠ 0).
What happens to the quadratic roots when b² − 4ac is negative, and why does the formula still apply?
The square root is of a negative number, so the two roots are complex conjugates; the formula still gives them, but they are not real.
How does the binomial coefficient relate to the expansion of (a+b)² ?
(a+b)² = Σ C(2,k) a^k b^{2−k} = a² + 2ab + b², where C(2,1) = 2 gives the middle coefficient.

notes.t: Key formulae: conics, number bases, error propagation, trig, waves, logs
pts: Hyperbola centred at (a,b) with horizontal transverse axis; the minus sign separates the two branches.
A number written in base d expands as a sum of digits times powers of d, with the rightmost digit multiplied by d^0.
Uncertainties add for sums, and relative errors add for products.
Angle conversion: multiply degrees by π/180° to get radians; the unit circle parametrised by t gives (cos t, sin t).
For polar conversion, θ = arctan(y/x) is only valid in the right-hand quadrant (x, y > 0); other quadrants need correction.
defs: Wave number k
Spatial analogue of angular frequency, k = 2π/λ, where λ is wavelength.
Angular frequency ω
ω = 2πf, where f is frequency in Hz.
Relative error
r_a = ε_a / a, the absolute error divided by the value a.
Hyperbolic cosine
cosh(x) = ½(eˣ + e⁻ˣ).
Hyperbolic sine
sinh(x) = ½(eˣ − e⁻ˣ).
Natural logarithm
ln(x) = log(x) = log_e(x), with base e.
eqs: x, y = coordinates; a, b = centre; r, s = semi-axis lengths (m)
a, b = values; ε_a, ε_b = absolute errors (same units as a, b); ε_ab = error in ab
y = displacement (m); A = amplitude (m); k = wave number (rad/m); x = position (m); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
tips: Unit trap: keep angles in radians when using ω = 2πf, k = 2π/λ and trig functions; mixing in degrees gives wrong answers.
Only use the error-propagation rules for independent, small errors; for sums, absolute errors add but for products it is relative errors that add.
rq: Why does the polar angle need a quadrant check when computed with arctan(y/x)?
Because arctan returns values only in (−π/2, π/2), so for x < 0 the true angle differs by π; the quadrant of (x, y) must be checked.
Why do relative errors add when multiplying two quantities, but absolute errors add when adding them?
For products, the relative changes compound multiplicatively, so ln-based relative errors add; for sums, absolute changes simply add.

units.name: 00 Intro Lecture - Block 2
units.ov: This introductory lecture for ENG1063 Block 2 sets out how to succeed in the block and which topics it covers: complex numbers and vector algebra, plus the role of computational tools. The notes contain no technical mathematics. They stress that tutorial engagement and a secure grasp of fundamentals matter more than software output. The mathematical content itself (complex numbers, vectors) comes in later lectures and is not in these notes.
must: Block 2 covers complex numbers and vector algebra, which are core tools across science and engineering
Block 2 has three tutorial sheets that combine textbook exercises with full solutions
Attending tutorials and feedback sessions is linked to higher exam marks
Tutorials are diagnostic workshops for resolving difficulties, not lectures that work solutions from scratch, so attempt problems before attending
Work problems actively in class, then check them against the provided solutions
Computer algebra systems and LLMs are aids for exploring and checking work, not replacements for understanding
Engineers must formulate models, interpret results and critically assess solutions, which needs rigorous grounding in fundamental mathematics
Answers from a tool you cannot justify will not earn exam credit, so always verify and understand the method
Mastery of fundamentals is what distinguishes an engineer from a technician
conn: Complex numbers and vectors are both used to represent quantities with magnitude and direction, such as phasors and 2D vectors, so questions often combine them
Computational tools can check algebra in complex-number and vector problems, but exam credit depends on showing the method yourself
Tutorial practice builds the manual fluency tested in exams, linking the study advice to exam performance
exq: Explain why a computer algebra system or LLM cannot replace understanding of fundamental mathematics when modelling an engineering problem. Give an example of a check you would perform on its output.
Describe how you would use the Block 2 tutorial sheets and their full solutions to diagnose and fix gaps in your understanding of complex numbers and vector algebra.
A software package returns an answer to a vector or complex-number problem. Outline how you would verify it independently and justify it in an exam script.
State the two main topic areas of Block 2 and give one engineering application of each.

notes.t: How to Succeed in ENG1063
pts: Block 2 has three tutorial sheets combining textbook exercises with full solutions.
Attendance at tutorials and feedback sessions is linked to higher exam marks.
Tutorials are diagnostic workshops for resolving difficulties, not lectures where solutions are worked from scratch.
Work tutorial problems actively in class, then review them against the provided solutions.
tips: Do not treat tutorials as passive lectures; come with attempted problems, since engagement is linked to exam performance.
rq: Why is attempting tutorial problems before looking at the solutions more effective for learning?
Attempting problems first exposes gaps in understanding (diagnostic); reviewing solutions afterwards then fixes and reinforces those specific gaps.

notes.t: Topics: Complex Numbers, Vector Algebra and Computational Tools
pts: Complex numbers and vector algebra are powerful mathematical tools used in science and engineering.
Computer algebra systems and LLMs make algebraic manipulation and calculation readily accessible, but they are aids for exploring and checking work.
Automated tools cannot replace understanding; formulating models, interpreting results and critically assessing solutions requires rigorous grounding in fundamental mathematics.
Mastery of fundamental mathematics is what distinguishes a technician from an engineer.
tips: Do not rely on software or LLM output without checking it yourself; an answer produced by a tool you cannot justify will not earn credit in an exam.
rq: Why can't using MATLAB or an LLM to get the answer be enough to show you understand a problem?
Tools can perform algebra and calculation, but understanding is needed to formulate the correct model, interpret the results and judge whether a solution is sensible.
How could you use a computer algebra system to check your work without letting it replace your reasoning?
Solve the problem by hand first, then use the tool to verify the result or explore variations, comparing outputs and explaining any discrepancy.

units.name: 1.1 Course overview and complex numbers outline
units.ov: The notes supplied contain only a title page ('Complex numbers: overview and course outline') and no worked content, so this report is based on the standard first-year syllabus for complex numbers rather than on the notes themselves. Complex numbers extend the reals through \(i^2=-1\); the Cartesian, polar and exponential forms are linked by Euler's formula. They underpin roots, loci, phasors, and the solution of differential equations in engineering.
must: Definition: \(i^2=-1\), \(z=x+iy\), with \(\operatorname{Re}z=x\) and \(\operatorname{Im}z=y\)
Argand diagram: \(z\) is the point \((x,y)\), with modulus \(|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and argument \(\theta=\arg z\) (principal value in \((-\pi,\pi]\))
Polar and exponential forms: \(z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=re^{i\theta}\) (Euler's formula \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\))
Conjugate: \(\bar z=x-iy\), with \(z\bar z=|z|^2\); use it to divide, \(\frac{a}{b}=\frac{a\bar b}{|b|^2}\)
Multiplication and division in polar form: moduli multiply or divide, arguments add or subtract
De Moivre's theorem: \(z^n=r^n e^{in\theta}\), used for powers and for trig identities
nth roots: \(z^{1/n}=r^{1/n}e^{i(\theta+2\pi k)/n}\), \(k=0,\dots,n-1\), equally spaced on a circle
Triangle inequality \(|z_1+z_2|\le|z_1|+|z_2|\) and the properties \(|z_1z_2|=|z_1||z_2|\), \(\overline{z_1z_2}=\bar z_1\bar z_2\)
Loci: \(|z-a|=r\) is a circle and \(\arg(z-a)=\alpha\) is a ray
Complex roots of real polynomials occur in conjugate pairs; \(\cos\theta=\frac{e^{i\theta}+e^{-i\theta}}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta=\frac{e^{i\theta}-e^{-i\theta}}{2i}\)
conn: Euler's formula links the polar form to de Moivre's theorem, which gives nth roots and multiple-angle trig identities
Conjugates link modulus, division and conjugate-pair roots of real polynomials, for example in quadratics with negative discriminant
The geometry of the Argand diagram links loci, modulus and argument, and the roots of unity form regular polygons
Complex exponentials \(e^{i\omega t}\) represent sinusoids as phasors, which links to vibrations and AC circuits
exq: Write \(z=\frac{3+4i}{1-2i}\) in the form \(x+iy\), then find \(|z|\) and \(\arg z\).
Express \(-1+i\sqrt3\) in polar form and use de Moivre's theorem to evaluate \((-1+i\sqrt3)^{6}\).
Find all roots of \(z^4=-16\), give them in the form \(x+iy\), and sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Sketch the locus \(|z-2i|=3\) and the region \(\arg(z-1)\le\pi/4\), and find where they intersect.
Use de Moivre's theorem to express \(\cos 3\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\).

units.name: 1.2 Why complex numbers: quadratics, Cardano's cubic formula and imaginary numbers
units.ov: The module starts from quadratics, where geometric (area) methods only give positive lengths, and moves to Cardano's cubic formula. Cardano's formula can force square roots of negative numbers even when all three roots are real, which motivates the imaginary unit \(j=\sqrt{-1}\) and complex numbers. It ends with the fundamental theorem of algebra: over \(\mathbb{C}\), a degree-\(n\) polynomial has exactly \(n\) roots counted with multiplicity.
must: Definition of the imaginary unit: \(j=\sqrt{-1}\), \(j^2=-1\), \(j^3=-j\), \(j^4=1\). Watch the sign errors in odd powers.

Depressed cubic \(x^3+px=q\) has Cardano root \(x=\sqrt[3]{\frac{q}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{q^2}{4}+\frac{p^3}{27}}}+\sqrt[3]{\frac{q}{2}-\sqrt{\frac{q^2}{4}+\frac{p^3}{27}}}\). The notes' printed '9/2' in the first radicand is a typo for \(q/2\).
If \(\frac{q^2}{4}+\frac{p^3}{27}<0\), the formula needs \(\sqrt{\text{negative}}\). This is the 'casus irreducibilis': three real roots, but complex intermediates.

Cube roots in the example: \((2+j)^3=8+12j-6-j=2+11j\), so \(\sqrt[3]{2+11j}=2+j\) and \(\sqrt[3]{2-11j}=2-j\). The sum is \(4\), because the imaginary parts of the conjugates cancel. (The notes pair the signs the other way round; verify by expanding.)
Cross-check by factorising: \(x^3-15x-4=(x-4)(x^2+4x+1)\), so the roots are \(4\) and \(-2\pm\sqrt3\). Once one real root is known, reduce to a quadratic.
Completing the square: add \((\tfrac{b}{2})^2\) to both sides. For \(x^2+26x=27\): \((x+13)^2=196\), so \(x=1\) or \(x=-27\). Check both roots by substitution, and do not discard negative roots.

Fundamental theorem of algebra: a degree-\(n\) polynomial over \(\mathbb{C}\) has exactly \(n\) roots counted with multiplicity. \(\mathbb{C}\) is algebraically closed, and 'no real roots' does not mean 'no roots'.

Historical point: Cardano saw square roots of negatives as useless, while Bombelli treated \(\sqrt{-1}\) as a new kind of number that is neither positive nor negative and cannot be ordered. The geometric proof fails, but the algebra still works.
conn: Cardano's formula, complex arithmetic and conjugates: cube roots of conjugate pairs are conjugates, so the sum is real.
Factorising a cubic after finding one root, and the quadratic formula: the discriminant sign decides real or complex roots. Use this to check Cardano's output.
Completing the square, the quadratic formula and the fundamental theorem of algebra: the number of roots, real or complex, with multiplicity.
Powers of \(j\) and expanding \((a+jb)^3\): the algebra needed to verify the cube roots.
exq: Use Cardano's formula to solve \(x^3-15x-4=0\). Show that \(\frac{q^2}{4}+\frac{p^3}{27}=-121\), verify that \((2+j)^3=2+11j\), and hence find the real root. Then find the other two roots by factorisation.
Solve \(x^2+26x=27\) by completing the square. Verify both roots by substitution and explain why one has no area interpretation.
Compute \(j^2, j^3, j^4, j^{25}\) and expand \((2-j)^3\). Hence state \(\sqrt[3]{2-11j}\).

For \(x^3+6x=20\), compute \(\frac{q^2}{4}+\frac{p^3}{27}\) and use Cardano's formula to find a real root (it is \(x=2\)). Then show that for \(x^3-12x-q=0\) the discriminant condition for complex intermediates is \(q^2<256\).
State the fundamental theorem of algebra. How many roots does \(x^3-15x-4=0\) have, and how many are real? Give an example of a quartic with no real roots.

notes.t: Complex numbers: motivation from quadratic equations and geometric areas
pts: Geometric (area-based) methods can solve quadratics, but they only give positive lengths, so negative 'solutions' lack a visual meaning.
The visual method completes the square: adding 169 to both sides turns the left side into a perfect square, here \((x+13)^2\).
Substituting x = 1 into x² + 26x = 27 confirms that x = 1 is a genuine root.
x = -27 also satisfies the equation algebraically, showing that a negative root can arise even though it has no direct area interpretation.
eqs: Quadratic equation being solved by completing the square (visual method)
x = unknown (dimensionless here, or m if a length); x² = area (m²)
Completed square after adding 169 to both sides
x = unknown (dimensionless); 196 = total square area (dimensionless here)
tips: Do not discard negative roots just because they lack a geometric interpretation; check them by substitution.
When completing the square, add (half the coefficient of x)² to both sides, not only to one side.
rq: Why does adding 169 to both sides of x² + 26x = 27 help solve the equation?
Because 169 = 13² makes the left side a perfect square, (x+13)² = 196, so x+13 = ±14 can be taken square-root-wise.
If a side length must be positive, why might a negative root still be a valid mathematical solution?
The algebra only requires the equation to hold; a negative value does satisfy it, so it is a solution even if it lacks a physical length meaning.
What would it mean physically for a square to have area -27?
No real geometric square can have negative area, which motivates extending the number system (leading to complex numbers).

notes.t: Why we need complex numbers: Cardano's formula
pts: Cubic equations of the form x³ + px = q led mathematicians to a closed-form solution, found in the early 1500s.
Cardano's formula gives the root of the depressed cubic as a sum of two cube roots, each containing a square root.
When the quantity under the square root is negative, the formula involves square roots of negative numbers, which motivates complex numbers.
defs: Depressed cubic equation
A cubic equation with no x² term, of the form x³ + px = q, which can be solved directly using Cardano's formula.
eqs: x = unknown root (dimensionless); p = coefficient of x (dimensionless in this context); q = constant term (dimensionless in this context)
Cardano's formula for the root of x³ + px = q
x = root; p, q = coefficients as above
tips: Cardano's formula as printed assumes p, q, x are positive; the general case needs care with signs and cube roots.
Do not assume the square root term is real: when \(\frac{q^2}{4}+\frac{p^3}{27}<0\), complex numbers are needed.
rq: Why might Cardano's formula require complex numbers even when the cubic has real roots?
If \(\frac{q^2}{4} + \frac{p^3}{27} < 0\), the inner square root is of a negative number, so intermediate steps need \(\sqrt{-1}\); the real root can only be reached through complex arithmetic.
What if p and q were allowed to be negative?
The formula's square root and cube root expressions change, and the discriminant \(\frac{q^2}{4} + \frac{p^3}{27}\) can become negative, so the same complex-number issue arises.

notes.t: Examples: Cardano's formula with complex numbers (cubic equation)
pts: A cubic can be factorised once one real root is known, reducing it to a quadratic that is solved directly.
Applying Cardano's formula directly to a cubic with three real roots produces square roots of negative numbers, so intermediate complex numbers appear even though the final roots are real.
The square root of a negative number is written using the imaginary unit, so \(\sqrt{-121}=11i\).
defs: Cardano's formula
A closed-form method for finding the roots of a cubic equation by writing the root as a sum of two cube roots, which may involve square roots of negative numbers (complex numbers).
eqs: Roots from the quadratic factor and linear factor
tips: Applying Cardano's formula to a cubic with three real roots forces \(\sqrt{\text{negative}}\); do not conclude the roots are complex.
Check the sign of the square root term: \(\sqrt{-121}=11i\) must be handled with \(i^2=-1\) when combining the cube roots.
rq: Why does Cardano's formula give \(\sqrt{-121}\) here even though all three roots are real?
Because the discriminant is negative (three distinct real roots, the casus irreducibilis), so the formula passes through complex intermediate values that cancel out to give real roots.
Why is factorising with a known root easier than using Cardano's formula?
It avoids complex intermediate numbers entirely; the remaining quadratic is solved with the ordinary quadratic formula.

notes.t: Historical origin of imaginary numbers (square root of negative numbers)
pts: Cardano viewed square roots of negative numbers as subtle but of no practical use.
Bombelli concluded that √(-1) cannot be classed as positive or negative, so it must be treated as a new kind of number.
Bombelli used the imagined unit j = √(-1) with its powers: j² = -1 and j³ = -j, allowing cube-root expressions with negative radicands to be manipulated algebraically.
Cardano's cubic formula combines two cube roots whose radicands contain √(-121), showing that intermediate complex quantities can yield a real result.
defs: Imaginary unit
The number j = √(-1), defined so that j² = -1; it is not a real number and is introduced to extend the number system to square roots of negative numbers.
eqs: Cardano/Bombelli cube-root expression for a real solution of a cubic
x = real root of the cubic (dimensionless); √(-121) = imaginary quantity (dimensionless)
Defining property of the imaginary unit
tips: Do not confuse j with a real number: j² = -1 but j is not a real value, so do not order it as positive or negative.
Watch the sign when cubing: (√(-1))³ = j·(-1) = -j, not +j.
rq: Why did Bombelli conclude that √(-1) cannot be called positive or negative?
Because squaring it gives -1, which is negative, yet no real number's square is negative; it therefore lies outside the ordering of real numbers and must be a new kind of number.
What if we ignored √(-1) entirely in Cardano's formula?
The intermediate terms would be undefined in the reals, so the method would fail even though the final value x is real; the imaginary parts must cancel out.

notes.t: Cardano's method and imaginary intermediate steps
pts: The imaginary unit j is defined as the square root of minus one, so its powers cycle: j² = −1 and j³ = −j.
Cardano's formula for a cubic can produce square roots of negative numbers even when the final root is real, so complex intermediates are needed.
The cube roots of complex conjugates 2 + j11 and 2 − j11 are the complex numbers 2 − j and 2 + j, whose cube reproduces the original values.
Adding the two complex conjugate cube roots gives a purely real result, because the imaginary parts cancel.
Cardano's method works algebraically, but the geometric proof that motivated it no longer applies once complex numbers appear.
defs: Imaginary unit j
j = √(−1), with j² = −1 and j³ = −j; used as the square root of minus one in complex numbers.
eqs: Cube of a complex conjugate pair used in Cardano's solution
j = imaginary unit (dimensionless); the equation verifies the cube root of 2 − j11
Real root of the cubic from Cardano's formula
x = real root (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
tips: Remember j³ = j²·j = −j, not +j; sign errors in powers of j are a common mistake.
Cardano's intermediate complex terms must be handled as complex numbers; do not discard them as meaningless negative areas.
rq: Why must we accept imaginary numbers as intermediate steps when the final answer is real?
Cardano's formula takes cube roots of expressions like 2 ± √−121, which contain square roots of negatives; these complex terms cancel in pairs, leaving a real answer.
Why does (2 − j)³ equal 2 − j11, and what step makes it simplify?
Expanding with j² = −1 and collecting real and imaginary parts: (2 − j)³ = 6 − j8 − j3 − 4 = 2 − j11.

notes.t: Algebraic closure of the complex numbers and the fundamental theorem of algebra
pts: The complex numbers form an algebraically closed field: every polynomial equation has a solution in the complex numbers, even when it has no real solution.
The complex number system is more complete than the real number system for solving equations and problems.
Fundamental theorem of algebra: a polynomial of degree n with complex coefficients has exactly n roots in the complex numbers (counted with multiplicity).
defs: Algebraically closed field
A field in which every non-constant polynomial with coefficients in the field has at least one root in the field. The complex numbers are algebraically closed.
Fundamental theorem of algebra
Every polynomial equation of degree n with complex coefficients has n roots (solutions) in the complex numbers.
tips: The theorem counts roots with multiplicity and in the complex numbers; do not conclude that a polynomial of degree n has n real roots.
Do not confuse 'no real solutions' with 'no solutions': complex solutions always exist.
rq: Why can a quadratic such as \( x^2+1=0 \) have no real solutions yet still be 'solved' within the complex system?
Because the complex numbers include \( i=\sqrt{-1} \), so the roots are \( x=\pm i \), which are complex numbers; the field is algebraically closed, so every such equation has roots there.
What would happen to the fundamental theorem of algebra if we restricted ourselves to real coefficients and real roots only?
Polynomials such as \( x^2+1 \) would have fewer than n real roots, so the statement 'n roots' would fail; the theorem only holds once we enlarge to the complex numbers.

units.name: 1.3 Real and imaginary parts and the Argand diagram
units.ov: This material introduces complex numbers in Cartesian form \(z = x + jy\), defines the real and imaginary parts (both real numbers), and shows how to plot them as points on the Argand diagram. The key idea is that a complex number is an ordered pair \((x, y)\), so algebraic statements about \(\operatorname{Re}(z)\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(z)\) translate directly into geometry in the plane.
must: Cartesian form: \(z = x + jy\) with \(x, y\) real and \(j^2 = -1\)
\(\operatorname{Re}(z) = x\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(z) = y\); the imaginary part is the real coefficient and does NOT include \(j\) (\(\operatorname{Im}(3 - 4j) = -4\), not \(-4j\))
Purely real means \(\operatorname{Im}(z)=0\) (e.g. \(2+0j\)); purely imaginary means \(\operatorname{Re}(z)=0\) (e.g. \(0+2j\))
Argand diagram: real part on the horizontal axis, imaginary part on the vertical axis; \(z\) is the point \(P(x, y)\)
Each complex number corresponds to exactly one point, and the origin is \(z=0\)
Sign rules: \(\operatorname{Re}>0\) is right of the imaginary axis, \(\operatorname{Re}<0\) left; \(\operatorname{Im}>0\) above the real axis, \(\operatorname{Im}<0\) below
Quadrants: \(5+j4\) is in Q1, \(6-j5\) in Q4, \(-3-j\) in Q3 (note \(-3-j\) has \(\operatorname{Im}=-1\))
Read coordinates as \((\operatorname{Re}, \operatorname{Im})\) in that order; swapping axes misplaces every point
Two complex numbers are equal only if both real parts and both imaginary parts match (the basis for equating parts in equations)
conn: Argand diagram plotting leads to modulus and argument: the point \((x,y)\) gives \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and \(\theta=\arctan(y/x)\), with the quadrant (from the signs) deciding the correct angle
Extracting \(\operatorname{Re}\) and \(\operatorname{Im}\) is the tool for solving complex equations: rationalise or expand, then equate real and imaginary parts to find unknowns
Real and imaginary parts underpin the conjugate \(\bar z = x - jy\) (reflection in the real axis), with \(z+\bar z = 2\operatorname{Re}(z)\) and \(z-\bar z = 2j\operatorname{Im}(z)\)
In engineering, the real and imaginary parts represent in-phase and quadrature components (e.g. resistance and reactance in AC impedance \(Z = R + jX\))
exq: State \(\operatorname{Re}(z)\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(z)\) for \(z = 6 - j5\), \(z=-3-j\) and \(z = 4j\), and classify each as purely real, purely imaginary, or neither.
Plot \(z_1 = 5+j4\), \(z_2 = 6-j5\), \(z_3 = -3-j\) on an Argand diagram, label the quadrant of each, and find the distance of each point from the origin.
Find real \(a\) and \(b\) such that \((a+2) + j(b-3) = 5 - 2j\), and state the real and imaginary parts of the result.
For what real value of \(k\) is \(z = (k^2-4) + j(k+1)\) (i) purely real, (ii) purely imaginary? Describe where \(z\) lies on the Argand diagram in each case.
Sketch the set of points satisfying \(\operatorname{Re}(z) = -2\), and the set satisfying \(\operatorname{Im}(z) > 1\), on one Argand diagram, and describe the region where both conditions hold.

notes.t: Complex Numbers: Properties (Real and Imaginary Parts)
pts: A complex number z is written as a real part plus j times an imaginary part, where both parts are real numbers.
The real part of z is x, written Re(z).
The imaginary part of z is y, written Im(z); it is a real number and does not include j.
If the real part is zero, z is purely imaginary.
If the imaginary part is zero, z is purely real.
defs: Complex number
A number z = x + jy with x and y real, where j is the imaginary unit (j² = −1).
Real part
The real number x in z = x + jy, written x = Re(z).
Imaginary part
The real number y (excluding j) in z = x + jy, written y = Im(z).
Purely imaginary
A complex number whose real part is zero (x = 0).
Purely real
A complex number whose imaginary part is zero (y = 0).
eqs: Cartesian (rectangular) form of a complex number
z = complex number; x = real part (dimensionless, real); y = imaginary part (real, excludes j); j = imaginary unit
x = real part of z; z = complex number
y = imaginary part of z (real number); z = complex number
tips: Do not write Im(z) as y·j; the imaginary part is the real coefficient y, without j.
Pure imaginary requires Re(z) = 0 exactly; a number like 0 + 2j is purely imaginary but a number like 2 + 0j is purely real.
rq: Why is Im(z) = y a real number rather than y·j, and what would go wrong in calculations if you included j in it?
Im(z) is defined as the coefficient of j, so it is real; including j would make it imaginary and the components would no longer be real numbers, breaking the separation of real and imaginary parts.
If z = 3 + 0j, what type of complex number is it, and why does its imaginary part not affect that classification?
It is purely real, since y = Im(z) = 0; the zero imaginary part means no j-term contributes.
Can a number be both purely real and purely imaginary? What must be true of x and y?
Only z = 0, since that requires x = 0 and y = 0 simultaneously.

notes.t: The complex plane (Argand diagram)
pts: A complex number z = x + jy is represented as a point P(z) in a plane, with x on the horizontal axis and y on the vertical axis.
The horizontal axis is the real axis, where x = Re(z) gives the real part.
The vertical axis is the imaginary axis, where y = Im(z) gives the imaginary part.
Each point in the plane corresponds to exactly one complex number, and the origin O corresponds to zero.
defs: Complex plane (Argand diagram)
A two-dimensional plane in which the complex number z = x + jy is plotted as the point with coordinates (x, y), the real part on the horizontal axis and the imaginary part on the vertical axis.
Real axis
The horizontal axis of the complex plane, on which values of Re(z) = x are plotted.
Imaginary axis
The vertical axis of the complex plane, on which values of Im(z) = y are plotted.
eqs: Cartesian form of a complex number (point P(z) location)
z = complex number (dimensionless); x = Re(z), real part (dimensionless); y = Im(z), imaginary part (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
tips: Plot x along the horizontal (real) axis and y along the vertical (imaginary) axis; swapping them gives the wrong point.
Use the imaginary part y itself (a real number), not jy, when reading coordinates from the diagram.
rq: Why is the complex plane called a 'plane' rather than a line, even though the real numbers form a line?
A complex number needs two independent real values (x and y), so it requires two dimensions; the real numbers alone need only one axis.
What point in the Argand diagram represents a purely real number such as z = 3, and why?
The point (3, 0) on the real axis, because its imaginary part y = 0.

notes.t: Representing complex numbers on the Argand diagram
pts: A complex number a + jb is plotted as the point with real part a on the horizontal axis and imaginary part b on the vertical axis.
Positive real parts lie to the right of the imaginary axis; negative real parts lie to the left.
Positive imaginary parts lie above the real axis; negative imaginary parts lie below it.
z₁ = 5 + j4 lies in the first quadrant, z₂ = 6 − j5 in the fourth quadrant, and z₃ = −3 − j in the third quadrant.
defs: Argand diagram
A plane whose horizontal axis represents the real part Re(z) and whose vertical axis represents the imaginary part Im(z), used to display complex numbers as points.
tips: Mind the signs: a negative imaginary part places the point below the real axis, a common error when plotting z₂ and z₃.
Read the real part along the horizontal axis first, then the imaginary part vertically; swapping them misplaces every point.
rq: Why does the point for z₃ = −3 − j appear in the lower-left region rather than the upper-right?
Both its real part (−3) and imaginary part (−1) are negative, so it lies left of the imaginary axis and below the real axis, i.e. the third quadrant.
What would change in the plot if you wrote z₂ = 6 + j5 instead of 6 − j5?
The point would move from the fourth quadrant to the first quadrant, reflected across the real axis.

units.name: 1.4 Equality of complex numbers
units.ov: This material covers the definition of equality for complex numbers in Cartesian form \(z = x + jy\). Two complex numbers are equal if and only if their real parts match and their imaginary coefficients match. An equality statement therefore becomes two real simultaneous equations. These can be solved for unknown real parameters such as \(a\) and \(b\), and the answer checked by substituting back.
must: Definition: \(z_1=z_2 \iff x_1=x_2\) and \(y_1=y_2\), i.e. \(\operatorname{Re}(z_1)=\operatorname{Re}(z_2)\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(z_1)=\operatorname{Im}(z_2)\).
One complex equation gives two real equations, so always write both. Missing the imaginary equation is the classic error.
Compare the coefficient of \(j\) (the real number \(y\)), not the whole term \(jy\). Never treat \(j\) as an ordinary real number.
First rearrange each side into the form (real expression) + \(j\)(real expression), expanding brackets, before matching parts.
Solve the resulting pair of real equations by substitution or elimination. Example: \(6a+1=b-4\) and \(2a=a+b\) give \(a=b\), then \(5a=-5\), so \(a=b=-1\).
Check by substituting back. With \(a=b=-1\), both sides read \(-5-2j\) (assuming the example is \(z_1=(6a+1)+j2a\), \(z_2=(b-4)+j(a+b)\)).
Watch signs when moving terms, e.g. \(5b=-5\) gives \(b=-1\), not \(+1\).
The parameters \(a\), \(b\) must be real for the matching rule to apply. The quantities are dimensionless.
A complex number equals zero iff both its real and imaginary parts are zero.
conn: Equality combined with multiplication or division: expand and simplify, e.g. \((a+jb)(2-j)=\dots\), into Cartesian form, then equate parts.
Equality combined with the complex conjugate: \(z=\bar z\) gives \(y=0\), and \(z=-\bar z\) gives \(x=0\).
Equating real and imaginary parts to solve for unknown \(z=x+jy\) in equations such as \(z^2=\dots\) or \(2z+\bar z=\dots\), which reduce to simultaneous equations.

Link to polar form: equal complex numbers have equal modulus and equal argument (up to \(2\pi\)), a second way to test equality. Equating parts also underlies AC circuit impedance and phasor matching.
exq: Find real \(a\) and \(b\) such that \((6a+1)+j\,2a=(b-4)+j(a+b)\), and verify your answer by substitution.
Find real \(x\) and \(y\) satisfying \((2x+3)+j(y-1)=(5-x)+j(3y+2)\).
Given \((a+j b)(2-j)=7+j\) with \(a,b\) real, expand the left side, equate parts and solve for \(a\) and \(b\).
Find the complex number \(z=x+jy\) satisfying \(2z+\bar z=6-j\).
Explain why \(3+j(2a-b)=a+j4\) cannot be solved by comparing the terms \(j(2a-b)\) and \(j4\) with the real parts mixed in. Then solve it correctly for real \(a\) and \(b\).

notes.t: Arithmetic of complex numbers: equality
pts: Two complex numbers are equal only when both their real parts and their imaginary parts are equal.
Complex numbers are written in Cartesian form, with a real part x and an imaginary coefficient y multiplying j.
defs: Equality of complex numbers
Two complex numbers z₁ = x₁ + jy₁ and z₂ = x₂ + jy₂ are equal if and only if x₁ = x₂ and y₁ = y₂.
eqs: Condition for equality of two complex numbers
z_1 = z_2 \iff x_1 = x_2 \text{ and } y_1 = y_2
z₁, z₂ = complex numbers (dimensionless); x₁, x₂ = real parts (dimensionless); y₁, y₂ = imaginary parts (dimensionless)
tips: Equality of complex numbers gives two separate real equations; do not forget to equate the imaginary parts as well as the real parts.
Only the coefficient of j is compared for imaginary parts: compare y₁ with y₂, not jy₁ with jy₂ as a whole mixed with real terms.
rq: Why can we not conclude z₁ = z₂ just because x₁ = x₂?
Equality requires both parts to match; the imaginary parts y₁ and y₂ must also be equal, since j is not a real number and the two parts cannot cancel each other.

notes.t: Equality of complex numbers: solving for real parameters
pts: Two complex numbers are equal exactly when their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal, giving two simultaneous equations.
Equating real parts and imaginary parts gives a system of equations in the unknown real parameters a and b, which is solved by substitution.
Once a and b are found, substitute back into z₁ and z₂ to read off their real and imaginary parts; for equal numbers these parts must match.
defs: Equal complex numbers
Two complex numbers z₁ = x₁ + jy₁ and z₂ = x₂ + jy₂ are equal if and only if x₁ = x₂ and y₁ = y₂ (real parts equal and imaginary parts equal).
eqs: Equality condition for complex numbers (real and imaginary parts matched)
z₁, z₂ = complex numbers (dimensionless); Re, Im = real and imaginary parts (dimensionless)
Solved system for the given example
tips: Do not equate the j-terms as if j were a real number; equate the real-part expression to the real-part expression and the coefficient of j to the coefficient of j.
Watch for sign errors when moving terms, e.g. 6b + 1 = b − 4 gives 5b = −5, not 5b = 5.
rq: Why must both the real parts and the imaginary parts be equated, rather than just one of them?
A complex number is defined by two independent real components; matching only one leaves the other free, so the numbers are not determined to be equal.
Why does the example yield z₁ = z₂ = −5 − j2 even though the original expressions looked different?
Equal complex numbers have identical real and imaginary parts; substituting a = −1 and b = −1 makes both expressions reduce to the same value.

units.name: 1.5 Addition, subtraction and multiplication
units.ov: This section covers the basic arithmetic of complex numbers in Cartesian form \(z = a + jb\): addition and subtraction, which act on real and imaginary parts separately, and multiplication, which uses ordinary expansion together with \(j^2=-1\). Addition and subtraction are linear component-wise operations, while multiplication mixes the components, so the real part picks up a sign change from \(j^2\). Accuracy with signs and the \(j^2\) substitution is the main skill.
must: Addition: \(z_1+z_2=(a_1+a_2)+j(b_1+b_2)\), combining real and imaginary parts separately
Subtraction: \(z_1-z_2=(a_1-a_2)+j(b_1-b_2)\), with the minus sign distributed over both parts of \(z_2\)
Multiplication: \((a+jb)(c+jd)=(ac-bd)+j(ad+bc)\)
Real part of a product = real×real minus imag×imag; imaginary part = sum of the cross terms \(ad+bc\)
\(\mathrm{Re}(z)=a\) and \(\mathrm{Im}(z)=b\) are both real numbers; \(\mathrm{Im}(z)\) excludes the \(j\)
A real scalar multiplier scales both parts: \(2(3+j2)=6+j4\) before subtracting in expressions like \(2z_1-z_2\)
Give the final answer in standard form \(a+jb\), then read off Re and Im directly
Check signs on negative components, such as \((4)(-2)\) in cross terms, and on negative real parts
conn: Scalar multiples feed into subtraction: in \(2z_1-z_2\), scale first, then distribute the minus sign over \(z_2\)
Multiplication relies on \(j^2=-1\) and then on collecting terms, which links to reading Re and Im for later work such as modulus, argument and division
Multiplication results are often combined with addition or subtraction in one expression, e.g. \(z_1z_2 - z_1\) or \(z_1^2+z_2\)
Component-wise addition corresponds to vector addition on the Argand diagram, whereas multiplication does not behave like vector addition (it leads to the polar form)
exq: Given \(z_1=3+j2\) and \(z_2=-1+j5\), calculate \(2z_1-z_2\) and state its real and imaginary parts.
Calculate \(z_1z_2\) for \(z_1=4+j5\) and \(z_2=-2+j2\), giving the answer in the form \(a+jb\).
Simplify \((2-j3)(4+j)+(1+j)\) and find Re and Im of the result.
Show that \((a+jb)(c+jd)=(ac-bd)+j(ad+bc)\), and find a case where the product is purely real with both factors non-real.
Find real \(x\) and \(y\) such that \((x+jy)(1+j2)=5+j5\).

notes.t: Adding and subtracting complex numbers (worked examples)
pts: Complex numbers are added or subtracted by combining their real parts and their imaginary parts separately.
Scaling a complex number by a real constant multiplies both its real and imaginary parts by that constant before subtracting.
Subtraction must distribute the minus sign over every term of the second complex number.
eqs: z_1 = a_1 + jb_1, z_2 = a_2 + jb_2 (dimensionless); a = real part, b = imaginary part
z_1 = a_1 + jb_1, z_2 = a_2 + jb_2 (dimensionless); a = real part, b = imaginary part
tips: Sign error trap: in z₁ − z₂ the imaginary part of z₂ is subtracted too, so (−1 + j5) gives −j5 contribution; keep track of negative real parts.
Check 2z₁ − z₂ carefully: the coefficient 2 must multiply both the real and imaginary parts of z₁ (giving 6 + j4).
rq: Why does (3 + j2) − (−1 + j5) give 4 − j3 and not 4 + j3?
The minus sign applies to the whole second number, so the imaginary part becomes 2 − 5 = −3; the real part becomes 3 − (−1) = 4.
Why must 2z₁ be computed before subtracting z₂ in part c?
The factor 2 multiplies only z₁ (operator precedence), giving 2z₁ = 6 + j4, which is then combined with z₂.

notes.t: Multiplying complex numbers (worked example: z1z2)
pts: To multiply two complex numbers, expand the brackets as for ordinary algebra, then replace j² with −1 and collect real and imaginary parts.
The real part of the product is the sum of the real×real term and the j²-term (imaginary×imaginary), since j² = −1 makes that term real.
The imaginary part collects the cross terms: (real of z1)(imag of z2) + (imag of z1)(real of z2).
Final result is written in the standard form a + jb, from which Re and Im are read directly.
defs: Real part, Re(z)
For z = a + jb, Re(z) = a, the coefficient of the non-j term; it is a real number.
Imaginary part, Im(z)
For z = a + jb, Im(z) = b, the real coefficient multiplying j (not including j itself).
eqs: Product of two complex numbers z1 = a + jb and z2 = c + jd
a, b, c, d = real numbers (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit with j² = −1
tips: Forgetting that j² = −1 when expanding (j4)(j2): the term must become −8, not +8 or j8.
Sign errors in the cross terms: (4)(−2) is negative, so keep the minus sign when combining with (5)(2).
rq: Why does the j²-term from (j4)(j2) contribute to the real part rather than the imaginary part?
Because j·j = j² = −1, which is a real number, so the product j4·j2 = −8 has no j and therefore lies on the real axis.
If z2 were −2 − j2 instead, which terms in the answer would change sign?

The imaginary-part cross terms would change, since they involve the sign of the imaginary part of z2; the real part would be recalculated with the same structure, giving a different real and imaginary result.

units.name: 1.6 Division and complex conjugate
units.ov: This material covers division of complex numbers by rationalising the denominator with the complex conjugate, and the properties of the conjugate, including how it behaves with products. It also covers extracting Re(z) and Im(z) once an expression is simplified to the form \(x+jy\). Everything rests on \(j^2=-1\) and on the fact that \(zz^*=a^2+b^2\) is real, so the conjugate removes j from the denominator.
must: Conjugate: for \(z=a+jb\), \(z^*=a-jb\). Only the sign of the imaginary part flips, e.g. the conjugate of \(2-j\) is \(2+j\), not \(-2-j\).
\(zz^*=a^2+b^2\) is real and non-negative (the modulus squared), which is why it works as a rationalising factor.
Division: \(\frac{z_1}{z_2}=\frac{z_1 z_2^*}{z_2 z_2^*}\). Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
Product expansion: \((a+jb)(c+jd)=(ac-bd)+j(ad+bc)\). Always apply \(j^2=-1\), e.g. \(6-j^2 2\) becomes \(6+2\).
Conjugate of a product: \((z_1z_2)^*=z_1^*z_2^*\). Verify by computing both sides separately; the example gives \(-4-j2\) on both sides.
Re and Im are taken only after simplifying to \(a+jb\): \(\operatorname{Re}(a+jb)=a\) and \(\operatorname{Im}(a+jb)=b\).
\(\operatorname{Im}(z)\) is a real number and does not include j. For example, a result of \(0+j2\) has Re = 0 and Im = 2.
Final answers must be in standard form \(x+jy\), with no \(j^2\) left and no j in the denominator. Split the fraction into \(\frac{8}{5}-j\frac{1}{5}\).
Sign errors in the conjugate propagate through the whole answer, so write the conjugate explicitly, e.g. \((-1-j2)^*=-1+j2\).
conn: Division with Re/Im: simplify the quotient to \(x+jy\) first, then read off Re and Im. Questions often ask for Im of a quotient.
Conjugate properties with multiplication: \((z_1z_2)^*=z_1^*z_2^*\) is checked using the product formula and \(j^2=-1\), and the same expansion skills apply in division numerators.
Conjugate with modulus: \(zz^*=|z|^2\) links division to the polar form and magnitude, so the denominator \(a^2+b^2\) is the modulus squared.
Solving equations in z (equating real and imaginary parts) uses division to reach standard form, followed by Re and Im comparison.
exq: Express \(\frac{3-j2}{2+j}\) in the form \(x+jy\) and state Re and Im of the result.
Given \(z_1=2-j3\) and \(z_2=-1-j2\), verify that \((z_1z_2)^*=z_1^*z_2^*\) by evaluating both sides.
Simplify \(\frac{1+j}{1-j}+\frac{1-j}{1+j}\) and find its real and imaginary parts.
Find \(\operatorname{Im}\left(\frac{5+j4}{3-j2}\right)\), showing the conjugate multiplication and the value of the denominator.
Find real x and y such that \(\frac{x+jy}{2+j}=1-j3\), by rationalising or cross-multiplying and equating real and imaginary parts.

notes.t: Division of complex numbers and finding real and imaginary parts
pts: To divide complex numbers, multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator to remove j from the denominator.
For z₂ = a + jb, the conjugate is z₂* = a − jb, and z₂z₂* = a² + b², which is real.
Using j² = −1 when expanding the numerator, the quotient is written as a single complex number of the form x + jy.
Re(z) gives the real part and Im(z) gives the imaginary part (a real number, not containing j) of the result.
defs: Complex conjugate
For z = a + jb, the complex conjugate is z* = a − jb; multiplying z by z* gives the real number a² + b².
Real part Re(z)
For z = x + jy, Re(z) = x, the real component of the complex number.
Imaginary part Im(z)
For z = x + jy, Im(z) = y, the real coefficient of j (not including j itself).
eqs: Division of complex numbers by rationalising the denominator
z₁, z₂ = complex numbers (dimensionless); z₂* = complex conjugate of z₂; j = imaginary unit
tips: Sign error: the conjugate of 2 − j is 2 + j, not −2 − j; only the imaginary part changes sign.
Forgetting j² = −1 when expanding the numerator leaves a wrong real part (e.g. 6 − j²2 must become 6 + 2).
rq: Why do we multiply by the complex conjugate of the denominator rather than by the denominator itself?
Multiplying by z₂* makes the denominator z₂z₂* = a² + b², a real number, so the j term is removed from the denominator and the result can be split into real and imaginary parts.
What happens to the j² term when expanding (3 − j2)(2 + j), and why?
Since j² = −1, the term −j²·2 becomes +2, which is why the numerator simplifies to 6 + 2 + j(3 − 4) = 8 − j.

notes.t: Complex conjugate of a product: verifying (z1 z2)* = z1* z2*
pts: The conjugate of a product equals the product of the conjugates; verify by computing both sides separately and comparing.
Multiply complex numbers using j² = −1 to simplify the real and imaginary parts.
Conjugating a number flips the sign of its imaginary part, so (−j2)* = j2 and (−1 − j2)* = −1 + j2.
Both sides give −4 − j2, confirming the identity for this example.
defs: Complex conjugate
For z = a + jb, the complex conjugate is z* = a − jb: the imaginary part changes sign while the real part is unchanged.
eqs: Conjugate of a product of two complex numbers
z_1, z_2 = complex numbers (dimensionless); * = complex conjugate operator
Product of complex numbers in rectangular form
a, b, c, d = real numbers (dimensionless); j² = −1
tips: Do not forget j² = −1 when expanding products; dropping it gives an incorrect real part.
Conjugate only the imaginary part: a + jb → a − jb; a sign error on the real part is a common slip.
rq: Why does j² = −1 matter when multiplying (−j2)(−1 − j2)?
The term (−j2)(−j2) = j²·4 = −4 produces a real part; without j² = −1 the real part would be lost and the product would be wrong.
What would change if you conjugated only one of the two numbers before multiplying?
The result would generally not equal (z1z2)*, since the identity requires conjugating each factor and conjugating the product to agree.

notes.t: Complex division via conjugate and real/imaginary parts
pts: To divide complex numbers, multiply numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator so the denominator becomes real.
The modulus squared of a complex number z = a + jb is the real number a² + b², obtained by multiplying z by its conjugate.
Simplify a complex expression by substituting j² = −1 and then separating the result into real and imaginary parts.
Re and Im of a complex number are taken after the expression is simplified to the form a + jb; here the real part is zero and the imaginary part is 2.
defs: Complex conjugate
For z = a + jb, the complex conjugate is z* = a − jb; it reverses the sign of the imaginary part and satisfies z·z* = a² + b².
Real part Re(z)
For z = a + jb, Re(z) = a, the real component of z.
Imaginary part Im(z)
For z = a + jb, Im(z) = b, the coefficient of j (a real number, not including j).
eqs: Division of complex numbers using the conjugate
z_1, z_2 = complex numbers (dimensionless); z_2^* = complex conjugate of z_2 (dimensionless)
a, b = real parts of z_2 (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Real part of a complex number
a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless)
Imaginary part of a complex number
a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless)
tips: Watch the sign when taking the conjugate: (−1 − j2)* = −1 + j2, and sign errors in the conjugate propagate through the whole answer.
Do not forget j² = −1 when simplifying; leaving j² in the answer means it is not in standard a + jb form.
rq: Why multiply by the conjugate of the denominator rather than by the denominator itself when dividing complex numbers?
Multiplying by the conjugate gives z·z* = a² + b², a real number, so the denominator becomes real and the result can be written in the form x + jy.
Why does the term 1/j become −j in part b)?
Since 1/j = j/j² = j/(−1) = −j, using j² = −1.
What if z were real, say z = 2? What would Im(z − 1/z) be?
Im(z − 1/z) = 0, because a real number has zero imaginary part and z − 1/z is then real.

units.name: 1.7 Quadratic roots and preview of Lecture 2
units.ov: This material covers solving real quadratics with the quadratic formula, and shows that a negative discriminant gives a pair of complex-conjugate roots written with j. It then previews Lecture 2, where complex numbers are written in polar form (modulus and argument) and linked to Euler's formula. Polar form makes multiplication, division and rotation on the Argand diagram much easier.
must: Quadratic formula: \( x=\dfrac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a} \), with \( a\neq0 \)
Discriminant \( \Delta=b^2-4ac \): \( \Delta>0 \) gives two distinct real roots, \( \Delta=0 \) a repeated root, \( \Delta<0 \) a complex-conjugate pair
For \( \Delta<0 \), \( \sqrt{-k}=j\sqrt{k} \), e.g. \( \sqrt{-8}=j2\sqrt2 \); never leave it as a real value
Complex conjugate: if \( x_1=p+jq \) then \( x_1^*=p-jq \); the roots of a real quadratic with complex roots satisfy \( x_2=x_1^* \)
Worked example: \( x^2-2x+3=0 \) has \( \Delta=4-12=-8 \) and roots \( 1\pm j\sqrt2 \)
Graphical meaning: no real roots means the parabola never crosses the x-axis (here the minimum value is 2, at \( x=1 \))
Polar form uses modulus and argument; multiplying by j rotates a number 90° anticlockwise on the Argand diagram
Euler's formula \( e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta \) gives the compact polar form; keep angles in consistent units (radians or degrees)
Find the argument in the correct quadrant when converting from rectangular to polar form
conn: Quadratic roots to polar form: the complex-conjugate roots \( p\pm jq \) have the same modulus and opposite arguments, so they lie symmetrically about the real axis on the Argand diagram
Discriminant sign to graph shape: \( \Delta<0 \) corresponds to a parabola that does not touch the x-axis, and the vertex value shows by how much
Conjugates and modulus: \( x_1x_1^*=|x_1|^2 \) is real and equals \( c/a \) for the quadratic, so the product and sum of the roots link back to the coefficients
Multiplication by j as a 90° rotation links to Euler's formula, since \( j=e^{j\pi/2} \)
exq: Solve \( x^2-2x+3=0 \) and show the discriminant working. Write the roots in the form \( p\pm jq \) and confirm that they are complex conjugates.
Find the roots of \( 2x^2+4x+10=0 \), giving the answers in the form \( p+jq \), and state the discriminant.
For \( x^2+bx+4=0 \), find the range of b for which the roots are (i) real and distinct, (ii) complex. Find the roots when \( b=2 \).
Show that the sum of the roots of \( x^2-2x+3=0 \) is \( 2 \) and the product is \( 3 \). Check these against \( -b/a \) and \( c/a \), and find \( |x_1|^2 \).
Plot the roots \( 1\pm j\sqrt2 \) on an Argand diagram. State the effect of multiplying \( 1+j\sqrt2 \) by j, and say which quadrant its argument lies in.

notes.t: Roots of quadratic functions
pts: For a quadratic with a ≠ 0, the roots come from the quadratic formula; a negative discriminant gives complex roots.
When the discriminant b² − 4ac is negative, the square root produces j, so the two roots are complex conjugates.
The quadratic x² − 2x + 3 = 0 has no real roots, since its graph never crosses the x-axis (minimum value 2).
Worked example: substituting a = 1, b = −2, c = 3 gives discriminant 4 − 12 = −8, so the roots are 1 ± j√2.
defs: Complex conjugate
For a complex number x₁ = p + jq, its complex conjugate is x₁* = p − jq; the two roots of a real quadratic with complex roots are complex conjugates of each other.
eqs: Quadratic formula giving the roots of a quadratic equation
x = root (dimensionless in pure maths); a, b, c = real coefficients of the quadratic (dimensionless), a ≠ 0
Conjugate relation between the two roots
x₁ = first root; x₂ = second root; * = complex conjugate
tips: Watch the sign: with b = −2, the term −b becomes +2, and b² = (−2)² = 4 must be squared correctly.
Write the square root of a negative number as j√(|…|) (e.g. √−8 = j√8 = j2√2), not as a real value.
rq: Why does a negative discriminant guarantee that the two roots are complex conjugates rather than two unrelated complex numbers?
Because the ± sign in the formula produces the same real part (−b/2a) with imaginary parts of equal size and opposite sign, i.e. p + jq and p − jq, which are conjugates.
What does the graph of x² − 2x + 3 tell you about its roots before calculating them?
The parabola has its minimum value 2 above the x-axis and never crosses it, so there are no real roots, only complex ones.

notes.t: Preview of Lecture 2: Polar Form of Complex Numbers
pts: Lecture 2 covers modulus and argument, which are needed to express complex numbers in polar form.
Polar form lets complex numbers be multiplied and divided using their moduli and arguments.
Multiplying by j corresponds to a rotation of 90 degrees anticlockwise on the Argand diagram.
Euler's formula links the exponential form to cosine and sine, giving the compact polar notation.
tips: Ensure the argument is measured in the correct quadrant when converting from rectangular to polar form.
Keep angles in consistent units (radians or degrees) when using Euler's formula and polar multiplication.
rq: Why is polar form convenient for multiplying complex numbers?
Because moduli multiply and arguments add, so the product is found without expanding brackets.
What do you expect multiplying by j to do to the argument of a complex number?
It adds 90 degrees (π/2 radians) to the argument, since j has modulus 1 and argument π/2.

units.name: 2.1 Recap and lecture outline
units.ov: This material recaps the algebra of complex numbers in Cartesian form on the Argand diagram: equality, addition, subtraction, multiplication using \(j^2=-1\), and division by rationalising with the conjugate. It then introduces Lecture 2, which moves to modulus, argument and polar form. Cartesian arithmetic is the foundation, since polar form is another way of describing the same point and makes multiplication and division easier.
must: A complex number \(z=x+jy\) is the point \(P(x,y)\) on the Argand diagram, with Re(z) on the horizontal axis and Im(z) on the vertical axis.
Two complex numbers are equal only if their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal. This gives two real equations from one complex equation.
Addition and subtraction work component-wise: add or subtract the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.
Multiplication: expand the brackets and use \(j^2=-1\), giving \(z_1z_2=(x_1x_2-y_1y_2)+j(x_1y_2+x_2y_1)\).
The conjugate is \(z^*=x-jy\), the reflection of z in the real axis. Also \(zz^*=x^2+y^2\), which is real.
Division: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator \(z_2^*\). Then \(\frac{z_1}{z_2}=\frac{(x_1x_2+y_1y_2)+j(x_2y_1-x_1y_2)}{x_2^2+y_2^2}\).
Common errors: forgetting \(j^2=-1\) (so the real part gets \(+y_1y_2\) instead of \(-y_1y_2\)), and using the conjugate of the numerator instead of the denominator.
Lecture 2 preview: modulus, argument and polar form give the same point as \((r,\theta)\) rather than \((x,y)\). Be ready to convert between the two forms.
conn: Conjugate and modulus: \(zz^*=x^2+y^2=|z|^2\), so the denominator in division is the squared modulus of \(z_2\).
Equality of complex numbers and algebra: solve equations such as \((a+jb)(1+j)=3-j\) by expanding, then equating real and imaginary parts to get simultaneous equations.
Cartesian and polar form: Cartesian form is best for addition and subtraction, while polar form is best for multiplication, division and powers. Questions often require converting between them.
Argand diagram geometry: conjugation is a reflection in the real axis, and addition is vector addition. These give a visual check on algebraic answers.
exq: Given \(z_1=3+4j\) and \(z_2=1-2j\), find \(z_1z_2\) and \(z_1/z_2\) in the form \(x+jy\).
Find real x and y such that \((x+jy)(2-j)=5+5j\).
Show that \(zz^*\) is real for any z, and use this to rationalise \(\frac{2+3j}{4-j}\).
Plot \(z=-2+3j\), \(z^*\) and \(z+z^*\) on an Argand diagram and describe the geometric relationship between them.
Simplify \(\frac{(1+j)^2}{1-j}+\frac{1-j}{1+j}\) and give the real and imaginary parts.

notes.t: Recap: complex plane, arithmetic and conjugates
pts: A complex number z = x + jy is plotted as the point P(x, y) on the Argand diagram, with x on the real axis and y on the imaginary axis.
Two complex numbers are equal only when their real parts and their imaginary parts are equal separately.
Addition and subtraction act component-wise: real parts combine with real parts and imaginary parts with imaginary parts.
Multiplication expands the brackets and uses j² = −1, giving real part x₁x₂ − y₁y₂ and imaginary part x₁y₂ + x₂y₁.
The complex conjugate z* = x − jy reflects z in the real axis and is used to rationalise division.
defs: Complex plane (Argand diagram)
A plane in which the horizontal axis represents the real part Re(z) and the vertical axis represents the imaginary part Im(z) of a complex number.
Complex conjugate
For z = x + jy, the complex conjugate is z* = x − jy; it has the same real part and the opposite imaginary part.
eqs: Division of complex numbers (rationalised using the conjugate of z₂)
z₁, z₂ = complex numbers; x₁, x₂ = real parts (dimensionless); y₁, y₂ = imaginary parts (dimensionless)
z₁ = x₁ + jy₁, z₂ = x₂ + jy₂; x, y = real and imaginary parts (dimensionless)
tips: Remember j² = −1 when expanding products; forgetting this gives a wrong real part (it becomes −y₁y₂, not +y₁y₂).
Division is only in standard form after multiplying by the conjugate of the denominator; dividing by the conjugate of the numerator instead is a common error.
rq: Why does dividing by z₂ require multiplying top and bottom by z₂*?
Because z₂z₂* = x₂² + y₂² is real, which removes the imaginary part from the denominator and leaves a result in the form a + jb.
What geometric change does taking the conjugate make on the Argand diagram?
It reflects the point z across the real axis, keeping Re(z) fixed and negating Im(z).

units.name: 2.2 Modulus and argument of a complex number
units.ov: This material defines a complex number \(z=x+jy\) as a point in the Argand plane. The modulus \(r=|z|\) is its distance from the origin, and the principal argument \(\theta\in(-\pi,\pi]\) is its direction from the positive real axis. The modulus comes from Pythagoras, or equivalently \(\sqrt{zz^*}\), and obeys product, quotient and triangle rules. The argument needs a quadrant-aware arctan, so a sketch is the key link between the two.
must: Modulus: \(|z|=r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\sqrt{zz^*}\). It is always real and non-negative, and the \(j\) is never squared into it (never \(x^2+(jy)^2\)).
Principal argument range: \(-\pi<\arg z\le\pi\), measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis. Give answers in this range and in radians unless degrees are requested (multiply by \(180/\pi\)).
Quadrant-corrected argument: \(\arctan(y/x)\) if \(x>0\); \(+\pi\) if \(x<0,\ y\ge0\); \(-\pi\) if \(x<0,\ y<0\). Plain arctan only returns \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\).
Axis cases: \(x=0,\ y>0\) gives \(\pi/2\); \(x=0,\ y<0\) gives \(-\pi/2\); a negative real number gives \(\pi\) (not \(-\pi\)); \(\arg 0\) is undefined (never write 0).
Always sketch the Argand diagram first to fix the quadrant, then check that the calculated \(\theta\) matches it. Example: \(-7+j7\) gives \(-\pi/4+\pi=3\pi/4=135^\circ\).
Product and quotient: \(|z_1z_2|=|z_1||z_2|\) and \(|z_1/z_2|=|z_1|/|z_2|\) with \(z_2\ne0\).
Triangle inequality: \(|z_1+z_2|\le|z_1|+|z_2|\), with equality only when \(z_1,z_2\) point in the same direction. Do not treat it as an equality.
\(zz^*=|z|^2\), e.g. \(|5+j4|=\sqrt{(5+j4)(5-j4)}=\sqrt{41}\). Signs of \(x\) and \(y\) do not make the modulus negative, e.g. \(|-3-j|=\sqrt{10}\).
Do not add components (\(5+4=9\)); use the root of the sum of squares.
conn: Conjugates and modulus: \(zz^*=|z|^2\) is used to rationalise \(z_1/z_2\), and it gives \(|z_1/z_2|\) directly without doing the division.
Modulus and argument together give polar form \(z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)\), and then \(re^{j\theta}\). The quadrant-correct \(\theta\) is what makes the conversion valid.
Argand geometry and the triangle inequality: addition is vector addition, so \(|z_1+z_2|\) is the third side of a triangle. Equality happens when the vectors are parallel (equal arguments).
Product and quotient rules for modulus lead on to the argument rules (arguments add or subtract). Final arguments then need reducing back into \((-\pi,\pi]\).
exq: Find the modulus and principal argument (in radians to 3 d.p. and in degrees) of \(z_1=5+j4\), \(z_2=-3-j\), \(z_3=-7+j7\) and \(z_4=-2j\). Sketch all four on one Argand diagram.
Let \(z_1=3+4j\) and \(z_2=1-j\). Calculate \(|z_1z_2|\) both directly and via \(|z_1||z_2|\), and \(|z_1/z_2|\) both ways, to verify the rules.
Take \(z_1=3+4j\) and \(z_2=-3+4j\). Show that \(|z_1+z_2|<|z_1|+|z_2|\). Then give a pair of non-zero complex numbers for which equality holds, and explain why.
A student states \(\arg(-1-j)=\arctan(1)=\pi/4\). Explain the error, give the correct principal value, and write a general rule for \(x<0\).
Use \(zz^*\) to show \(|z|^2=x^2+y^2\). Hence find all \(z=x+jy\) with \(|z|=5\) and \(\arg z=-\pi/2\), and state why \(\arg 0\) cannot be assigned.

notes.t: Modulus and argument of a complex number
pts: A complex number z = x + jy is a point P(x, y) in the Argand plane, with x on the horizontal axis and y on the vertical axis.
The modulus r is the distance from the origin O to the point P, and measures the size of z.
The argument θ is the angle the line OP makes with the positive real axis, using the principal value range.
The modulus can be found from z multiplied by its complex conjugate, since zz* = x² + y² is always real and non-negative.
The argument must be chosen by quadrant: arctan(y/x) alone gives the wrong angle when x < 0, so add or subtract π accordingly.
defs: Modulus of z
The distance of the point representing z from the origin, \( |z| = r = \sqrt{x^2+y^2} \), always real and non-negative.
Argument of z
The angle θ = arg(z) measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis to the line joining O to P(z), with principal value −π < arg z ≤ π.
Principal value of the argument
The unique value of arg z lying in the interval −π < θ ≤ π.
eqs: r = modulus (dimensionless); x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); z* = complex conjugate of z
Argument of z = x + jy (principal value)

\theta = \arg(x+jy) = \begin{cases} \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) & x>0 \\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+\pi & x<0,\ y\ge 0 \\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)-\pi & x<0,\ y<0 \\ +\frac{\pi}{2} & x=0,\ y>0 \\ -\frac{\pi}{2} & x=0,\ y<0 \\ \text{undefined} & x=0,\ y=0 \end{cases}
θ = argument (rad); x = real part; y = imaginary part
tips: Always check the quadrant before using arctan(y/x); forgetting the ±π correction for x < 0 gives the wrong argument.
Argument is an angle in radians within (−π, π]; do not give a value outside this range when asked for the principal value.
rq: Why can't we simply write θ = arctan(y/x) for every complex number?

arctan returns values only in (−π/2, π/2), so it cannot distinguish points in the left half-plane from those in the right; for x < 0 the point lies in quadrant II or III and π must be added or subtracted.
Why is the modulus always real even though z is complex?
Because zz* = (x+jy)(x−jy) = x² + y², which contains no j term, so its square root is real and non-negative.
What happens to θ when the point lies on the imaginary axis with y < 0?
θ = −π/2, since the point lies directly below the origin on the negative imaginary axis.

notes.t: Common mistakes when finding modulus and argument
pts: The modulus of z is the square root of x squared plus y squared, not x plus jy.
The j part is already accounted for in the Argand diagram representation, so it must not be squared in the modulus.
The argument θ is easily placed in the wrong quadrant, so check the quadrant before finalising arg z.
Sketching the Argand diagram showing where the number lies is the recommended way to avoid quadrant errors.
eqs: x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); |z| = modulus (dimensionless)
tips: Do not square the j in the modulus: use x² + y², never x² + (jy)².
Always sketch the Argand diagram to identify the correct quadrant before stating arg z.
rq: Why would squaring jy (giving -y²) inside the modulus produce a wrong answer?
Because the modulus is a length in the Argand plane, always non-negative; using x² + (jy)² = x² − y² can be negative or misrepresents the distance, so the correct form is x² + y².
If z = −1 + j, why can't a calculator's arctan(y/x) alone give the correct argument?
arctan(y/x) = arctan(−1) = −π/4 lies in the fourth quadrant, but the point (−1, 1) is in the second quadrant, so the argument must be 3π/4; sketching the diagram reveals this.

notes.t: Modulus of a complex number
pts: The modulus of z = x + jy is its distance from the origin, r = √(x² + y²), and it satisfies zz* = |z|².
Multiplicative property: the modulus of a product is the product of the moduli.
Modulus of a quotient equals the quotient of the moduli, provided the denominator is non-zero.
Triangle inequality: the modulus of a sum is at most the sum of the moduli.
defs: Modulus
The modulus |z| of a complex number z = x + jy is its magnitude, the distance from the origin in the Argand diagram: |z| = r = √(x² + y²).
eqs: Modulus of a complex number squared (from zz*)
z = complex number (dimensionless); z* = complex conjugate of z; x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless)
tips: The quotient rule |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂| only applies when z₂ ≠ 0; dividing by zero is undefined.
Do not confuse the triangle inequality with equality: |z₁ + z₂| is generally strictly less than |z₁| + |z₂|, with equality only when z₁ and z₂ point in the same direction.
rq: Why does zz* give a real number, and why is that useful for finding the modulus?
Since z* = x − jy, zz* = (x + jy)(x − jy) = x² + y² (the j terms cancel), which is real and equals |z|², so the modulus follows as √(zz*).
Why can the modulus of a sum be strictly less than the sum of the moduli?
Moduli add only when the vectors point in the same direction; otherwise the triangle formed by the vectors in the Argand diagram makes the resultant shorter than the sum of the two sides.

notes.t: Modulus of a complex number (similar to Example 3.10)
pts: The modulus of z = x + jy is the distance of the point (x, y) from the origin in the Argand diagram, found by Pythagoras.
The modulus can be computed as the square root of z multiplied by its complex conjugate, which gives x² + y² with no imaginary part.
Each of the four given complex numbers is plotted in the Argand diagram, and its modulus is the length of the line from the origin to its point.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
The distance from the origin to the point representing z in the Argand diagram, written |z| = r = √(x² + y²) for z = x + jy.
eqs: r = modulus (dimensionless); x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless)
tips: Modulus is always non-negative and is a length; do not take the sign of the real or imaginary part into account, e.g. |−3 − j| = √10, not −√10.
Do not add the components directly (e.g. 5 + 4 = 9); the modulus uses the sum of squares under a square root.
rq: Why does multiplying z by its conjugate give a real number, and why is this useful for finding the modulus?
(x + jy)(x − jy) = x² + y², since the j-terms cancel, so the result is real and equals |z|²; taking the square root gives |z|.
For −7 + j7, why is the modulus 7√2 and not 7 or 14?
r = √((−7)² + 7²) = √98 = 7√2; the two components are both 7 in size, so they combine by Pythagoras, not by simple addition.

notes.t: Principal value of the argument
pts: The single-argument arctan function only returns angles in the interval (−π/2, π/2), so it cannot by itself give the correct argument of a complex number with x<0.
The principal argument of x+jy is found piecewise, using arctan(y/x) and adding or subtracting π depending on the quadrant.
Special cases x=0 must be handled separately: the argument is +π/2 if y>0, −π/2 if y<0, and undefined if both x and y are zero.
defs: Principal value of the argument
The angle θ = arg(x+jy), taken in the principal range (−π, π], that correctly places a complex number in its quadrant; it is obtained from arctan(y/x) with a π correction when x<0.
Argument (arg)
The angle θ measured from the positive real axis to the point representing x+jy in the Argand diagram.
eqs: Principal argument of a complex number x+jy

\theta=\arg(x+jy)=\begin{cases}\arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) & \text{if } x>0\\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+\pi & \text{if } x<0 \text{ and } y\ge 0\\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)-\pi & \text{if } x<0 \text{ and } y<0\\ +\frac{\pi}{2} & \text{if } x=0 \text{ and } y>0\\ -\frac{\pi}{2} & \text{if } x=0 \text{ and } y<0\\ \text{undefined} & \text{if } x=0 \text{ and } y=0\end{cases}
θ = argument (rad); x = real part (dimensionless, same units as y); y = imaginary part (dimensionless, same units as x)
θ = tangent value (dimensionless); arctan output in radians
tips: Always check the quadrant of x+jy before using arctan(y/x); a calculator's arctan alone gives the wrong angle for x<0.
The argument is undefined at the origin (x=0, y=0); do not write θ = 0 there.
rq: Why can't we simply write arg(x+jy) = arctan(y/x) for every complex number?

Because arctan only returns angles between −π/2 and π/2, which covers only the right half-plane (x>0). For x<0 the point lies in the left half-plane, so π must be added or subtracted to reach the correct angle.
Why do x<0 points need +π when y≥0 but −π when y<0?
