The π shift moves the arctan result into the correct quadrant: for y≥0 (second quadrant) the angle must lie in (π/2, π], and for y<0 (third quadrant) it must lie in (−π, −π/2), so the shift direction depends on the sign of y.
What happens if x=0 and you compute y/x?
Division by zero is undefined, so the formula fails; instead the argument is directly ±π/2 according to the sign of y, and it is undefined when both x and y are zero.

notes.t: Modulus and argument of complex numbers (principal value)
pts: The modulus r of z = x + jy is the distance from the origin, r = √(x² + y²).
The argument θ is the angle the vector makes with the positive real axis; its principal value lies in (−π, π].
Choose the quadrant-correct formula for θ using the signs of x and y, since arctan alone gives only (−π/2, π/2).
Points on the imaginary axis have special arguments: +π/2 when y > 0 and −π/2 when y < 0.
The argument of z = 0 is undefined, since no direction can be assigned to the origin.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
The length r = |z| of the vector from the origin to the point x + jy in the Argand diagram, given by r = √(x² + y²).
Argument of a complex number
The angle θ = arg(z) measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis to the vector representing z.
Principal value of the argument
The unique value of arg(z) satisfying −π < arg(z) ≤ π.
eqs: \theta = \arg(x+jy) = \begin{cases} \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) & x>0 \\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+\pi & x<0,\ y\ge 0 \\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)-\pi & x<0,\ y<0 \\ +\frac{\pi}{2} & x=0,\ y>0 \\ -\frac{\pi}{2} & x=0,\ y<0 \end{cases}
θ = argument (rad); x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless)
r = modulus (dimensionless); x = real part; y = imaginary part
tips: Unit trap: the argument is in radians in the formulas, but answers are often requested in degrees; multiply by 180/π.
Quadrant trap: always add or subtract π for x < 0 (e.g. 5 + j4 is first quadrant, but −7 + j7 needs +π, giving 3π/4 = 135°).
rq: Why must we check the signs of x and y before using arctan(y/x) for the argument?
arctan returns values only in (−π/2, π/2), so it cannot distinguish opposite quadrants; the sign of x and y decides whether to add or subtract π.
What goes wrong if you compute the argument of −3 − j as arctan(1/3) alone?
You get about +0.32 rad, placing the point in the first quadrant; the correct point is in the third quadrant, so θ = arctan(1/3) − π ≈ −2.82 rad.
Why is the argument of 0 undefined, while the modulus is defined?
The modulus is the distance from the origin (zero), but no direction from the origin to itself exists, so no angle can be defined.

units.name: 2.3 Polar form of complex numbers
units.ov: This material shows how to describe a complex number z = x + jy by its modulus r (distance from the origin) and argument θ (anticlockwise angle from the positive real axis), giving z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) = r∠θ. The key skill is converting from rectangular to polar form, which means using Pythagoras for r and arctan for θ, with a quadrant check. Polar form is the basis for Euler's formula and for easier multiplication, division and powers.
must: Polar form: \(z = r(\cos\theta + j\sin\theta) = r\angle\theta\)
Modulus: \(r = |z| = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\), always non-negative
Polar to rectangular: \(x = r\cos\theta,\; y = r\sin\theta\)
Argument: \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) is correct only in quadrants 1 and 4 (a > 0); always sketch the Argand diagram first
Quadrant correction: for a < 0 add \(\pi\) (b > 0, 2nd quadrant) or subtract \(\pi\) (b < 0, 3rd quadrant) to the arctan value
Worked example: \(z=5+j4\) has \(r=\sqrt{41}\approx 6.40\) and \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(4/5)\approx 0.675\) rad \(\approx 38.7^\circ\)
Worked example: \(z=-3-j\) has \(r=\sqrt{10}\) and \(\theta=\tan^{-1}(1/3)-\pi\approx -2.82\) rad (principal value)
The argument is only defined up to multiples of \(2\pi\); state the principal range used, usually \((-\pi,\pi]\)
Keep angles in consistent units (rad or deg) when evaluating cos, sin and tan⁻¹; convert with \(180/\pi\) only when degrees are asked for
Special points lie on the axes, e.g. \(z=j\) has \(r=1\) and \(\theta=\pi/2\), where arctan(b/a) is undefined for a = 0 and the argument must be read from the diagram
conn: Quadrant checking links the Argand diagram to arctan: a sketch decides whether to add or subtract \(\pi\), so most lost marks come from skipping it
Polar form leads directly to Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\), so \(z=re^{j\theta}\) and exam questions often ask you to switch between all three forms
Polar form makes multiplication, division, powers and roots simple (multiply moduli and add arguments, as in de Moivre), which questions often pair with a conversion step
In engineering applications such as AC phasors and oscillations, modulus is amplitude and argument is phase angle, so unit consistency (rad vs deg) matters
exq: Express \(z=-3-j\) in polar form \(r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)\), giving r exactly and θ in radians to 3 s.f. in the principal range, and sketch it on an Argand diagram.
Convert \(z_1=5+j4\) and \(z_2=-2+j2\) to polar form, giving angles in both radians and degrees.
Convert \(z=6\angle 120^\circ\) to rectangular form \(x+jy\), giving x and y to 3 s.f.
Find the modulus and argument of \(z=-j\) and of \(z=-4\), and explain why \(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) cannot be used directly in each case.
A student writes \(\arg(-3-j)=\tan^{-1}(1/3)=0.322\) rad. Identify the error, correct it, and verify by evaluating \(r\cos\theta\) and \(r\sin\theta\).

notes.t: Polar form of a complex number
pts: A complex number P(x, y) = P(z) can be located by its distance r from the origin and its angle θ from the positive real (x) axis.
Rectangular components follow from right-angled triangle trigonometry: x equals r cos θ and y equals r sin θ.
Substituting these into z = x + jy gives the polar form, written either as r(cos θ + j sin θ) or in shorthand as r∠θ.
defs: Modulus r
The distance from the origin O to the point representing the complex number on the Argand diagram, equal to √(x² + y²).
Argument θ
The angle measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis to the line joining the origin to the point representing the complex number.
eqs: x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad)
Polar form of a complex number
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); j = imaginary unit
z = complex number; r = modulus; θ = argument (rad)
tips: Watch the quadrant when finding θ from arctan(y/x): the calculator value alone may place the point in the wrong quadrant.
Keep θ in consistent units (radians or degrees) throughout; mixing them when evaluating cos θ and sin θ is a common error.
rq: Why does the right-angled triangle in the diagram give x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ, rather than the other way round?
θ is the angle between r and the x-axis, so x is the adjacent side (cos θ × hypotenuse r) and y is the opposite side (sin θ × hypotenuse r).
If you know x and y, how would you find θ, and why must you check the quadrant?
Use θ = arctan(y/x), but the arctan gives only values between −90° and 90°, so you must adjust by 180° if x < 0 to place the point in the correct quadrant.

notes.t: Expressing complex numbers in polar form
pts: A complex number z = a + jb is written in polar form using its modulus r = √(a²+b²) and argument θ, with z = r(cos θ + j sin θ).
The argument θ must be found from the quadrant the point lies in; tan⁻¹ alone gives the wrong angle for points in the second or third quadrant.
For z = 5 + j4 the point lies in the first quadrant, so θ = tan⁻¹(4/5) directly gives the argument.
Angles can be given in radians or degrees; convert using 180/π to move between them.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
The distance of z = a + jb from the origin in the Argand diagram, r = √(a²+b²), always non-negative.
Argument of a complex number
The angle θ between the positive real axis and the line from the origin to z, measured anticlockwise, usually taken in the principal range.
Polar form
Representation z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) of a complex number using its modulus r and argument θ.
eqs: r = modulus (dimensionless); a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless)
Argument of z = a + jb (first quadrant)
θ = argument (rad); b = imaginary part; a = real part
Polar form of a complex number
z = complex number; r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad)
tips: Check the quadrant before using tan⁻¹: for a negative real part add π (or subtract π) to get the correct argument.
Keep angle units consistent: convert 0.67 rad to degrees with 180/π only when degrees are requested, and never mix radians and degrees in cos and sin.
rq: Why does θ = tan⁻¹(−1) need +π added for z = −7 + j7?
Because −7 + j7 lies in the second quadrant; tan⁻¹ returns an angle in the fourth quadrant, so π is added to move it to the correct quadrant, giving 3π/4.
Why is the modulus r = √41 for z = 5 + j4 and not 5 + 4?
The modulus is the distance from the origin, found by Pythagoras, √(5²+4²), not by adding the components.

notes.t: Polar form of complex numbers: modulus and argument
pts: Any complex number can be written in polar form using its modulus r and argument θ.
The modulus r is the distance from the origin, found by Pythagoras on the real and imaginary parts.
The argument θ is found from the arctangent of the imaginary part over the real part, adjusted to the correct quadrant.
For z = −3 − j, the point lies in the third quadrant, so π must be subtracted from the arctangent to get the correct argument.
Writing z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) gives the polar form, which is the basis for Euler's formula.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
For z = a + jb, the modulus is |z| = r = √(a² + b²), the distance of z from the origin of the Argand diagram.
Argument of a complex number
The angle θ that the line from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise; it is defined only up to multiples of 2π (principal value usually in (−π, π]).
Polar form
The representation of a complex number as z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), giving its modulus and argument.
eqs: Polar form of a complex number
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus, distance from origin (dimensionless); θ = argument, angle from positive real axis (rad); j = imaginary unit
r = modulus (dimensionless); a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless)
Argument of z = a + jb (first-quadrant form)
θ = argument (rad); a = real part; b = imaginary part; valid only when quadrant is correct, otherwise adjust by ±π
tips: Do not take the arctangent result directly as θ; check the quadrant of z and add or subtract π where needed.
Keep the argument in radians when using it in polar or exponential form, and state the principal value range you are using.
rq: Why must we subtract π when finding the argument of −3 − j, even though tan⁻¹(1/3) is a valid number?

tan⁻¹ returns angles only in (−π/2, π/2), so it cannot distinguish the third quadrant; since both real and imaginary parts are negative, the true angle lies in the third quadrant and must be shifted by π.
What happens to the modulus if we multiply z by −1, and why?
The modulus is unchanged, since r = √(a² + b²) depends only on squares of the parts, while the argument shifts by π, because −z is the reflection through the origin.

units.name: 2.4 Multiplication and division in polar form
units.ov: This material derives and applies the rules for multiplying and dividing complex numbers in polar form: moduli multiply or divide, and arguments add or subtract. The rules follow from the compound-angle identities for cos and sin, with conjugates used to handle division. Worked examples show the full routine: convert to modulus-argument form (checking the quadrant), apply the rule, reduce the argument to the principal range, and convert back to \(a+jb\) if asked.
must: Product rule: \(z_1z_2=r_1r_2[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)]\), so moduli multiply and arguments add
Quotient rule: \(\frac{z_1}{z_2}=\frac{r_1}{r_2}[\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2)]\), so moduli divide and arguments subtract, in the order \(\theta_1-\theta_2\)
Modulus and argument results: \(|z_1z_2|=|z_1||z_2|\), \(\arg(z_1z_2)=\arg z_1+\arg z_2\), \(|z_1/z_2|=|z_1|/|z_2|\), \(\arg(z_1/z_2)=\arg z_1-\arg z_2\)
Modulus \(r=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) and argument measured anticlockwise from the positive real axis, with principal range \((-\pi,\pi]\)
Find the argument by checking the quadrant first, because \(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) alone is wrong when \(a<0\). Example: \(-7+j7\) has modulus \(7\sqrt2\) and argument \(3\pi/4\)
Reduce the final argument to \((-\pi,\pi]\) by adding or subtracting \(2\pi\) whenever the sum or difference falls outside it
Use radians throughout or degrees throughout, and never mix them when combining angles

Derivation: expand the brackets and apply the \(\cos(\alpha\pm\beta)\) and \(\sin(\alpha\pm\beta)\) identities; for division, multiply by the conjugate \(\cos\theta_2-j\sin\theta_2\) and use \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\)
Moduli multiply but do not add: \(|z_1+z_2|\neq|z_1|+|z_2|\) in general. Also do not divide the cos/sin brackets directly
Convert the polar answer back to \(a+jb\) with \(a=r\cos\theta\), \(b=r\sin\theta\), and check the signs against the quadrant
conn: Argand diagram geometry and polar form: multiplying by \(z\) scales by \(|z|\) and rotates by \(\arg z\), and dividing does the reverse. This links to rotations and phasors in mechanical vibrations

Compound-angle trig identities and complex algebra: the product and quotient rules are proofs by those identities. Questions may ask for a derivation or use the results to get exact values of \(\cos\) and \(\sin\) of sums

Quadrant-aware argument finding and principal-value reduction: a correct modulus can still give a wrong final answer if the argument is in the wrong quadrant or outside \((-\pi,\pi]\) after adding or subtracting
Polar multiplication and division lead on to De Moivre's theorem, powers and roots, and the exponential form \(re^{j\theta}\), where the same add/subtract-argument rules apply
exq: Let \(z_1=5+j4\) and \(z_2=-7+j7\). Find the modulus and principal argument of each, then give \(z_1z_2\) in polar form, and convert it to \(a+jb\) to check against direct multiplication.
Find \(z_1/z_2\) for \(z_1=6-j5\) and \(z_2=-3-j\). Give the answer in polar form with the principal argument and in rectangular form, stating the quadrant of each argument you use.

Prove that \(\frac{z_1}{z_2}=\frac{r_1}{r_2}[\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2)]\) by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator and using the compound-angle identities.

Given \(z_1=3\left(\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}+j\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\) and \(z_2=2\left(\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}+j\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\), find \(z_1z_2\) and \(z_1/z_2\), reducing each argument to \((-\pi,\pi]\).
Show that \(|z_1+z_2|\neq|z_1|+|z_2|\) in general using a numerical counterexample such as \(z_1=1+j\), \(z_2=-1+j\), and explain why the product rule for moduli does not carry over to sums.

notes.t: Multiplication in polar form
pts: Write each complex number as modulus times (cos θ + j sin θ); the moduli multiply and the arguments add when multiplying.
Expanding the product of the two brackets and collecting real and imaginary parts gives a result that depends on the sum of the angles.
The compound-angle identities for cos(α+β) and sin(α+β) reduce the expanded form to a single bracket in θ_1 + θ_2.
eqs: Product of two complex numbers in polar form
z_1, z_2 = complex numbers (dimensionless); r_1, r_2 = moduli (dimensionless); θ_1, θ_2 = arguments (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Angles must be consistent (both in radians or both in degrees) before adding them; mixing units gives wrong arguments.
The sum θ_1+θ_2 may exceed 2π or π; reduce it to the principal argument range if the question requires it.
rq: Why do the arguments add rather than multiply when two complex numbers are multiplied in polar form?
Because the product expansion uses the compound-angle identities for sin and cos, which combine the angles additively: cos θ_1 cos θ_2 − sin θ_1 sin θ_2 = cos(θ_1+θ_2).
What would happen to the moduli if you multiplied z_1 by z_2 where |z_2| = 1?
The modulus of the product stays equal to r_1, since r_1 r_2 = r_1 when r_2 = 1; only the argument is shifted by θ_2.

notes.t: Multiplying complex numbers in polar form
pts: Product of two complex numbers in polar form: moduli multiply and arguments add.
Modulus of a product equals the product of the moduli.
Argument of a product is the sum of the arguments.
Point P(x,y) or P(z) has modulus r and argument θ measured from the positive x-axis.
defs: Modulus r of z
The distance from the origin O to the point representing z; r = |z| = √(x²+y²).
Argument θ of z
The angle the line from O to P(z) makes with the positive real (x) axis, measured anticlockwise.
eqs: Polar form of a product of two complex numbers
z_1, z_2 = complex numbers; r_1, r_2 = moduli (dimensionless); θ_1, θ_2 = arguments (rad); j = imaginary unit
|z| = modulus (dimensionless); r_1, r_2 = moduli of z_1, z_2
arg z = argument (rad); θ_1, θ_2 = arguments of z_1, z_2
tips: Arguments add but may need reducing to the principal range (−π, π] before stating the final answer.
Moduli multiply, not add: |z_1 + z_2| ≠ |z_1| + |z_2| in general, so do not confuse the product rule with the sum.
rq: Why can we add the arguments when multiplying complex numbers, but not when adding them?

Multiplication corresponds to a rotation plus a scaling: the moduli scale the length and the arguments rotate the point, so rotations accumulate by addition. Addition of complex numbers is vector addition of their components, which has no simple effect on the argument.
What happens to the point representing z if we multiply by a number with modulus 1 and argument θ?
Its modulus is unchanged and it is rotated anticlockwise through angle θ about the origin.

notes.t: Multiplying complex numbers in polar form
pts: Convert each complex number to modulus–argument (polar) form before multiplying.
When multiplying in polar form, multiply the moduli and add the arguments.
The modulus of z1 = 5 + j4 is √(5² + 4²) = √41, and its argument is about 0.67 rad.
The modulus of z2 = −7 + j7 is 7√2, and its argument is 3π/4 rad (135°) because it lies in the second quadrant.
Final answer is expressed in polar form with the product modulus and argument.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
The distance from the origin to the point representing z in the Argand diagram, |z| = √(a² + b²) for z = a + jb.
Argument of a complex number
The angle the vector from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, measured anticlockwise, usually taken in (−π, π].
eqs: Product of two complex numbers in polar form
tips: Check the quadrant of each complex number before finding its argument; arctan alone gives the wrong angle for negative real parts.
Keep angles in consistent units (radians here) and reduce the final argument to the principal range (−π, π] if required.
rq: Why can we multiply the moduli and add the arguments, rather than multiplying the real and imaginary parts separately?

Because the modulus measures scaling and the argument measures rotation; multiplying by z2 scales by |z2| and rotates by arg z2, which follows from the polar/Euler form z = r e^{jθ} and the exponent rule e^{jθ1}e^{jθ2} = e^{j(θ1+θ2)}.
What would change if z2 = 7 − j7 instead of −7 + j7?
Its modulus stays 7√2 but its argument becomes −π/4, so the product argument would be 0.67 − π/4 instead of 0.67 + 3π/4.

notes.t: Division of complex numbers in polar form
pts: Dividing complex numbers in polar form divides the moduli; the bracketed cos + j sin factors multiply.
The reciprocal of cos θ + j sin θ is cos θ − j sin θ, found by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate.
The identity cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 simplifies the denominator when rationalising a unit-modulus term.
Hence z₁/z₂ = (r₁/r₂)(cos θ₁ + j sin θ₁)(cos θ₂ − j sin θ₂), which combines into a modulus ratio and an angle difference.
defs: Complex conjugate of cos θ + j sin θ
The conjugate cos θ − j sin θ; the product of a number with its conjugate equals its squared modulus, here 1.
eqs: Polar form of a complex number
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad)
Quotient of two complex numbers in polar form
z₁, z₂ = complex numbers; r₁, r₂ = moduli (dimensionless); θ₁, θ₂ = arguments (rad)
tips: Watch the sign: the conjugate of the denominator uses −j sin θ₂, not +j sin θ₂.
Divide only the moduli r₁/r₂; do not divide the cos/sin brackets directly.
rq: Why does multiplying by cos θ − j sin θ remove the j from the denominator?
Because (cos θ + j sin θ)(cos θ − j sin θ) = cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, which is real.
Why does the modulus divide but the angles do not simply subtract when the form is written this way?
The expression keeps the angles as separate cos/sin products; combining them gives the angle difference θ₁ − θ₂ via the addition formulae.

notes.t: Division of complex numbers in polar form
pts: Dividing complex numbers in polar form divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.
The division is carried out by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, using cos and sin addition identities.
The modulus of a quotient equals the ratio of the moduli.
The argument of a quotient equals the difference of the arguments.
eqs: Division of complex numbers in polar form
z_1, z_2 = complex numbers (dimensionless); r_1, r_2 = moduli (dimensionless); θ_1, θ_2 = arguments (rad)
tips: Subtract the arguments in the correct order (θ_1 − θ_2); reversing them gives the wrong sign.
Check that the resulting angle is in the required range (e.g. −π < θ ≤ π) when giving the principal argument.
rq: Why can we subtract the arguments when dividing, but add them when multiplying?
Dividing by z_2 undoes the rotation by θ_2, so the angles subtract; multiplying applies both rotations, so the angles add.
Why is multiplying by the conjugate of z_2 useful in the derivation?
It removes the imaginary part from the denominator, turning the quotient into a form that the cos and sin identities simplify.

notes.t: Division of complex numbers in polar form
pts: Convert each complex number to modulus–argument (polar) form before dividing.
Dividing in polar form divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.
The result must be converted back to rectangular form a + jb, using cos and sin of the new argument.
defs: Modulus of a complex number
The distance from the origin to the point representing z = a + jb in the Argand diagram, r = |z| = √(a² + b²).
Argument of a complex number
The angle θ that the line from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, so that tan θ = b/a with correct quadrant.
eqs: Division of complex numbers in polar form
z_1, z_2 = complex numbers (dimensionless); r_1, r_2 = moduli (dimensionless); θ_1, θ_2 = arguments (rad)
tips: Ensure arguments are taken with the correct quadrant (e.g. tan⁻¹ alone gives the wrong angle for 6 − j5 and −3 − j) before subtracting.
Convert the final polar result back to rectangular form a + jb and check the signs of the real and imaginary parts match the quadrant.
rq: Why do we subtract the arguments rather than add them when dividing, but add them when multiplying?
Division is the inverse of multiplication: multiplying multiplies moduli and adds arguments, so dividing divides moduli and subtracts arguments.
Why is the calculated argument −0.69 − (−2.82) = 2.13 rad, and what does it tell you about the quadrant of the answer?
Subtracting a negative angle adds it, giving 2.13 rad (about 122°), which lies in the second quadrant, consistent with the negative real part −1.31.

units.name: 2.5 Multiplication by j and powers of j
units.ov: This material shows that multiplying a complex number by \(j\) rotates it 90° anticlockwise about the origin, so powers of \(j\) cycle with period 4 through \(1, j, -1, -j\). Negative powers run the rotation clockwise, and the reciprocal \(1/j=-j\) follows from \(j^2=-1\). This geometric picture underlies phasor rotation and simplifying complex expressions.
must: Definition: \(j^2=-1\), where \(j\) is the imaginary unit (engineering notation for \(i\)).
Multiplying by \(j\) rotates a complex number by \(90^\circ\) anticlockwise about the origin, with its modulus unchanged.
Powers cycle with period 4: \(j^0=1,\ j^1=j,\ j^2=-1,\ j^3=-j,\ j^4=1\).
To evaluate \(j^n\), reduce \(n\) modulo 4 (e.g. \(j^{27}=j^3=-j\)).
Reciprocal: \(j^{-1}=1/j=-j\), because \(j\cdot(-j)=-j^2=1\).
Negative powers rotate clockwise: \(j^{-1}=-j,\ j^{-2}=-1,\ j^{-3}=j,\ j^{-4}=1\). Reduce modulo 4 here too.
Each power sits on an axis of the unit circle: \(1\) on +Re, \(j\) on +Im, \(-1\) on −Re, \(-j\) on −Im.
Common errors: \(1/j=-j\), not \(j\); \(j^2=-1\), not \(+1\); keep track of signs, e.g. \((-j)^2=-1\).
Multiplying by \(j^n\) rotates by \(n\times 90^\circ\): \(z=a+jb\) becomes \(jz=-b+ja\).
conn: Rotation by \(j\) is the special case of multiplying by \(e^{j\theta}\) with \(\theta=90^\circ\). This leads to polar form, where multiplying multiplies moduli and adds arguments.
Rationalising \(1/(a+jb)\) uses the same idea as \(1/j=-j\): multiply by the conjugate to remove \(j\) from the denominator.
Phasors in AC circuits: multiplying by \(j\) gives a 90° phase lead and dividing by \(j\) gives a 90° lag. This appears in \(Z_L=j\omega L\) and \(Z_C=1/(j\omega C)=-j/(\omega C)\).
Differentiating a sinusoid, which leads it by 90°, corresponds to multiplying its phasor by \(j\omega\).
exq: Evaluate \(j^{15}\), \(j^{42}\), \(j^{-7}\) and \(j^{-10}\), stating the modulo-4 reasoning used in each.
Simplify \((3+2j)\,j^3\) and sketch both the original and rotated numbers on an Argand diagram, marking the rotation angle.
Show that \(1/j=-j\) both algebraically and geometrically. Hence simplify \(\dfrac{5}{j}+\dfrac{2}{j^3}-j^{-2}\).
Starting from \(z=4+3j\), find the result of multiplying by \(j\), \(j^2\), \(j^3\) and \(j^4\). Give the argument of each and explain why the sequence repeats.
Evaluate \(S=1+j+j^2+\dots+j^{20}\) by grouping terms in cycles of four.

notes.t: Geometrical representation of multiplication by j
pts: Multiplying by j rotates a complex number by 90° anticlockwise about the origin, so the powers of j cycle through 1, j, −1, −j.

Each successive power of j moves one quarter-turn around the unit circle: j⁰ = 1 on the positive real axis, j¹ = j on the positive imaginary axis, j² = −1 on the negative real axis, j³ = −j on the negative imaginary axis.
Because four quarter-turns return to the start, j⁴ = 1, and the pattern repeats every four powers.
Negative powers run the rotation the other way (clockwise), giving j⁻¹ = −j and j⁻² = −1.
defs: Imaginary unit j
The number satisfying j² = −1, used to represent the vertical (imaginary) direction in the complex plane.
tips: Do not confuse j⁻¹ with j: the reciprocal 1/j equals −j, not j.
Remember j² = −1 (not +1) when simplifying powers; reduce exponents modulo 4 before evaluating.
rq: Why does multiplying by j rotate a point 90° rather than stretching or shrinking it?
Since |j| = 1, multiplication by j preserves modulus; its argument increases by 90° (π/2), so the point is rotated, not scaled.
What happens to the point 1 after multiplying by j four times, and why?
It returns to 1 because four 90° rotations total 360°, so j⁴ = 1.

notes.t: Powers of j and the rotating phasor picture
pts: Powers of j cycle with period 4: 1, j, −1, −j, then repeat.
Negative powers follow from the reciprocal: j^(−1) = 1/j = −j.
Multiplying by j rotates a phasor by 90° anticlockwise in the complex plane.
defs: Imaginary unit j
j is defined by j² = −1 (engineering notation for i); its successive powers cycle through 1, j, −1, −j.
tips: Do not confuse j^(−1) = −j with j^(−1) = j; the reciprocal of j is −j because j·(−j) = 1.
Remember j^(−2) = 1/j² is not 1/(−j)² in the sense of sign errors: (−j)² = −1 gives the same result, but keep track of signs carefully.
rq: Why does j^4 return to 1 rather than producing a new value?
Since j² = −1, j⁴ = (j²)² = (−1)² = 1, so the powers repeat every four steps.
What is j^(−2), and why is it equal to −1?
j^(−2) = 1/j² = 1/(−1) = −1, the same as j², because the reciprocal of −1 is −1.

units.name: 2.6 Euler's formula and exponential form
units.ov: This material introduces Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\), which lets any complex number be written compactly in exponential (polar) form \(z=re^{j\theta}\). Converting from Cartesian form \(a+jb\) relies on finding the modulus and a correctly chosen argument, and the special case \(\theta=\pi\) gives Euler's identity \(e^{j\pi}+1=0\). Radians and quadrant awareness underpin every step.
must: Euler's formula: \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\) for real \(\theta\), with \(\theta\) in radians
Exponential form: \(z=re^{j\theta}\), where \(r=|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\) and \(\theta=\arg z\)
Conversion procedure: find \(r\), find \(\theta\) from \(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\), check the quadrant, then write \(z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)=re^{j\theta}\)
Quadrant trap: \(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) is wrong when \(a<0\); add or subtract \(\pi\) to place \(\theta\) correctly (e.g. \(-7+j7\) has \(\theta=3\pi/4\), not \(-\pi/4\))
Worked example 1: \(5+j4=\sqrt{41}\,e^{j0.67}\) (first quadrant, \(\theta\approx0.67\) rad)
Worked example 2: \(-7+j7=7\sqrt2\,e^{j3\pi/4}\) (second quadrant, \(3\pi/4=135^\circ\))
Euler's identity: \(e^{j\pi}=\cos\pi+j\sin\pi=-1\), so \(e^{j\pi}+1=0\)
Always use radians in \(e^{j\theta}\) and in calculator mode; degrees give wrong values (e.g. \(\cos\pi=-1\) only in radian mode)
Know radian-degree conversions (\(\pi\leftrightarrow180^\circ\), \(3\pi/4\leftrightarrow135^\circ\)) and that \(j=\sqrt{-1}\) is used in engineering rather than \(i\)
conn: Argand diagram and trigonometry: the modulus and argument come from Pythagoras and inverse tangent, and the quadrant sets the correct angle
Exponential form simplifies multiplication, division, powers and roots (multiply moduli and add arguments; De Moivre's theorem)
Euler's formula links to sinusoids and phasors: \(\cos\theta=\mathrm{Re}(e^{j\theta})\), used in vibrations and AC analysis
Special angles in Euler's formula (\(\pi\), \(\pi/2\), \(2\pi\)) give values like \(e^{j\pi/2}=j\) and connect to the identity
exq: Express \(z=-3+j3\sqrt3\) in exponential form \(re^{j\theta}\), giving \(\theta\) in radians, and state the quadrant.
Write \(z=-7-j7\) in exponential form, and explain why \(\tan^{-1}(b/a)\) alone gives the wrong argument.
Using Euler's formula, show that \(e^{j\pi}+1=0\), and evaluate \(e^{j\pi/2}\) and \(e^{j3\pi/2}\).
Convert \(6e^{j5\pi/6}\) to the form \(a+jb\), giving exact values.
Given \(z_1=5+j4\) and \(z_2=-7+j7\), write both in exponential form and use this to find \(z_1z_2\) in exponential form, giving the modulus and argument.

notes.t: Exponential (polar) form of complex numbers via Euler's formula
pts: Convert a complex number z = a + jb to polar form by finding its modulus √(a²+b²) and argument θ, then write z = r e^{jθ}.
Euler's formula links the exponential to sine and cosine, so r(cos θ + j sin θ) equals r e^{jθ}.
The argument must be chosen to match the quadrant of the point; for (a) it lies in the first quadrant, for (b) in the second.
Angles can be given in radians, e.g. 3π/4 corresponds to 135°.
defs: Euler's formula
For real θ, e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ, so any complex number can be written in exponential form as r e^{jθ}, where r is the modulus and θ the argument.
Exponential form
The representation z = r e^{jθ} of a complex number, with modulus r = |z| and argument θ = arg z.
eqs: θ = argument angle (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Quadrant trap: tan⁻¹(b/a) gives the wrong argument for points with a < 0; add or subtract π to place θ in the correct quadrant.
Angle units: keep θ in radians when writing e^{jθ}; mixing degrees and radians gives wrong results.
rq: Why is the argument of −7 + j7 equal to 3π/4 rather than −π/4, even though both give the same tangent?
The point lies in the second quadrant (negative real, positive imaginary), so the principal argument is between π/2 and π; tan⁻¹ alone gives −π/4, which must be shifted by π to 3π/4.
Why is the modulus of 5 + j4 equal to √41 and not 9?
The modulus is √(a²+b²) = √(25+16) = √41; adding the components directly (5+4=9) is incorrect because the real and imaginary parts combine by Pythagoras.
What does the modulus r represent geometrically in the Argand diagram?
It is the distance from the origin to the point representing z, and θ is the angle that line makes with the positive real axis.

notes.t: Euler's identity and the constants π and e
pts: Euler's formula links the complex exponential to sine and cosine, and at θ = π it gives a famous identity relating five fundamental constants.
Substituting θ = π into e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ gives cos π = −1 and sin π = 0, so e^{jπ} = −1.
The identity e^{jπ} + 1 = 0 combines e, j, π, 1 and 0 in one equation.
eqs: Euler's identity (special case of Euler's formula at θ = π)
e = Euler's number (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless); π = circular constant (dimensionless)
Euler's formula evaluated at θ = π
tips: Angles in Euler's formula must be in radians: sin π = 0 and cos π = −1 only hold with θ = π rad, not 180 in degree mode.
Do not confuse j (engineering notation for √−1) with the index i; in mechanical engineering j is used throughout.
rq: Why does e^{jπ} equal a real number even though the exponent is imaginary?
Because Euler's formula gives e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ; at θ = π the imaginary part sin π = 0, leaving cos π = −1.
What would change if the identity used e^{jπ/2} instead of e^{jπ}?
The result would be cos(π/2) + j sin(π/2) = j, a purely imaginary number, so the identity would no longer give −1 and the +1 = 0 form would not follow.

units.name: 3.1 Recap: Argand diagram, modulus, argument and polar form
units.ov: This recap covers complex numbers z = x + jy as points on the Argand diagram, their Cartesian arithmetic and conjugates, and their modulus, argument and polar/exponential forms. Cartesian form suits addition and subtraction, while polar form makes multiplication and division simple (multiply or divide moduli, add or subtract arguments). Euler's formula ties the trigonometric and exponential forms together, and the conjugate links the two representations through \( zz^*=|z|^2 \).
must: Argand diagram: \( z=x+jy \) is the point \( (x,y) \), with real part on the horizontal axis and imaginary part on the vertical axis; equality requires real and imaginary parts to match separately
Modulus: \( |z|=r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\ge 0 \)

Argument: \( \theta=\arctan(y/x) \) only for \( x>0 \); add \( \pi \) if \( x<0,\ y\ge0 \), subtract \( \pi \) if \( x<0,\ y<0 \); \( \pm\pi/2 \) for \( x=0 \); undefined at 0. Always sketch the quadrant
Polar form \( z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta) \) and Euler's formula \( e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta \), so \( z=re^{j\theta} \)
Polar product: \( z_1z_2=r_1r_2[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)] \), i.e. moduli multiply and arguments add
Polar quotient: \( z_1/z_2=(r_1/r_2)[\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2)] \), i.e. moduli divide and arguments subtract
Cartesian product: \( z_1z_2=(x_1x_2-y_1y_2)+j(x_1y_2+x_2y_1) \), using \( j^2=-1 \)
Conjugate: \( z^*=x-jy \) (only the sign of the imaginary part changes); \( zz^*=x^2+y^2 \) is real
Division: multiply top and bottom by \( z_2^* \) to get denominator \( x_2^2+y_2^2 \) (not \( x_2+y_2 \)); the result is \( \frac{(x_1x_2+y_1y_2)+j(x_2y_1-x_1y_2)}{x_2^2+y_2^2} \)
Keep angles in radians in polar and Euler forms; addition and subtraction are component-wise in Cartesian form
conn: Converting between Cartesian and polar form needs both \( r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2} \) and the correct quadrant for \( \theta \); an error in \( \theta \) carries into every later product, quotient or power
Division can be done either by the conjugate in Cartesian form or by dividing moduli and subtracting arguments in polar form; the two answers should agree, which gives a check
Euler's formula unifies the polar product and quotient rules with the index laws \( e^{j\theta_1}e^{j\theta_2}=e^{j(\theta_1+\theta_2)} \)
The conjugate links to modulus via \( zz^*=|z|^2 \) and to the Argand diagram as a reflection in the real axis, with \( \arg z^*=-\arg z \)
exq: Given \( z_1=3-4j \) and \( z_2=-1+2j \), find \( z_1z_2 \) and \( z_1/z_2 \) in the form \( x+jy \), and plot \( z_1,z_2 \) on an Argand diagram
Find the modulus and argument (in radians, in \( (-\pi,\pi] \)) of \( -2-2j \) and of \( -\sqrt3+j \). Write each in polar and exponential form
Let \( z_1=2(\cos\frac{\pi}{3}+j\sin\frac{\pi}{3}) \) and \( z_2=4(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}+j\sin\frac{\pi}{6}) \). Find \( z_1z_2 \) and \( z_1/z_2 \) in polar form, then convert to Cartesian form
Express \( \frac{2+3j}{1-j} \) in Cartesian form, then in polar form. Verify using the polar quotient rule
Find the real numbers \( x \) and \( y \) such that \( (x+jy)(2-j)=5+5j \). Hence state \( |x+jy| \) and \( \arg(x+jy) \)

notes.t: Complex numbers: Argand diagram, arithmetic, and conjugates (recap)
pts: A complex number z = x + jy is plotted as the point P(x, y) on the Argand diagram, with x on the real axis and y on the imaginary axis.
Two complex numbers are equal only when their real parts and their imaginary parts are separately equal.
Addition and subtraction act component-wise: real parts combine with real parts, imaginary parts with imaginary parts.
Multiplication is found by expanding the brackets and using j² = −1, giving real part x₁x₂ − y₁y₂ and imaginary part x₁y₂ + x₂y₁.
Division is performed by multiplying numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator, so the denominator becomes the real number x₂² + y₂².
defs: Complex conjugate
For z = x + jy, the complex conjugate z* = x − jy is obtained by reversing the sign of the imaginary part; z z* = x² + y² is real.
Argand diagram (complex plane)
A plane on which the complex number x + jy is represented by the point with horizontal coordinate x (real axis) and vertical coordinate y (imaginary axis).
eqs: z₁, z₂ = complex numbers (dimensionless); x₁, x₂ = real parts (dimensionless); y₁, y₂ = imaginary parts (dimensionless)
z₁, z₂ = complex numbers (dimensionless); x₁, x₂ = real parts; y₁, y₂ = imaginary parts (all dimensionless)
z* = conjugate of z (dimensionless); x = real part; y = imaginary part (dimensionless)
tips: Watch the sign of the imaginary part in the conjugate: only the j-term changes sign, not the real part.
Remember j² = −1 during multiplication; forgetting it leaves a wrong real part, and in division the final denominator must be x₂² + y₂², not x₂ + y₂.
rq: Why does multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of z₂ make division easier?
It turns the denominator into the real number x₂² + y₂², so the result can be written in the form a + jb by simply separating real and imaginary parts.
What happens to the point P(x, y) on the Argand diagram when you take the complex conjugate?
It reflects across the real axis, since the imaginary part changes sign while the real part stays the same.
Why does j² appear in multiplication, and how is it handled?
Because j² = −1, the term y₁y₂ j² becomes −y₁y₂, which moves into the real part of the product.

notes.t: Recap: Modulus, Argument and Polar Form of Complex Numbers
pts: The modulus of z = x + jy is its distance from the origin, found by Pythagoras; it is always non-negative.
Writing z in polar form gives z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), so multiplying complex numbers multiplies moduli and adds arguments.
In polar form, the product z₁z₂ has modulus r₁r₂ and argument θ₁ + θ₂.
The argument θ must be chosen using the quadrant of (x, y), because arctan(y/x) alone only gives values in one range.
Euler's formula e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ links the exponential and trigonometric forms, and division divides moduli and subtracts arguments.
defs: Modulus of z
The distance of the point x + jy from the origin in the Argand diagram, |z| = r = √(x² + y²), always ≥ 0.
Argument of z
The angle θ = arg(x + jy) between the positive real axis and the line from the origin to z, measured anticlockwise, with the branch chosen by the quadrant of (x, y).
eqs: z = complex number; x = real part (dimensionless); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); r = modulus (dimensionless)

\theta = \arg(x + jy) = \begin{cases} \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) & x>0 \\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)+\pi & x<0,\ y\ge 0 \\ \arctan\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)-\pi & x<0,\ y<0 \\ +\frac{\pi}{2} & x=0,\ y>0 \\ -\frac{\pi}{2} & x=0,\ y<0 \\ \text{undefined} & x=0,\ y=0 \end{cases}
θ = argument (rad); x, y = real and imaginary parts (dimensionless)
Polar form of a complex number
z = complex number; r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad)
Product of two complex numbers in polar form
r₁, r₂ = moduli (dimensionless); θ₁, θ₂ = arguments (rad)
Quotient of two complex numbers in polar form
r₁, r₂ = moduli (dimensionless); θ₁, θ₂ = arguments (rad)
tips: Do not use arctan(y/x) directly without checking the quadrant; add or subtract π when x < 0 to get the correct argument.
Angles are in radians in these formulas; keep θ in radians when using the polar product and quotient rules, and handle the x = 0 cases with ±π/2 separately.
rq: Why must the argument be chosen by checking the quadrant of (x, y) rather than just computing arctan(y/x)?
arctan(y/x) returns values only in (−π/2, π/2), so it cannot distinguish points that differ by π, such as (1, 1) and (−1, −1), which have the same ratio y/x but opposite positions.
What would happen to the modulus and argument of z₁z₂ if you instead divided the moduli and added the arguments?

You would get the modulus of the quotient z₁/z₂ and the argument of z₁/z₂ wrongly combined; the correct rule is that products multiply moduli and add arguments, and quotients divide moduli and subtract arguments.
Why does the formula z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) combined with Euler's formula make multiplication so simple?
Since z = re^{jθ}, the product of exponentials adds exponents: r₁e^{jθ₁} · r₂e^{jθ₂} = r₁r₂e^{j(θ₁+θ₂)}, so the angles simply add.

units.name: 3.2 Euler's formula and circular–hyperbolic function relationships
units.ov: Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\) lets cos and sin be written as complex exponentials. Substituting an imaginary argument (\(\theta\to jx\)) into these forms gives the hyperbolic functions cosh, sinh and tanh, which are defined directly from \(e^{x}\) and \(e^{-x}\). Circular and hyperbolic functions are therefore one family, linked by \(x\to jx\), and their identities differ mainly by sign changes.
must: Euler's formula: \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\), and so \(e^{-j\theta}=\cos\theta-j\sin\theta\)
\(\cos\theta=\dfrac{e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta}}{2}\) and \(\sin\theta=\dfrac{e^{j\theta}-e^{-j\theta}}{2j}\) (do not drop the \(j\) in the sine denominator)
Definitions: \(\cosh x=\dfrac{e^{x}+e^{-x}}{2}\), \(\sinh x=\dfrac{e^{x}-e^{-x}}{2}\), \(\tanh x=\dfrac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}\)
Circular of imaginary argument: \(\cos jx=\cosh x\), \(\sin jx=j\sinh x\), \(\tan jx=j\tanh x\)
Hyperbolic of imaginary argument: \(\cosh jx=\cos x\), \(\sinh jx=j\sin x\), \(\tanh jx=j\tan x\). Only the cos/cosh results are free of \(j\)
Hyperbolic identity: \(\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1\) (minus sign), compared with \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\)

Hyperbolic addition formulas: \(\sinh(x\pm y)=\sinh x\cosh y\pm\cosh x\sinh y\) and \(\cosh(x\pm y)=\cosh x\cosh y\pm\sinh x\sinh y\). The cosh formula keeps the same sign as the left side, unlike circular \(\cos(x\pm y)\), which has \(\mp\)
Parity: cos and cosh are even, sin and sinh are odd. \(\cosh 0=1\), \(\sinh 0=0\), and \(\cosh x\ge1\) (catenary shape)
Method: to evaluate \(\sin\) or \(\cos\) of a complex \(z=a+jb\), use the exponential definitions or the addition formulas together with \(\cos jb=\cosh b\) and \(\sin jb=j\sinh b\)
Do not confuse \(\cos jx=\cosh x\) with \(\cosh jx=\cos x\). Both are true, but check which function you start with. Angles must be in radians
conn: Osborn's rule: any circular identity converts to the hyperbolic one by \(x\to jx\). Since \(\sin^2 jx=-\sinh^2x\), \(\cos^2+\sin^2=1\) becomes \(\cosh^2-\sinh^2=1\), so a hyperbolic product of sinh terms flips sign relative to the circular one

Euler's formula and the exponential forms of cos/sin are used to prove trig identities, to find powers like \(\cos^3\theta\) as sums of multiple angles, and to get the real and imaginary parts of complex expressions
Complex \(\sin(a+jb)\) and \(\cos(a+jb)\) combine the circular addition formulas with \(x\to jx\) to give real and imaginary parts, such as \(\sin(a+jb)=\sin a\cosh b+j\cos a\sinh b\)
Solving equations such as \(\cos z=2\) needs the exponential definitions, a quadratic in \(e^{jz}\), and logarithms of complex numbers
exq: Starting from Euler's formula, derive \(\cos\theta=(e^{j\theta}+e^{-j\theta})/2\) and \(\sin\theta=(e^{j\theta}-e^{-j\theta})/(2j)\), then use them to prove \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\)
Show from the exponential definitions that \(\cosh^2x-\sinh^2x=1\) and \(\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y\)
Show that \(\cos(jx)=\cosh x\) and \(\sin(jx)=j\sinh x\). Hence express \(\sin(2+3j)\) in the form \(a+jb\), giving a and b to 3 d.p.
Use the exponential forms to express \(\sin^3\theta\) in terms of \(\sin\theta\) and \(\sin3\theta\)
Find all complex z satisfying \(\cos z=2\), by writing cos in exponential form, solving the quadratic in \(e^{jz}\), and taking logarithms

notes.t: Relationship between circular and hyperbolic functions (Euler's formula)
pts: Euler's formula links the exponential of an imaginary angle to cosine and sine, so cosine and sine can be written in terms of complex exponentials.
Adding e^{jθ} and e^{-jθ} cancels the imaginary parts, leaving twice the cosine; subtracting them leaves twice j times the sine.
Cosine is an even function and sine is an odd function, which follows from the symmetry of the exponential form.
This exponential form is the route to defining sin(z) and cos(z) for complex numbers z, not just real angles.
defs: Euler's formula
e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ, which relates the complex exponential to circular functions for real θ.
eqs: Cosine in terms of complex exponentials
Sine in terms of complex exponentials
tips: Do not forget the 2j in the denominator of the sine formula; using 2 instead of 2j gives the wrong result.
Euler's formula is stated for real θ here; extending to complex z requires the same exponential definitions, not a simple substitution of degrees.
rq: Why does adding e^{jθ} and e^{-jθ} give the cosine but not the sine?
The imaginary parts j sin θ and −j sin θ cancel on addition, leaving only 2 cos θ; subtraction cancels the real cos θ parts instead, leaving 2j sin θ.
Why must sin(−θ) equal −sin θ when cos(−θ) equals cos θ?
Replacing θ by −θ swaps e^{jθ} and e^{-jθ} in Euler's formula, which leaves the sum unchanged (even cosine) and flips the sign of the difference (odd sine).

notes.t: Relationship between circular and hyperbolic functions
pts: Euler's formula links circular functions of real angles to exponentials, which is the basis for evaluating sin and cos of complex numbers.
Substituting θ → jθ into the exponential forms of cos and sin turns circular functions into hyperbolic functions.
Setting θ → jθ gives cos(jθ) = cosh θ, so cosine of an imaginary angle is a real hyperbolic function.
Setting θ → jθ gives sin(jθ) = j sinh θ, so the sine of an imaginary angle is purely imaginary.
Dividing gives tan(jθ) = j tanh θ, and replacing θ by x gives the standard identities for real x.
defs: Hyperbolic functions
Functions defined from exponentials: cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2, sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, tanh x = sinh x / cosh x.
eqs: Cosine in terms of complex exponentials (Euler form)
Sine in terms of complex exponentials (Euler form)
θ = real argument (dimensionless); cosh θ = hyperbolic cosine (dimensionless)
θ = real argument (dimensionless); sinh θ = hyperbolic sine (dimensionless)
x = real argument (dimensionless); tanh x = hyperbolic tangent (dimensionless)
tips: Watch the factor j: sin(jx) = j sinh x, not sinh x; forgetting j is a common error when converting between circular and hyperbolic results.
Do not confuse cos(jx) = cosh x with cosh(jx) = cos x; the substitution direction matters and the formulas are only valid for the stated forms.
rq: Why does replacing θ with jθ turn cos into cosh but sin into j·sinh?

Because (jθ)·j = −θ inside the exponent gives e^{−θ} and e^{θ}; cos is symmetric in the exponent signs so it gives a real sum over 2, while sin is antisymmetric and picks up the factor 1/(2j), producing j·sinh θ.
How could you use cos(jx) = cosh x to evaluate cos(z) for a complex z = a + jb?
Use the addition formula cos(a+jb) = cos a cos(jb) − sin a sin(jb), then substitute cos(jb) = cosh b and sin(jb) = j sinh b, giving cos a cosh b − j sin a sinh b.
What happens to the sign of sin(jx)'s imaginary part if x is negative?
sinh is an odd function, so sinh(−x) = −sinh x and sin(j(−x)) = −j sinh x; the result stays purely imaginary but changes sign.

notes.t: Relationship between circular and hyperbolic functions
pts: Hyperbolic functions are defined in terms of exponentials, giving cosh x as the average of eˣ and e⁻ˣ and sinh x as their half-difference.
cosh x is an even function with minimum value 1 at x = 0, and sinh x is an odd function passing through the origin.
The hyperbolic identity cosh²x − sinh²x = 1 parallels the circular identity cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, but with a minus sign.
Addition formulas for hyperbolic functions have the same structure as those for circular functions, with the sign pattern of the sinh product changing in the cosh formula.
defs: Hyperbolic cosine
cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2, an even function with cosh 0 = 1 and graph a catenary-shaped curve.
Hyperbolic sine
sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, an odd function with sinh 0 = 0.
eqs: x = real argument (dimensionless); cosh x = hyperbolic cosine (dimensionless)
x = real argument (dimensionless); sinh x = hyperbolic sine (dimensionless)
tips: Watch the sign: cosh²x − sinh²x = 1 (minus), not cosh²x + sinh²x = 1.
Do not confuse the addition formulas: the sinh(x ± y) expansion has no minus sign on the product term when the operator is +, while cosh(x ± y) keeps the ± sign on sinh x sinh y.
rq: Why does cosh²x − sinh²x = 1 hold, and how does this differ from the circular identity?

Substituting the exponential definitions gives ((eˣ+e⁻ˣ)² − (eˣ−e⁻ˣ)²)/4 = 4/4 = 1; the circular version is cos²θ + sin²θ = 1, so the hyperbolic one has a minus sign, tracing a hyperbola rather than a circle.
What happens to the sign in the cosh addition formula compared with the sinh one, and why?
In cosh(x ± y) the product sinh x sinh y carries the ± sign, while sinh(x ± y) has cosh x sinh y with the ± sign, because sinh is odd and cosh is even.

notes.t: Circular and hyperbolic functions via x → jx
pts: Replacing x by jx in the exponential definitions of cosh and sinh converts them into circular (trigonometric) functions, since e^{jx} = cos x + j sin x.
Hyperbolic functions of an imaginary argument reduce to ordinary cos and sin, so cosh jx is a real-valued cosine.
Circular functions of an imaginary argument become hyperbolic functions, with a factor j appearing for sin and tan.
The relationships are reversible: the same substitution x → jx links each circular function with its hyperbolic counterpart.
defs: Hyperbolic cosine
cosh x = (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2, the even part of eˣ.
Hyperbolic sine
sinh x = (eˣ − e⁻ˣ)/2, the odd part of eˣ.
eqs: x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit; cosh = hyperbolic cosine (dimensionless)
x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit; sinh = hyperbolic sine (dimensionless)
x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit; tanh = hyperbolic tangent (dimensionless)
x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit; cos = circular cosine (dimensionless)
x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit; sin = circular sine (dimensionless)
x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit; tan = circular tangent (dimensionless)
tips: Do not forget the factor j: sin jx = j sinh x and sinh jx = j sin x, whereas cos jx and cosh jx carry no j.
Check which functions carry the j: the cosine-type results are real, while sine- and tangent-type results need j.
rq: Why does cosh jx come out as a real cosine while sinh jx picks up a factor of j?
cosh is the even combination (eˣ + e⁻ˣ)/2, and substituting jx gives (e^{jx} + e^{−jx})/2 = cos x, which is real; sinh is the odd combination, giving (e^{jx} − e^{−jx})/2 = j sin x.
If you know sin jx = j sinh x, how would you find sinh x for real x?
Divide both sides by j: sinh x = sin(jx)/j, or equivalently rearrange the identity directly.

units.name: 3.3 Circular and hyperbolic functions of complex arguments
units.ov: This module extends sine, cosine and their hyperbolic counterparts to complex arguments z = x + jy. It uses the addition formulae together with the imaginary-argument conversions (cos jy = cosh y, sin jy = j sinh y, cosh jx = cos x, sinh jx = j sin x) to split each function into real and imaginary parts built from real trig and hyperbolic functions. Circular and hyperbolic functions are thus two faces of one family, and the conversions let you evaluate them numerically as a + jb.
must: \(\sin(x+jy)=\sin x\cosh y + j\cos x\sinh y\): derive it from the addition formula and state it from memory
\(\sinh(x+jy)=\sinh x\cos y + j\cosh x\sin y\): the hyperbolic counterpart, derived the same way
Imaginary-argument conversions: \(\cos jy=\cosh y\), \(\sin jy=j\sinh y\)
The reverse conversions: \(\cosh jx=\cos x\), \(\sinh jx=j\sin x\)
Do not confuse \(\sin jy=j\sinh y\) with \(\sinh jy=j\sin y\); the j stays in both, and the function type swaps
Method for numerical questions: expand with the addition formula, convert the imaginary-argument terms, evaluate each real term separately, then write the answer as \(a+jb\)
Use radians for x in the trig terms; the hyperbolic terms take y as a plain number
Hyperbolic addition formula: \(\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y\)
\(\sin z\) is unbounded for complex z (\(|\sin z|\) can exceed 1 when \(y\neq0\)), unlike real sine
Under \(w=\sin z\) a rectangular grid maps to a curvilinear grid: lines of constant x and constant y become hyperbolas and ellipses
conn: Addition formulae plus imaginary-argument identities: every derivation uses both, and they produce the real/imaginary split
Real and imaginary parts feed into modulus and argument, so a question may ask for \(|\sin z|\) or the polar form of \(\sinh z\)
Euler's formula and the exponential definitions of sinh and cosh underpin the conversions and let you check results
Solving equations such as \(\sin z = w\) means equating real and imaginary parts, which uses the hyperbolic identities and the unboundedness of sin z
exq: Express \(\sinh(5+j4)\) in the form \(a+jb\), giving a and b to 3 decimal places (use radians).
Derive \(\sin(x+jy)=\sin x\cosh y+j\cos x\sinh y\) from the sine addition formula and the identities for \(\cos jy\) and \(\sin jy\).
Find \(\sin(2+j3)\) in Cartesian form and hence its modulus. Explain why a modulus greater than 1 is possible.
Show that \(\sinh(x+jy)=\sinh x\cos y+j\cosh x\sin y\), and find all real x, y for which \(\sinh z\) is purely imaginary.
Describe the image under \(w=\sin z\) of the lines \(x=\pi/4\) and \(y=1\), writing u and v in terms of x and y.

notes.t: Circular functions of complex numbers: sin z
pts: Write z = x + jy and apply the sine addition formula to split sin z into real-variable trigonometric and hyperbolic parts.
Use cos(jy) = cosh y and sin(jy) = j sinh y to convert imaginary-argument terms into hyperbolic functions.
The result separates into real and imaginary parts: sin x cosh y is real and cos x sinh y is multiplied by j.
The mapping of a rectangular grid in the z-plane under sin z produces a curvilinear grid, illustrating how complex functions transform regions.
eqs: Sine of a complex number z = x + jy expressed in real and imaginary parts
\sin z = \sin x\cosh y + j\sinh y\cos x
z = complex variable (dimensionless); x = real part (rad); y = imaginary part (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
Sine addition formula used in the derivation
Hyperbolic conversion of cosine with imaginary argument
Hyperbolic conversion of sine with imaginary argument
tips: Do not confuse cos(jy) = cosh y with cos(y) = cosh y; the imaginary unit j must be carried through, giving sin(jy) = j sinh y.
Sin z is not bounded for complex z, unlike sin x for real x; the modulus can exceed 1 when y ≠ 0.
rq: Why does sin z have a hyperbolic function of y in its real part, while the trigonometric function of x stays in the real part too?
Because sin(x+jy) expands into sin x cos(jy) + sin(jy) cos x, and cos(jy) = cosh y is real, so sin x cosh y is real; the imaginary-argument sine gives j sinh y.
What happens to the modulus of sin z as y grows large, and why does this differ from sin x for real x?
|sin z| grows like cosh y / 2 for large |y|, since cosh y is unbounded, whereas |sin x| ≤ 1 for real x.

notes.t: Circular and hyperbolic functions of complex numbers
pts: The sine of a complex number x + jy splits into a real part using cosh y and an imaginary part using sinh y.
The hyperbolic sine of a sum expands like the trigonometric identity, using sinh and cosh of each part.
Hyperbolic functions of an imaginary argument convert to circular functions: sinh jx gives j sin x and cosh jx gives cos x.
Use these conversions to rewrite sinh(5 + j4) as real and imaginary parts, then evaluate numerically.
Numerical results are found by evaluating each real trig and hyperbolic term separately before combining real and imaginary parts.
defs: Complex sine
For z = x + jy, sin z = sin x cosh y + j sinh y cos x, which is a complex number with real part sin x cosh y and imaginary part sinh y cos x.
Complex hyperbolic sine
For z = x + jy, sinh z = sinh x cos y + j cosh x sin y, obtained by expanding sinh(x + jy) with the addition formula and sinh jx = j sin x, cosh jx = cos x.
eqs: x = real part of the angle (rad); y = imaginary part of the angle (rad, dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
x, y = arguments (dimensionless); sinh, cosh = hyperbolic functions
x = real argument (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Do not confuse sin(jy) with sinh(jy); sin(jy) = j sinh y, while sinh(jy) = j sin y.
Check that cosh and sinh are evaluated with radians, and that the final answer is written as a + jb with both parts numerical.
rq: Why does sin(x + jy) have cosh y in the real part rather than cos y?
Because sin(jy) = j sinh y and cos(jy) = cosh y; the real part comes from cos(jy) = cosh y multiplying sin x.
Why is sinh(j4) equal to j sin 4 and not sin 4?
Since sinh(jx) = j sin x, the factor j is carried through from the definition of the hyperbolic sine of an imaginary argument.
What if you used the sinh addition formula but forgot to convert sinh(j4) and cosh(j4)?
You would leave complex-argument hyperbolic terms unevaluated, so the result would not be in the form a + jb with real a and b.

units.name: 3.4 Logarithm of a complex number
units.ov: This material defines the logarithm of a complex number by writing z in polar/exponential form, \(z=|z|e^{j\theta}\), so that \(\ln z=\ln|z|+j\theta\). Because the argument is only defined modulo \(2\pi\), the logarithm is multivalued; the general solution adds \(2n\pi\) to the argument, and the principal value restricts \(\theta\) to \(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\). The key skills are finding \(|z|\) and the correct-quadrant argument from \(x+jy\), then assembling the real and imaginary parts.
must: Principal value: \(\ln z=\ln|z|+j\theta\), with real part \(\ln|z|\) and imaginary part the principal argument \(\theta\).
Principal argument range is \(-\pi<\arg z\le\pi\); always give the principal value in this interval.

General solution: \(\ln z=\ln|z|+j(\theta+2n\pi)\), with n any integer (positive, negative or zero), not just \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) as the notes write it. Only the imaginary part changes between branches.
Modulus: \(|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\), so the real part of \(\ln z\) is \(\tfrac12\ln(x^2+y^2)\); e.g. \(\ln(5+j4)\) has real part \(\ln\sqrt{41}\), not \(\ln 5\).
Argument needs quadrant care: \(\arctan(y/x)\) alone is wrong for \(x<0\); add or subtract \(\pi\) so that \(\theta\) lies in the correct quadrant and in the principal range.
Euler's formula \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\) links polar form \(|z|(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)\) and exponential form \(|z|e^{j\theta}\).
\(\ln 0\) is undefined because arg 0 is undefined; ln z exists only for \(z\ne0\).
Worked example: \(\ln(5+j4)=\ln\sqrt{41}+j(0.67+2n\pi)\), principal value \(\approx1.61+0.67j\) (angle in radians).
Work in radians and check the answer by exponentiating: \(e^{\ln z}=z\) for every branch.
conn: Cartesian to polar conversion (modulus, arctan with quadrant correction) feeds straight into the log formula, so errors in \(\theta\) propagate to the imaginary part.
Euler's formula explains why the \(2\pi\) periodicity of \(e^{j\theta}\) makes the logarithm multivalued.
Solving equations like \(e^{w}=z\) or \(\ln z=a+jb\) needs the general solution, then the principal value is picked from it.
Complex powers \(z^w=e^{w\ln z}\) and logs of negative real numbers, e.g. \(\ln(-1)=j\pi\), reuse the same branch ideas.
exq: Find the principal value of \(\ln(-3+j3)\) and state its modulus and argument in the form a + jb.
Find all values of \(\ln(5+j4)\), then state the principal value to 2 decimal places.
Evaluate \(\ln(-2)\), \(\ln(j)\) and \(\ln(-j)\), giving general solutions and principal values.
Solve \(e^{w}=1-j\sqrt3\) for all complex w, and identify the value with imaginary part in \((-\pi,\pi]\).
Explain why \(\ln z\) is multivalued and why the principal argument of \(z=-4-j4\) is \(-3\pi/4\) rather than \(\pi/4\) from \(\arctan(y/x)\).

notes.t: Logarithm of a complex number
pts: Write a complex number in polar form z = |z|e^{jθ}; the modulus is the distance from the origin and θ is the argument.
The principal value of ln z combines the real log of the modulus with the argument: the real part is ln|z| and the imaginary part is θ.
The argument θ is only defined modulo 2π, so the principal value is taken with θ in a fixed range (e.g. −π < θ ≤ π).
Adding 2πk to θ (k an integer) gives the same z, so ln z has infinitely many values differing by 2πjk.
The quadrant of z determines θ; arctan(y/x) alone is insufficient and must be adjusted by π for x < 0.
defs: Modulus |z|
The magnitude of z = x + jy, given by √(x² + y²), the distance of the point from the origin in the Argand diagram.
Argument θ = arg(x + jy)
The angle the vector from the origin to z makes with the positive real axis, found using arctan(y/x) with quadrant corrections.
Principal value of ln z
The single value of the complex logarithm obtained by using the principal argument θ, giving ln z = ln|z| + jθ.
eqs: Polar form of a complex number
z = complex number; |z| = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); j = imaginary unit
Principal logarithm of a complex number
ln z = complex logarithm (dimensionless); |z| = modulus; θ = principal argument (rad)
x = real part; y = imaginary part; |z| = modulus (same unit as x, y)
tips: Watch the quadrant when finding θ: arctan(y/x) gives the wrong argument when x < 0; apply the ±π correction.
Undefined: arg is undefined at z = 0 (x = 0, y = 0), so ln z cannot be evaluated there.
rq: Why does e^{jπ} = e^{j(π±2π)} both equal −1, and what does this imply for ln z?
Cosine and sine are periodic with period 2π, so θ can differ by 2πk without changing z; hence ln z is multivalued, with the principal value chosen by restricting θ to one period.
Why can't you find θ for z = x + jy with x < 0 just by computing arctan(y/x)?
arctan returns values only in (−π/2, π/2), so for x < 0 the point lies in the left half-plane and π must be added or subtracted depending on the sign of y.

notes.t: Complex logarithm: general and principal value solutions
pts: The complex logarithm is multivalued: each non-zero z has infinitely many logarithms, differing by multiples of 2πj.
The general solution adds 2nπ to the argument θ for every integer n, giving all branches of ln z.
The principal value is obtained by restricting the argument to a single interval, so ln z is single-valued.
Principal value uses arg z in the range −π < arg z ≤ π, so the imaginary part lies in that interval.
The real part ln|z| is the same for every branch; only the imaginary part changes between branches.
defs: Multivalued function
A function that assigns more than one output to a single input; for the complex logarithm, every non-zero z has infinitely many values of ln z.
Principal value of ln z
The single branch of the complex logarithm obtained by taking the argument in the interval −π < arg z ≤ π.
Principal argument
The value of arg z restricted to −π < arg z ≤ π, used to define the principal logarithm.
eqs: General solution (all branches) of the complex logarithm
z = complex number (dimensionless); |z| = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer branch index (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Principal value of the complex logarithm
z = complex number (dimensionless); |z| = modulus of z (dimensionless); arg z = principal argument of z (rad); j = imaginary unit
tips: Do not forget the 2nπ term when asked for all values of ln z; quoting only the principal value gives an incomplete answer.
Take the principal argument within −π < arg z ≤ π when asked for the principal value, not any angle that happens to represent z.
rq: Why does ln z have infinitely many values, while ln x for real x > 0 has only one?
Because z = |z|e^{j(θ+2nπ)} for every integer n, so the same point z is reached by adding any multiple of 2π to the argument; for real positive x the argument is fixed at 0, so only one value arises.
What would change if the principal range were 0 ≤ arg z < 2π instead of −π < arg z ≤ π?

The principal value would still be single-valued, but it would differ from the original branch for points with negative real part (the branch cut would move from the negative real axis to the positive real axis).
Why does the real part of ln z not depend on the branch chosen?
Because ln|z| depends only on the modulus, and adding 2nπ j changes only the imaginary part of the logarithm.

notes.t: Logarithm of a complex number: ln z in Cartesian form
pts: The modulus of ln z is ln|z|, and the argument θ of z gives the imaginary part.
Convert z = x + jy to polar/exponential form to find |z| and θ before applying the log formula.
The principal value uses the principal argument of z, giving a single answer.
The general solution adds multiples of 2π to the argument, since the argument of z is not unique.
defs: Principal value of ln z
The logarithm of z using the principal argument θ (usually −π < θ ≤ π), giving a single value.
Polar form of a complex number
z = |z|(cos θ + j sin θ), where |z| is the modulus and θ the argument.
Exponential form of a complex number
z = |z| e^{jθ}, equivalent to the polar form via Euler's formula.
eqs: Logarithm of a complex number in terms of modulus and argument
z = complex number (dimensionless); |z| = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); j = imaginary unit
General value of ln(5 + j4) in Cartesian form
n = non-negative integer (dimensionless); 0.67 = principal argument of 5 + j4 (rad)
tips: Forgetting the 2nπ shifts in the general solution: the argument is multi-valued, so include ±2nπ with n ∈ ℕ.
Using the real part of z directly as the modulus: |z| = √(x² + y²), so the real part of ln z is ln√41 = ½ ln 41, not ln 5.
rq: Why does ln z have infinitely many values, while ln of a positive real number has only one?

Because the argument of z is defined only up to multiples of 2π, so θ can be shifted by ±2nπ, each giving a different value of ln z. A positive real number has argument 0 (principal), so its log is unique.
To find ln(5 + j4), why must you first find |z| and θ rather than directly taking ln of the real and imaginary parts?
Because ln is not applied componentwise to x + jy; the log of a complex number is defined via ln|z| + jθ, which requires the modulus and argument.

units.name: 3.5 Powers of complex numbers and De Moivre's theorem
units.ov: This material covers De Moivre's theorem: for \(z=r(\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)=re^{j\theta}\) and integer \(n\), \(z^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta)=r^ne^{jn\theta}\). It extends the polar multiplication rule (multiply moduli, add arguments) to repeated multiplication. The workflow is to convert to polar form, apply the power, then convert back to Cartesian form if needed.
must: De Moivre's theorem: \(z^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+j\sin n\theta)\) for integer \(n\)
Exponential form: \(z=re^{j\theta}\), so \(z^n=r^ne^{jn\theta}\), using \(e^{j\theta}=\cos\theta+j\sin\theta\)
The modulus is raised to the power \(n\) (\(r^n\)) and the argument is multiplied by \(n\) (\(n\theta\)). The common errors are \(nr\) and \(\theta^n\)
Polar product rule: \(z_1z_2=r_1r_2[\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)+j\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)]\). Squaring squares the modulus and doubles the angle
Find \(r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and \(\theta\) with the correct quadrant. For \(-3-j\) (third quadrant), \(\theta=-\pi+\arctan(1/3)\approx-2.82\) rad, not \(\arctan(1/3)\)
Keep angles in one unit (radians, with the calculator in rad mode) for \(n\theta\) and for evaluating cos and sin
Reduce \(n\theta\) to the principal range (\(-\pi<\theta\le\pi\)) by adding or subtracting \(2\pi k\) when asked. For example \(-8.46+2\pi\approx-2.18\)
Worked example: \((-3-j)^3\) has modulus \(10^{3/2}\approx31.62\) and angle \(\approx-8.46\) rad. Converting back gives \(-18-26j\) exactly
Check by direct expansion: \((-3-j)^2=8+6j\), and \((8+6j)(-3-j)=-18-26j\). The notes' \(-18.01-25.99j\) is only rounding error, so give exact integers where possible
conn: Cartesian ↔ polar conversion, including quadrant choice for the argument, is the first step of every De Moivre question, and an error there carries through to the final answer
Euler's formula links the polar and exponential forms, so \(z^n\) can be done with \(e^{jn\theta}\) and then converted back to Cartesian form

The product rule for polar forms generalises to powers. Together with division, it also gives trig identities such as \(\cos 3\theta\) and \(\sin 3\theta\) by equating real and imaginary parts of \((\cos\theta+j\sin\theta)^3\)
Powers in polar form lead to roots of complex numbers (fractional \(n\)), which have \(n\) values spaced by \(2\pi/n\) on a circle in the Argand diagram, and to rotating phasors in engineering
exq: Express \(z=-3-j\) in polar form and use De Moivre's theorem to find \(z^3\) in Cartesian form. Verify by direct expansion.
Given \(z=1+j\sqrt3\), find \(z^6\) and \(z^{-2}\), giving answers in both polar and Cartesian form.
Use De Moivre's theorem with \(n=3\) to derive expressions for \(\cos3\theta\) and \(\sin3\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\) and \(\sin\theta\).
Write \(z_1=2e^{j\pi/6}\) and \(z_2=\sqrt2\,e^{-j\pi/4}\) in Cartesian form. Find \(z_1^4z_2^3\) and give its modulus and principal argument.
Find \((\sqrt3-j)^{5}\), reducing the argument to the principal range. Explain why using \(\theta^5\) or \(5r\) would be wrong.

notes.t: Powers of complex numbers: De Moivre's theorem
pts: De Moivre's theorem gives the nth power of a complex number written in polar form by raising the modulus to n and multiplying the argument by n.
In polar form a complex number z with modulus r and argument θ is written as r(cos θ + j sin θ), so its nth power keeps the same angle structure with nθ.
Using exponential form z = re^{jθ}, raising to the power n simply multiplies the modulus by r^n and the exponent by n, giving z^n = r^n e^{j(nθ)}.
The two forms are equivalent because e^{jθ} = cos θ + j sin θ, so the polar and exponential results agree.
defs: De Moivre's theorem
For a complex number z = r(cos θ + j sin θ) and integer n, z^n = r^n(cos nθ + j sin nθ).
eqs: De Moivre's theorem in polar form (nth power of a complex number)
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
Exponential form of a complex number
z = complex number; r = modulus (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); j = imaginary unit
z = complex number; r = modulus; θ = argument (rad); n = integer power
tips: The formula applies with θ in radians when using the exponential form; mixing degrees and radians gives wrong angles.
Remember the modulus is raised to the power n (r^n), not multiplied by n; the argument is multiplied by n, not raised to n.
rq: Why does raising z to the power n multiply the argument by n rather than adding n to it?
Because z^n = r^n e^{jθ} multiplied n times, and exponents add when bases are multiplied: e^{jθ}·e^{jθ}… gives e^{jnθ}, so the angle accumulates as nθ.
What happens to the modulus when you raise a complex number to a power n?
It becomes r^n, since each multiplication multiplies the moduli together.

notes.t: Powers of complex numbers in polar form (De Moivre's theorem)
pts: Squaring a complex number in polar form squares the modulus and doubles the argument.
Multiplying complex numbers in polar form multiplies their moduli and adds their arguments.
Raising z to the power n gives modulus rⁿ and argument nθ, which generalises the squaring result to any integer n.
defs: Polar form of a complex number
z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), where r = |z| is the modulus and θ is the argument of z.
eqs: Product of two complex numbers in polar form
r₁, r₂ = moduli (dimensionless); θ₁, θ₂ = arguments (rad); j = imaginary unit
Power of a complex number (De Moivre's theorem)
z = complex number; r = |z| (dimensionless); θ = argument (rad); n = integer exponent
tips: Raise the modulus to the power n (rⁿ), not multiply it by n; only the argument is multiplied by n.
Make sure θ is in the correct units and range (radians or degrees consistently) before applying nθ, and reduce the final angle to the principal range if required.
rq: Why does squaring z double the argument rather than the modulus?
Squaring means multiplying z by itself; in polar form the moduli multiply (r·r = r²) and the arguments add (θ+θ = 2θ), so the modulus is squared and the angle is doubled.
What happens to |z|ⁿ if |z| = 1 and n is large?
Since |z|ⁿ = 1ⁿ = 1, the modulus stays 1 for every power; only the argument changes, giving nθ.

notes.t: Powers of complex numbers (De Moivre's theorem)
pts: Write the complex number in modulus-argument (polar) form before raising it to a power.
The modulus of z = -3 - j is √10, so the modulus of z³ is (√10)³ = 10^{3/2} ≈ 31.62.
Raising to the power n multiplies the argument by n, so the angle becomes 3 × (-2.82) ≈ -8.46 rad.
Convert the polar result back to Cartesian form by evaluating cos and sin of the new angle and multiplying by the modulus.
The final answer is the Cartesian form obtained by expanding the bracket: real part -18.01 and imaginary part -25.99.
defs: Modulus-argument (polar) form
A complex number written as z = r(cos θ + j sin θ), where r = |z| is the modulus and θ is the argument.
eqs: De Moivre's theorem: power of a complex number in polar form
z = complex number (dimensionless); r = modulus of z (dimensionless); θ = argument of z (rad); n = integer power (dimensionless); j = imaginary unit
tips: Do not raise the argument to the power n; multiply it by n. Raising θ to the power n is a common error.
Angles from calculators may be in radians or degrees; the power rule and the cos/sin evaluation must use the same unit (here radians).
rq: Why must the complex number be converted to polar form before applying the power rule, rather than multiplying out directly?
Because in polar form the power rule reduces to raising the modulus to n and multiplying the argument by n, which avoids repeated expansion of (a + jb)ⁿ and handles large or fractional powers easily.
If the argument of z is -2.82 rad, why is the argument of z³ not simply -2.82 cubed?
The argument is multiplied by n (here 3), not raised to the power n, so the new argument is 3 × (-2.82) ≈ -8.46 rad.

units.name: 3.6 nth roots of complex numbers
units.ov: This material finds all n nth roots of a nonzero complex number, using the cube roots of \(j\) as the worked example. Two methods are shown. The algebraic one factorises \(w^n - z = 0\) after spotting one root. The geometric one uses polar form, where the roots lie on a circle and are equally spaced in argument. The two methods give the same roots, so each can check the other.
must: An nth root of \(z\) is any \(w\) with \(w^n = z\); a nonzero \(z\) has exactly \(n\) distinct roots, so a single root is an incomplete answer.
Polar formula: if \(z = re^{j\theta}\) then \(w_k = r^{1/n} e^{j(\theta+2k\pi)/n}\), \(k=0,\dots,n-1\).
The roots all have modulus \(r^{1/n}\) and are spaced \(2\pi/n\) apart in argument, forming a regular n-gon on a circle centred at the origin.
Cube roots of \(j\): \(j=e^{j\pi/2}\), so the roots have modulus 1 and arguments \(-\pi/2,\ \pi/6,\ 5\pi/6\).
Rectangular forms of the cube roots of \(j\): \(-j\), \(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\tfrac{j}{2}\), \(-\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}+\tfrac{j}{2}\).
Algebraic method: spot a root (here \(w=-j\)), factor \(w^3-j=(w+j)(w^2-jw-1)\), then solve the quadratic with the quadratic formula.
The quadratic factor gives \(w=\dfrac{j\pm\sqrt{(-j)^2+4}}{2}=\dfrac{j\pm\sqrt3}{2}\); the discriminant is \(-1+4=3\) because \((-j)^2=-1\).
Quote arguments in the principal range \((-\pi,\pi]\), and add the angle step before reducing (\(3\pi/2\equiv-\pi/2\)).
The cube roots of \(j\) are the cube roots of 1 rotated by \(\pi/6\); do not confuse the two sets.
Check answers by cubing a root, or by confirming that the roots sum to zero and each has the right modulus.
conn: Polar/exponential form links to the algebraic factorisation: a root found by inspection (e.g. \(-j\)) gives \(w_1\), and multiplying by \(e^{j2\pi/3}\) generates the others, which must match the quadratic's roots.
Modulus and argument (Argand diagram) link to de Moivre's theorem: taking an nth root divides the argument by \(n\) and takes the nth root of the modulus, with \(2k\pi\) added to give all branches.
Converting between polar and rectangular form (\(\cos\pi/6=\sqrt3/2\), \(\sin\pi/6=1/2\)) is needed to give exact answers.
Solving \(w^n=z\) is a polynomial-root problem, so the complex quadratic formula and the fact that a degree-\(n\) polynomial has \(n\) roots both apply.
exq: Find all cube roots of \(j\) in both polar and rectangular form, and sketch them on an Argand diagram.
Show that \(w=-j\) is a root of \(w^3-j=0\), factorise the cubic as \((w+j)(w^2-jw-1)\), and solve the quadratic to find the other two roots.
Find all fourth roots of \(-16\) in the form \(a+jb\), and state their moduli and principal arguments.
Find the cube roots of \(-8j\) and show that their sum is zero.
Explain why the cube roots of \(j\) are the cube roots of unity rotated by \(\pi/6\), and use this to write down the cube roots of \(j\) from \(1,\ e^{j2\pi/3},\ e^{j4\pi/3}\).

notes.t: Calculating nth roots of complex numbers (heuristic approach)
pts: The nth root w of z satisfies w^n = z, so solve the polynomial equation w^n − z = 0 to find all roots.
Factor the polynomial by spotting a known root; here w = −j is a root because (w + j) is a factor of w³ − j.
