The notes give only qualitative detail, so a top-grade student should derive the quantitative results from the definitions of average and RMS.
must: Period \(T\) is the time for one complete cycle and frequency is \(f=1/T\); read T from the time axis, checking its scale first.
Waveform shape, amplitude and frequency are independent properties: two waves can share a shape but differ in size or repetition rate.
Sawtooth: linear rise from 0 to 1.0 V over T, then an abrupt drop to 0 V. Its equation is \(v(t)=V_{pk}\,t/T\) for \(0\le t<T\).
Square wave: abrupt switching between two fixed levels (here +1.0 V and -1.0 V) with constant peak values, used in digital signalling.
Symmetric square wave (±V): \(V_{RMS}=V_{pk}\) because \(v^2\) is constant, and the average over a full cycle is 0.
General definitions: \(V_{avg}=\frac1T\int_0^T v\,dt\) and \(V_{RMS}=\sqrt{\frac1T\int_0^T v^2\,dt}\). Use these for any waveform.
Sawtooth 0 to 1 V (derived from the definitions): \(V_{avg}=0.5\) V and \(V_{RMS}=1/\sqrt3\approx0.577\) V. Note it is not \(V_{pk}/\sqrt2\).
The sinusoid relations \(V_{RMS}=V_{pk}/\sqrt2\) and \(V_{avg}=0.637V_{pk}\) (half-cycle) do not apply to other shapes; the ratio of peak to RMS depends on shape (form and crest factors).
Sawtooth and square waves are harmonically rich, whereas a sine wave is single-frequency. This explains their different sound in synthesisers.
Applications: sawtooth for TV raster scanning and oscilloscope time bases; square wave for digital signals; sine, sawtooth and square from oscillators in synthesisers.
conn: RMS and power: RMS gives the equivalent DC heating value, so \(P=V_{RMS}^2/R\). A ±1 V square wave across R dissipates \(1/R\), while a 0 to 1 V sawtooth dissipates only \(1/(3R)\).
Average versus RMS: the sawtooth has a non-zero average (DC offset) while the symmetric square wave averages zero. This matters when AC-coupling or when reading a meter that assumes a sine wave.
Period and frequency with the oscilloscope: the time-base sawtooth sweeps the trace, and you read T from the time-axis scale to find f and then compare it with amplitude.
Waveform shape and harmonic content: abrupt edges (the sawtooth drop and square-wave switching) imply high-frequency harmonics, which links to Fourier ideas and to circuit bandwidth.
exq: A sawtooth rises linearly from 0 to 1.0 V over T = 2 ms then drops to 0 V. Find its frequency, average value and RMS value by integration.
A symmetric square wave of ±1.0 V and period 10 µs is applied across a 50 Ω resistor. Determine f, V_RMS and average power. Compare with a 1 V peak sinusoid.
Derive the RMS value of the sawtooth \(v=V_{pk}t/T\) and explain why it is not \(V_{pk}/\sqrt2\). Calculate the crest factor.

From an oscilloscope trace showing 4 divisions per cycle at 0.5 ms/div and 2 V/div peak amplitude, state T, f and the peak, average and RMS values if the waveform is (a) a ±V square wave, (b) a 0 to V sawtooth.
A sawtooth (0 to 1 V) and a square wave (±1 V) have equal period. Compare their average and RMS values and the power dissipated in the same resistor, and explain the differences.

notes.t: AC Waveforms: Non-Sinusoidal Waveforms (Sawtooth)
pts: AC circuits are not limited to sinusoidal voltages; other periodic waveforms can be used.
The sawtooth waveform rises linearly from 0 V to 1.0 V over each period and then drops abruptly back to 0 V, repeating every period T.
Sawtooth waveforms are used in TV raster scanning and in oscilloscope time bases.
defs: Sawtooth waveform
A periodic waveform that increases linearly over one period and then falls abruptly to its starting value, repeating each period T.
Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform before it repeats.
tips: Do not assume AC means sinusoidal: the period T is the same for all periodic waveforms, but the shape determines the relationship between peak and average values.
rq: Why is a sawtooth waveform useful for a TV raster scan or an oscilloscope time base?
Its linear rise sweeps the beam across the screen at a constant rate, and the abrupt drop resets it quickly to the start for the next sweep.
How does the sawtooth differ from a sinusoid in terms of the rate of change of voltage?
A sawtooth has a constant rate of change (constant slope) during its rise, whereas a sinusoid's rate of change varies continuously with time.

notes.t: AC Waveforms: Non-Sinusoidal Waveforms (Square Wave)
pts: AC circuits do not have to use sinusoidal waveforms; other waveform shapes are possible.
The square wave switches abruptly between two fixed voltage levels, here +1.0 V and −1.0 V, with a period T.
Square waves are widely used in digital signals, where the voltage is either high or low.
defs: Square wave
A periodic waveform that alternates abruptly between two constant voltage levels with equal-or-specified durations, widely used in digital signalling.
Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform before the pattern repeats.
tips: Do not assume every AC waveform is sinusoidal; read the voltage–time graph to find peak values and period.
Remember that the peak values for a square wave are constant, unlike a sinusoid, so RMS calculations differ (RMS equals the peak value for a symmetric square wave).
rq: Why might a circuit designer choose a square wave rather than a sinusoid for a digital system?
Square waves have abrupt transitions between two defined levels, which map directly onto binary high and low states and are easy to detect reliably.
If the square wave in the figure has a period of T, what fraction of each period is it at +1.0 V?
From the plot, the signal is at +1.0 V for half the period (T/2) and at −1.0 V for the other half, so the duty cycle is 50%.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms
pts: This page introduces AC waveforms, which are the periodic signals that alternating current circuits use; the page itself shows only a video link rather than explanatory content.
tips: The page only links to an external video; the content relevant to exams (waveform shapes, period, frequency, amplitude) must be learned from the video or following slides, not assumed from this page alone.
rq: Why might a video be used to introduce waveforms before any equations are given?
Watching how voltage or current varies over time builds an intuitive picture of periodic waveforms (shape, repetition, amplitude) that makes later mathematical descriptions easier to understand.

notes.t: Alternating current waveforms: sine, sawtooth and square
pts: Waveforms such as sine, sawtooth and square are alternating signals that vary periodically over time.
Synthesisers and electronic music generate these common waveform shapes using oscillators.
The sine wave is the smooth, single-frequency waveform that repeats its shape each cycle.
The sawtooth wave rises linearly and then drops sharply, giving a bright, harmonically rich sound.
The square wave switches abruptly between two fixed levels, alternating between positive and negative values.
defs: Waveform
The shape of a signal plotted as a function of time, describing how its value varies over each cycle.
tips: Do not confuse waveform shape with amplitude or frequency; two waves can share a shape but differ in size or rate of repetition.
Read the time axis scale on waveform plots before estimating period or frequency.
rq: Why does a square wave sound harsher than a sine wave when played on a synthesiser?
A square wave contains sharp transitions and strong higher-frequency harmonics, whereas a sine wave is a pure single frequency with no harmonics.
What would you expect to change in the sawtooth waveform if its frequency were doubled?
The waveform would repeat twice as often, so each cycle would occupy half the time while its amplitude stays the same.

units.name: 1.5 Sine and cosine from circular motion
units.ov: This material builds sine and cosine from right-angled triangle ratios, then places the triangle inside a circle so that the radius is the hypotenuse and its horizontal and vertical projections give cosine and sine. A point rotating around the circle then traces sinusoidal waveforms, with one revolution equal to one period. These ideas underlie later work on harmonic motion, phasors and AC signals.
must: Right-triangle definitions: \(\sin\theta = o/h\) and \(\cos\theta = a/h\), so \(o = h\sin\theta\) and \(a = h\cos\theta\)
Identify opposite and adjacent relative to the angle \(\theta\), not by their position on the page; swapping them is the commonest error
In the circle, the hypotenuse is the radius \(r\): horizontal projection \(x = r\cos\theta\), vertical projection \(y = r\sin\theta\)
For a unit circle (\(r=1\)), \(\cos\theta\) is the x-coordinate and \(\sin\theta\) is the y-coordinate of the rotating point
Plotting a projection against angle (or time) gives a sinusoid that oscillates between \(+r\) and \(-r\); the amplitude equals the radius
One full revolution (\(360^\circ = 2\pi\) rad) equals one period \(T\) of the waveform
Key cosine values: maximum 1 at \(0^\circ\) and \(360^\circ\), minimum -1 at \(180^\circ\), zero at \(90^\circ\) and \(270^\circ\); sine is the same wave shifted by \(90^\circ\)
Amplitude (radius) and frequency (rotation speed) are different things: radius sets the height, rotation rate sets how quickly the wave repeats
Keep the calculator in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians) and use one unit consistently throughout
conn: Vector resolution in statics and dynamics: a force or velocity of magnitude \(h\) at angle \(\theta\) has components \(h\cos\theta\) and \(h\sin\theta\), which is the same projection idea as the circle
Rotating point to waveform: with \(\theta = \omega t\), the projection becomes \(A\cos(\omega t)\), linking angle, angular frequency, period \(T = 2\pi/\omega\) and simple harmonic motion
Degrees versus radians: converting a revolution to \(2\pi\) rad connects the period, arc length and angular velocity, and calculator mode errors affect all of these
Sine and cosine as phase-shifted versions of one wave leads to phase angles and phasor representations of oscillating quantities
exq: A ladder of length 4.0 m rests at \(65^\circ\) to the horizontal. Find the height it reaches up the wall and the horizontal distance of its foot from the wall, stating which side is opposite and which is adjacent to the angle.

A point moves around a circle of radius 0.5 m, starting at \(\theta = 0\). Find its horizontal and vertical positions at \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(120^\circ\) and \(225^\circ\), and sketch the vertical projection against angle for one revolution.

A crank of radius 150 mm rotates at constant speed. Write the expression for the vertical displacement of its end, state the amplitude, and give the angles in one revolution where the displacement is maximum, minimum and zero.
Explain why one revolution of a rotating point corresponds to one period of the cosine wave. If the point completes a revolution in 0.02 s, find the period and the angular speed in rad/s.
A force of 200 N acts at \(35^\circ\) above the horizontal. Calculate its horizontal and vertical components, and show how the answer changes if the calculator is wrongly set to radians.

notes.t: Origin of sine and cosine from a right-angled triangle
pts: Sine and cosine are ratios of the sides of a right-angled triangle relative to an angle θ.
The opposite side equals the hypotenuse multiplied by sin(θ).
The adjacent side equals the hypotenuse multiplied by cos(θ).
defs: Hypotenuse (h)
The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
Opposite side (o)
The side across from the angle θ in a right-angled triangle.
Adjacent side (a)
The side next to the angle θ that is not the hypotenuse.
eqs: Opposite side from hypotenuse and angle
o = opposite side (m); h = hypotenuse (m); θ = angle (rad or °)
Adjacent side from hypotenuse and angle
a = adjacent side (m); h = hypotenuse (m); θ = angle (rad or °)
tips: Check the angle mode: θ must be in radians or degrees consistently with your calculator setting.
Identify o and a relative to θ, not by position; swapping them gives the wrong sine/cosine.
rq: Why does dividing the opposite side by the hypotenuse give a value that depends only on θ?
Similar right-angled triangles with the same angle have proportional sides, so the ratio o/h is fixed by θ alone.
If θ is fixed and h doubles, what happens to o and a?
Both o and a double, since each is h multiplied by a constant depending only on θ.

notes.t: Origin of sine and cosine from a right-angled triangle in a circle
pts: Sine and cosine describe the side ratios of a right-angled triangle formed by a radius at angle θ within a circle.
The hypotenuse h is the radius of the circle; the adjacent side a is the horizontal projection of h, so a = h·cos(θ).
The opposite side o is the vertical projection of h, giving o = h·sin(θ) and linking sine to height on the circle.
defs: Cosine (cos θ)
Ratio of the adjacent side to the hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle: cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.
Sine (sin θ)
Ratio of the opposite side to the hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle: sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.
eqs: Horizontal (adjacent) component of a vector of length h at angle θ
a = adjacent side (m or same unit as h); h = hypotenuse / radius (m); θ = angle from horizontal (rad or °)
tips: Check which side is adjacent to θ before choosing sine or cosine; mixing them up is the most common error.
Ensure the calculator is in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians) when evaluating cos θ.
rq: Why does the adjacent side equal h·cos(θ) rather than h·sin(θ)?
Cosine is defined as adjacent/hypotenuse, and the adjacent side lies next to the angle θ measured from the horizontal axis.
What happens to a and o as θ increases from 0° towards 90°?
a = h·cos θ decreases from h to 0, while o = h·sin θ increases from 0 to h.

notes.t: Rotation around a circle (sinusoid from circular motion)
pts: A point rotating around a unit circle has its horizontal projection following the cosine of the angle and its vertical projection following the sine.
The vertical projection of the rotating point traces a sinusoidal waveform between +1 and -1 as the angle increases.
The amplitude of the resulting waveform equals the radius of the circle, here 1.
tips: Do not confuse the radius of the rotating circle (the amplitude) with the frequency of rotation, which determines how fast the waveform repeats.
rq: Why does the vertical projection of a rotating point produce an AC waveform rather than a constant value?
Because the vertical coordinate of the point changes continuously with the angle as it rotates, giving \( \sin\theta \), which oscillates periodically between -1 and +1.

notes.t: Rotation around a circle and the sinusoidal waveform
pts: A point rotating once around a unit circle through 360° traces one full cycle of a cosine wave when its horizontal position is plotted against angle.
One complete revolution of the rotating point corresponds to one period (T) of the waveform on the right.
The vertical value of the waveform equals the projection of the rotating point onto the horizontal axis, which ranges between -1 and 1.
The waveform reaches its maximum value of 1 at 0° and 360°, and its minimum value of -1 at 180°.
defs: Period (T)
The time or angle taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform; for a rotation this is one full revolution of 360°.
tips: Do not confuse the horizontal axis of the waveform (angle or time) with the vertical axis, which shows the projected amplitude between -1 and 1.
Ensure the angle is measured consistently in degrees or radians when relating a full rotation to the period.
rq: Why does the plotted waveform return to its starting value after 360°?
Because the rotating point completes one full revolution and returns to its original position on the circle, so its projection repeats.
What would happen to the period if the point rotated twice as fast around the circle?
The period would halve, since one full cycle would be completed in 180° of rotation-equivalent time instead of 360°.

units.name: 1.6 Radians, angular frequency and phase
units.ov: This material defines the radian as the ratio of arc length to radius (so 2π rad = 360°), then uses it as the natural angle unit for sinusoids. Angular frequency \(\omega\) links period T, frequency f and the sine argument, and phase offsets \(\phi\) are shifts along the angle axis that are equivalent to time shifts \(\Delta t\). Everything ties together through one cycle = 2π rad = one period T.
must: Radian definition: \(\theta = s/r\), dimensionless; one full turn is \(2\pi r/r = 2\pi\) rad
Conversions: \(\pi\) rad = 180°, \(\theta_{rad}=\theta_{deg}\times\pi/180\); never confuse π rad with π degrees
Sinusoid: \(V=V_o\sin(\omega t)\), with amplitude \(V_o\) (peak value) and the argument \(\omega t\) in radians
\(\omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f\), so \(T=2\pi/\omega = 1/f\); \(\omega\) in rad/s, f in Hz
Write in terms of frequency as \(V=V_o\sin(2\pi f t)\); never put f directly into \(\sin(\omega t)\) without the 2π
Phase shift: \(y=\cos(\omega t+\phi)\); positive \(\phi\) shifts the curve left, so the wave leads (e.g. \(\cos(\theta+\pi/2)\) leads by a quarter cycle)
Phase and time shift: \(\phi=\omega\Delta t = 2\pi\Delta t/T\) and \(\Delta t=\phi T/2\pi\)
Phase difference \(\Delta\phi\) between two waves of the same frequency is usually all that matters, not absolute phase
Check the calculator is in radian mode when \(\omega t\) is in rad; 2π ≈ 6.28 rad, and one period = 360° = 2π rad
Keep units consistent: s and r in the same units, \(\Delta t\) and T in the same units (ms with ms)
conn: Frequency, period and angular frequency: converting between f, T and \(\omega\) is needed before evaluating \(\sin(\omega t)\) or finding a phase
Phase shift and time shift: \(\phi=\omega\Delta t\) turns an oscilloscope time offset into a phase angle in rad or degrees, and back
Radians and calculator mode: evaluating \(V_o\sin(\omega t+\phi)\) at a given time needs \(\omega t\) and \(\phi\) in radians, so degree/radian conversion matters
Lead/lag sign convention: \(+\phi\) means earlier (leads), a minus sign means later (lags), which links the graph shift to the equation
exq: An arc of length 15 cm subtends an angle at the centre of a circle of radius 6 cm. Find the angle in radians and degrees.
A voltage is \(V=325\sin(2\pi\times 50\,t)\). State the amplitude, \(\omega\), f and T, and find V at t = 3 ms (radian mode).
Two sinusoids of the same frequency 200 Hz are offset by 0.5 ms. Find the phase difference in radians and degrees, and state which one leads.
Express a quarter-cycle lead of \(\cos(\omega t)\) with \(\omega=100\pi\) rad/s as \(\cos(\omega t+\phi)\), and find the equivalent time shift \(\Delta t\) in ms.
A waveform has period T = 20 ms and is shifted by \(\Delta t = 2\) ms. Calculate the phase angle in rad and in degrees, and write the shifted waveform for \(V_o=5\) V.

notes.t: Radians: measuring angles using the radius and arc length
pts: A radian compares an arc length to the radius of the same circle, so it is a ratio and has no units.
One radian is the angle subtended at the centre when the arc length equals the radius.
A full turn corresponds to one circumference divided by the radius, giving 2π radians.
Radians come from the geometry of the circle, and conversion uses 2π radians = 360°.
defs: Radian
The angle at the centre of a circle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius; equivalently, the ratio of arc length to radius.
Radius
The distance from the centre of a circle to any point on its circumference.
eqs: Number of radians subtended by an arc
θ = angle in radians (dimensionless); s = arc length (m); r = radius (m)
θ = angle for a full turn (rad); r = radius (m)
π = pi (dimensionless); θ in rad and degrees
tips: Ensure the arc length and radius are in the same units before dividing, otherwise the result is wrong.
Do not confuse π radians (180°) with π degrees; always convert using 180° = π rad.
rq: Why is a radian described as dimensionless even though it is built from lengths?
Because it is a ratio of arc length to radius, both in metres, so the units cancel.
If the radius doubles but the arc length also doubles, how many radians is the angle?
Unchanged: the ratio s/r stays the same, so the angle is the same number of radians.

notes.t: Degrees and radians
pts: One full period of a sine wave corresponds to 360° or 2π radians.
Radians measure angle as arc length on the unit circle, so one cycle spans 2π rad.
Sine waves plotted against degrees and radians have identical shape; only the horizontal axis scaling changes.
Two periods of a sine wave span 720° or 4π radians.
Amplitude of the sine wave oscillates between +1.0 and −1.0.
defs: Period
The time or angle over which a periodic waveform repeats exactly; for a sine wave in angle this is 360° or 2π radians.
Radian
The angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc equal in length to the radius; 2π radians equals 360°.
eqs: \(\theta_{\text{rad}}\) = angle in radians (rad); \(\theta_{\text{deg}}\) = angle in degrees (°)
tips: Do not mix units: when using sin or cos on a calculator, check whether it is set to degree or radian mode.
A period of 2π is about 6.28 rad; do not confuse it with 2 rad or 360 rad.
rq: Why does a sine wave repeat every 2π radians rather than every 360 radians?

Because radian measure is defined by arc length on the unit circle; a full revolution is a circumference of 2π, so one complete cycle corresponds to 2π rad, while 360 rad would be about 57 full turns.
If a sine wave has a period of 2π rad, what is its period in degrees, and why is the graph shape unchanged?
360°; only the labelling of the horizontal axis changes, since the same physical rotation is expressed in different units.

notes.t: Sinusoidal waveform: amplitude, angular frequency and period
pts: The sine wave V = Vo sin(ωt) has amplitude Vo, which sets the peak value of the signal.
The argument of the sine must be in radians, so ωt is measured in radians, with ω in radians per second and t in seconds.
Angular frequency ω is measured in radians per second and is linked to the period: one full cycle is completed when ωt = 2π.
For ω = 2π rad/s, one cycle takes exactly 1 s, so the period T = 1 s; the plot confirms one cycle is complete after 1 s.
defs: Angular frequency (ω)
The rate of change of the sine's phase angle, measured in radians per second; ω = 2π/T where T is the period.
Amplitude (Vo)
The maximum magnitude of the sinusoidal signal, measured from the zero line to the peak.
eqs: Instantaneous value of a sinusoidal voltage
V = instantaneous voltage (V); V_o = amplitude (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
t = period T (s); ω = angular frequency (rad/s)
tips: Keep the sine argument in radians: ωt must be in radians, not degrees, when using ω in rad/s.
Do not confuse angular frequency ω (rad/s) with frequency f (Hz); ω = 2πf, so a 1 Hz signal has ω = 2π rad/s.
rq: Why must the argument ωt be in radians rather than degrees?
Because ω is defined in radians per second, so ωt is dimensionless only when the angle is in radians; the sine function's natural argument is radians, and the cycle condition ωt = 2π relies on it.
If the frequency doubles, what happens to the period and to ω?
ω doubles (ω = 2πf), and the period T = 2π/ω halves, so the waveform completes cycles twice as fast.

notes.t: Frequency vs angular frequency
pts: One cycle is complete when the argument of the sine has advanced by 2π radians.
The period T is the time taken to complete one cycle, found from t = 2π/ω.
Angular frequency ω (rad/s) is related to ordinary frequency f (Hz) by ω = 2πf, so the sinusoid can be written in terms of f.
defs: Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of a periodic waveform; T = 2π/ω = 1/f.
Angular frequency (ω)
The rate of change of phase of a sinusoid in radians per second, ω = 2π/T = 2πf.
eqs: Sinusoidal voltage in terms of angular frequency
V = instantaneous voltage (V); V_o = peak voltage amplitude (V); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
ω = angular frequency (rad/s); T = period (s); f = frequency (Hz)
Sinusoidal voltage in terms of frequency
V = instantaneous voltage (V); V_o = peak voltage amplitude (V); f = frequency (Hz); t = time (s)
tips: Angular frequency is in rad/s while frequency is in Hz; do not substitute f directly into sin(ωt) without multiplying by 2π.
Remember that T = 2π/ω and f = 1/T are different forms; using ω where f is required (or vice versa) is a common unit trap.
rq: Why does one full cycle correspond to ωt = 2π rather than some other value?
A sine function repeats every 2π radians, so the phase must advance by 2π for the waveform to return to its starting point.
If a signal has f = 50 Hz, what is its angular frequency and period, and why must ω be in rad/s rather than Hz?
ω = 2π(50) ≈ 314 rad/s and T = 1/50 = 0.02 s; ω must be in rad/s because the sine argument is an angle in radians, and only the 2π factor converts cycles into radians.
What would happen to the period if the angular frequency doubled?
The period halves, since T = 2π/ω, and the frequency doubles because f = ω/2π.

notes.t: Phase and phase difference of waves
pts: Phase describes where a wave is within its cycle at a given point.
In most cases we only need the phase difference between two waves, not absolute phase.
Adding a phase offset to the angle input shifts the cosine curve to the left, so features occur earlier.
Adding π/2 to θ in cos(θ + π/2) makes the wave lead cos(θ) by a quarter cycle.
defs: Phase
The position of a periodic waveform within its cycle at a given instant, usually expressed as an angle in radians or degrees.
Phase difference (Δφ)
The angular offset between two waves of the same frequency, measuring how far one leads or lags the other along the angle axis.
eqs: y = instantaneous value (dimensionless); θ = angle (rad); φ = phase offset (rad)
y = instantaneous value (dimensionless); θ = angle (rad); π/2 = phase offset (rad)
tips: Shifting left versus right: cos(θ + φ) moves the graph left by φ, not right; a minus sign would move it right.
Phase offsets must be in radians consistently with θ; mixing degrees and radians gives wrong shifts.
rq: Why does adding +π/2 inside the cosine move the curve to the left rather than the right?
Because the output at angle θ equals the original output at θ + π/2, so each feature of the original curve is reached π/2 earlier in θ, i.e. it appears further left.
Why is only the phase difference between two waves usually meaningful?
Absolute phase depends on the arbitrary choice of time or angle origin; the relative offset between waves of the same frequency is what is physically measurable and affects their interaction.

notes.t: Phase shift as a time shift in sinusoids
pts: A phase shift φ in a cosine wave is equivalent to shifting it in time by Δt, since the phase can be written as ω multiplied by a time offset.
Phase and time shift are linked by φ = ω·Δt, so a phase of π/2 corresponds to a quarter-period time shift.
Expressing the phase in terms of period T gives φ = 2π(Δt/T), and inverting gives Δt = φT/(2π).
eqs: Sinusoid with phase shift written as a time shift
y = instantaneous value (dimensionless here); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s); φ = phase shift (rad)
Time shift equivalent to phase shift
Δt = time shift (s); ω = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
Phase from time shift and period
φ = phase shift (rad); Δt = time shift (s); T = period (s)
Time shift from phase and period
Δt = time shift (s); φ = phase shift (rad); T = period (s)
tips: Keep consistent units: use 2π with radians and 360 with degrees when converting between phase and time shift.
Remember the sign: cos(ωt + φ) with positive φ means the wave is shifted earlier in time (leads), not later.
rq: Why does a phase shift of π/2 in cos(ωt + π/2) correspond to a quarter period time shift?
Because φ = 2π(Δt/T); with φ = π/2, Δt/T = 1/4, so Δt = T/4.
If a wave is shifted by one full period, what phase change does this produce and why?
A phase change of 2π (360°), since Δt = T gives φ = 2π, leaving the waveform unchanged.

notes.t: Alternating Current Circuits - Waveforms: phase angle
pts: Phase angle φ is the fraction of one full period elapsed, expressed in radians (one period = 2π radians).
The phase angle is found by dividing the time shift Δt by the period T and multiplying by 2π.
defs: Period (T)
The time taken for one complete cycle of an alternating waveform, measured in seconds.
eqs: Phase angle of a waveform shifted in time by Δt
φ = phase angle (rad); Δt = time shift (s); T = period (s)
tips: Keep Δt and T in the same units (here both in ms or both in s) before dividing, otherwise the phase angle is wrong by a power of 10.
Give the answer in radians; a phase of 0.1π rad is not the same as 0.1 degrees.
rq: Why is the period multiplied by 2π rather than the frequency being used directly in the phase formula?
Because one full cycle corresponds to 2π radians, so the time shift as a fraction of the period gives the fraction of 2π; using frequency would require ω = 2πf instead.

units.name: 1.7 Circuit effects on signals: speaker crossover filters
units.ov: This material introduces speaker crossovers as practical filter circuits built from resistors, capacitors (and inductors) that separate audio signals into frequency bands for woofers and tweeters. It explains that circuits alter an AC signal's magnitude, phase, or both, and that this effect depends on frequency, which is what makes filtering possible. Note: pages 40-50 of the notes contained no extractable content, so topics such as transfer functions, cutoff frequency and Bode plots are not covered here and should be checked against the original slides.
must: A crossover divides the audio signal into frequency bands and routes each band to the suitable driver (woofer for low, tweeter for high).
A filter passes some frequency ranges and blocks or attenuates others; it is built from R, C and/or L.
Filter behaviour is frequency-dependent, not an absolute on/off block: attenuation is gradual and varies with frequency.
A circuit can leave an AC signal unchanged, change its magnitude, shift its phase, or change both.
Phase difference (lag) \( \phi \) is the angular or time offset between corresponding points of input and output sinusoids of the same frequency.
Magnitude change (volts, e.g. \( V_o < V_i \)) and phase change (degrees or radians) are independent quantities; a phase shift alone does not reduce the peak voltage.
Always check both gain \( V_o/V_i \) and phase \( \phi \); knowing only that \( V_i > V_o \) says nothing about phase lag.
The same component impedes low and high frequencies differently (e.g. a capacitor's impedance depends on frequency), which is the physical basis of frequency separation.
Component colour in photos does not indicate type or function; identify components by labels and symbols.
conn: Frequency-dependent impedance of R, C, L leads to gain and phase changes, which together determine the filter's low-pass or high-pass behaviour.
Amplitude ratio \( V_o/V_i \) and phase lag \( \phi \) combine to describe the output sinusoid: \( V_o(t)=V_{o,peak}\sin(\omega t-\phi) \).
Crossover design links filter type (low-pass for woofer, high-pass for tweeter) to the practical choice of which driver receives which band.
Time offset between waveforms converts to phase angle via \( \phi = 360^\circ f\,\Delta t \) (or \( 2\pi f\Delta t \) rad), linking oscilloscope readings to circuit analysis.
exq: Explain what a speaker crossover does and why a woofer and a tweeter need different filters. State which filter type feeds each driver.
An input sinusoid has a 5 V peak and the output has a 3 V peak and lags by 1 ms at 250 Hz. Calculate the gain and the phase lag in degrees.
Describe the three ways a circuit can alter an AC input signal, with a sketch of input and output waveforms for each.
A student states that because the output peak is smaller than the input, the circuit has introduced a phase lag. Critique this statement.
Explain why a capacitor-resistor circuit can separate low and high frequencies, and why the separation is gradual rather than an abrupt block.

notes.t: Filter circuits in HiFi speaker crossovers
pts: A speaker crossover is a circuit that separates the different electrical signal frequencies and routes each band to the appropriate speaker driver.
Crossover circuits are filters: they block current flow for some frequencies while letting others pass.
In the pictured crossover, resistors (white) and capacitors (yellow) are among the components used to build these filters.
Filters are frequency-dependent: the same component impedes low and high frequencies differently, which is what makes frequency separation possible.
defs: Crossover
A circuit in a loudspeaker system that divides the audio signal into frequency bands and directs each band to the appropriate driver (e.g. woofer, tweeter).
Filter
A circuit that passes signals within certain frequency ranges while blocking or attenuating others, built from resistors, capacitors and/or inductors.
tips: Do not confuse the colours in the photo with component types; the labels identify them here, but in general component colour does not define function.
Filters block current for some frequencies: remember the behaviour is frequency-dependent, not an absolute on/off block.
rq: Why must a tweeter be protected from low-frequency signals by a crossover, and what component would block them?
Low frequencies carry large excursions that can damage a small tweeter; a high-pass filter, typically a series capacitor, blocks low frequencies from reaching it.
Why would a capacitor and resistor be used together in a filter rather than resistors alone?
Resistors dissipate power equally at all frequencies, whereas capacitors have frequency-dependent impedance, so only a reactive component can selectively block or pass frequency bands.

notes.t: AC Circuits - Waveforms: how circuits alter an input signal
pts: A circuit can leave an AC input signal unaltered, so the output matches the input exactly.
A circuit can change the magnitude (amplitude) of the input signal so the output peak is smaller than the input peak.
A circuit can shift the waveform in time, creating a phase difference (lag) between input and output, without necessarily changing its amplitude.
Most circuits affect the input signal by altering its magnitude, its phase, or both.
defs: Phase difference (phase lag)
The angular or time offset between corresponding points of an input and output sinusoidal waveform of the same frequency, usually given as the angle \( \phi \).
tips: Do not confuse a change in magnitude (amplitude, measured in volts) with a phase change (measured in degrees or radians); a phase shift does not reduce the peak voltage.
Comparing \( V_i > V_o \) only tells you the output is smaller; it does not tell you whether a phase lag exists too, so check both quantities.
rq: If a circuit reduces the peak voltage from \( V_i \) to \( V_o \), has its frequency changed?
No. Changing magnitude alters only the amplitude; the frequency (and period) of the sinusoid stay the same.
Why can two waveforms with identical amplitudes still be different signals?
Because they can differ in phase, i.e. one is shifted in time relative to the other by a phase angle \( \phi \).

units.name: 1.8 Phasors and phase rotation
units.ov: This module introduces phasors as rotating vectors that encode the amplitude (length) and phase (angle) of a sinusoid, with the vertical projection giving the instantaneous value. Because all phasors of the same frequency rotate at the same \(\omega\), their relative angle (the phase difference) stays fixed, so phase shifts from components like capacitors and inductors become simple vector rotations instead of trigonometric manipulation. The key link is between phasor angle, waveform shift and time delay.
must: A phasor is a rotating vector whose length is the amplitude and whose angle is the phase of a sinusoid
The instantaneous angle is \(\theta(t)=\omega t\), with \(\omega=2\pi f\) in rad/s
The instantaneous value of the sinusoid is the vertical projection of the rotating phasor, e.g. \(v(t)=V_m\sin(\omega t+\phi)\)
Phase offset is the constant angle between two same-frequency phasors, so one waveform is a shifted copy of the other
Phasor comparison is valid only for equal frequencies; different frequencies give a changing angle
Time delay converts to phase by \(\phi = 2\pi f\,\Delta t\) (radians), or \(\phi=360^\circ f\Delta t\) in degrees; the angle is a phase difference, not a time
The sign of the angle shows lead or lag: a phasor ahead in the rotation direction leads, one behind lags
Capacitors and inductors shift the phase of voltage relative to current, and this shift is treated as a fixed rotation on the phasor diagram
Phasors avoid repeated trig identities because phase shifts become geometric rotations and amplitudes become lengths
conn: Phasor angle and time delay: converting between phase difference and \(\Delta t\) needs the frequency, which links \(\omega\), \(f\) and period \(T\)
Rotating phasor and waveform: the vertical projection over time traces the sine wave, so reading a phase from a plot matches reading an angle on the phasor diagram
Phase shift in components: the voltage-current phase difference in capacitors and inductors is a phasor rotation, which leads into impedance and AC circuit analysis
Same-frequency condition: adding or comparing sinusoids by phasors requires equal \(\omega\), otherwise the relative angle varies with time
exq: Two voltages \(v_1=10\sin(100\pi t)\) V and \(v_2=6\sin(100\pi t-\pi/3)\) V. Draw the phasor diagram, state which leads and by how many degrees, and find the time offset between the waveforms.
A 50 Hz sinusoid lags a reference by 2 ms. Calculate the phase difference in radians and degrees, and sketch both phasors.
Explain why the phase offset between two phasors stays constant if they have the same frequency, but not if they have different frequencies. Illustrate with 50 Hz and 60 Hz signals after 10 ms.
A rotating phasor of length 5 V turns at \(\omega=200\) rad/s starting at 30° from the reference. Find the instantaneous value at \(t=5\) ms and write the expression for \(v(t)\).
Describe how a capacitor or inductor changes the phase of the voltage relative to the current, and show how a phasor diagram makes this simpler than using trigonometric functions.

notes.t: Phase change and phasor rotation
pts: Phasor vectors representing the two sinusoids rotate about the origin at the same angular rate ωt, so their relative geometry is fixed.
The angle between the two rotating vectors is the phase offset (shift); it remains constant over time, so the waveforms are shifted copies of each other.
Components such as capacitors and inductors shift the phase of the applied voltage or current wave relative to the other.
Representing phase as a rotating vector avoids repeatedly manipulating trigonometric functions, allowing phase shifts to be handled as simple vector rotations.
defs: Phase offset (phase shift)
The constant angle between two sinusoidal waveforms of the same frequency, measured between their corresponding vectors on the phasor diagram.
eqs: Instantaneous angle of a rotating phasor at time t
\theta = instantaneous angle (rad); \omega = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s)
tips: The phase offset is only constant when both waves have the same frequency; comparing waves of different frequencies gives a changing angle.
rq: Why does a constant angle between two rotating vectors correspond to a fixed phase difference between the two waves?
Both vectors rotate at the same ωt, so their angular separation never changes; the waves therefore keep the same time displacement, a constant phase offset.

notes.t: Phasors: representing phase and amplitude
pts: A phasor is a graphical way to represent the amplitude and phase of a sinusoidal function.
The length of a phasor arrow encodes the amplitude of the sinusoid.
The angle between two phasor arrows encodes the phase difference between the two sinusoids.
Rotating phasor's vertical projection traces the sinusoid over time: the projection of the rotating arrow onto the vertical axis gives the instantaneous value.
defs: Phasor
A rotating vector in the complex plane whose length represents the amplitude of a sinusoid and whose angle represents its phase, used to represent sinusoidal quantities graphically.
Phase difference
The angular difference between two sinusoids of the same frequency, shown as the angle between their phasor arrows; it determines how far one waveform leads or lags the other.
tips: Phasor angles only have meaning relative to each other for sinusoids of the same frequency; comparing phasors of different frequencies is invalid.
Be careful the angle is a phase difference, not a time difference; converting requires the frequency (phase in radians = 2π × frequency × time delay).
rq: Why is the phasor's length, rather than its direction, used to represent amplitude?
Because the length (magnitude) of the arrow is constant as it rotates, so it directly equals the peak value of the sinusoid; the direction changes with time and encodes phase.
If two phasors have equal length but are 90° apart, what does this say about their waveforms?
They have the same amplitude and frequency but are 90° out of phase, so one is a quarter cycle ahead of the other (e.g. sine vs cosine).

units.name: 1.9 Complex numbers and impedance
units.ov: This material introduces complex numbers as a tool for describing AC phasors: j = √(−1) acts as a 90° rotation operator on the Argand diagram, and a complex number a + jb encodes both magnitude and phase. It extends Ohm's law to \(\tilde{V} = \tilde{I}Z\) with complex impedance Z, so multiplying by Z scales and rotates a phasor in one step. Circuits are then seen as operators that leave a signal unchanged or alter its amplitude, its phase, or both.
must: \(j=\sqrt{-1}\), \(j^2=-1\); multiplying by j rotates a phasor 90° anticlockwise, and \(j^2\) gives 180°, the same as multiplying by −1
Rectangular form \(Z=a+jb\): plot as the point (a, b) with real part on the horizontal axis and imaginary part on the vertical axis (e.g. 3 + j1 is at (3, 1))
Generalised Ohm's law for AC: \(\tilde{V}=\tilde{I}Z\), with Z complex in ohms. Never use V = IR directly on AC phasors
Impedance \(Z=R+jX\): the real part is resistance and the imaginary part is reactance, both in Ω
Multiplying complex numbers changes both magnitude and phase: magnitudes multiply and angles add. Expand the brackets term by term, then apply \(j^2=-1\)
Worked example: \(I=1+j0\), \(Z=0.5j\) gives \(V=0.5j\), a 90° rotation with magnitude halved, so V leads I by 90°
Worked example: \(\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\tfrac{j}{\sqrt2}\right)^2=\tfrac12+j-\tfrac12=j\); two 45° unit phasors give 90°, and the \(j\cdot j\) term is \(-\tfrac12\)
Magnitude is the length of the line from the origin and phase is the angle from the real axis; lead and lag depend on the direction of rotation of the output relative to the input
A circuit acts on an AC signal by leaving it unchanged, changing its magnitude, or changing its phase, and the output phasor is compared with the input reference along the real axis
Notation and units: use j rather than i, state units (V, A, Ω), and compare peak with peak or RMS with RMS
conn: Phasor rotation and impedance: multiplying by j (a 90° turn) is exactly what a purely reactive Z = jX does to a current phasor, so reactive components give a voltage lead or lag of 90°
Complex multiplication and phase addition: the angle of V is the angle of I plus the angle of Z, and \(|V|=|I||Z|\). Exam questions often switch between rectangular and polar form to do this
Generalised Ohm's law and circuit effect on waveforms: the gain \(|V_o|/|V_i|\) and phase shift come from the magnitude and argument of a complex ratio
Algebra and geometry: sign errors from \(j^2=-1\) show up directly as wrong quadrants on the Argand diagram, so sketching the answer checks the algebra
exq: Given \(\tilde{I}=2+j0\) A and \(Z=3j\) Ω, find \(\tilde{V}\) in rectangular form, its magnitude and phase, and state whether V leads or lags I. Sketch the phasor diagram.
Expand and simplify \((1+j)(1+j)\) and \(\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}+\tfrac{j}{\sqrt2}\right)^3\). Verify each result using magnitude and angle, and plot them on an Argand diagram.
Plot \(3+j1\), \(-2+j2\) and \(-1-j3\) on an Argand diagram, state the quadrant of each, and find each magnitude and angle.
A circuit has input phasor \(1+j0\) V and output phasor \(0.5j\) V. Find the gain and phase shift, and the impedance if the current is 1 A. Explain why this is not a simple resistance.
Show that multiplying a phasor by \(j^2\) is equivalent to a 180° rotation, and use this to find the result of multiplying \(V_1=1+j0\) by \(j\), \(j^2\), \(j^3\) and \(j^4\).

notes.t: Complex number system for phase rotation
pts: Multiplying a phasor by j rotates it by 90° anticlockwise on the complex plane.
Multiplying by −1 rotates a phasor by 180° (π radians), which is the same as two successive 90° turns.
Phasors are represented as points on the complex plane: the horizontal axis holds the real part and the vertical axis holds the imaginary part.
Multiplying by j twice gives j² = −1, so the phase rotation of two 90° steps is equivalent to multiplying by −1.
A complex number is written as a real part plus j times an imaginary part, so V1 = 1 + j0, V2 = 0 + j1 and V3 = −1 + j0 represent the three phasors at 0°, 90° and 180°.
defs: Complex number
A number of the form a + jb, where a is the real part and b is the imaginary part, with j = √(−1).
Imaginary unit j
The operator j = √(−1), so j² = −1; multiplying by j rotates a phasor by 90°.
Imaginary number
A number multiplied by j, lying on the vertical (j) axis of the complex plane.
eqs: Z = complex number (dimensionless in phasor representation); a = real part (same unit as Z); b = imaginary part (same unit as Z); j = imaginary unit
V_3 = rotated phasor (same unit as V_1); V_1 = original phasor (same unit as V_3)
Phase rotation of 180° via two 90° turns
V_3 = rotated phasor; V_1 = original phasor; j = imaginary unit (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse j (engineering notation for √−1) with the current symbol i; in electrical engineering j is used to avoid clashing with current.
Remember that j² = −1 only; j is not a real number, so you cannot simply treat jb as a real quantity when comparing magnitudes.
rq: Why does multiplying by j rotate a phasor by 90° rather than stretching it?

Because j has magnitude 1 and lies on the unit circle at 90°; multiplying complex numbers adds their angles and multiplies their magnitudes, so the magnitude stays unchanged and the phase shifts by 90°.
What would happen to V1 = 1 + j0 if it were multiplied by j three times?
j³ = −j, so V1 × j³ = −j, i.e. 0 − j1, which is a 270° rotation (equivalently −90°) pointing along the negative imaginary axis.
Why is it useful to write 180° as j² rather than simply −1?
Writing it as j² shows the rotation as two successive 90° steps, making the phase-shift interpretation explicit and generalising to any angle as repeated multiplication by j.

notes.t: Complex plane (Argand diagram)
pts: Complex numbers can be plotted as points or vectors on a plane with a real axis (horizontal) and an imaginary axis (vertical, labelled j).
A complex number a + jb is located by moving a units along the real axis and b units along the imaginary axis from the origin.
The sign of each component sets the quadrant: positive real and imaginary parts plot in the first quadrant, negative parts in the third.
Each complex number can be drawn as a line from the origin, so its magnitude is the length of that line and its phase is the angle from the real axis.
defs: Argand diagram
A plane whose horizontal axis represents the real part and whose vertical axis represents the imaginary part (multiplied by j) of a complex number, used to represent complex numbers geometrically.
Imaginary unit j
The operator j = √(−1) used in electrical engineering in place of i, so that a complex number is written as a + jb.
eqs: Rectangular form of a complex number
z = complex number (dimensionless); a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless); j = √(−1) (dimensionless)
tips: Don't confuse the real and imaginary coordinates: in 3 + j1 the real part is 3, not 1, so the point lies at (3, 1).
Remember that j stands for √(−1) in engineering notation; using i in exam answers may be marked inconsistently with the course convention.
rq: Why does the point −1 − j3 lie in the third quadrant rather than the second?
Both its real part (−1) and its imaginary part (−3) are negative, so it lies left of the origin and below the real axis, which is the third quadrant.
What happens to the plotted position if the real and imaginary parts of 3 + j1 are swapped to form 1 + j3?

The point moves from the lower-right region to the upper-left of the first quadrant, mirroring the position across the 45° line: the real and imaginary coordinates determine the location, not their order of reading.

notes.t: Complex numbers: phase and amplitude in AC circuits
pts: A complex number I₁ = 1 + j0 lies on the real axis, so it has zero phase and unit magnitude.
Multiplying by the complex impedance Z = 0.5j rotates the phasor by 90° and scales its magnitude by 0.5, producing a voltage that leads the current.
Multiplying complex numbers changes both phase and amplitude, so a complex impedance acts as a single operator on a phasor.
Because j² = −1, the product of j with itself becomes a real number, which is what lets the imaginary term collapse to a purely imaginary result here.
eqs: Voltage phasor from current phasor and impedance (Ohm's law in complex form)
\underline{V}_1 = voltage phasor (V); \underline{I}_1 = current phasor (A); Z = complex impedance (Ω)
Worked result: voltage phasor for I₁ = 1 and Z = 0.5j
tips: Remember j² = −1: do not leave j² terms unsimplified, as the term j²·0 vanishes only because it is multiplied by zero.
Phasor diagrams show magnitude and angle; always state units (V, A, Ω) when reading V₁ and I₁ from the diagram.
rq: Why does multiplying by 0.5j shift the phase by 90° rather than just making the number smaller?
Multiplying by j rotates a complex number 90° anticlockwise in the Argand diagram; the 0.5 factor scales the magnitude by 0.5. Both effects happen together.
What would happen to V₁ if Z were −0.5j instead?
The result would be −0.5j, a 90° rotation in the opposite direction (phase −90°) with the same magnitude 0.5 V.

notes.t: AC Circuits - Effect of Circuits on Waveforms
pts: Most electrical circuits act on an input AC signal in one of three ways: leaving it unaltered, changing its magnitude, or changing its phase.
A circuit may change the magnitude of the input signal so that the output amplitude is smaller than the input amplitude (Vi > Vo in the figure).
A circuit may introduce a phase difference (lag) between input and output, shown as a rotation of the output phasor relative to the input phasor.
In the phasor diagrams, the input is shown as a reference phasor Vin along the horizontal axis, and the output phasor Vout is compared against it.
defs: Phase difference (lag)
The angular difference, in degrees or radians, between the corresponding points of an output waveform and the input waveform; a lag means the output reaches its peak after the input.
tips: Do not confuse a phase lag (output behind input) with a lead; check the direction of rotation of the output phasor.
Ensure the magnitude comparison uses consistent units (peak or RMS) for both Vi and Vo.
rq: Why is a phasor diagram useful for showing what a circuit does to an AC signal?
It represents each sinusoid as a rotating vector, so magnitude changes appear as length changes and phase shifts appear as angular rotation relative to the input phasor.
If a circuit output has the same amplitude as the input but lags by 90°, which of the three effects has it produced?
Only a phase change; the magnitude is unaltered, so the output phasor is simply rotated clockwise relative to Vin.

notes.t: Complex numbers and impedance in AC circuits
pts: Ohm's law is extended for AC: voltage and current are related through a complex impedance Z rather than a real resistance R.
Impedance Z is a complex number, so it can account for components that change the phase of a signal.
Voltage and current in AC circuits are phasors, representing both magnitude and phase of a sinusoidal function.
Using complex numbers avoids the messy trigonometric identities needed to combine sinusoids.
defs: Impedance (Z)
The complex generalisation of resistance in AC circuits, Z = a + jb, measured in ohms, whose real part is resistance and whose imaginary part is reactance.
Phasor
A complex number representing the magnitude and phase of a sinusoidal voltage or current, allowing AC quantities to be manipulated algebraically.
eqs: Generalised Ohm's law for AC circuits (phasor form)
\tilde{V} = phasor voltage (V); \tilde{I} = phasor current (A); Z = impedance (Ω)
Z = impedance (Ω); a = real part, resistance (Ω); b = imaginary part, reactance (Ω); j = imaginary unit (√-1)
tips: Do not apply V = IR directly to AC signals; use the phasor form with complex impedance Z.
Keep the real and imaginary parts of Z distinct: the real part is resistance, the imaginary part is reactance, both in ohms.
rq: Why does a purely real resistance R become a complex impedance Z when the signal is sinusoidal?
Some components shift the phase between voltage and current, which a single real number cannot represent; the imaginary part of Z captures this phase change.
Why are phasors more convenient than working directly with sinusoidal time functions?
Phasors turn differentiation and integration into algebra, so sinusoids can be added and divided without trigonometric identities.

notes.t: Complex numbers: multiplication worked example (polar/phasor view)
pts: A complex number a + jb can be written as a point or phasor in the complex plane; here each factor has magnitude 1 and lies at 45°.
Multiplying two complex numbers is done by expanding brackets term by term, just like ordinary algebra, then using j² = −1.
The product of two unit-magnitude phasors at 45° each gives a phasor at 90° (pointing along +j), so the answer is j.
Multiplying complex numbers adds their angles, a key shortcut for AC phasor analysis.
defs: j
The imaginary unit, defined by j² = −1 (used in electrical engineering instead of i).
eqs: Product of two complex numbers in the example, expanded term by term
tips: Forgetting that j² = −1 turns the j·j term into −1/2 (not +1/2); a sign error here changes the real part of the answer.
Multiplying the magnitudes is correct, but students often forget to also add the phase angles when working in polar form.
rq: Why does the product of the two factors come out purely imaginary (equal to j) rather than having a real part?
Each factor is at 45°, so their angles add to 90°; a phasor at 90° has zero real part and unit magnitude, i.e. it equals j. The real terms 1/2 and −1/2 cancel the 1/2 from the j·j term leaving zero.
What would happen to the product's angle if one factor were rotated to 30° instead of 45°?
The angles add, giving 30° + 45° = 75°, so the product would be cos75° + j sin75° rather than j.

units.name: 1.10 Lecture 1 summary
units.ov: This lecture introduces how speakers reproduce sound by driving them with time-varying (AC) voltage and current, where individual sinusoidal waves superimpose to form complex music. Because circuits with reactive elements respond differently to different frequencies and phases, resistance is generalised to complex impedance \(Z = a + jb\). The sinusoid \(V(t)=V_0\sin(\omega t+\phi)\) describes the signal, and impedance describes how the circuit acts on it.
must: Sinusoidal voltage: \(V(t) = V_0 \sin(\omega t + \phi)\), with \(V_0\) the peak amplitude (V), \(\omega\) the angular frequency (rad/s) and \(\phi\) the phase angle (rad)
Convert frequency to angular frequency with \(\omega = 2\pi f\), and keep \(\omega\) in rad/s (not Hz) in all formulae
Impedance is complex: \(Z = a + jb\,\Omega\), where \(a\) is the resistance (real part) and \(b\) is the reactance (imaginary part)
Do not treat impedance as plain resistance when the circuit contains reactive elements; the imaginary part affects amplitude and phase
\(j\) is the imaginary unit (\(j^2=-1\)), used in engineering instead of \(i\)
Sound is produced by varying the voltage and current sent to the speaker, and multiple waves superimpose or interfere to give complex music
Phase angle \(\phi\) shifts the wave in time and determines how waves add (constructive or destructive interference)
Impedance and resistance share the unit ohm (\(\Omega\)) but only the real part dissipates energy as resistance
conn: Sinusoid parameters (\(\omega\), \(\phi\)) link to impedance: a reactive element's \(b\) depends on \(\omega\), so the same circuit responds differently at different frequencies
Phase angle links superposition and impedance: complex impedance causes a phase shift between voltage and current, which changes how waves combine
Rectangular form \(a+jb\) connects to magnitude and phase (polar form), so impedance can be used with the \(\phi\) of the sinusoid
Frequency conversion \(\omega = 2\pi f\) is a prerequisite step in nearly every impedance calculation
exq: A speaker is driven by a 1 kHz sinusoidal signal of peak amplitude 5 V and phase \(\pi/6\). Write \(V(t)\) and find \(V\) at \(t = 0.2\) ms.
Convert frequencies of 50 Hz, 440 Hz and 20 kHz to angular frequency in rad/s, and state the period of each.
A speaker circuit has impedance \(Z = 6 + j8\,\Omega\). Identify the resistance and reactance, and find the magnitude \(|Z|\) and phase angle of the impedance.
Explain why treating the impedance \(Z = 4 + j3\,\Omega\) as a 4 Ω resistor gives the wrong current for a given AC voltage, and compute the correct peak current for \(V_0 = 10\) V.
Two sinusoidal waves of equal amplitude differ in phase by \(\pi\). Describe and show mathematically the resulting superposition, and relate it to sound from two speakers.

notes.t: Lecture 1 Summary: AC waves and impedance in speaker circuits
pts: Sound is reproduced by creating waves, achieved by varying the voltage and current sent to the speakers.
The individual waves interfere or superimpose to produce the complex music we hear.
For many circuit designs, impedance rather than resistance must be considered, because it is a complex quantity with real and imaginary parts.
eqs: Sinusoidal voltage as a function of time
V(t) = instantaneous voltage (V); V_0 = peak amplitude (V); \omega = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s); \phi = phase angle (rad)
Z = impedance (\Omega); a = real part, resistance (\Omega); b = imaginary part, reactance (\Omega); j = imaginary unit
tips: Impedance is written in ohms (Ω) but is complex; do not treat it as a plain resistance when the circuit contains reactive elements.
Keep angular frequency ω in rad/s; converting from frequency f in Hz requires ω = 2πf.
rq: Why is a sinusoidal function such as V(t) = V_0 sin(ωt + φ) a suitable way to describe the signal sent to a speaker?
Sound is a wave, and a sinusoid captures its oscillation: amplitude sets loudness, frequency ω sets pitch, and phase φ sets the timing offset between waves, which determines how they interfere.
Why does a speaker circuit need impedance rather than plain resistance?
Speakers contain inductive and capacitive effects that change with frequency, so the opposition to current has a frequency-dependent phase shift that resistance alone cannot describe.

units.name: 2.1 Lecture 1 recap and need for complex impedance
units.ov: This material recaps Lecture 1: sound as superposed waves produced by varying voltage and current, and AC signals described as sinusoids with amplitude, angular frequency and phase. It then motivates complex impedance Z = a + jb as the generalisation of resistance, so that Ohm's law becomes V = IZ and phase shifts can be handled with complex numbers instead of trigonometric identities.
must: An AC voltage is \( V(t) = V_0 \sin(\omega t + \phi) \), with \(V_0\) the peak amplitude (V), \(\omega\) the angular frequency (rad/s) and \(\phi\) the phase (rad)
Generalised Ohm's law for AC: \( V = IZ \), reducing to \( V = IR \) when Z is purely real (a resistor)
Impedance is complex: \( Z = a + jb \ \Omega \), where \(a\) is the resistive (real) part and \(b\) is the reactive (imaginary) part that accounts for phase shift
Z is measured in ohms, but it is not a scalar resistance: keep both real and imaginary parts in calculations
The imaginary unit is \( j = \sqrt{-1} \) (the engineering notation, rather than i)
Complex numbers avoid cumbersome trigonometric identities when analysing phase-shifting AC circuits
Keep the angle \( \omega t + \phi \) in radians when \(\omega\) is in rad/s; do not mix in degrees
Sound reproduction needs time-varying voltage and current to drive the speaker; waves superimpose and the combined pattern is perceived as music
Components that shift phase need impedance rather than resistance, so AC circuit design must consider impedance
conn: Sinusoid parameters (amplitude, \(\omega\), \(\phi\)) link to impedance: the phase shift between V and I is carried by the imaginary part of Z
Generalised Ohm's law \( V = IZ \) combines with complex arithmetic: dividing or multiplying complex quantities gives both magnitude and phase of the response
Superposition of sinusoids (sound waves) links to using complex representation to add signals of the same frequency but different phases
Resistor as the special case of impedance (b = 0) links the DC Ohm's law to the AC form
exq: Write the general expression for a sinusoidal voltage. For \( V_0 = 5\,\text{V} \), \( f = 1\,\text{kHz} \) and \( \phi = \pi/6 \), find \(\omega\) and V(t) at \( t = 0.2\,\text{ms} \), stating the angle units used.
Explain why resistance alone is insufficient in AC circuit design and define impedance, identifying its real and imaginary parts and their physical meaning.
A component has \( Z = 30 + j40\,\Omega \). Find the current phasor for an applied voltage of \( 10\,\text{V} \) (taking V as the reference), using \( V = IZ \).
State how Ohm's law generalises from DC to AC. For what values of a and b does Z reduce to a pure resistor?
Why are complex numbers preferred to trigonometric identities for AC analysis? Illustrate with the sum of two sinusoids of the same frequency but different phases.

notes.t: Lecture 1 Summary: Sound waves and AC circuit quantities
pts: Reproducing sound requires creating waves by varying the voltage and current sent to the speaker.
Sound waves interfere or superimpose, and this combined pattern is what we perceive as music.
An alternating voltage can be described as a sinusoid with amplitude, angular frequency and phase.
In AC circuit design, impedance rather than resistance must be considered, since it is complex (real and imaginary parts).
eqs: Instantaneous voltage of a sinusoidal AC signal
V(t) = instantaneous voltage (V); V_0 = peak amplitude (V); \omega = angular frequency (rad/s); t = time (s); \phi = phase angle (rad)
Z = impedance (\Omega); a = resistive (real) part (\Omega); b = reactive (imaginary) part (\Omega); j = imaginary unit
tips: Impedance is in ohms (Ω) but is a complex quantity; do not treat it as a simple scalar like resistance.
Ensure the angle in sin(ωt + φ) is in radians when ω is in rad/s, not degrees.
rq: Why does a speaker need a time-varying voltage and current rather than a constant one to produce sound?
A constant voltage produces a steady displacement with no vibration; sound requires the cone to oscillate, so the voltage must vary periodically to create pressure waves.
Why is resistance alone insufficient for describing a speaker circuit with AC signals?
Speaker coils have inductance and capacitive effects that shift the phase and depend on frequency; impedance captures both magnitude and phase.

notes.t: Complex numbers and impedance
pts: Ohm's law V = IR holds for resistors, but components that shift signal phase need a generalised form.
Replacing R with impedance Z gives V = IZ, which accounts for phase changes in signals.
Impedance Z is a complex number, with a real part a and an imaginary part jb, measured in ohms.
Using complex numbers avoids the more cumbersome trigonometric identities when analysing AC circuits.
defs: Impedance (Z)
The generalised resistance in AC circuits, a complex quantity Z = a + jb (Ω) whose real part is resistance and whose imaginary part accounts for phase shift.
eqs: V = voltage (V); I = current (A); R = resistance (Ω)
Generalised Ohm's law for AC circuits with phase change
V = voltage (V); I = current (A); Z = impedance (Ω)
Z = impedance (Ω); a = real part (Ω); b = imaginary part (Ω); j = imaginary unit (√-1)
tips: Do not treat impedance Z as a plain real resistance; it is complex, so keep both real and imaginary parts when calculating.
Remember Z is measured in ohms (Ω) like R, so the units in V = IZ are unchanged.
rq: Why can't a plain resistance R describe a component that changes signal phase?
A resistor keeps voltage and current in phase, so a real-valued R cannot represent a phase shift; the complex impedance Z adds an imaginary part that encodes it.
Why are complex numbers preferred over trigonometric identities for AC circuits?
Complex arithmetic lets phase shifts be handled as simple algebra (multiplication and addition) instead of combining sine and cosine terms with trig identities.

units.name: 2.2 Phasors as rotating vectors
units.ov: This material introduces phasors: rotating arrows in the complex plane whose length gives a sinusoid's amplitude and whose angle gives its phase. All the waves must share one angular frequency, so the phase offset between them stays fixed. The vertical (or horizontal) projection of a rotating phasor gives the instantaneous sine or cosine value, which links circular motion to waveforms and lets sinusoids be treated as fixed vectors in AC analysis.
must: A phasor is a rotating arrow in the complex plane: length = amplitude, angle = phase, rotating at a common angular frequency \(\omega\)
Projecting the phasor onto the vertical axis gives a sine wave, \(y(t)=A\sin(\omega t+\phi)\); projecting onto the horizontal axis gives a cosine wave
Phase difference is the angle between two phasors, e.g. \(\pi/4\) rad = 45°, and it corresponds to a time shift \(\Delta t=\Delta\phi/\omega\)
Phasors only apply when all waves have the same \(\omega\); for different frequencies the phase difference is not constant and has no meaning
Always state whether the reference is sine or cosine, because \(\sin(\omega t)=\cos(\omega t-\pi/2)\), a 90° shift in the stated phase
Arrow length (amplitude) and angle (phase) are independent: a larger angle does not mean a larger signal
A positive phase angle means the phasor leads (is ahead, anticlockwise) and a negative one means it lags
Because the phase offset is constant, each sinusoid reduces to a fixed vector at \(t=0\), which is the basis of AC analysis
Converting between a phasor diagram and a waveform plot: read amplitude from length, read phase from the angle at \(t=0\)
conn: Phasors with complex numbers: \(Ae^{j(\omega t+\phi)}\) has the sinusoid as its imaginary (sine) or real (cosine) part, so phase shifts become multiplication by \(e^{j\phi}\)
Phasors with simple harmonic motion: SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion, so \(\omega=2\pi f=2\pi/T\) links rotation rate, frequency and period
Phase difference with time shift: an angle on the phasor diagram corresponds to a horizontal offset between plotted waveforms, via \(\Delta t=\Delta\phi/\omega\)
Adding sinusoids of the same frequency with phasors: vector addition of the arrows gives the resultant amplitude and phase, which is also used for superposition and AC circuits
exq: Two signals \(y_1=3\sin(100t)\) and \(y_2=5\sin(100t+\pi/4)\) are drawn as phasors. Give the length of each phasor, the angle between them, which one leads, and the time shift between the waveforms in ms.
Write \(y=4\cos(\omega t)\) as a sine function with a phase angle, and say how the phasor diagram changes if the reference is switched from cosine to sine.
Explain why a phasor diagram cannot be used to find a fixed phase difference between a 50 Hz wave and a 60 Hz wave. What happens to the angle between their arrows over time?
Add \(2\sin(\omega t)\) and \(3\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)\) using phasors. Find the amplitude and phase of the resultant and sketch the diagram.
A rotating phasor of length 2 rotates at \(\omega=10\) rad/s starting at 30° above the horizontal axis. Write the vertical projection as a function of time and find its value at \(t=0.1\) s.

notes.t: Phasors
pts: Two sinusoids of the same angular frequency keep a fixed phase offset between them, shown here as the angle π/4 between the rotating arrows.
Because the phase offset is constant, a rotating arrow (phasor) can represent the amplitude and phase of a (co)sinusoidal function.
Projecting each phasor onto the vertical axis as it rotates gives the instantaneous value of the corresponding sine or cosine wave.
defs: Phasor
A rotating arrow in the complex plane whose length gives the amplitude and whose angle gives the phase of a (co)sinusoidal function, all at a common angular frequency.
tips: Phasors only apply when all waves have the same angular frequency; the phase relationship is meaningless between waves of different frequencies.
Be clear whether the reference is sine or cosine, since a 90° difference changes the phase angle stated.
rq: Why can we drop the time-varying rotation and describe each sinusoid by a fixed arrow?
All the waves share the same angular frequency, so the relative angle between their arrows never changes; only the common rotation differs, which can be ignored, leaving amplitude and phase.

notes.t: Phasors: representing sinusoids as rotating vectors
pts: A phasor is a rotating arrow (vector) in the complex plane whose projection onto one axis gives a sinusoidal function of time.
The length of the phasor encodes the amplitude of the sinusoid.
The angle between two phasors encodes the phase difference between the two sinusoids, so the waveforms are shifted in time relative to each other.
The vertical projection of a rotating phasor traces out the sine (or cosine) waveform, which is why the diagram links the circle to the plotted curves.
defs: Phasor
A rotating vector whose length represents the amplitude of a sinusoid and whose angle represents its phase, used to represent sinusoidal signals as fixed vectors in AC analysis.
Phase difference
The angular difference between two sinusoids of the same frequency, shown as the angle between their phasors.
tips: Phasor angles only have meaning when comparing signals of the same frequency; phasors at different frequencies cannot be compared on one diagram.
Do not confuse the arrow length (amplitude) with the angle (phase); a larger angle does not mean a larger signal.
rq: Why does a rotating phasor let us compare two AC signals at a glance?
Because amplitude is shown by length and phase difference by the angle between the arrows, so both can be read directly from the geometry without plotting waveforms.
What would happen to the phasor diagram if the two signals were at the same frequency but one was delayed?
The delayed signal's phasor would be rotated by an angle equal to the phase shift relative to the other, while both keep their lengths.

units.name: 2.3 Complex numbers: j-operator, rectangular and polar forms
units.ov: This module introduces the j-operator (j = √−1, j² = −1) as a 90° anticlockwise rotation on the complex plane. It builds rectangular form Z = a + jb and polar form Z = |Z|∠θ, with conversions between them via Pythagoras and arctan. Polar form makes multiplication and division simple (multiply or divide magnitudes, add or subtract angles), which is applied to phasor Ohm's law V = IZ in AC circuits.
must: Definition of j: \( j=\sqrt{-1} \), \( j^2=-1 \); multiplying by j rotates a phasor 90° anticlockwise without changing its size (|j|=1)
Two j-rotations give 180°: \( V_3=V_1\times j^2=-V_1 \); never write j = −1
Rectangular form \( Z=a+jb \): a is the real (horizontal) part, b is the imaginary (vertical) coefficient of j
Magnitude \( |Z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2} \) and phase angle \( \phi=\arctan(b/a) \)
Quadrant check: arctan(b/a) from a calculator is wrong when a < 0 (add 180° or use the sketch of the complex plane)
Polar form \( Z=|Z|\angle\theta \); convert to the rectangular form with \( a=|Z|\cos\theta \), \( b=|Z|\sin\theta \)
Polar multiplication: \( Z_1Z_2=r_1r_2\angle(\theta_1+\theta_2) \)
Polar division: \( Z_1/Z_2=(r_1/r_2)\angle(\theta_1-\theta_2) \)
Phasor Ohm's law \( V=IZ \): amplitude scales by |Z| and phase shifts by arg Z; e.g. \( 1\angle0^\circ\times0.5j=0.5\angle90^\circ \)
Keep angles in consistent units (degrees or radians), convert purely imaginary numbers such as 0.5j to 0.5∠90° before multiplying, and normalise the final angle
conn: Rectangular and polar forms: use rectangular form for addition and subtraction, polar form for multiplication and division, so a single problem often requires converting both ways
j² = −1 and the rotation picture: expanding (a+jb)(c+jd) in rectangular form gives the same result as multiplying magnitudes and adding angles in polar form, so you can use one to check the other
Complex impedance and phasor Ohm's law: Z = jX (e.g. 0.5j) gives a +90° phase shift of V relative to I, linking complex algebra to AC circuit phase and amplitude
Arctan and quadrants: the sign of a and b determines the angle, which affects the phase result in circuit calculations
exq: Convert Z = −3 + j4 to polar form, giving the magnitude and the angle in degrees (check the quadrant), then convert 10∠−60° to rectangular form.
Starting from a phasor V₁ = 5∠0°, find V₂ = V₁·j and V₃ = V₁·j² and sketch all three on the complex plane. Explain why j ≠ −1.
A current I = 2∠30° A flows through an impedance Z = 3 + j4 Ω. Find the voltage phasor V = IZ in polar form, giving its amplitude and phase.
Given Z₁ = 8∠70° and Z₂ = 2∠−20°, calculate Z₁Z₂ and Z₁/Z₂ in polar form, then express the answers in rectangular form.
Show that (1 + j0)(0.5j) = 0.5j, write the result in polar form, and state the amplitude scaling and phase shift produced by the impedance 0.5j Ω.

notes.t: Complex numbers and the complex plane (j-operator rotations)
pts: Multiplying a phasor by j rotates it 90° anticlockwise on the complex plane.
Multiplying by −1 rotates a phasor through 180°, so two j-rotations give a half turn.
A complex number has a real part a and an imaginary part b, written as a sum with j attached to b.
Numbers multiplied by j are imaginary; the j-coefficient gives the vertical (imaginary-axis) component.
Phasors V1, V2, V3 sit at 0°, 90° and 180° on the complex plane, written as a + jb coordinates.
defs: Imaginary unit j
The operator j = √(−1), satisfying j² = −1; multiplying by j rotates a phasor by 90° anticlockwise.
Complex number
A number Z = a + jb with a real part a and imaginary part b, plotted as a point or vector on the complex plane.
Real number
The real-valued component a of a complex number Z = a + jb, lying on the horizontal axis.
Imaginary number
A number of the form jb (b real), i.e. a real number multiplied by j; lies on the vertical axis.
Complex plane
A two-dimensional plane with real numbers on the horizontal axis and imaginary (j) numbers on the vertical axis, used to represent complex numbers and phasors.
eqs: Rectangular form of a complex number
Z = complex number (dimensionless); a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless)
V_1 = starting phasor; V_3 = rotated phasor (same unit as V_1)
V_1 = starting phasor; V_2 = rotated phasor (same unit as V_1)
tips: Do not confuse rotation with scaling: j has magnitude 1, so multiplying by j changes direction, not size.
Remember that 180° = two 90° turns (j² = −1), not j = −1; a common error is writing j = −1.
rq: Why does multiplying by j rotate a phasor by 90° rather than scaling it?
Because j² = −1, so applying j twice gives −1 (a 180° turn); j acts as a unit-magnitude operator that advances the angle by 90° with no change in length.
What would happen to V1 = 1 + j0 if you multiplied it by j² instead of j?
j² = −1 gives V3 = −1 + j0, a 180° rotation to the opposite side of the real axis.
How can you tell from a + jb alone which quadrant or axis a complex number lies on?
The sign and size of a (horizontal) and b (vertical) locate the point; b = 0 means on the real axis, a = 0 means on the imaginary axis.

notes.t: Complex numbers: rectangular and polar forms
pts: A complex number can be written in rectangular form as a real part plus j times an imaginary part, locating a point on the complex plane.
The magnitude of a complex number is the distance from the origin to the point, found by Pythagoras.
The phase angle is the angle the line from the origin makes with the real axis, found using arctangent of b over a.
Polar form expresses a complex number by its magnitude and angle, which simplifies multiplication, division and many circuit calculations.
defs: Rectangular form
Representation of a complex number as Z = a + jb, where a is the real part and b is the imaginary part.
Polar form
Representation of a complex number by its magnitude and phase angle, Z = |Z|∠θ.
Argument (phase angle)
The angle φ between the positive real axis and the line from the origin to the complex number, φ = arg(Z).
eqs: Phase angle of a complex number
φ = phase angle (rad or °); a = real part (dimensionless); b = imaginary part (dimensionless)
|Z| = magnitude (same unit as Z); a = real part; b = imaginary part
Z = complex number; |Z| = magnitude; θ = phase angle (rad or °)
tips: Check the quadrant when finding θ from arctan(b/a); a calculator gives the wrong angle for a < 0.
Keep angles consistent in degrees or radians throughout a calculation.
rq: Why does arctan(b/a) give the correct angle only when a is positive?
arctan returns angles between −90° and +90°, so for points in the left half-plane (a < 0) you must add 180° (or use atan2) to get the correct quadrant.
Why is polar form more convenient than rectangular form for multiplying impedances in a circuit?
In polar form you multiply magnitudes and add angles, which is simpler than expanding products of real and imaginary parts.

notes.t: Complex numbers: phase and amplitude in a system
pts: Multiplying a complex current by a complex impedance gives the voltage; the result's amplitude and phase both change.
Here I₁ = 1 (real, angle 0°) multiplied by Z = 0.5j (angle 90°) gives V₁ = 0.5j, so the phase shifts by +90° and the amplitude is scaled by 0.5.
Multiplying by j rotates a phasor by 90° anticlockwise, and j·j = −1 turns the product back into a real number.
defs: j (imaginary unit)
The operator j satisfying j² = −1, used to represent a 90° phase rotation in complex-number phasor notation.
eqs: Voltage from current and impedance (Ohm's law in complex form)
V_1 = phasor voltage (V); I_1 = phasor current (A); Z = complex impedance (Ω)
tips: Don't forget that j² = −1; dropping the j² term or treating it as +1 gives the wrong real part.
Phase angles are in degrees with the reference phasor at 0°; a result of 0.5∠90° means the amplitude is 0.5 and the phase is 90°, not 0.5 rad.
rq: Why does multiplying the real number 1 by 0.5j produce a voltage that lags or leads the current, rather than just a smaller real voltage?
