formulas.vars: R_1, R_2 = resistances (Ω)
formulas.use: Exactly two parallel resistors

formulas.name: Current divider
formulas.vars: I_tot = total current into the pair (A); R_1, R_2 = branch resistances (Ω)
formulas.use: Two parallel branches; larger share through smaller resistance

formulas.name: Parallel branch currents (KCL)
formulas.vars: I_T = total current (A); V_B = common voltage (V)
formulas.use: Parallel circuit with common voltage

formulas.name: Series-parallel reduction
formulas.vars: R_{eq} = equivalent resistance (Ω); R_1 in series with R_2∥R_3
formulas.use: Reduce step by step, then find source current and work back with Ohm's law/dividers

formulas.name: Thévenin equivalent
formulas.vars: V_T = Thévenin voltage (V); R_T = Thévenin resistance (Ω); v_oc = open-circuit voltage (V); i_sc = short-circuit current (A)
formulas.use: Replace any linear two-terminal network; R_T also found by zeroing sources (voltage sources short, current sources open) and combining resistors

formulas.name: Load current/voltage with Thévenin source
formulas.vars: i_L = load current (A); V_L = load voltage (V); R_L = load resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: After replacing the circuit by its Thévenin equivalent

formulas.name: Norton equivalent / source transformation
formulas.latex: I_N = i_{sc} = \frac{V_T}{R_T},\quad R_N = R_T,\quad V_T = R_T I_N
formulas.vars: I_N = Norton current (A); R_N = Norton resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Convert between Thévenin and Norton forms

formulas.name: Practical source terminal voltage
formulas.latex: V_L = I R_L = V_o - I R_o
formulas.vars: V_o = ideal source voltage (V); R_o = internal resistance (Ω); I = load current (A)
formulas.use: Source with internal resistance; terminal voltage drops with load

formulas.name: Maximum power transfer condition
formulas.vars: R_L = load resistance (Ω); R_T = Thévenin resistance (Ω)
formulas.use: Load receives maximum power when equal to source resistance (from dP/dR_L = 0)

formulas.name: Load power
formulas.vars: P_L = load power (W); V_T = Thévenin voltage (V)
formulas.use: Power vs R_L; at matching, P_max = V_T²/(4R_T)

formulas.name: Superposition
formulas.vars: r_k = response (V or A) due to source k alone; r_T = total response
formulas.use: Linear circuits; set other voltage sources to short, current sources to open; add signed responses

formulas.name: Delta to star
formulas.vars: R_1,R_2,R_3 = delta resistors (Ω); R_A,R_B,R_C = star arms (Ω)
formulas.use: Each star arm = product of two adjacent delta resistors over the sum; for bridge networks

formulas.name: Star to delta
formulas.vars: R_A,R_B,R_C = star arms (Ω); R_1,R_2,R_3 = delta resistors (Ω)
formulas.use: Delta resistor = sum of pairwise products over opposite star arm

formulas.name: Two-mesh equations (standard form)
formulas.vars: i_1, i_2 = clockwise mesh currents (A); R_3 = shared resistor (Ω); V_A, V_B = source voltages (V)
formulas.use: KVL per mesh: self-resistance × own current − shared resistance × neighbour current = source EMF

formulas.name: Cramer's rule
formulas.vars: det(R) = determinant of resistance matrix; det(R_i) = determinant with column i replaced by voltage vector
formulas.use: Solve [R][I] = [V]

formulas.name: 2×2 determinant
formulas.latex: \begin{vmatrix} a & b\\ c & d\end{vmatrix} = ad - bc
formulas.vars: a, b, c, d = matrix entries
formulas.use: Evaluate Cramer's rule determinants

formulas.name: Branch current from mesh currents
formulas.latex: I_R = i_k - i_m \ (\text{shared}),\quad I_R = i_k \ (\text{outer branch})
formulas.vars: I_R = current in resistor (A); i_k, i_m = adjacent mesh currents (A)
formulas.use: After solving; sign shows direction

formulas.name: Mesh with a current source
formulas.vars: I_S = current source value (A)
formulas.use: Source in only one mesh fixes that mesh current; write KVL for remaining meshes

formulas.name: Three-mesh matrix form
formulas.vars: i_k = mesh currents (A); R = resistances (Ω); V = source voltages (V)
formulas.use: Example of three-mesh circuit; diagonal = sum of mesh resistances, off-diagonal = −shared

rep.ov: Mechanical Design 1 (ENG1016) first covers basic fluid machines and thermal/transmission elements: valves (globe, gate, butterfly, relief), pumps (positive displacement and centrifugal) and pumps in systems, heat exchangers (plate and shell-and-tube), clutches (positive contact, friction, overrunning, fluid coupling), then mountings and gearboxes. Each topic follows the same pattern of purpose, principle, types, construction, materials and design considerations. Pump work builds on valves and system resistance through system curves, static/dynamic head and operating points. Clutch work builds on torque-power-speed relations. Concept selection (PDS and decision matrices) and engineering drawing and fluid-diagram standards support the Semester 2 project. Note that assessment is coursework only (30% set exercises, 70% design project), so the Moodle quizzes and in-class exercise test this content.
must: Pump classification: positive displacement (fluid enclosed once per cycle, flow set by speed, pressure set by system, blocks flow when stopped, needs a relief valve) versus centrifugal (impeller gives kinetic energy, volute converts it to pressure, flow set by system, no relief valve needed)
System curve: head required vs flow, \( H = H_{static} + kQ^2 \); starts at the origin if there is no static head and above zero if there is; best/worst cases as valves change
Operating point = intersection of pump curve and system curve; PD pump curve is near-vertical, centrifugal falls with flow; selecting a pump means matching it to the required duty
Static head \( H_{static} = H_{suction} + H_{discharge} \) (elevation only, in m of fluid, independent of density) versus dynamic head (friction, rises with flow squared) and TDH as their sum

Theoretical suction lift \( H = \frac{P}{\rho g} \approx 10\) m for water; practical lift is lower because of vapour pressure, friction, leakage and cavitation (NPSH); the specific gravity effect on lift
Piston pump flow \( \dot v = (AK - V)S \) with consistent SI units (rev/s not rpm); pulsating delivery and accumulators; gear, lobe, vane and screw pumps

Valve types and duty: globe (linear, throttling, S-shaped path), gate (on/off only, low loss when fully open), butterfly (quarter-turn disc), relief and non-return; the four functions of on/off, rate, pressure, direction; globe lift \( h = D/4 \) from \( \pi R^2 = 2\pi R h \); dynamic seals (packing, PTFE) vs static seals

Heat exchanger conduction \( Q/t = kA\Delta T/d \) and the design drivers (large area, thin wall, high k, no mixing, thermal expansion); \( Q = UA\,\mathrm{LMTD} \); counter-flow is more effective than parallel-flow

Plate vs shell-and-tube exchangers: construction (corrugated plates, gaskets; tubes, tube plates, headers, floating end with O-rings and tell-tale), materials (SS 304/316, titanium, Hastelloy; NBR/EPDM seals), pros and cons, cleaning, vents, drains and sacrificial anodes

Clutch classification by engagement (positive contact, friction, overrunning, magnetic, fluid coupling) and by actuation; operating principle and applications of each, including centrifugal drum, multi-plate wet/dry disc, ratchet/roller/sprag and fluid coupling

Clutch torque analysis: \( P = T\omega \) (rad/s), place the clutch on the high-speed, low-torque side, inertial torque \( T = mk^2\alpha \), heat generated during slip, steady-state vs accelerating conditions

Gearbox power transmission needs both lubrication to the highest-loaded parts and cooling; concept selection with a PDS-weighted decision matrix; drawing standards (BS 5070-3, BS 1553, SI units, cross-over methods)
conn: Valves and pump systems: opening or closing a globe or gate valve changes system resistance, shifting the system curve and hence the operating point
Static head, suction lift and the system curve: a suction-side limit of about 10 m plus friction and NPSH constrains the pump and the static head offset of the curve
Heat exchanger conduction equation with LMTD and flow configuration: sizing area from Q, U and LMTD, linked to material conductivity and wall thickness

Clutch torque, power and gearbox position: \( P = T\omega \) fixes torque on each side of a gearbox, which sets clutch torque capacity; engagement heat from inertial torque links to wet/dry and cooling choices; gearbox heat links to lubrication
Material and seal selection recurs everywhere (valves, plate exchangers, pumps); it ties to corrosion, temperature and fluid compatibility, and feeds the decision matrix in concept selection
exq: A pump lifts water 4 m on the suction side and 12 m on the discharge side, with friction head 6 m at 20 m³/h and friction proportional to Q². Calculate the static head, sketch the system curve, and find the head and flow where it meets a given pump curve.

A single-acting piston pump has piston diameter 50 mm, stroke 80 mm, runs at 300 rpm with leakage 2 cm³ per stroke. Calculate the volumetric flow rate in m³/s and explain why the discharge is pulsed and how an accumulator helps.
Derive the maximum theoretical suction lift of water at 101 kPa. State and explain why the practical lift is lower, and how it changes for diesel with SG 0.86.

A copper wall of area 2 m², thickness 3 mm and k = 390 W/m K separates fluids with ΔT = 40 K. Calculate the heat transfer rate, then compare the effect of a stainless steel wall; compare counter-flow and parallel-flow arrangements using given terminal temperatures and LMTD.

A motor delivers 10 kW at 1500 rpm through a 5:1 reduction gearbox. Calculate the torque on each side, say where the clutch should be placed, and find the inertial torque needed to accelerate a load of known mass and radius of gyration to speed in a given time.

Compare gate, globe and butterfly valves for a clean-water shut-off supply. State the choice of valve, materials and seals, and justify them; or explain how a sprag clutch, a centrifugal drum clutch and a fluid coupling each operate and where each is suited.
weak: Reading and constructing system and pump curves: students mix up which curve is which, forget that static head offsets the curve, and misplace the operating point when valves change
Clutch torque, power and speed: unit slips between rpm and rad/s, squared radius of gyration, and deciding which side of the gearbox carries the lower torque; combining steady and accelerating cases
Head vs pressure and suction lift: head in metres is independent of density while pressure is not; the limit of about 10 m, vapour pressure and NPSH versus theoretical lift are easy to muddle

units.name: 7.1 Machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes (summary notes)
units.ov: This material introduces design considerations for machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes, using a pump-motor set on a common rigid steel baseframe as the example. It then focuses on what power transmission does to a gearbox: meshing teeth generate heat and wear, so lubrication and cooling are both needed. The linking idea is that the enclosure and mounting must keep components aligned while supporting lubrication and heat removal. Note that the source pages are brief and give no formulas.
must: A pump, coupling/guard and electric motor are mounted together on a rigid steel baseplate (common baseframe) so that their shafts stay aligned
Meshing gear teeth generate large amounts of heat, and the gearbox must be designed to remove it
Without lubricant between the teeth, meshing teeth damage each other mechanically (wear, scuffing)
Lubrication and cooling are two separate requirements, and lubrication alone is not sufficient
The lubrication system must deliver lubricant to the highest-loaded parts, not just be present in the gearbox generally
The gearbox needs a system that removes all the generated heat, not just some of it
The coupling is guarded and sits between the driver (motor) and the driven machine (pump) on the baseframe
Mounting and enclosure choices are driven by function: alignment, support, protection, and lubricant and heat management
conn: Baseframe rigidity links to shaft alignment, which affects coupling and bearing loads and so gear tooth loading, heat generation and wear
Power transmitted links to heat generated, which sets the required cooling capacity and the lubricant system design
Lubricant has a dual role: it separates the teeth to prevent mechanical damage and carries heat away, so lubrication and cooling are designed together
The enclosure must contain the lubricant, protect the gears and allow heat to be rejected, so it ties together mounting, lubrication and cooling
exq: Explain why a pump, coupling and electric motor are mounted on a common rigid steel baseframe, and describe what could go wrong if the baseplate were flexible.
List the main effects of transmitting power on a gearbox and state the design provisions needed to deal with each.
Why is lubrication alone insufficient for a gearbox? Describe how the lubrication system should deal with the highest-loaded parts and how the generated heat is removed.
Describe what happens to meshing gear teeth when lubricant is absent, and discuss how this affects gearbox life.
Sketch a pump-motor set on a baseframe, labelling the pump, coupling guard, motor and baseplate, and comment on the function of each.

notes.t: Machinery Mountings, Enclosures, and Gearboxes – Design Points
pts: This section introduces design considerations for machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes, illustrated by a pump-motor set on a common baseframe.
The pump, coupling/guard and electric motor are mounted together on a rigid steel baseplate so their shafts stay aligned.
tips: The page contains only a heading and a photo; do not invent specific design formulas or rules that are not shown on this page.
rq: Why does a pump-motor set need a rigid common baseplate rather than individual floor mountings?
A rigid common baseplate keeps the pump and motor shafts aligned and limits relative movement and vibration, which would otherwise cause coupling wear and bearing failure.

notes.t: Effects of Transmitting Power on a Gearbox
pts: Meshing gear teeth generate large amounts of heat, so the gearbox must remove this heat.
Without lubricant between the teeth, meshing teeth damage each other mechanically.
Gearboxes need lubrication systems that deliver lubricant to the highest-loaded parts.
Gearboxes need systems that remove all the generated heat, i.e. cooling as well as lubrication.
tips: Lubrication and cooling are both required; do not treat lubrication alone as sufficient.
Lubricant must reach the highest-loaded parts, not just be present in the gearbox generally.
rq: Why does lubricant serve a dual role (protection and heat removal) in a gearbox rather than just reducing friction?

Lubricant separates the meshing teeth to prevent metal-to-metal contact and damage, and it also carries away the heat generated by meshing, so it must be circulated to the highest-loaded contact points.
What would happen to a gearbox transmitting high power if its cooling system failed but lubrication continued?
Heat would build up faster than it could be removed, raising the oil and component temperature, thinning the lubricant film and risking tooth damage and failure.

units.name: 7.2 Fluid system diagrams and engineering drawing requirements (summary notes)
units.ov: This module covers the conventions that make fluid system diagrams and engineering drawings unambiguous: the British standards for symbols (BS 5070-3, BS 1553, BS ISO 1219-1, BS EN 61082-2), rules for line cross-overs and junctions, and flow diagram layout. It then moves to the drawing hierarchy (diagrams, general arrangement, detail, manufacturing, single-part and assembly drawings) governed by BS 8888, with dimensioning rules, abbreviations and orthographic views. The unifying idea is that each drawing type has a defined purpose and content, and standards ensure it is read consistently.
must: Match standard to symbol set: BS 5070-3 for fluid flow diagrams, BS 1553 for general engineering graphical symbols, BS ISO 1219-1 for pneumatics, BS EN 61082-2 for electrical symbols
BS 1553 parts: Part 1 piping systems and plant (including heating and ventilation), Part 2 power generating plant (steam and IC engines, turbines), Part 3 compressing plant

Cross-overs: drawn at right angles with no change of direction; use one of the three methods (1, 2 or 3) consistently across a diagram set; with the hump method (2) the jumper preferably sits on the horizontal line
Junctions: no more than two lines meet at a point, and the dot is the preferred marking

Flow diagram: shows all essential parts so physical characteristics can be analysed and calculated, independent of physical layout; cause-to-effect runs left to right, and vertical orientation is shown with arrow symbols

Diagrams show flow and linkage, not physical position; the two types are control systems and main flow; general arrangement drawings show overall views, dimensions, weights, services and a list of associated drawings, and are used to check access, transport and installation
Detail drawings are fully dimensioned and describe a part for manufacture; manufacturing/fabrication drawings are process-specific and annotated (weld codes, bolt torques, lubrication, stress relief)
BS 8888:2000 is current and replaced BS 308 (withdrawn 2000); number format uses spaces for thousands and a comma for the decimal
Single-part drawings need shape, dimensions, tolerances, material/heat treatment and surface finish; assembly drawings need a parts list and use hatching to distinguish parts

Dimensioning rules: dimension each feature once only, on one view, outside the outline, with enough dimensions to machine without calculation, and watch error build-up in series dimensions; know the abbreviations A/F, PCD, CSK, SFACE, NTS, UCUT; distinguish dashed hidden detail from chain centre lines and identify the view before deducing hole positions
conn: Standards and symbols link to diagram type: BS 5070-3 and BS 1553 symbols are used in flow diagrams, and consistent symbol and cross-over conventions make the diagram readable

General arrangement, detail, manufacturing and assembly drawings are cross-referenced; the GA gives the parts list and references, and the detail drawings supply the dimensions and tolerances for manufacture
Orthographic views, line types and dimensioning rules combine in reading a part drawing, for example locating holes by centre lines and PCD and deciding which view to dimension on
BS 8888 ties to drawing practice: the numeric format and the referenced standards apply to every drawing type
exq: State which British standard applies to each of: fluid flow diagrams, pneumatic circuits, electrical symbols and piping system symbols. Name the three BS 1553 parts and what each covers.
Sketch the three acceptable methods of showing a line cross-over and a junction. State the rules on right angles, number of lines at a junction, and mixing methods in a diagram set.
Define a flow diagram and explain how it differs from a general arrangement drawing. State what information a GA drawing must carry and its uses.

Distinguish between detail, manufacturing/fabrication, single-part and assembly drawings, listing the content required for each. Explain why BS 308 should not be cited and how BS 8888 writes the number 3213.8 mm.

A block drawing has a row of five holes of decreasing diameter on one centre line and a central through hole in the end view. Explain how you would dimension it (PCD, one-view, external, avoiding series error build-up), distinguish the line styles used, and explain what NTS means for reading dimensions.

notes.t: Basic Fluid Systems: diagram standards and line cross-overs/junctions
pts: Engineering fluid diagrams follow named British standards, with BS 5070-3 covering mechanical/fluid flow diagram drawing practice.
Pneumatic control circuits use BS ISO 1219-1 symbols, while electrical symbols follow BS EN 61082-2.
A cross-over without joining is drawn at right angles without change of direction; only one of three acceptable methods may be used per diagram set.
When method 2 (hump/bridge) is used, the jumper should preferably sit on the horizontal line.
No more than two connecting lines should meet at a point to form a junction, with a dot marking the preferred junction method.
defs: Line cross-over
Two lines crossing on a diagram without being connected; shown at right angles with no change of direction, using one consistent drawing method (method 1, 2 or 3) across the diagram set.
Line junction
A point where connecting pipe lines meet and are joined; recommended to involve no more than two connecting lines, shown with a dot as the preferred method.
tips: Do not mix cross-over methods 1, 2 and 3 within one diagram or set of diagrams.
Know which standard applies to which symbol set: BS 5070-3 for fluid flow diagrams, BS ISO 1219-1 for pneumatics, BS EN 61082-2 for electrical symbols.
rq: Why does the standard insist that only one cross-over method is used on any one diagram set?
So that the reader never has to guess whether a crossing is joined or not; mixing methods causes ambiguity in interpreting the drawing.
Why is a junction with more than two connecting lines discouraged?
Too many lines meeting at one point make it hard to tell which connections exist and how flow is routed, so the diagram becomes ambiguous.

notes.t: BS 1553 graphical symbols and fluid/flow diagram guidelines
pts: BS 1553 is a multi-part standard of graphical symbols for general engineering; the key parts here are Part 1 (piping systems and plant, including heating and ventilation), Part 2 (power generating plant) and Part 3 (compressing plant).
Part 2 covers steam and internal combustion engines, turbines and auxiliary plant.
A flow diagram depicts all essential parts of a process or equipment so that physical characteristics can be analysed and calculated, arranged to show operation clearly regardless of physical layout.
Flow diagrams should be drawn so that the sequence from cause to effect runs from left to right; vertical orientation depends on pressure facilities and sequences and is indicated by arrow symbols.
BS 1553-1:1977 graphically shows all symbols used in piping systems and is used to prepare system diagrams.
defs: Flow diagram

A diagram depicting all essential parts of a process or item of equipment, arranged to show operation clearly and to enable analysis and calculation of physical characteristics, independent of physical layout.
tips: Use symbols consistently throughout a diagram; mixing symbols for the same component is a common mistake.
Vertical orientation of a flow diagram is not the default: it depends on pressure facilities and sequences and must be indicated with arrow symbols.
rq: Why should a flow diagram ignore the physical layout of the equipment?
Because its purpose is to show the process operation and sequence clearly, so the logic of cause and effect is not obscured by the physical positions of items.
Why is it good practice to use the simplest symbol that gives all the detail needed?
Simple symbols keep the diagram clear and readable, while still conveying every piece of information the reader requires; unnecessary detail adds clutter.

notes.t: Requirements for Engineering Drawings, Diagrams, and Models
pts: Engineering information is conveyed graphically through sketches, diagrams, general arrangement drawings, detail drawings and models (real or 3D virtual).
Diagrams are their own class of engineering drawing that convey the flow of something and how items are linked, not their physical placement in space.
Diagrams come in two types: those showing control systems and those showing the main flow.
General arrangement drawings show overall views of equipment and are used to produce detail drawings and to check access, transportation and installation.

General arrangement drawings carry overall dimensions, installation details, overall weight/mass, subsystem weights, service supply details, a list of associated drawings, and labels or reference numbers for assemblies and parts.
defs: Schematic / block diagram
A diagram conveying how items are linked and the flow of something, where item placement on the page need not match physical placement.
General arrangement drawing
A drawing showing overall views of equipment (layout, assembly, exploded view) used to produce detail drawings and check access, transportation and installation.
Detail drawing
A fully dimensioned drawing specific to a manufacturing process such as casting, fabrication, welding or machining.
tips: Do not assume the position of items in a diagram reflects their physical position in space.
Detail drawings must be fully dimensioned and specific to the manufacturing process (casting, fabrication, welding, machining).
rq: Why can a diagram's layout be misleading if read as a physical layout?
Because diagrams show flow and links between items, so the placement of items on the page often has no practical link to their placement in space.
Why is a general arrangement drawing useful beyond producing detail drawings?
It also serves as a check for access, transportation and installation, since it shows overall views and dimensions of the whole equipment.

notes.t: Detail Drawings, Manufacturing Drawings and Drawing Standards (BS 8888)
pts: A detailed drawing fully describes a part so it can be manufactured; complex parts may need several linked drawings that reference each other.

Manufacturing (fabrication) drawings form part of the detail drawings and are often drawn for a specific process or step, annotated with process notes such as weld codes, bolt torques, lubrication and stress-relieving requirements.

The old standard BS 308 was withdrawn in 2000 but remains downloadable; the current standard is BS 8888:2000, a harmonised standard that is essentially a list of other standards covering individual areas of drawing detail.
BS 8888 introduced a harmonised change in number formatting: thousands are separated by spaces and decimals by commas.
defs: Detailed drawing
A drawing that contains all the information required to fully describe a part so that it can be manufactured; several may be needed for one part, cross-referenced to each other.
Manufacturing (fabrication) drawing
A drawing that forms part of the detail drawings, prepared for a specific manufacturing process or step and annotated with process-specific notes.
The current UK harmonised standard for Technical Product Documentation, specifying how products are defined, specified and graphically represented by referencing a set of supporting standards.
BS 308
The former UK Engineering Drawing Practice standard, withdrawn in 2000 and superseded by BS 8888.
tips: Do not use the old BS 308 standard in answers; the current standard is BS 8888:2000, even though BS 308 is still downloadable.
Remember the BS 8888 number format: spaces separate thousands and a comma marks the decimal, unlike the usual UK 3,213.8 mm notation.
rq: Why might one part need several drawings rather than a single one, and what must they do to work together?
Because the level of detail and the number of manufacturing steps can exceed what one sheet can show; the drawings must reference one another so the complete description of the part is traceable.
Why is BS 8888 described as a list of other standards rather than a complete standard in itself?
It acts as an umbrella that points to specific standards (e.g. BS ISO 10209-1, BS EN ISO 5456-2, BS EN ISO 128-20) covering individual areas of drawing detail.

notes.t: Drawing Abbreviations, Single Part and Assembly Drawings, Dimensioning Principles
pts: A single part drawing must contain all information needed to produce the part: shape, dimensions, tolerances, material/heat treatment and surface finish.
An assembly drawing shows a complete assembly or subassembly and must include a parts list.
Hatching is used on assembly drawings to distinguish different parts.
Enough dimensions must be given so the component can be machined without extra calculations.
Dimensions should appear on only one view, be placed external to the drawing, and build-up of errors must be considered for series dimensions.
defs: A/F
Across flats: the distance between opposite flat faces of a hexagon or square section.
PCD
Pitch circle diameter: the diameter of the circle on which the centres of a set of holes or bolts lie.
CSK
Countersunk: a conical recess machined so a screw head sits flush with the surface.
SFACE / SF
Spotface: a flat-bottomed circular machined recess providing a bearing surface for a bolt head or nut.
NTS
Not to scale: indicates the drawing is not dimensionally accurate and dimensions must be relied upon.
UCUT
Undercut: a groove cut at the end of a shoulder or thread to allow clearance for a tool or mating part.
tips: Do not repeat the same dimension on several views; each dimension should appear once only.
Remember that 'NTS' means the drawing is not to scale, so measured lengths must not be used.
rq: Why must dimensions appear on only one view rather than on every view?
Repeating dimensions adds clutter and creates risk of conflicting values if one is changed; one clear placement keeps the drawing readable and unambiguous.
Why does build-up of errors matter when dimensioning a series of features?
Chained tolerances accumulate, so the final feature's position can deviate far more than any single tolerance; this must be considered when choosing how to dimension in series.
Why is a parts list essential on an assembly drawing but not required on a single part drawing?
An assembly combines several components that must each be identified and quantified; a single part is one item, so its identity is given in the title block.

notes.t: Basic Machine Elements – orthographic drawing of a block with through holes
pts: The page shows three orthographic views (plan/elevation style) of a rectangular block, with hidden detail drawn as dashed lines and centre lines drawn as chain lines.
The front-view square outline contains a single central circular hole, located by crossing centre lines, indicating a through-hole along the axis of the block.
The long rectangular view carries a row of five circular holes of decreasing diameter, all sharing one horizontal centre line, showing a stepped series of hole sizes.
tips: Do not confuse hidden-detail dashed lines with centre lines; they use different line styles and meanings.
Check which view you are reading (plan, front, side) before deducing hole positions, since a circle in one view appears as a line in another.
rq: Why are centre lines drawn as chain lines, and why do the dashed lines in the top view indicate hidden features?
Chain (centre) lines mark axes of symmetry and hole centres; dashed lines represent edges or features behind the visible surface that cannot be seen directly in that view.
If the five holes in the long view are all the same depth through the block, what does the decreasing diameter tell you about the drilling sequence?

Each hole is a different size, so they would typically be produced by separate drilling/boring operations with progressively smaller tools (or the block is a stepped/counterbored form), not one tool pass.

units.name: 7.3 Lec 11 drawing fault files course ENG 1016
units.ov: This lecture covers how to read and interpret engineering drawings from a set of example parts (plug plate, ratchet, cannon head, flange, bar, park layout, vane pump, steering head assembly). It covers orthographic, section, detail and isometric views, how dimensions, units, scales and title-block notes define a part, and how assembly drawings use parts lists and balloons. The common thread is that the stated dimensions and notes, not the printed image, define the part, so units and scale must be checked before any value is used.
must: 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS': read stated dimensions only and never measure the printed image
Check units first: most drawings are mm, but the cannon head is in cm and the park layout is in m
Scale is drawing:real. A detail view has its own scale (e.g. 5:1, 2:5, 1:2), but stated dimensions are already real sizes and must not be rescaled
Orthographic projection uses several 2D views (plan, front, side) at right angles. Elevation views give heights and plan views give footprint
Section views (e.g. A-A, B-B, shown by a cutting-plane line) reveal internal geometry; detail views enlarge small features
Isometric view is pictorial with equal foreshortening of the three axes. It aids visualisation but is not used for dimensioning
Dimensioning notation: R = radius, Ø = diameter, and angles and tolerances are given for linear and angular dimensions. Do not confuse R27 with Ø50, or R25 with Ø25

The title block holds drawing number, material (e.g. SUS303, austenitic stainless), scale, tolerances, surface finish and sheet number. General notes include 'deburr and break sharp edges' to remove burrs and reduce stress concentrations
Assemblies use an exploded view with balloons plus a bill of materials (item, part number, description, quantity). Check quantities such as 16 off M6 bolts and 4 off vanes
Standard components are specified by designation, e.g. key ISO 2491 6x4-50 (6 wide, 4 high, 50 long), bolts ISO 4014 M6x40 and ISO 4762 M8x16, and pipe thread BS EN 10226-2
conn: Units and scale combine in a single question: cm vs mm on the cannon head, or the 1:250 park scale with real areas and heights in m
Detail view scale vs main scale: a 5:1 detail of the ratchet keyway (3 mm wide, 2.86 mm deep, R0.25) shows a feature 5 times larger on the page but still carries its real dimensions
Plan and elevation views must be combined to build the 3D shape and overall size (e.g. 15.5 x 14.0 m footprint, heights of 2.5 and 3.0 m), with the isometric view used to check it
Assembly drawing links the parts list, balloons and standard fastener designations to the quantity and material in the title block; keys and crank length also tie in with torque transmission
exq: The cannon head drawing gives a 30 cm diameter outline and a 22.91 cm inner circle. Convert both to mm, state the radial wall thickness, and explain why the printed drawing must not be measured.
A park plan is drawn at 1:250 and its footprint is 15.5 m by 14.0 m. Calculate the footprint area in m², and the length a 3.0 m high structure would have on the sheet in mm.

Explain what is shown by detail A of the ratchet (5:1, 3 mm wide keyway, 2.86 mm deep, R0.25). What real size is a feature that measures 15 mm on the printed detail, and why is the 5 mm thickness read from the side view?

For the flange (150 mm square, 5 mm thick, 10 mm corner radius, Ø50 tube, gussets to R27, height 40 mm, drawn at 1:2), state which values are real sizes and sketch the plan and front views with the key dimensions.
Describe the information in a bill of materials and title block for the steering head assembly, and decode the designations 'ISO 2491 6 x 4 - 50' and 'ISO 4762 M8 x 16'.

notes.t: Engineering drawing: dimensioning and reading a 3J CentreModulePlug technical drawing
pts: The drawing is a multi-view orthographic projection (plan, front/side section and an isometric view) of a square plug plate with a central boss below it.
Dimensions are given in millimetres unless otherwise specified, so all values read from the drawing are in mm.
The plate is 116 mm square with four corner holes of diameter 4 mm located at the corners of the plate.
The lower boss is 100 mm wide and sits offset 10 mm from the plate edge, with a total thickness of 20 mm including the 5 mm plate.
Sharp edges must be deburred and broken, and the drawing must not be scaled; dimensions alone define the part.
defs: Isometric view
A pictorial projection in which the three principal axes are foreshortened equally, giving a 3D impression of the part; used alongside orthographic views to aid visualisation.
Tolerance
The permissible variation in a dimension, specified in the title block for linear and angular dimensions, within which a part is acceptable.
Surface finish
The specified texture and quality of a machined surface, given in the title block as a requirement for the finished component.
tips: Do not measure dimensions from the drawing image; always read the stated values, since the drawing is not to scale.
Check the unit note in the title block (millimetres) before converting any value.
rq: Why must the drawing not be scaled, even though the views look proportional?
Printed drawings may be reproduced at a different scale, so measuring them gives unreliable sizes; only the stated dimensions are authoritative.
What does the 4 mm diameter callout tell a machinist about the corner features, and how would you confirm their position?
It defines four through-holes of 4 mm diameter at the corners; their position is set by dimensions from the plate edges shown in the plan view.

notes.t: Engineering drawing of a stainless steel ratchet (drawing 4(c)): dimensions, details and t
pts: The drawing gives the main ratchet outline with radii R25 (outer) and R10 (hub/boss), plus a 6.50 mm dimension locating the tooth/feature at the top.
Detail A shows a keyway/slot on the central bore: 3 mm wide and 2.86 mm deep, with a corner radius R0.25, drawn at scale 5:1.
Detail B shows a small circular feature (pin/hole) with radius R0.50, also drawn at scale 5:1 to make small features legible.
The part is 5 mm thick, shown in the side view, and the material is SUS303 stainless steel.
The title block states the note 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS', so all sizes must be taken from the stated dimensions, not measured on the page.
defs: Detail view
An enlarged view of a small feature, drawn at a stated scale (here 5:1) so its dimensions can be shown clearly.
Radius (R)
Distance from the centre of a circle or arc to its edge, dimensioned with the prefix R on engineering drawings.
Deburr and break sharp edges
A general note instructing removal of burrs and rounding of sharp edges after machining, for safety and to avoid stress concentrations.
Do not scale drawings
A drawing note meaning dimensions must be read from the annotated values; measuring the printed drawing is not reliable.
tips: Use the stated dimensions, not measurements taken from the image, because the drawing says not to scale it.
Keep units consistent: all dimensions are in millimetres unless otherwise specified.
rq: Why does the drawing give a separate Detail A and Detail B at 5:1 instead of only the main view?
The features (keyway and small hole) are too small to dimension clearly at the main view scale, so an enlarged view shows them legibly.
Why must the note 'Do not scale drawings' be followed when making the part?
The printed drawing may be distorted by reproduction or scaling, so only the stated dimensions are reliable for manufacture.

notes.t: Engineering drawing dimensions and views of a perimeter cannon head
pts: All dimensions on this drawing are given in centimetres, not millimetres, so unit conversion must be considered when reading values.
The drawing includes a detail view at a stated scale, and the drawing itself must not be scaled, so the printed dimensions govern.
The head is shown in several orthographic views, including a front view with a 30 cm diameter circular outline and a 20 cm overall height, with a rectangular cut-out of 25 cm width and 10 cm offset.
A 15° angled feature and an R20 radius are dimensioned on the side view, showing how angles and radii are specified on a drawing.
The bottom view shows a 22.91 cm diameter inner circle inside a 30 cm outer circle, with notches at the edge, indicating how concentric features are dimensioned.
defs: Detail view
An enlarged view of a small region of a drawing, drawn at a different scale (here 2:5) and labelled with a letter to show where it applies.
Scale
The ratio between a dimension on the drawing and the real size of the object, written as drawing:real.
Orthographic projection
A method of representing a 3D object by several 2D views (front, side, top) projected at right angles to one another.
Tolerance
The permitted variation in a dimension, specified on the drawing for linear and angular measurements.
Deburr and break sharp edges
A finishing instruction to remove burrs and sharp corners from machined edges for safety and fit.
tips: Mixing units: dimensions here are in cm, while many engineering drawings use mm; always check the units note before calculating.
Do not measure the page to find sizes; the drawing states it must not be scaled, so use the written values.
rq: Why does the drawing state 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS' when a scale is given?
Printed copies may be reproduced at a different size, so only the dimensions written on the drawing are reliable; measuring with a ruler can give wrong sizes.
If a student measures the 30 cm outer diameter and gets a different length on a printout, what should they do?
Use the printed dimension (30 cm) rather than the measured length, because the drawing is not to scale.

notes.t: Engineering drawing of a flange (Water Chimes, drawing 2.2)
pts: The flange is a 150 mm square plate with 10 mm radius corners, 5 mm thick, carrying a central tube and four radial gussets.
The central tube has a 50 mm diameter, and the four gussets are 5 mm thick and project to a radius of 27 mm.
The gussets are inclined at 30° to the base, and the overall height of the component is 40 mm.
Dimensions are given in millimetres at a scale of 1:2, so the drawn sizes are half the real sizes.
tips: Dimensions on the drawing are in mm and represent real sizes even though the sheet is drawn at 1:2; do not convert them by the scale again.
Do not confuse the 27 mm radius (gusset extent) with the 50 mm diameter (central tube).
rq: Why is the scale 1:2 important when reading dimensions from this drawing?
Lengths drawn on paper are half the real size, so dimensions must be read from the printed values, not measured on the sheet, to get true sizes in mm.
What would change if the gusset angle were 45° instead of 30°?
The gussets would be steeper, reducing their base footprint and changing the sloped profile seen in the side view; the stated height and radius would constrain the new geometry.

notes.t: Engineering drawing conventions: reading dimensioned views and title block of a tubular be
pts: Orthographic views (front, side) plus sectional and detail views together fully define the geometry of a component.
Dimensions are given in millimetres unless otherwise specified, so all values on the sheet are read in mm.
A section view shows internal or cut geometry, here the row of holes in the bar, and is referenced by a cutting-plane line labelled B–B.
A detail view magnifies a small area at a different scale, indicated by a circled region and its own scale label.
The title block records material, drawing number, scale and sheet count, which must be checked before manufacture.
defs: Section view
A view formed by an imaginary cut through a part, shown with hatching or outline to reveal internal features such as holes or slots.
Detail view
An enlarged view of a small region of a drawing, drawn at a larger scale than the main view so that small features can be dimensioned clearly.
Deburr and break sharp edges
A general note instructing removal of burrs and rounding of sharp edges after machining for safety and handling.
tips: Watch the scale: the sheet is 1:5 unless otherwise stated, so a detail labelled 1:2 or 1:15 must be read with its own scale.
Do not measure from the printed drawing; use the dimension values given, as the note states DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS.
rq: Why is the note 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS' included even though the sheet is drawn to a stated scale?
Printing and copying can change the physical size of the drawing, so measuring with a ruler may give wrong values; the stated dimensions must be used instead.
What would you need to check if a detail view showed a feature at a different scale from the main view?
Read the scale label under that view (e.g. 1:5 or 1:2) and use it to interpret any measurements taken from it, rather than the main sheet scale.

notes.t: Engineering drawing: reading a park layout (plan and elevation views)
pts: The drawing shows the park in an isometric view, a plan view and two elevation views, each with dimensions in metres.
Overall plan dimensions are 15.5 m by 14.0 m of the park footprint, with the site boundary drawn in the plan view.
The scale is 1:250, so drawn lengths must be multiplied by 250 to obtain real sizes.
The elevation views give a maximum overall width of 25.0 m, and the structures sit at heights including 2.5 m and 3.0 m above the ground line.
Units are metres (M), and the drawing is numbered 6.1 and dated 04/04/19.
defs: Plan view
A view looking directly down onto the object, showing horizontal positions and footprint dimensions.
Elevation view
A view looking horizontally at the side of an object, showing heights and vertical dimensions.
Isometric view
A pictorial 3D projection in which the three principal axes are equally foreshortened, giving an overall impression of the object.
tips: Do not mix units: all dimensions are in metres, so convert consistently before calculating areas or heights.
Do not measure the printed drawing to get real sizes; always use the dimensioned values or apply the 1:250 scale factor.
rq: Why must dimensions be read in metres rather than from the drawn size on the page?
Because the drawing is at scale 1:250, so printed measurements are reduced; real dimensions are the stated values in metres, not measured drawing lengths.
Why are several views (plan and elevations) needed to fully define the park?
A single view cannot show both horizontal footprint and vertical heights; the plan gives layout and the elevations give heights and widths.

notes.t: Engineering drawing of a rotary vane pump (dimensions, materials, fittings)
pts: The drawing gives a multi-view layout (front section A-A, side and isometric views) so that the pump's internal cavity, rotor and shaft can be understood alongside its external fittings.
Internal geometry is specified by radii: the cavity radius R48, rotor radius R44 and shaft radius R10 define the clearances the vanes run in.
The pump is driven by hand through a crank arm of length 152 mm acting on pedals, so the crank length sets the lever arm for the input torque.
The inlet/outlet connection is a 50 mm pipe thread to BS EN 10226 2, which is welded to a weld neck flange in service.
Drive is transmitted to the shaft through a parallel key to ISO 2491, 6 x 4 - 50, and the base is fixed with four M8 bolts at normal clearance.
defs: A standard parallel key 6 mm wide by 4 mm high, 50 mm long, fitted into keyways in shaft and hub to transmit torque.
Weld neck flange
A flange with a long tapered hub welded to the pipe or body, giving good stress transfer at the joint.
Austenitic stainless steel
A corrosion-resistant steel with a face-centred cubic austenite structure, used here for the pump body.
tips: Read dimensions as millimetres and do not scale the drawing, since the sheet states DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS.
Do not confuse the crank arm length (152) with the diameter Ø50 of the pipe connection.
rq: Why does the drawing specify both a cavity radius (R48) and a rotor radius (R44) rather than only one?
The difference (48 − 44 = 4 mm) sets the eccentric clearance space in which the vanes slide and trap fluid, so both radii are needed to define the working chamber.
What would happen to the required hand force if the crank arm were made shorter than 152 mm?
For the same input torque, a shorter lever arm requires a larger force at the pedal, so the operator works harder.

notes.t: Engineering drawing parts list and title block (Square Vane Rotary Steering Head assembly)
pts: The parts list (bill of materials) identifies every component by item number, part number, description and quantity, and links to the balloons on the exploded view.
The title block records drawing number, material, title, scale and sheet number, giving the identity and manufacturing information for the whole drawing.
The drawing is annotated 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS', so all dimensions must be taken from stated values, not measured from the image.
Two square housing halves (top and bottom case) enclose four square stator vanes and a carrier ring, sealed with rubber strip seals and an O-ring.
Fasteners are called up by standard designations (e.g. ISO 4014 M6 x 40, ISO 4762 M8 x 16), and the notes call for deburring and breaking sharp edges.
defs: Exploded view
A drawing in which the parts of an assembly are shown separated along their assembly axis, with leader lines and balloons identifying each item.
Bill of materials (parts list)
A table listing each component of an assembly with its item number, part number, description and quantity required.
Title block
The information panel on an engineering drawing giving drawing number, material, title, scale, tolerances, and approval signatures.
tips: Do not measure dimensions from the drawing image; use the dimensions stated on it, as the drawing says not to scale it.
Check the quantity column: several items appear in multiples (e.g. 16 off M6 bolts, 4 off vanes), and counts must match when describing the assembly.
rq: Why does the drawing say 'DO NOT SCALE DRAWINGS' even though it is a precise technical drawing?
The image may be distorted or reproduced at a changed size, so only the stated dimensions are reliable; measuring from the drawing can give wrong sizes.
If you needed to order replacement seals, which items on the parts list would you check and why?
Items 7 and 8 (strip rubber seals, single and triple flange, 4 each) plus item 12 (O-ring 250x5.3) and item 4 (lip seals), using their part numbers and quantities.

units.name: 7.4 Concept Selection Preparation Notes
units.ov: These notes cover a structured, repeatable approach to concept selection in design: choosing a limited set of high-level criteria tied to PDS statements, scoring concepts on a consistent scale, weighting criteria, and totalling a decision matrix. The ideas connect as a pipeline: PDS gives criteria, criteria are weighted (e.g. digital logic), concepts are scored, and the weighted totals are then reviewed with engineering judgement rather than accepted blindly.
must: Concept selection must be methodical and repeatable, not ad hoc: choose key elements, score concepts, find an initial winner, then analyse and redesign until a clear winner emerges.
Digital logic weighting: compare every criterion pairwise, award 1 to the more important and 0 to the less important, and count each criterion's positive decisions.
Weighting factor \( \alpha = \frac{\text{positive decisions of criterion}}{\text{total positive decisions of all criteria}} \); the factors must sum to 1 (use this as a check).
For n criteria there are \( \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \) pairwise comparisons, which equals the total positive decisions (useful for checking the denominator).
Weighted score = rating (1-5) × \( \alpha \); the total is the sum of weighted scores, not of raw scores.
Use one common scoring scale and method throughout a matrix (e.g. relative -2 to +2 against the existing system, with 0 meaning no better and no worse, or 1-5 ratings); never mix methods.
Ranking gives each concept a unique score, so it cannot show large differences between concepts, and its scale equals the number of concepts.
Use only a limited number of high-level criteria (matrix of about 5-10 concepts), each justified and linked to specific measurable PDS statements so that a high score is clearly defined.
A minimum criterion (disqualifying condition) removes a concept automatically, before any weighting or scoring; discard clearly weak concepts first.
The highest total is not automatically the final design: review and analyse the result with engineering judgement, and set weights through group discussion.
conn: PDS statements and importance levels feed into criteria selection, which then determines the weighting (digital logic) and how scores are defined in the matrix.
Pairwise digital logic scoring (1/0) is distinct from the 1-5 rating scale, yet both are combined in the weighted score calculation, so questions often test whether you keep them separate.
Minimum criteria act as a filter before the matrix, while the choice of scoring method (ranking vs relative vs 1-5) affects how well the matrix distinguishes concepts.
Matrix results lead to analysis and redesign, linking the quantitative totals back to the iterative selection process and engineering judgement.
exq: Four criteria (cost, safety, weight, usability) are compared pairwise using digital logic. Construct the comparison table from the given preferences, calculate each weighting factor \( \alpha \), and verify they sum to 1.
Given a decision matrix with five concepts, 1-5 ratings and your calculated weightings, compute the weighted scores and totals and identify the best concept. Then explain why you might not select it.
Explain why a student who sums raw scores instead of weighted scores gets a misleading result, and show with a numerical example how the ranking could change.
Compare ranking with a relative -2 to +2 scale for scoring concepts. State one advantage and one limitation of each, and explain why methods must not be mixed in one matrix.
Why should you not use every PDS item as a criterion? Describe how you would choose and justify high-level criteria, and where a minimum criterion would be applied in the process.

notes.t: Advice for Concept Selection: Overview and Choosing Design Criteria
pts: Concept selection must follow a methodical, repeatable process rather than an ad hoc choice of design.
A good matrix compares roughly 5 to 10 concepts; discard clearly weak or unwanted concepts first.
Selection proceeds by choosing key design elements, scoring each concept against them, finding an initial winner, then analysing and redesigning until a clear winner emerges.
Use only a limited number of high-level, important criteria, with documented reasons and an importance level for each PDS statement, so the matrix stays manageable and accurate.
Simple headings such as cost or usability are a starting point; criteria should be defined through the specific PDS statements they relate to, since a high score must be clearly defined.
defs: PDS (Product Design Specification)
A document listing the requirements and attributes a design must satisfy, each of which can be given an importance level and used as a selection criterion.
tips: Do not use every PDS item in the matrix; select a limited set of high-level criteria and justify the choice.
Simplified headings like 'cost' must be linked to specific measurable PDS statements to score consistently.
rq: Why can't all PDS items be used directly as selection criteria in the matrix?
Using every PDS item makes the selection process unwieldy and inaccurate, so only a limited set of high-level, important criteria should be chosen and documented.
Why is a simple criterion such as 'cost' insufficient on its own for scoring?
Because the statement does not define what a high score must achieve; criteria need to be made specific, e.g. energy usage per litre of water produced.

notes.t: Scoring Concepts and Criteria Weighting in Decision Matrices
pts: A decision matrix identifies the best-meeting solution, but results must still be reviewed with engineering judgement before selecting a final design.
A common scale must be used for all criteria, and the same scoring method must be applied to every criterion in one matrix.
A relative scale of −2 to +2 scores each solution against the existing system, with 0 meaning no better and no worse.
Ranking gives each concept a unique score, so big differences between solutions cannot be shown clearly and the scale equals the number of concepts.
Criteria weighting is not equal; weights should be set as a group activity through discussion, since discussion is the most valuable way to judge importance.
defs: Decision matrix
A tool used to decide which solution to a problem best meets the criteria set out by the design statement and PDS; its result is not automatically the final design.
Minimum criterion (disqualifying condition)
A requirement where a product that cannot achieve a certain value must be automatically removed from the selection process.
Ranking method
Scoring solutions by ordering them from best (highest score) to worst (score 1), with each score used once.
tips: Do not mix scoring methods within one matrix; every criterion must be rated using the same method.
Weightings from the percentage method must total 100%, and each criterion should be justified rather than simply assigned.
rq: Why might a rating scale let more than one solution share the same score, while a ranking scale cannot?
A rating scale scores each concept on absolute merit, so equally performing concepts can receive the same score; ranking forces each concept to occupy a distinct position, so no score can repeat.
What does a score of 0 mean on the −2 to +2 scale, and why is it useful?
It means the new solution is no better and no worse than the existing system for that criterion, providing a baseline for comparison with the current design.
Why is a weighting of 0 a problem in the digital logic method?
Every criterion must carry a non-zero weighting to be considered, so a zero result must be manually changed, meaning the method alone does not guarantee valid weights.

notes.t: Criteria Weighting by the Digital Logic Method and the Decision Matrix
pts: Each criterion is pairwise compared with every other; the more important scores 1, the less important scores 0.
A property's weighting factor is its positive decisions divided by the total positive decisions for all criteria.
Weighting factors across all criteria should sum to 1, as a check on the calculation.
Decision matrix multiplies each solution's score (1 to 5) by its weighting to give a weighted score; the weighted scores are summed for a total.
The highest total is not automatically the answer; results must be fully analysed before choosing a solution.
defs: Positive decisions
The count of pairwise comparisons in which a criterion was judged more important (scored 1), summed for each criterion.
Weighting factor (α)
A criterion's positive decisions divided by the total positive decisions across all criteria, giving its relative importance.
Weighted score
The rating of a solution on a criterion multiplied by that criterion's weighting factor.
eqs: \alpha = \frac{\text{property's positive decisions}}{\text{total positive decisions for all criteria}}
α = weighting factor (dimensionless); positive decisions = count of pairwise wins (dimensionless)
tips: Do not confuse the 1/0 pairwise scoring with the 1–5 rating scale used in the decision matrix.
Weighted score = score × weighting; a common error is summing raw scores instead of weighted scores.
rq: Why must a justification accompany each pairwise decision in the table?
Without justification the decisions lack validity; the scoring is only credible if the reasoning for each choice is recorded.
If the total of weighting factors does not equal 1, what has gone wrong?
The positive decision counts or the totals were miscalculated, since weighting factors are shares of the total positive decisions.

units.name: 1.1 Welcome, lecturer and class conduct
units.ov: These notes are the Week 1 introduction to Mechanical Design 1 (ENG1016). They cover the lecturer's profile (Professor in Ultrasonic Engineering, Adviser of Studies, Chartered Engineer) and the expected standards of class conduct. They contain no technical engineering content such as design methods, equations or calculations. The two pages connect through professionalism: knowing who to approach for guidance, and behaving as a professional engineer would.
must: The module is Mechanical Design 1, code ENG1016, in the James Watt School of Engineering at Glasgow.
The lecturer is a Professor in Ultrasonic Engineering and works in the Centre for Medical and Industrial Ultrasonics (C-MIU) and the Materials and Manufacturing Research Cluster (MMRC).
The lecturer is Adviser of Studies for Mechanical Engineering students, so is your first point of contact for academic guidance and welfare.
The lecturer's credentials are Chartered Engineer, Fellow of the IMechE and Senior Member of the IEEE. This shows the professional route open to Mechanical Engineering graduates.
The lecturer has industry experience, mainly in aerospace, and collaborates extensively with industry, so expect design content with industrial relevance.
Students are expected to engage actively with scheduled content and activities.
Class etiquette: keep a respectful and focused atmosphere, use devices only when necessary, and stay until the lecturer ends the class.
Contribute positively and professionally in all interactions.
Staff may ask a student to leave if their behaviour disrupts others' learning.
The notes contain no formulas or quantitative methods. Do not expect marks for this material beyond awareness. Spend revision time on later technical weeks.
conn: Adviser of Studies role and professional conduct: knowing when to seek guidance early, such as for difficulties with workload or attendance, supports good performance and professional development.
Lecturer's IMechE/Chartered Engineer status and class conduct: professional registration requires ethical, respectful behaviour, which classroom expectations mirror.
Aerospace and industry experience and the ultrasonics research: this links the design module to real applications in materials, manufacturing and medical or industrial ultrasonics.
Active engagement and exam preparation: attending, focusing and participating in scheduled activities is how technical design content is actually learned.
exq: Name the professional bodies of which the lecturer is a Chartered Engineer, Fellow or Senior Member, and explain what Chartered Engineer status represents for a mechanical engineer.
Describe the two research groups the lecturer belongs to and give one way their work could relate to mechanical design.
State four behaviour expectations for students in class and justify why each matters for a professional engineering environment.
Explain the role of an Adviser of Studies and describe a situation in which you would contact yours.
Reflect on how industrial experience, for example in aerospace, might shape the way mechanical design is taught. Give two examples.

notes.t: About me – lecturer profile
pts: The lecturer is a Professor in Ultrasonic Engineering in the James Watt School of Engineering.
The lecturer works within the Centre for Medical and Industrial Ultrasonics (C-MIU) and the Materials and Manufacturing Research Cluster (MMRC).
The lecturer is Adviser of Studies for Mechanical Engineering students, so is a point of contact for student guidance.

The lecturer has industry experience, mainly in aerospace, and extensive collaborative research with industry.

notes.t: Respectful engagement in class
pts: Students should actively engage with scheduled class content and activities.
Maintaining a respectful and focused atmosphere is expected of everyone.
Devices should be used only when necessary, and students should stay until the lecturer ends class.
Students should contribute positively and professionally in all interactions.
Staff may ask individuals to leave if their behaviour disrupts others' learning.
rq: Why might a student who finds the guidelines challenging be encouraged to speak to staff rather than simply stop following them?
Staff such as the Adviser of Studies or course coordinator can help resolve concerns, so the student can keep engaging appropriately rather than being disruptive or leaving.

units.name: 1.2 Purpose, engineering skills and course aims
units.ov: This introductory material sets out why the course exists, which skills engineers need, and what the course will teach. It frames engineering as creative, systematic problem solving that combines technical and non-technical skills. The specific aims (design process, sustainability and ethics, basic fluid machines, engineering drawing, group project) show how lectures feed into the collaborative design project. The notes contain no equations or calculations, so questions will probably be descriptive or applied.
must: Engineering is more than maths and physics: it is creative problem solving applied to real needs.
Design follows a systematic, learnable process, and the course introduces the design processes used in mechanical engineering.
Mistakes are treated as a learning tool within design, so iteration and refinement are part of the process.
Core engineering skills span technical knowledge, problem solving and computation.
Non-technical skills (teamwork, communication, leadership) are as essential as technical ones.
Analysis, creative thinking and attention to detail underpin sound engineering judgement.
A capacity for lifelong learning lets engineers keep pace with evolving technology.
Sustainability and ethics are core themes that shape how designs are developed, not optional add-ons.
Basic fluid machines are studied through their design, construction and operation, not general fluid theory alone.
Students must be able to use and interpret sketches and engineering drawings; the group project applies lecture knowledge to a real design problem.
conn: The systematic design process links to the group project: the project is where the process is applied and where mistakes and iteration serve as learning.
Sustainability and ethics apply to every design decision, including the design and operation of fluid machines.
Sketches and engineering drawings are the means of communicating design ideas, which links technical skill to teamwork and communication in the project.
Fluid machines serve as the worked example in which design, construction, operation and drawing skills come together.
exq: Describe the stages of a systematic engineering design process and explain how iteration and learning from mistakes improve the final design.
Discuss why non-technical skills such as teamwork, communication and leadership are as important as technical knowledge for a mechanical engineer. Give examples from a group design project.
Explain how sustainability and ethical considerations could influence the design of a basic fluid machine such as a pump. Give at least three specific design decisions affected.
Sketch a simple fluid machine (e.g. a centrifugal pump) and label its main components. State what information an engineering drawing must convey so that it can be built.
Compare the design, construction and operation of a basic fluid machine, and say which engineering skills are needed at each stage.

notes.t: Purpose of the course
pts: Engineering is broader than just maths and physics; it involves creative problem solving.
Students learn common engineering solutions to recurring problems.
Design follows a systematic process that can be learned and applied.
Imagination and personal ideas are encouraged, and students get hands-on design opportunities.
Mistakes are treated as a learning tool within the design process.
tips: This page states course aims rather than technical content, so exam questions are unlikely to ask for these points verbatim; focus on the technical topics that follow.
rq: Why does the course stress that engineering is more than maths and physics?
Because real engineering design also requires creativity, practical judgement, and the ability to choose sensible solutions, not just solve equations.
What might be the benefit of following a defined design process rather than designing ad hoc?
It structures the work into repeatable steps, making problems easier to define, solutions easier to evaluate, and errors easier to find and correct.

notes.t: What are engineering skills?
pts: Engineering requires a set of core skills spanning technical knowledge, problem solving and computation.
Non-technical skills such as teamwork, communication and leadership are equally essential for engineers.
Analysis, creative thinking and attention to detail support sound engineering judgement.
A capacity to learn lets an engineer keep pace with evolving technology throughout a career.
rq: Why might a graduate with strong technical knowledge still struggle in an engineering job?
Because engineering work also depends on teamwork, communication, management and leadership, which technical knowledge alone does not provide.

notes.t: Specific course aims
pts: The course introduces the design processes used in mechanical engineering.
Sustainability and ethics are core themes that shape how designs are developed.
Basic fluid machines are studied in terms of their design, construction and operation.
Students learn to use and interpret sketches and engineering drawings.
A collaborative project applies lecture knowledge to a real engineering design problem.
tips: Note that the course covers fluid machines as "basic machines" focused on design, construction and operation, not general fluid theory alone.
rq: Why does the course pair technical design processes with sustainability and ethics?
Engineering designs affect society and the environment, so sustainability and ethical considerations must be built into design decisions from the start, not added afterwards.

units.name: 1.3 Course structure and timetables
units.ov: This material describes how engineering design is organised in first-year Mechanical Engineering at Glasgow. Mechanical Design 1 (unique design elements, in two parts: fundamental machines/systems, and the design process leading to a real-world project) is paired with Design and Manufacture 1 (repetitive elements). The notes also cover the Semester 1 timetable and the Semester 2 Design Project timetable, but the extracted pages contain no technical formulae and no timetable detail.
must: Mechanical Design 1 covers the more unique elements of design; Design and Manufacture 1 covers the more repetitive elements. Do not swap them.
The two courses are deliberately designed as partners and should be treated as complementary, not separate.

units.name: 1.6 AI caution, ethics and expectations of engineers
units.ov: This material covers three linked themes: cautious and honest use of AI tools in coursework, the four ethical principles the UK Engineering Council and Royal Academy of Engineering set for engineers, and the wider skills and attitudes industry and academia expect of 21st-century engineers. The ideas connect through integrity and rigour. Verifying and declaring AI output is a small-scale example of the professional ethics that protect safety, public trust and reputation.
must: AI use is not prohibited, but undeclared use or submitting generated output as your own is misconduct and plagiarism, with severe penalties.

Industry seeks skilled, reliable and industrious people, so maintaining high standards is key.

units.name: 1.7 Course introduction and contents (summary notes)
units.ov: This is the introduction to Basic Machine Elements. It outlines the course topics: valves and pumps, pumps in systems, heat exchangers, clutches, machinery mountings and gearboxes, plus basic fluid systems and engineering drawing. It also sets the conventions for communicating technical information (SI units, number formatting). The notes are only an outline, so the technical content below comes from what the contents pages list and from standard knowledge of these topics.
must: Use SI units throughout and convert every quantity before substituting into formulas; unit errors give answers wrong by orders of magnitude
Number format: decimal point is a full stop, and no commas as thousands separators (write 12500 or 12.5, not 12,500)
Pump-system matching: the operating point is where the pump curve intersects the system curve
System curve: \(H_{sys}=H_{static}+kQ^2\), so with static head it starts at a non-zero height on the head axis; check for static head first
Suction lift and static head both affect the pump duty and must be included in the system analysis
Heat exchanger types: plate and shell-and-tube, each with its own advantages, disadvantages and materials, so be ready to compare and justify a choice
Clutch types by purpose: dog, overrunning, sprag, drum and disc friction, fluid coupling
Clutch analysis separates steady state (\(P=T\omega\), torque balance) from accelerating conditions (\(T-T_{load}=I\alpha\), which must include inertia)
Machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes: transmitting power loads the gearbox, so consider the effects of the transmitted torque and power
conn: Pump curve with system curve (static head plus friction) gives the operating point, and suction lift limits where the pump can be placed
Clutch torque, power and speed link to gearbox loading: \(P=T\omega\) sets the torque transmitted through the gearbox and onto its mountings
Accelerating clutch engagement needs inertia, \(T=I\alpha\), and the slipping energy dissipated is a heating problem, which links to thermal management
Unit consistency underlies all of these calculations (pressure to head, rpm to rad/s, kW to W)
exq: A pump delivers water through a pipe system with 15 m static head and friction losses \(kQ^2\). Given the pump curve data, plot both curves and find the operating flow rate and head.
Explain how suction lift affects pump selection and positioning, and state what changes in the system curve when static head is added.
Compare plate and shell-and-tube heat exchangers in terms of advantages, disadvantages and materials, and recommend one for a stated application.

A friction clutch connects a motor of known power and speed to a load of known inertia. Calculate the steady-state torque transmitted, then the torque needed to accelerate the load to speed in a given time.
Describe how a sprag clutch (overrunning) and a fluid coupling work and give one suitable application for each.

notes.t: Table of contents: Pumps in Systems, Heat Exchangers, Clutches, Machinery Mountings
pts: The notes cover pump-system matching, including system curves and pump curves, with static head and suction lift considered.
Heat exchangers are split into plate type and shell and tube type, each with its own advantages, disadvantages and materials.
Clutches are organised by purpose and type, including dog, overrunning, sprag, drum and disc friction, and fluid couplings.
Torque, power and speed are treated separately for steady state and accelerating conditions in clutch analysis.
The final section covers machinery mountings, enclosures and gearboxes, including the effects of transmitting power on a gearbox.
tips: Do not confuse the steady-state and accelerating torque conditions; accelerating analysis must include inertia effects.
Check whether a pump problem includes static head before drawing the system curve, as the curve starts at a different height.
rq: Why would a dog clutch be unsuitable for engaging while the shafts are rotating at different speeds?
Dog clutches have interlocking teeth that must align; with a speed difference the teeth would clash and cause shock loading and damage, so they are engaged at rest or near matched speed.
What is the key difference between steady-state and accelerating torque in a clutch?
Steady-state torque is what the clutch transmits at constant speed; accelerating torque additionally includes the torque needed to change the rotating inertia's speed.

notes.t: Communicating Technical Information in this Course
pts: Always use SI units, whatever is customary in your home country.
Write the decimal point as a full stop, not a comma.
Do not use commas to separate thousands in numbers, to avoid confusion with European decimal commas.
tips: Unit trap: convert all quantities to SI units before substituting into formulas, otherwise answers will be wrong by orders of magnitude.
Number formatting: write 12500 or 12.5 rather than 12,500 or 12,5 so markers read values unambiguously.
rq: Why does a comma used as a thousands separator cause problems in an international engineering context?
Because in many European countries the comma is the decimal point, so 1,500 could be read as 1.5 rather than 1500, risking a serious numerical error.

units.name: 2.2 Purposes of valves
units.ov: This module introduces the four basic purposes of valves in fluid systems: starting or stopping flow, regulating flow rate, setting or limiting pressure, and selecting flow direction or path. Valves appear across everyday and industrial settings, from taps and irrigation to oil and gas. The notes are purely qualitative, so top marks depend on naming the specific function precisely and linking it to a suitable example. The notes do not cover valve types, equations or numerical data.
must: The four functions of a valve: on/off, flow rate, pressure, direction. Exam answers often list these exactly.
On/off (isolation) function: a valve stops or starts the flow of fluid in a line.
Flow-rate function: a valve regulates how fast fluid moves through a system, usually by varying the opening, i.e. throttling.
Pressure function: a valve sets, regulates or limits pressure in a system, as in pressure-relief or pressure-regulating roles.
Direction function: a valve selects or changes the path the fluid takes, determining which way it flows.
Name the specific function in an answer. 'Controls flow' alone is too vague and loses marks.
The four roles are distinct. Do not conflate stopping/starting, rate, pressure and direction.
Applications span everyday and industrial use: taps, irrigation, and oil and gas.
Be able to link each function to a concrete example. Taps and irrigation suit on/off and flow rate; oil and gas suit pressure limiting and routing.
conn: Flow rate and pressure are linked: throttling a valve to change flow rate also changes the pressure drop across it, so the two functions often occur together.
On/off and flow-rate functions both act on the valve opening. Full open/closed gives isolation, while partial opening gives regulation.
Direction control (path selection) works with on/off, since diverting flow means closing one path and opening another.
Pressure limiting is a safety function that complements normal flow control in industrial systems such as oil and gas.
exq: List and briefly describe the four main purposes of valves in a fluid system. (4 marks)

For each of the following applications, state which valve function is primary and justify it: a kitchen tap, a garden irrigation system, an oil pipeline relief valve, a diverter in a pipework network.
Explain the difference between a valve that regulates flow rate and one that regulates pressure, giving an example of each.
Why is the statement 'a valve controls flow' an insufficient answer to 'state the purpose of a valve'? Rewrite it as a full-mark answer.
Describe how a single system, such as an industrial oil and gas line, might use all four valve functions, naming where each would be applied.

notes.t: Purposes of valves
pts: Valves can stop or start the flow of a fluid in a line.
Valves regulate how fast fluid moves through a system.
Valves set or limit the pressure within a system.
Valves select or change the path the fluid takes through a system.
tips: Remember the four functions as: on/off, flow rate, pressure, and direction; exam answers often list these exactly.
rq: Why would a system need a valve that controls flow rate rather than simply an on/off valve?
Some processes need a specific, adjustable amount of fluid delivered over time, so a throttling valve sets the rate continuously rather than only fully open or fully closed.

notes.t: What valves are used for
pts: Valves can stop or start the flow of a fluid.
