Valves regulate how fast fluid flows through a system.
Valves set or regulate the pressure within a system.
Valves determine which direction the fluid flows.
Valves are found in many everyday and industrial applications, from taps and irrigation to oil and gas.
tips: Distinguish the four functions clearly: stopping/starting, rate, pressure and direction are different roles, and an exam answer should name the specific function rather than just 'controls flow'.
rq: Why would a system need a valve to control direction of flow rather than simply stopping flow?
A direction-control valve lets fluid be routed to different paths or reversed (e.g. to change the motion of an actuator) without the flow having to be shut off entirely.

units.name: 2.3 Design principles: fluid mechanics, materials and statics
units.ov: The module links three areas of design: fluid mechanics (pressure difference, resistance, turbulence and flow-rate in pipes), materials (corrosion and erosion resistance for valves and meters) and statics (strength to contain pressure, plus the machine elements that make a valve work). A valve or flow meter shows how they combine. The fluid sets the pressure and velocity, which sets the material and strength requirements, and the machine elements (stem, seals, fasteners, bearings) deliver the function. The ultrasonic flow meter is the worked example of measurement.
must: Flow-rate is set by the driving pressure difference and the total system resistance together: \(Q \propto \Delta p/R\) in the simple picture. A pump supplies the \(\Delta p\).

Pressure drop accumulates along the pipe, so for the same flow rate \(\Delta p \propto L\) and doubling length doubles the pressure needed. Check the units: 1 m of water head \(\approx 0.1\) bar (\(p=\rho g h\approx 9.81\) kPa).

Resistance rises with internal roughness (measured in microns), with bends, corners and fittings, and with turbulence. Deviation from a circular bore raises resistance through secondary flows. The design aim is minimum resistance when a valve is fully open.
Turbulence is irregular swirling mixing caused by corners, high velocity and drag. It increases drag, noise, resistance and erosion, but it can help heat transfer and mixing, so it is not always bad.

Corrosion is chemical or electrochemical attack, while erosion is mechanical wear by the moving fluid, often carrying particles. A material can resist one and not the other, so choose it to match the fluid and conditions as well as the strength needed.

Typical materials: stainless steel, aluminium, bronze, copper and galvanised steel for corrosion and erosion resistance. Valves are commonly made from brass, bronze, cast iron and steel alloys, balancing strength, cost and compatibility.
Statics requirement: the valve body must be strong enough to resist internal pressure (stress from pressure must stay below the material's strength, with a safety factor).

Ultrasonic transit-time flow meter: pulses cross the pipe at an angle (60° to the flow axis in the notes), and the transit-time difference gives the velocity component along the beam. Correct for the angle with the geometry, e.g. \(v=\dfrac{L}{2\cos\theta}\dfrac{t_{up}-t_{down}}{t_{up}t_{down}}\) with \(\theta\) measured from the flow axis. Calibration is judged against the ideal \(y=x\) line, which the notes show holding over 0–40 m/s.
A valve is an assembly of machine elements: stems or shafts transmit motion to the closure, and fasteners join parts (bolts and washers are non-permanent).

Seals and bearings: static seals sit between parts that do not move relative to each other, and dynamic seals between parts that do. Bearings either constrain motion or reduce friction, so state which in an answer.
conn: Turbulence, resistance and erosion: corners and high velocity cause turbulence, which raises \(\Delta p\) (so a bigger pump is needed) and erodes surfaces. This feeds directly into material choice and the geometry of valve and pipe interiors.
Pressure and strength: the system pressure from the pump and the head sets the load on the valve body, which links fluid mechanics to wall-thickness and material-strength checks in statics.

Valve function and machine elements: the stem passing through the body needs a dynamic seal and bearings, the body joints need static seals and bolts, and all of these must be compatible with the fluid (corrosion) and the pressure (strength).

Flow measurement and geometry: the meter's accuracy depends on beam angle and path length (geometry), on the flow profile (turbulence and pipe shape) and on a body material that resists corrosion and erosion so the calibration does not drift.
exq: A pump must deliver a given flow through a pipe run. Explain how the required pressure difference changes if the length is doubled, and convert a 15 m head of water into bar and kPa.
List four factors that increase flow resistance in a pipe system. Discuss two situations where turbulence is a disadvantage and one where it is an advantage.

Distinguish corrosion from erosion. For a valve handling water with suspended particles at high velocity, recommend and justify a body material from stainless steel, bronze, cast iron or galvanised steel.

An ultrasonic meter has path length \(L\), beam angle 60° to the flow axis and measured up- and downstream transit times. Derive or use the transit-time expression to find the flow velocity, and explain why the angle correction is needed.
Name the machine elements in a gate or globe valve. State the function of each and explain the difference between static and dynamic seals, with a location for each in the valve.

notes.t: Engineering design principles: fluid mechanics
pts: Flow resistance in a pipe increases when the cross-section deviates from circular, because secondary flows raise the pressure drop.
Water can only flow through a pipe system if a pressure difference exists, usually supplied by a circulation pump.
Flow-rate depends on two primary factors, which the slide asks students to identify (for example, the pressure difference driving the flow and the resistance of the pipe system).
tips: Do not assume pressure drop is independent of pipe shape; any deviation from a circular bore increases resistance.
Flow-rate is not set by pressure alone; always consider the resistance of the system as well.
rq: Why does a non-circular pipe cross-section increase the pressure drop for the same flow?
Non-circular sections create secondary flows and local velocity variations, adding energy losses so a larger pressure difference is needed to maintain the same flow-rate.
What would happen to water flow in a pipe system if the circulation pump were removed?
There would be no pressure difference to drive the flow, so the water would stop flowing (apart from gravity-driven flow if there is a height difference).

notes.t: Fluid mechanics: resistance, pressure difference and flow-rate in pipes
pts: Flow through a pipe system requires a pressure difference, usually supplied by a circulation pump.
Flow-rate depends on the pressure difference between two points and the total restriction of the pipe.
Pressure drop accumulates with every metre of pipe, so doubling the length doubles the pressure needed for the same flow rate.
Non-circular cross-sections cause secondary flows that increase the pressure drop (Venturi effect).
defs: Pressure head
The height of a fluid column that produces a given pressure; here 1 m of water corresponds to 0.1 bar.
tips: Keep track of units: 1 m of water head is about 0.1 bar, not 1 bar.
Flow rate depends on pressure difference and total restriction together, not on pressure alone.
rq: Why does doubling the length of a pipe double the pressure needed for the same flow rate?
Because every metre of pipe adds a pressure drop (friction/restriction), and these drops accumulate along the length, so the total pressure required scales with length.
What would happen to the flow rate if the pipe bore were non-circular but the pressure difference stayed the same?
The flow rate would fall, because secondary flows increase the pressure drop and so the total restriction rises.

notes.t: Fluid mechanics: flow resistance and turbulence in pipes
pts: Resistance to flow depends on the internal roughness of a pipe, measured in microns.
Resistance to flow increases with turbulence and when the fluid stream changes shape.
Turbulence is mixing of fluid through swirls, caused by corners, high velocities and drag.
Turbulence causes erosion on the internal surfaces of a pipe.
Design aim is to minimise flow resistance in an open condition.
defs: Turbulence
Irregular, swirling mixing of a fluid's flow, which increases flow resistance and can erode pipe surfaces.
Roughness (of a pipe)
The measure of internal surface smoothness of a pipe, typically expressed in microns, which governs resistance to flow.
tips: Roughness is measured in microns, a length unit; do not confuse it with flow velocity or pressure.
Turbulence is caused by geometry (corners), high velocity and drag, not by smoothness alone.
rq: Why does a sharp corner in a pipe increase flow resistance?
It changes the fluid stream's shape, creating swirling turbulence that mixes the flow and dissipates energy, raising resistance.
Why might a smoother pipe lower the energy needed to pump a fluid, even at the same flow rate?
Smoother internal surfaces reduce turbulence and friction at the wall, so less energy is lost to swirling and drag.

notes.t: Engineering design principles: fluid mechanics and turbulent flow
pts: Turbulent flow can be either advantageous or disadvantageous in a design.
Turbulence increases air resistance (drag) and noise, which are usually undesirable in products.
Turbulence can also speed up heat conduction and thermal mixing, which may be beneficial.
Designers must understand, handle and control turbulent flows to achieve successful product design.
tips: Do not state that turbulence is always bad; the page stresses it can be advantageous depending on the application.
rq: Why might a designer deliberately create turbulence in one product but try to eliminate it in another?

Turbulence raises drag and noise (undesirable where streamlined, quiet operation matters) but enhances heat transfer and mixing (desirable in heat exchangers or mixing systems), so the design goal determines whether it is wanted.

notes.t: Engineering design principles and ultrasonic flow measurement
pts: Good engineering design draws on fluid mechanics, materials (including corrosion and erosion behaviour) and statics, particularly strength.
An ultrasonic flow meter infers fluid velocity by sending sound pulses across the pipe at an angle and measuring their transit times; an array of paths improves the measurement.
The measured flow velocity from the ultrasonic array closely tracks the reference velocity across the full range of 0 to 40 m/s, showing good linearity.
A single transducer fires at 60° to the flow axis, so the path length and the velocity component along the flow must be accounted for in the calibration.
defs: Corrosion
Chemical or electrochemical degradation of a material by its environment, reducing its section and strength over time.
Erosion
Progressive material loss caused by the mechanical action of a moving fluid, often carrying particles, on a surface.
Strength
The ability of a material or component to resist failure under applied stress, a key concern of statics in design.
tips: Ultrasonic transit-time velocity uses only the component of flow along the beam; with the transducer at 60° the measured velocity must be corrected by the geometric factor.
Corrosion and erosion are different mechanisms: corrosion is chemical/electrochemical, erosion is mechanical wear by the fluid.
rq: Why does the ultrasonic meter use several measurement paths across the diametral plane rather than one?
Flow velocity is not uniform across the pipe cross-section, so multiple chordal paths sample the profile and give a more representative mean velocity.
Why must corrosion and erosion be considered alongside fluid mechanics when designing a flow meter body?
Fluid flow can wear or chemically attack the meter wall, changing its geometry and strength, which would alter the measured flow and the structural integrity.

notes.t: Engineering design principles: materials for valves and flow-meter bodies
pts: Materials chosen for corrosion and/or erosion resistance, e.g. stainless steel, aluminium, bronze, copper and galvanised steel, suit fluid-handling components.
Valves are commonly made from brass, bronze, cast iron and steel alloys, balancing strength, cost and fluid compatibility.

Ultrasonic flow measurement uses transducers that send ultrasound obliquely across the pipe; the flow velocity is inferred from the transit times, and the measurement is compared against a reference velocity to check accuracy.
defs: Corrosion resistance
The ability of a material to withstand chemical or electrochemical attack from the surrounding fluid or environment without significant loss of material or function.
Erosion resistance
The ability of a material to withstand progressive material loss caused by the mechanical action of a flowing fluid, often carrying particles or at high velocity.
tips: Distinguish corrosion (chemical attack) from erosion (mechanical wear by flow); materials may resist one but not the other.
Material choice must match the fluid and operating conditions, not just strength.
rq: Why might a valve be made of bronze rather than plain carbon steel in a water line?
Bronze resists corrosion in water and is easy to cast and machine, so it lasts longer in wet, possibly aggressive environments.
Why are the ultrasonic transducers mounted at an angle (60°) rather than straight across the pipe?
The angled path lets the ultrasound travel partly along the flow, so the difference in transit times upstream and downstream gives the flow velocity.

notes.t: Engineering design principles: mechanics (statics) and ultrasonic flow measurement
pts: Valve bodies must have enough strength to resist the internal pressure of the system.
Opening and closing mechanisms for valves need basic mechanical components to operate.
Ultrasonic flow meters infer flow velocity from ultrasound travelling diagonally across the meter body at an angle to the flow; the measured velocities track the reference flow velocity closely.
tips: Do not confuse the 'strength to resist pressure' requirement (statics) with the flow measurement principle; the page covers both in one slide.
The reference line on the flow calibration graph is the ideal y = x relation; measured values should lie close to it.
rq: Why must the meter body be designed in statics as well as for flow measurement?
Because it is a pressure-containing part, so its wall and structure must resist the system pressure without failing, independent of how well it measures flow.
Why is the ultrasonic beam angled (about 60°) to the flow rather than sent straight across the pipe?
An angled path has a component along the flow, so the transit time difference between upstream and downstream beams depends on flow velocity and can be used to measure it.

notes.t: Machine elements required for valves
pts: A valve is an assembly of smaller machine elements, not a single part.
Shafts (stems) transmit motion to the valve closure element.
Seals prevent leakage; static seals sit between non-moving parts, dynamic seals between moving parts.
Fasteners connect parts together; non-permanent fasteners such as bolts and washers allow disassembly.
Bearings either constrain motion or reduce friction between moving surfaces.
defs: Static seal
A seal that prevents leakage between two surfaces that do not move relative to each other.
Dynamic seal
A seal that prevents leakage between surfaces that move relative to each other, such as a rotating or sliding stem.
Non-permanent fastener
A fastener, such as a bolt with a washer, that connects parts and can be removed without damaging them.
tips: Do not confuse static and dynamic seals: the key distinction is whether the sealed surfaces move relative to each other.
Bearings serve two different purposes (constraining motion and reducing friction); state which purpose applies in an answer.
rq: Why does a valve need both static and dynamic seals rather than just one type?
Static seals stop leakage at joints between fixed parts (e.g. body and bonnet), while dynamic seals are needed where the moving stem passes through the body, so the seal must tolerate motion.
What would happen to a valve stem if it had no bearing?
Friction between the stem and body would be high, causing wear and high actuation force, and the stem could move off-axis unless motion is constrained by the bearing.

units.name: 2.4 Globe valve construction and operation
units.ov: This module covers the globe valve, a linear-motion throttling valve whose disc moves perpendicular to a seat set across an S-shaped flow path. It explains the main components (body, seat, disc, spindle, gland, gasket, bonnet) and how the disc-spindle connection decides whether the valve is a screw-down stop valve or a screw-down non-return (SDNR) valve. The ideas connect through flow direction, pressure below the disc, and sealing of the moving stem. The notes for the SDSL vs SDNR comparison (p15) and technology changes (p16) contain no detail, so those topics need to be filled in from lectures.
must: Definition: a globe valve is a linear-motion valve in which a disc or plug moves perpendicular to a seat set at right angles to the flow axis, used to throttle or shut off flow
Flow path is S-shaped, so flow changes direction in the bulbous body; this gives good throttling but a higher pressure drop
Liquid is normally admitted from below the seat, so the bonnet side and gland are not pressurised when the valve is closed, which eases gland sealing and maintenance
Operation: the handwheel turns the threaded spindle, which raises or lowers the disc to open or close the gap between the disc (disc ring) and the seat
Gland and packing (e.g. PTFE) form a dynamic seal around the moving spindle; the gasket is a static seal between body and bonnet. Do not mix them up
SDNR action: if the disc is not fixed to the spindle, it closes when screwed down but only lifts when pressure beneath it acts on it, so raising the spindle alone does not open it
Under reverse flow or pressure the unfixed disc closes automatically, preventing backflow (SDNR); a screw-down stop valve with a fixed disc can be positively opened and closed by the spindle

Distinguish valve types: a globe valve is linear and used for throttling; a gate valve is linear but lifts parallel to the flow and is used for full open or closed isolation; a butterfly valve is rotary
Typical use: ship suction lines, where isolation, flow regulation and prevention of backflow matter
Definitions to quote accurately: gland, gasket, valve seat, SDNR
conn: Disc-spindle connection and pressure direction: whether the disc is fixed decides whether the valve is a stop valve or an SDNR, and the direction of the pressure under the disc decides whether it lifts or closes
Flow from below the seat and sealing: the bonnet is unpressurised when closed, so the gland and packing see less pressure, which links to leakage along the spindle and ease of maintenance
S-shaped flow path and application: flow direction changes give throttling ability but a pressure loss, which is why globe valves suit regulation while gate valves suit isolation
Static versus dynamic seals: the gasket (body-bonnet joint) and the gland packing (moving spindle) are often asked about together as leakage paths
exq: Describe with a labelled sketch the construction of a globe valve, naming the body, seat, disc, spindle, gland, packing, gasket, bonnet and handwheel, and state the function of each.
Explain why liquid is directed from below the seat in a globe valve and what would change if it entered from above when the valve was closed.
Explain how a screw-down non-return valve works. What happens when the spindle is raised with no pressure under the disc, and what happens if the flow reverses?
Compare a globe valve with a gate valve and a butterfly valve in terms of disc motion, flow path, and typical use (throttling or isolation).
Distinguish between a gland and a gasket, giving the material typically used for gland packing and explaining why the gland is a dynamic seal.

notes.t: The globe valve
pts: Globe valves are widely used on ships, for example in suction lines.
A globe valve is a linear motion valve, so its disc moves straight along the flow axis to regulate fluid flow.
The bulbous (globe-shaped) body houses the valve seat and the disc that together control flow.
defs: Globe valve
A linear motion valve with a bulbous body that contains a seat and disc, used to regulate fluid flow by moving the disc towards or away from the seat.
tips: Do not confuse a globe valve (linear motion, throttling) with a gate valve (also linear, but mainly for full open/closed isolation) or a butterfly valve (rotary motion).
rq: Why is a globe valve suited to regulating flow rather than simply isolating it?
Its linear disc movement relative to the seat allows a graduated, throttling change in flow area, whereas a simple on/off isolation valve is designed for full open or closed positions.
Why might a globe valve be placed in a suction line on a ship?
It provides reliable regulation and shut-off of the pump suction flow, and its robust bulbous body suits the marine service environment.

notes.t: The globe valve: construction and operation
pts: The valve seat and disc (or plug) are arranged at right angles to the valve axis, so the flow path is S-shaped and flow must change direction.
Lifting the disc away from the seat opens a gap between disc and disc ring, allowing flow; the valve is opened by perpendicular movement of the disc.
Liquid is directed from below the seat so the upper chamber (bonnet side) is not pressurised when the valve is closed, which eases gland sealing and maintenance.
A gland with packing (a dynamic seal, e.g. PTFE) surrounds the spindle to stop leakage along the moving stem; the handwheel turns the threaded spindle to raise or lower the disc.

If the disc is not fixed to the spindle, it closes when turned down but will not lift when the spindle is raised unless pressure acts beneath the disc; if flow reverses, the disc closes automatically, giving a screw-down non-return valve (SDNR) action.
defs: Globe valve
A linear-motion valve in which a disc or plug moves perpendicular to a seat set at right angles to the flow axis, used to throttle or shut off flow.
Gland
A sealing assembly around the valve spindle that holds packing (e.g. PTFE) to prevent leakage along the moving stem.
Gasket
A seal fitted between the valve body and bonnet that prevents leakage at the joint.
Screw down non-return valve (SDNR)
A globe valve whose disc closes automatically under reverse pressure, preventing backflow.
Valve seat
The fixed sealing surface against which the disc or plug closes to stop flow.
tips: Do not confuse the globe valve's disc action (perpendicular to flow, S-shaped path) with gate valves, which lift parallel to the flow.
Remember the disc will not open by raising the spindle alone if it is not connected to it; positive pressure below the disc is required.
rq: Why is the liquid directed from below the valve seat rather than above it?
So the upper chamber (bonnet and gland) is not pressurised when the valve is closed, reducing leakage stress on the packing and making the valve easier to maintain.
What would happen to a globe valve with a disc not attached to the spindle if the spindle is raised with no pressure below the disc?
The disc would stay seated and the valve would not open, since it needs positive pressure below the disc to be lifted with the flow.

units.name: 2.5 Gate, butterfly, relief and three-way valves
units.ov: This material covers four valve types and the duty each is suited to: the gate valve (on/off, low loss), the butterfly valve (quarter-turn, throttling, large lines), the relief valve (spring-set overpressure protection) and the three-way valve (mixing, diverting, switching). The unifying idea is matching valve construction to function, weighing pressure drop, controllability, directionality, sealing and wear. The gate valve is repeatedly contrasted with the globe valve.
must: Gate valves are for fully open or fully closed service only; never use them for throttling, because a part-open gate causes large losses, vibration and fast seal wear.
A fully open gate valve gives almost no obstruction, so its pressure drop is negligible. This low loss is the main reason to choose one.
Gate valves are multidirectional (flow either way), whereas globe valves are unidirectional.

Gate operation: a threaded spindle turns, and the thrust collar is trapped in the valve cover so it cannot move axially. The rotation therefore lifts or lowers the gate, which is guided in casing channels so it cannot rotate.

Under a large pressure drop across the closed gate, the gate is pushed downstream and jams its guides against the channel sides. Guide and channel surfaces must be smooth and matched to limit friction and wear.
Butterfly valve: a rotary quarter-turn (90°) disc valve that suits throttling and large valves with automatic actuators. The disc always stays in the flow, so it is never full bore.
Butterfly seats: rubber hardens and distorts over time, which degrades sealing; metal seats erode.
Relief valve: a spring acting on the stem holds the disc closed, and the spring compression sets the opening pressure. The setting must be tamper-proof (e.g. capped), and the valve must be testable.
Relief valve types are proportional lift (opening proportional to overpressure) and high lift. The valve can be designed to reclose below the set pressure, so opening and reseating pressures differ.

Three-way valve: one inlet with two outlets (diverting or splitting), or two inlets with one outlet (mixing). Closing one port while opening another switches flow between paths, and the function depends on how the valve is connected.
conn: Gate versus globe versus butterfly valve selection: on/off with low loss points to a gate valve, throttling or control points to a globe or butterfly valve, and the choice also depends on directionality and seal wear.
The gate valve's closed-gate pressure drop links to guide jamming and friction, so the pressure load drives the need for matched, smooth bearing surfaces.
Relief valve spring compression links to set pressure, lift type and reseating, so spring stiffness and setting determine safety behaviour.
Three-way valve function (mix or divert) links to system layout, because the same body works either way depending on port connection, as in temperature control by mixing.
exq: A system needs minimal pressure loss, on/off duty and flow in either direction. Justify the choice of a gate valve over a globe valve, and state why it is unsuitable for throttling.

Explain with a sketch how rotating the spindle lifts the gate in a gate valve. Describe the roles of the thrust collar and the guides, and explain what happens when there is a large pressure difference across the closed gate.
Compare butterfly valve seat materials (rubber versus metal) and explain why a butterfly valve is suited to large pipelines with automatic actuators but cannot give a full-bore opening.

Describe the construction of a spring-loaded relief valve. How is the opening pressure set and protected from tampering, and how do proportional lift and high lift types differ? A spring is compressed to give a set pressure; how does changing the compression change the opening pressure?
Sketch a three-way valve used (a) as a mixing valve and (b) as a diverting valve. Describe how the valve position switches flow between two pipes.

notes.t: The gate valve
pts: Gate valves are used only for fully open or fully closed (on/off) service, not for regulating flow.
A fully open gate valve offers almost no resistance to flow, so it causes negligible extra pressure drop.
Because the flow path is essentially unobstructed, the gate valve permits flow in either direction.
tips: Do not select a gate valve for flow regulation or throttling; choose a globe or similar valve for control duties.
Low pressure drop applies only when the gate valve is fully open; a partly open valve adds significant losses.
rq: Why would a gate valve be a poor choice for throttling flow to a set rate, even though it has low pressure loss when open?

Partially closing a gate valve produces turbulent, high-velocity flow past the partly open gate and can cause vibration and erosion of the seat and gate; it does not give a stable, proportional flow-rate control, so it is designed for full open/closed operation.
What would happen to the pressure drop across a gate valve if it were only partly open, and why does this matter for the on/off rule?
Pressure drop rises sharply as the valve closes, because the restriction increases; this is why the valve should be fully open to keep losses negligible.

notes.t: The gate valve: construction and operation
pts: The threaded spindle turns to raise or lower the gate (plug), opening or closing the flow path.
The thrust collar is trapped in the valve cover so it cannot move axially, so turning the stem drives the gate vertically.
The gate is guided on both sides so it cannot rotate while being lifted; guides slide in channels in the casing.
A large pressure drop across the closed gate can push it along the flow direction, jamming guides against the channel sides.
Guide and channel bearing surfaces must be smooth and suitably matched to minimise friction and wear.
defs: Gate (plug)
The sliding closure element of a gate valve, either parallel or wedge-shaped in section, that seats against a matching seat to stop flow.
Thrust collar
A collar at the top of the threaded spindle, trapped between parts of the valve cover so it transmits stem rotation into vertical gate travel without axial movement.
tips: Do not confuse the gate (plug) with the seat: the gate lifts, while the seat is fixed in the body.
Remember the gate is guided to prevent rotation; a rotating gate would not move correctly on the threaded spindle.
rq: Why are guides needed on the gate, and what would happen without them?
They stop the gate rotating with the threaded stem, so turning the spindle lifts it linearly; without them the gate would twist and fail to seat or move properly.
Why might a large pressure drop across a partly opened gate valve be dangerous?
The fluid pressure can push the gate along the flow direction, forcing the guides hard against the channel sides and causing high friction, jamming and wear.

notes.t: The gate valve: design points and limitations
pts: Gate valves suit applications where low pressure drop is the top priority, because a fully open gate offers almost no obstruction to flow.
Gate valves are multidirectional, so they can be fitted to pass flow either way, unlike the unidirectional globe valve.
Gate valves are prone to significant vibration when part-way open, and their seals wear faster than those of a globe valve.
The size of the valve plug sets the overall height of the gate valve.
Gate valves are not suitable for flow regulation; they are designed for fully open or fully closed operation.
tips: Do not select a gate valve for flow regulation; a globe valve is the correct choice when throttling is needed.
Remember the contrast: gate valves are multidirectional, while globe valves are unidirectional and better where large pressure changes are not an issue.
rq: Why is a gate valve a poor choice for regulating flow even though it can be partly opened?

Partly open, the flow past the gate creates turbulence and vibration, and the seat and seals erode quickly; the gate's geometry does not give a controllable, stable flow characteristic, so it is intended for on/off service.
What happens if a gate valve is only half opened?
Flow is still restricted and turbulent, causing significant vibration and accelerated wear of the seals and seating surfaces, and the flow is not reliably controlled.

notes.t: The butterfly (disc) valve
pts: A rotary valve whose seating element is a disc that rotates 90° to open or close flow.
Well suited to throttling service and large valves that use automatic actuators.
Cannot give a non-obstructed (full bore) opening, because the disc stays in the flow path.
Seats can be metal or rubber; rubber hardens and distorts over time, degrading sealing, while metal can erode.
defs: Butterfly (disc) valve
A quarter-turn rotary valve in which a disc-shaped closure element rotates 90° about a central stem to open or close flow, typically used for throttling large pipelines.
tips: Do not confuse the butterfly valve's 90° quarter-turn with a ball valve or gate valve; the disc always stays in the flow.
Remember the trade-off of seat material: rubber seats degrade by hardening, metal seats by erosion.
rq: Why can't a butterfly valve be used where full, unobstructed flow is required?
The disc remains in the flow path even when fully open, so it always partially obstructs the bore and causes a pressure loss.
Why are butterfly valves preferred for large sizes with automatic actuators?
A 90° quarter-turn is simple to automate and the valve is compact and lighter than gate or globe valves at large diameters.

notes.t: The relief valve: construction and key design points
pts: A relief valve is a safety device that prevents excess pressure from building up in a system.
The valve disc is held closed by a spring arrangement acting on the stem, and the spring compression sets the pressure at which the valve opens.
The spring setting must be tamper-proof (e.g. with a cap) so that the set opening pressure cannot be altered unsafely.
The shape of the valve plug determines how the valve lifts; in a proportional lift valve the opening is proportional to the overpressure.
Relief valves can be designed to reclose at a pressure below the set (safe) pressure, and the two main types are proportional lift and high lift safety valves.
defs: Relief valve
A pressure-activated safety valve that opens when system pressure exceeds a set value, releasing fluid to prevent overpressure.
tips: Do not confuse the set (opening) pressure with the pressure at which the valve reseats; a valve can be designed to reclose below the safe pressure.
Remember the valve must be testable for safety, so testing provision is a design requirement, not optional.
rq: Why must the spring setting be made tamper-proof?
So that nobody can alter the compression and hence the opening pressure, which would otherwise allow dangerous overpressure or premature venting.
What would happen to a proportional lift valve if the overpressure doubled?
Its lift would increase in proportion to the overpressure, so the opening would be larger, releasing more fluid to bring pressure back down.

notes.t: The three-way control valve
pts: A three-way valve has one inlet and two outlets, or two inlets and one outlet, so it can route, mix or divert fluid between three pipes.
Shutting flow in one pipe while opening flow in another lets the valve switch fluid between two paths.
Used in reverse, the valve splits a single pipe's flow into two separate pipes.
tips: Identify the flow direction before answering: the same valve can mix (two inlets to one outlet) or divert (one inlet to two outlets) depending on how it is connected.
rq: Why would a plant engineer choose one three-way valve instead of two separate two-way valves?
One three-way valve saves space, cost and connecting pipework, and can switch or blend flow between three pipes in a single unit.

units.name: 2.6 Activity: valve selection for a water supply system
units.ov: This short activity applies engineering design thinking to choosing a valve for a building's shut-off water supply. The valve type, wetted materials, seal materials and operating conditions (pressure, flow, temperature) all follow from the duty and from the requirement to keep the water clean. A strong answer justifies each choice against these criteria.
must: Design criteria for the system: valve selection, materials, and operational parameters (pressure, flow rate, temperature), plus water quality
Water quality is a design criterion in its own right: wetted materials must not contaminate the supply
Gate valves suit simple on/off service where precise flow control is not needed
Gate valves should not be used for throttling, because partial opening causes wear and vibration
Stainless steel is a suitable wetted material for clean water because it resists corrosion and so protects water quality
Low operating temperature allows nitrile elastomer for static seals and PTFE for dynamic seals
Seal choice depends on temperature and on whether the seal is static or dynamic
Low flow rate and pressure suit quick shut-off, and a robust closing handle ensures reliable operation
Extras such as filters and flow metering may be added depending on requirements
Justify every choice against the duty (shut-off), the fluid (clean water) and the operating conditions
conn: Valve duty (on/off vs throttling) links to valve type and to wear and vibration, and so to long-term reliability
Fluid and operating temperature link to material and seal selection (corrosion resistance, nitrile static seals, PTFE dynamic seals)
Pressure and flow rate link to the handle or actuator design and to how quickly the valve can safely close
Water quality links materials choice to the added features (filters, metering) in the overall system design
exq: Propose a valve for a building's shut-off water supply. Justify the valve type, the wetted material and the seal materials against the design criteria.
Explain why a gate valve is unsuitable for throttling flow, and state what happens if it is used that way.
Why is stainless steel suitable for a clean-water supply valve? Describe what could go wrong with a material that corrodes.
Compare the requirements for static and dynamic seals in a low-temperature water valve. Why are nitrile and PTFE appropriate respectively?
List the operational parameters you would specify when selecting a shut-off valve and explain how each affects the design. Say when a filter or flow meter would be added.

notes.t: Break and activity: designing a shut-off water supply system
pts: A simple building water supply should let the user shut off flow quickly, so valve choice matters.
Key design criteria include valve selection, choice of materials and operational parameters.
Materials must be suitable for providing clean water, so they should not contaminate the supply.
Working in small groups of 2 or 3 to sketch or propose a system before comparing with a model answer.
tips: Students often forget that water quality (clean water) is a design criterion, not just flow and pressure.
Consider operational parameters such as pressure and flow rate when selecting valves, not only their shut-off function.
rq: Why would a quick-acting shut-off valve be important in a building water supply?
It lets the user isolate the supply rapidly during leaks, maintenance or emergencies, limiting water damage and wastage.
How might the choice of pipe material affect the quality of the water delivered?
Some materials can leach metals or support bacterial growth, so materials must be selected to keep the water clean and safe.

notes.t: Valve selection and design considerations for a clean-water system
pts: A gate valve is a reasonable choice when precise flow control is not required, since it is designed for simple on/off service.
For clean water, wetted materials must resist corrosion so they do not degrade water quality; stainless steel is a suitable choice.
Low operating temperatures allow elastomer static seals (nitrile) and PTFE dynamic seals.
Low flow rates and pressures suit quick shut-off, and a robust closing handle is needed for reliable operation.
Additional features such as filters and flow metering may be needed depending on requirements.
tips: Choose valve type by duty: gate valves are for full open/closed service, not throttling, which causes wear and vibration.
Match seal materials to operating temperature and whether the seal is static or dynamic.
rq: Why would stainless steel be preferred over a cheaper metal for a valve body in a clean-water system?
Stainless steel resists corrosion, so it does not leach contaminants or degrade water quality over time.
Why is precise flow control not needed in this design, and what does that imply for valve choice?
The duty is essentially on/off, so a gate valve suffices; a globe valve, better for throttling, is unnecessary.

units.name: 2.7 Design considerations for specific valves
units.ov: This module covers the mechanical design considerations that are specific to globe, gate, butterfly and relief valves: how each valve's geometry sets its flow control, sealing, bearing and failure behaviour. The common thread is matching valve type to duty (throttling, on/off isolation, low-disturbance flow, or overpressure protection) and managing seals, wear, jamming and leakage. Two quantitative anchors are the globe valve lift rule and the relief valve spring force balance.
must: Globe valve full-flow lift rule: set annular area equal to port area, \( \pi R^2 = 2\pi R h \), giving \( h = R/2 = D/4 \)
Be able to derive the lift rule and keep R and D straight: \( h=R/2 \) and \( h=D/4 \) are the same result, and the annulus area is the flow area
Globe valve: fine flow control via seat geometry; design must avoid plug jamming; erosion is expected in the high-velocity annular gap between plug and seat
Relief valve lift pressure from a force balance: \( p_{lift}A = k x_0 + F_{preload} \); include the spring force at the seat (preset compression) and use the area the fluid acts on

Relief valve design: adjuster locked against tampering, body-bonnet seals only (no bearings), outlet safe yet showing the valve has opened, remote manual lift in hazardous areas, legally required on positive displacement pumps
Gate valve: straight-through open bore gives low disturbance, low blockage risk and low pumping loss, but only when fully open; it is for on/off isolation, not throttling

Gate valve sealing: one dynamic packing seal (spindle, with gland follower) plus at least two static gasket seals (bonnet-body, seat); distinguish static (no relative motion) from dynamic (relative motion)

Gate valve mechanics: threaded spindle converts rotation to linear plug motion; the thrust collar constrains the stem to rotate only and may jam (needs bearing surfaces, lubrication, alignment); high force is needed to unseat the plug; plug and seat are a matched set; flow can go either way; plug diameter sets valve height
Closed gate valves are not perfectly tight: leakage depends on seat wear and packing condition

Butterfly valve: seals on the disc edge against the seat with rubber gaskets at the flanges; the bushing is a radial bearing, not a seal; low disturbance, but rubber hardening and edge erosion or bearing wear raise torque and cause leaks
conn: Globe valve lift rule links to flow area and velocity: restricting the annulus raises velocity, which links to the erosion location and to fine control via the seat

Relief valve force balance links to pump protection: a positive displacement pump must have a relief valve, so the lift pressure \( p_{lift} \) is set by spring stiffness and compression to sit below the system pressure limit
Sealing ideas (static vs dynamic, packing, gaskets) link wear and leakage across the gate, butterfly and relief valves, and also link to the torque or force needed for actuation
Valve selection combines flow resistance and control: fully open gate or butterfly gives low losses, while throttling needs a globe valve, and a partly closed gate greatly raises losses
exq: Derive the rule-of-thumb plug lift for a globe valve with a 50 mm bore by equating port area with annular flow area, and state where erosion is most likely and why.

A spring-loaded relief valve has a seat area of 4×10⁻⁴ m², spring stiffness 20 kN/m, and an initial compression of 25 mm. Calculate the lift pressure, and explain how you would adjust the design to raise it by 20%.
Compare gate and butterfly valves for isolating a pumped water line: discuss flow disturbance, blockage, sealing method, and long-term leakage or torque problems.
Sketch a gate valve and identify each static and dynamic seal, explaining the function of the thrust collar, the packing and gland follower, and how jamming could be avoided.

Explain why a gate valve is unsuitable for flow regulation and why it needs a large force to open after sealing, and state what design features make a relief valve safe to use in a hazardous environment.

notes.t: Design considerations for the globe valve
pts: Globe valve design must avoid plug jamming, locate likely erosion, and allow fine flow control via seat geometry.
A quick rule of thumb sets the plug lift at a quarter of the port diameter so the annular flow area equals the port area for full flow.
Erosion is expected where high-velocity fluid passes through the restricted annular gap between plug and seat.
eqs: Rule-of-thumb lift for full flow through a globe valve (annular area equals port area)
h = plug lift/opening (m); R = pipe bore radius (m); D = pipe bore diameter (m)
Equating port area to annular flow area around the plug
R = pipe bore radius (m); h = plug lift (m)
tips: Keep units consistent: the rule uses radius R in the area equation but diameter D in the final form, so h = R/2 and h = D/4 are different expressions for the same result.
The area balance πR² = 2πRh assumes the flow area is the annulus around the plug; ignoring the plug's own surface area or using the wrong radius gives the wrong lift.
rq: Why does the lift h = R/2 give full flow, and what does it compare?
The annular flow area around the lifted plug, 2πRh, is set equal to the bore (port) area πR², so the gap is no longer the flow restriction.
Why might a plug jam, and how does design prevent it?
Jamming arises from misalignment or debris in the guided stem; a properly guided plug with clearance in its bore prevents it from seizing.
How could the seat be redesigned for very fine flow control?
Use a contoured (e.g. parabolic or linear-characteristic) plug and seat so that flow area changes gradually with lift, giving small, predictable flow changes per unit of travel.

notes.t: Design considerations for the gate valve
pts: Plug diameter sets the valve height, since plug size follows the pipe bore diameter.
The thrust collar constrains the stem so it can only rotate, not move vertically.
Fully open, the straight-line flow path causes very little disturbance to the fluid.
Sealing needs one dynamic packing seal plus at least two static gasket seals.
Flow is possible from either direction through the valve.
tips: Do not treat the plug and seat as interchangeable; they are a matched set, so regrinding is limited.
Gate valves need considerable force to release the plug from the seat after sealing, a common oversight when estimating actuation torque.
rq: Why does a gate valve need a thrust collar rather than just a plain stem?
The collar stops the stem moving vertically, so turning the handwheel opens/closes the plug by rotation alone, using the threaded stem to lift the gate.
Why can the seats only be reground a limited number of times?
The plug and seat form a matched set whose angle is critical for sealing; each regrind removes material and changes that angle and the fit.

notes.t: Design considerations for the gate valve
pts: Static seals are needed where parts do not move relative to each other, such as the bonnet-to-body joint and the seat seals around the valve plug.
Dynamic seals are needed where a moving part passes through the pressure boundary, such as the spindle through the bonnet, which is sealed by packing and a gland follower.
The threaded spindle converts the rotary handwheel motion into linear motion of the valve plug; force is transmitted through the spindle collar, which bears on the bonnet.
The thrust collar may jam under load or from poor lubrication or misalignment, so design should ensure adequate bearing surfaces, lubrication and alignment.
A closed gate valve is only as liquid tight as the plug-to-seat contact and the packing, so leakage is an expected design concern rather than something to assume away.
tips: Do not assume a closed gate valve is perfectly liquid tight; seat wear and packing condition determine leakage.
Distinguish clearly between static seals (no relative motion) and dynamic seals (relative motion, e.g. the spindle).
rq: Why does the gate valve need both static and dynamic seals rather than just one type?
Static seals stop leakage at fixed joints (bonnet to body, seat to body), while dynamic seals (packing around the moving spindle) must allow motion while still preventing leakage.
What would happen to the spindle force path if the thrust collar jammed while the handwheel was turned?
The torque and axial force could not reach the plug, so the handwheel would turn without closing the valve, or the spindle/threads would be overloaded and damaged.

notes.t: Gate valve advantages in pumped water systems
pts: A gate valve has a low chance of blockage because its open bore offers an unobstructed path for the fluid.
When water is pumped through a fully open gate valve, the flow meets low resistance, so pumping losses stay small.
Gate valves are best suited to systems where precise flow control is not needed, typically used as on/off isolation valves.
tips: Gate valves are for on/off isolation, not throttling; do not justify them by precise flow regulation.
Low resistance applies when the valve is fully open; a partly closed gate greatly increases losses.
rq: Why does a gate valve's low resistance to flow matter specifically when water is being pumped?
A pump must supply energy to overcome friction and minor losses; a fully open gate valve adds little loss, so less pump head/power is wasted and flow is maintained.
Why is a gate valve a poor choice for throttling flow even though it causes little resistance when open?
Partial opening produces turbulence and vibration around the partly closed gate and the flow change is non-linear, so fine control is difficult; it is designed for fully open or fully closed service.

notes.t: Butterfly valve design considerations
pts: Rubber gaskets at each pipe flange end provide the seal, and the valve sits between two flanges held by bolts running through them.
The disc seals against the seat on its edge rather than its face, so sealing depends on the disc edge meeting the seat.
The bushing acts as a radial bearing supporting the valve stem, allowing the disc to be turned smoothly.
A butterfly valve causes only a low level of disturbance to flow in the system because the disc remains in the flow path even when open.
Maintaining a proper seal over time is difficult because rubber seals harden, and disc edges can erode or bearings can wear, increasing the torque needed to turn the disc.
tips: Do not confuse the bushing (radial bearing supporting the stem) with the seal; the seal provides leak-tightness, the bushing provides support.
Remember the disc seals on its edge, so erosion of the disc edge or seat causes leakage paths.
rq: Why does a butterfly valve create only a low level of flow disturbance compared with other valves?
Its disc is a streamlined shape kept in the flow path even when open, so flow is only mildly obstructed and redirected.
What would happen to the torque needed to operate the valve if the rubber seal hardened and the bearing wore?
The disc would need more force to be pushed into the seal and turned, so operating torque increases and sealing may fail.

notes.t: Design considerations for the relief valve
pts: Lift pressure is set by spring compression; the adjuster must be locked against unauthorised access.
Seals are needed between body and bonnet; no bearings are required in this valve.
Outlet must discharge somewhere safe, yet opening must be detectable.
In dangerous environments the manual lift should be operated remotely in case the valve fails.
A relief valve is legally required on a positive displacement pump.
eqs: Force balance predicting the lift (cracking) pressure of a spring-loaded relief valve

p_lift = lift pressure (Pa); A = area on which the fluid acts (m²); k = spring stiffness (N/m); x_0 = spring compression at seat (m); F_preload = spring force at closed position (N), i.e. k x_0 when the spring is preset
tips: Lift pressure depends on spring compression, so the spring force at the seat must be included in the force balance.
Remember the outlet must be safe for people and the environment yet still show when the valve has opened.
rq: Why must the spring adjuster be inaccessible to unauthorised personnel?
Changing spring length changes the lift pressure; an unauthorised change could let system pressure exceed safe limits or cause premature lifting.
Once the valve opens, what happens to the force balance and why is this a problem?

Opening moves the valve so the fluid acts on a larger area and the spring compresses further; the fluid force rises suddenly and the valve can snap open and chatter or fail to reseat at the set pressure.
How would you redesign the valve to stop this sudden change in force balance?
Add a balancing feature such as a larger effective area on the spring side or a pressure-relief/ground-area correction, so the net force stays stable as the valve lifts.

units.name: 2.8 Valves summary
units.ov: This summary covers valve types (globe, gate, butterfly/disc, relief) and the components used to build them (shafts, seals, fasteners, bearings). Valve design combines fluid mechanics (flow and pressure), materials (selection for pressure, temperature and corrosion) and statics (forces and moments on components). The key idea is to match valve function (regulate, isolate, one-way flow, pressure relief) to the right type and design it so that all three disciplines are satisfied together.
must: Valve types: globe, gate, butterfly/disc and relief valves, and the main function of each
Valve function categories: flow control in one direction, simple shut-off (isolation), and pressure relief
A shut-off valve is not necessarily a relief valve, and a relief valve is not used for routine flow regulation
Valve design depends on fluid mechanics, materials and statics together, never on just one

Construction components and their roles: shafts (transmit torque or motion to the closure element), seals (prevent leakage), fasteners (hold the body and bonnet together against pressure), bearings (support and allow motion)
Statics: pressure force \(F = pA\) acting on the closure element and fasteners, and the resulting torque or moment on the shaft
Fluid mechanics: pressure drop and flow through the valve depend on its geometry and how far it is open
Materials: choose for pressure rating, temperature, corrosion and wear, especially at seals and seats
Be able to justify a valve choice for a given duty (throttling, isolation, backflow prevention or overpressure protection)
conn: Pressure from fluid mechanics gives the force \(F = pA\) on the closure, which statics turns into shaft torque, bearing loads and fastener tension
Materials selection links to seal and seat performance, since fluid temperature, pressure and chemistry determine which materials survive and so how well the valve seals
Valve type depends on function: a relief valve is set by the pressure at which it opens, whereas gate and globe valves are chosen for isolation or throttling
Fastener and bearing sizing combine statics (loads) with materials (strength, fatigue, wear) in one design calculation
exq: Compare globe, gate, butterfly and relief valves in terms of function and typical application, and recommend a valve type for (a) routine flow regulation, (b) full isolation of a pipeline, (c) overpressure protection of a vessel.

A valve disc of diameter 100 mm is subjected to a pressure difference of 10 bar. Calculate the force on the disc and the torque on a shaft if the force acts at a given offset, and comment on the shaft and bearing requirements.
Explain how fluid mechanics, materials and statics each influence the design of a valve for hot corrosive fluid at high pressure.
Describe the roles of shafts, seals, fasteners and bearings in a valve, and explain what could go wrong if each failed.
A colleague proposes using a shut-off valve as the pressure-relief device on a pressurised tank. Explain why this is inappropriate and what should be used.

notes.t: Valves: Summary
pts: Fluid mechanics, materials, and statics principles are all important in valve design
Valve types include globe, gate, butterfly/disc, and relief valves
Shafts, seals, fasteners, and bearings are used in the construction of valves
Some valves control flow in one direction, others simply shut off flow, and others provide pressure-relief
tips: Do not confuse valve function: a valve that shuts off flow is not necessarily a pressure-relief valve, and a relief valve is not used for routine flow regulation.
Remember that valve design depends on three disciplines together (fluid mechanics, materials, statics), not on any single one.
rq: Why must fluid mechanics, materials, and statics all be considered together when designing a valve?

A valve must handle the flow and pressure of the fluid (fluid mechanics), withstand the pressure and loads without failing (statics), and resist the fluid's corrosion, temperature and wear (materials). Neglecting any one can cause leakage or failure.
What is the key difference between a valve used for flow control and one used for pressure relief?
A flow-control valve is set to regulate or direct flow in one direction, while a pressure-relief valve opens automatically when pressure exceeds a set limit to protect the system.

units.name: 2.9 Valves: globe, gate, butterfly and relief (summary notes)
units.ov: This module covers the main valve types (globe, gate, butterfly and relief/safety) and how each one's construction determines its function: on/off isolation, throttling, non-return flow or overpressure protection. The recurring trade-off is sealing and control against flow resistance (pressure drop), plus the operating effort (torque) and the sealing of the spindle or stem. Selecting a valve means matching these properties to the duty.
must: Match valve to duty: globe = on/off plus accurate throttling with full seal but high pressure drop; gate = on/off isolation only with very low resistance when fully open; butterfly = quarter-turn disc, on/off with some control; relief = automatic overpressure protection
Globe valves have high flow resistance because of the tortuous internal passage, so they give a large pressure drop. Saying they are low-loss is a common error

SDSL (screw-down screw-lift): spindle fixed to disc, so the handwheel positively lifts and lowers it. SDNR (screw-down non-return): disc free of spindle, opens only when upstream pressure exceeds downstream and closes on backflow
In a globe valve, flow enters below the seat so the upper chamber (gland and bonnet) is not pressurised when closed

Gate valves must not be used to throttle: partial opening gives poor control, large losses and vibration. Guides in casing channels stop the gate rotating and must be smooth and low-friction because pressure pushes the gate against them

Butterfly valve parts: disc (rotating closure), seat (fixed, rubber or metal), stem (sealed by packing, bushing, retainer, thrust washer and retaining ring). It always causes some resistance even when fully open

Butterfly sealing problems: the disc pushes against a rubber seat, can jam when closed, and seal quality degrades over time. Butterfly valves cannot be made one-way, so they are unsuitable where non-return is required
Handle length sets the operating torque, \(T = F\times L\), so longer handles give more torque. It does not set flow rate
Relief valve: a spring holds the disc shut and spring compression sets the opening pressure. The setting must be tamper-proof yet testable in service

Proportional-lift valves lift in proportion to the pressure above the set value. High-lift valves lift fully and stay open until pressure falls well below the over-pressure value, so they show hysteresis-like reseating
conn: Pressure drop versus function: low-loss gate valves suit full-bore isolation, while globe valves accept high loss in exchange for throttling and tight sealing. Justify choices using resistance
SDSL versus SDNR versus butterfly: positive mechanical operation versus pressure-driven non-return action versus no one-way capability. Questions on backflow combine these
Torque and sealing: handle length, spindle thread, gland packing friction and seat material (rubber or metal) all affect operating effort and leakage
Relief valve spring setting, plug shape and lift behaviour together determine opening pressure, discharge capacity and reseating pressure
exq: Compare globe, gate and butterfly valves for a pipeline needing isolation and occasional flow control. Give advantages, disadvantages and pressure-drop behaviour, and recommend one with justification
Explain with a sketch the difference between an SDSL and an SDNR globe valve. State how each opens and closes, and which would protect a pump from backflow
A butterfly valve handle is 0.5 m long and a hand force of 100 N is applied. Calculate the torque available, and explain why longer handles are used and what limits sealing over time
Describe how a spring-loaded relief valve works. Explain how the spring sets the opening pressure and contrast proportional-lift and high-lift types, including reseating behaviour
Label the main parts of a globe stop valve (body, seat, disc, spindle, bonnet, gland, handwheel) and state which joints are bolted and which sealed by packing. Explain why flow enters below the seat

notes.t: Valves: purpose, design principles and basic types
pts: Valves start, stop, or control the flow of liquids and gases
Valves control flow quantity, pressure, and direction, and provide system safety
Valve design must account for fluid resistance, direction changes and surface finish causing erosion
Valve materials must suit the fluid and erosion; wall thickness governs strength against fluid pressure
Valve operation requires an effort (torque) that is typically expected for opening and closing
defs: Valve
A device that stops, starts, or regulates the flow, pressure, or direction of a fluid (liquid or gas) in a system.
Pressure relief valve
A safety valve that opens to release fluid when system pressure exceeds a set limit, protecting the system.
Non-return valve
A valve that allows flow in one direction only, preventing backflow.
Globe valve
A valve with a linear-motion plug or disc that throttles flow; also known as SDSL and SDNR in this course.
Butterfly valve
A quarter-turn valve using a rotating disc to regulate flow; also known as a disc valve.
tips: Distinguish valve functions clearly: stopping/starting flow, controlling quantity, controlling pressure, controlling direction, and providing safety are different purposes.
Globe, gate and butterfly valves are often confused; remember butterfly valves are quarter-turn disc valves.
rq: Why does a change in fluid direction cause erosion inside a valve, and how might a designer reduce it?
The flowing fluid's momentum strikes the wall at the change in direction, eroding material; smoother, gradual curves and suitable erosion-resistant materials reduce it.
Why must valve wall thickness be considered alongside material choice?
Thickness determines the strength and ability to withstand internal fluid pressure, so a thin wall may fail even in a strong material.

notes.t: Globe Valves
pts: Globe valves are primarily ON/OFF valves that can also accurately throttle flow and seal completely when closed.
Their main drawback is a large pressure drop because of high flow resistance through the internal passages.
Liquid is directed to enter from below the valve seat so the upper chamber is not pressurised when closed, reducing load on the gland and bonnet.
In a screw-lift (SDSL) valve the spindle is joined to the valve disc, so turning the handwheel positively raises or lowers the disc.
In an SDNR valve the disc is not attached to the spindle, so it closes by pressure backflow and only opens when upstream pressure exceeds downstream pressure.
defs: Globe valve
A valve with a spherical body enclosing a seat and disc (plug) that can fully shut off, throttle, or regulate flow, at the cost of high flow resistance.
SDNR (screw-down non-return valve)
A globe valve in which the disc is not connected to the spindle; it closes under reverse pressure and prevents backflow.
Screw-lift valve (SDSL)
A globe valve in which the spindle is fixed to the disc so the disc is positively raised and lowered by the threaded spindle.
Valve gland
Packing sealed around the spindle where it exits the bonnet to prevent leakage along the moving stem.
tips: Do not confuse SDSL (disc fixed to spindle, positively opened) with SDNR (disc free, opens only with positive upstream pressure).
Globes are chosen for control and sealing, not for low-loss flow; stating they have low resistance is a common error.
rq: Why does the flow direction through a globe valve matter when the valve is closed?
Flow enters from below the seat, so the pressure acts on the underside of the disc and the upper chamber stays unpressurised, easing gland sealing and handling when shut.
Why does a globe valve have a higher pressure drop than a gate valve, even though both can shut off flow fully?
The globe's internal passages force the fluid to change direction through the seat, creating high resistance to flow and a large pressure loss.

notes.t: Design Points (globe/stop valve illustration)
pts: The page shows two orthographic views (front section and side/cross views) of a cast globe-type stop valve, used as a worked example of machine-element drawing.
The valve body has flanged inlet and outlet ends with a horizontal flow passage whose internal curved shape guides the fluid and the valve seat sits across the flow path.
A vertical spindle passes through a bonnet/yoke and is turned by a hand wheel; rotating it lowers or lifts the disc onto the seat to control flow.
Sealing between the spindle and bonnet is provided by a gland/packing region; the bonnet is bolted to the body to allow assembly and maintenance.
tips: Do not confuse the flanged end faces with the bonnet joint; state which joints are bolted and which are sealed by packing.
Engineering drawings are shown in orthographic projection; read section lines to identify internal features rather than external outlines.
rq: Why is the flow passage in a globe valve made with a curved, S-shaped path rather than a straight bore?
The curved path changes flow direction gently, reducing pressure loss and turbulence, while the seat lies across the passage so the disc can throttle flow accurately.
What would happen to sealing if the spindle packing were omitted?
Fluid would leak along the spindle to atmosphere, so the valve would fail to contain pressure.

notes.t: Gate Valves
pts: A gate valve is primarily an ON/OFF isolation valve that can achieve a complete seal with very little flow resistance.
Because it causes almost no extra resistance when fully open, it adds negligible pressure drop to the system.
It is unsuitable for throttling because partial opening gives poor flow control.
Turning the threaded spindle raises or lowers the gate (plug) against a matching seat; the thrust collar is trapped by the cover so it cannot move axially.

Guides on either side of the gate slide in channels in the casing to stop it rotating; high pressure drop can push the gate against these guides, so their bearing surfaces must be smooth and low-friction.
defs: Gate valve
A valve in which a parallel or wedge-shaped gate (plug) is raised or lowered by a threaded spindle to open or close the flow path against a matching seat, used mainly for on/off isolation.
tips: Do not select a gate valve for flow regulation; it is designed only as an ON/OFF valve.
A gate valve's low pressure drop applies only when fully open; partial opening causes large losses and vibration.
rq: Why must the guide and channel surfaces be smooth and made of suitable materials?
A large pressure drop can force the gate sideways against the guides; rubbing surfaces with high friction would cause jamming and wear, so smooth, low-friction materials are needed.
Why does a gate valve require extra height in the system?
The plug must lift fully out of the flow stream to avoid obstructing flow and causing pressure drop when open, which needs vertical clearance.

notes.t: Butterfly Valves: Design Points and Aspects
pts: A butterfly valve's basic purpose is as a simple ON/OFF valve, though it can also be used to control flow.
A butterfly valve can achieve a 100% seal, but sealing becomes harder to maintain over time.
Any butterfly valve causes some resistance to flow, even when fully open.
Full closure is difficult because the disc often must push against a rubber seat, and the disc can jam in the closed position.
The handle length sets the opening or closing torque that can be generated, so long handles are often needed.
tips: Do not confuse the handle length with the flow rate: handle length governs the force needed to operate the valve, not how much fluid passes.
Butterfly valves cannot be made one-way only, so do not propose them where strict non-return flow is required.
rq: Why does a longer valve handle make the valve easier to operate?
The handle acts as a lever arm; a longer arm gives a greater moment (torque) for the same hand force, so a larger opening or closing force can be generated.
Why might a butterfly valve that seals 100% when new later leak?
The rubber seat wears and the disc repeatedly pushes against it, so the seal degrades over time and full closure becomes harder.

notes.t: Butterfly valve construction
pts: A butterfly valve regulates flow with a disc rotated on a stem inside the body.
The disc sits against a seat in the body; the seat may be rubber or metal.
The stem passes through packing, bushing and stem retainer, sealed by a thrust washer and retaining ring.
Two principal versions exist: rubber-seated and metal-seated.
defs: Butterfly valve
A quarter-turn valve in which a circular disc, mounted on a rotating stem, controls flow when turned against a seat within the body.
Disc
The circular closure element of a butterfly valve that rotates on the stem to open or shut the flow path.
Seat
The sealing surface in the body against which the disc closes, either rubber or metal.
Stem
The shaft connecting the actuator to the disc, passing through the body and sealed by packing.
tips: Do not confuse the disc (the rotating closure) with the seat (the fixed sealing surface in the body).
Identify the seat type (rubber or metal) before stating leakage or temperature limits.
rq: Why does the stem need packing, bushing and a stem retainer rather than passing straight through the body?
Packing seals against leakage, the bushing supports the stem and reduces friction, and the retainer locates the stem axially so it cannot be pushed out under pressure.
What trade-off would you expect between a rubber-seated and a metal-seated butterfly valve?
Rubber seats give tight, bubble-tight shut-off at lower pressures and temperatures but wear and degrade; metal seats tolerate high temperatures and pressures and are more durable but may leak more.

notes.t: Relief (safety) valves – construction and design
pts: Relief valves prevent excess pressure building up in pipe systems by opening automatically.
The valve disc is held closed by a spring arrangement on the stem; spring compression sets the opening pressure.
The spring setting must be tamper-proof yet still allow the valve to be tested in service.
The shape of the valve plug determines how the valve lifts: proportionally to over-pressure, or fully lifted with hysteresis-like staying open until pressure falls well below the set value.
Two main types exist: proportional-lift safety valves and high-lift safety valves.
defs: Relief valve
A pressure-activated valve that opens when system pressure exceeds a set value to vent fluid and prevent over-pressurisation of a pipe system.
Proportional-lift safety valve
A safety valve whose disc lift is proportional to the amount by which pressure exceeds the set (opening) pressure.
High-lift safety valve
A safety valve designed to fully lift once over-pressure is detected and to remain open until pressure drops significantly below the over-pressure value.
tips: Do not confuse the set (opening) pressure with the over-pressure value; the high-lift valve reseats only well below the over-pressure level.
Be clear that the spring compression, not the plug shape alone, sets the pressure at which the valve begins to open.
rq: Why must the spring setting be tamper-proof but still testable?
Tamper-proofing prevents unauthorised changes to the set pressure, which could allow dangerous over-pressure; testability ensures the valve is confirmed to open correctly in service.
What would happen if the valve plug shape were changed to a high-lift design on a system needing gradual pressure relief?
The valve would fully open at set pressure and stay open until pressure drops well below it, causing a larger, abrupt discharge rather than a proportional release.

units.name: 3.1 Pump purpose, machine elements and background principles
units.ov: This material introduces why pumps are used (circulating fluid, moving it, raising pressure and increasing flow rate) and the machine elements they are built from (shafts, seals, bearings, gears, crankshafts). It then sets out the background principles: pressure (static) head and dynamic (friction) head from fluid mechanics, and the gas laws from thermodynamics. These provide the tools for sizing a pump against a system and for distinguishing positive displacement from centrifugal pumps.
must: Pressure head: \( H = \dfrac{P}{\rho g} \), in metres; P in Pa, \( \rho \) in kg/m³, g in m/s²
Head depends on fluid density: the same pressure gives a different head for different liquids
Static (pressure) head is the potential energy per unit weight of fluid at rest; dynamic head is the head loss from friction that the pump must overcome in addition

Pump duties: circulate fluid in a closed loop, transfer fluid between locations, raise pressure, increase volumetric flow rate; pumps add energy to a liquid (unlike compressors for gases or fans for small pressure rises)
Centrifugal pump flow depends strongly on the system head curve, not just speed; do not treat the two pump families alike (positive displacement vs centrifugal)
Machine elements: shafts transmit rotation and torque, bearings support shafts and reduce friction, gears/crankshafts transmit and convert motion, seals prevent leakage
Seal types: dynamic (between moving parts) vs static (between stationary parts)
Boyle's law: \( P_1V_1 = P_2V_2 \) at constant T; Charles's law: \( V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2 \) at constant P
Avogadro's law: \( V_1/n_1 = V_2/n_2 \) at constant T and P; ideal gas law: \( PV = nRT \)
Use absolute temperature (K) and consistent SI units (Pa, m³) in gas law calculations; °C is a common error
conn: Total pump head requirement = static head (from \( P/\rho g \)) plus dynamic head (friction losses); this sets the duty point where the pump curve meets the system head curve, which determines centrifugal pump flow
Pressure head conversion links fluid mechanics to pump selection: a pressure rise in Pa converts to metres of head only via the fluid's density
Gas laws apply where a gas is present (e.g. a compressible pocket or a compressor/fan comparison); Boyle's law for compression, Charles's for heating, PV = nRT combining them
Machine elements connect to pump type: crankshafts and gears convert motion in positive displacement mechanisms, while shafts, bearings and dynamic seals serve the rotating parts of centrifugal pumps
exq: A pump must raise a pressure of 300 kPa in water (\( \rho = 1000 \) kg/m³). Calculate the pressure head in metres, and the head if the fluid were oil with \( \rho = 850 \) kg/m³.
Explain the difference between static (pressure) head and dynamic head, and state how each contributes to the total head a pump must deliver.
Distinguish between positive displacement and centrifugal pumps, explaining why flow in a centrifugal pump depends on the system head curve.
Describe the roles of shafts, bearings, gears/crankshafts and seals in a pump, and distinguish dynamic from static seals with examples.

A gas at 100 kPa and 20 °C occupies 0.5 m³. It is compressed isothermally to 300 kPa, then heated at constant pressure to 80 °C. Find the final volume, stating the laws used and converting temperatures to kelvin.

notes.t: Intended learning outcomes: pumps
pts: Distinguish positive displacement pumps from centrifugal pumps
Understand the engineering principles used in pump design
Identify the different types of pump
Identify key pump performance characteristics
tips: Do not confuse the two pump families: flow in a centrifugal pump depends strongly on the system head curve, not just on speed.
rq: Why does a positive displacement pump deliver a roughly constant flow regardless of outlet pressure, whereas a centrifugal pump's flow falls as pressure rises?

A positive displacement pump traps a fixed volume each cycle and forces it out, so flow depends on speed and geometry (leakage aside). A centrifugal pump relies on impeller-generated head, so its delivered flow varies with the system resistance it works against.

notes.t: What pumps are used for
pts: Pumps circulate a fluid around a closed system, such as a heating or cooling loop.
Pumps move a fluid from one location to another, e.g. supplying water to a point of use.
Pumps raise the pressure of the fluid within a system.
Pumps increase the volumetric flow rate of the fluid through a system.
tips: Pumps add energy to a fluid; do not confuse their function with that of a compressor, which handles gases, or a fan, which produces only small pressure rises.
rq: Why does a fire hydrant or a tyre-inflating pump need to increase pressure rather than just move fluid?

Delivering water to a height or through hoses needs enough pressure to overcome gravity and friction losses; air in a tyre must be pressurised to a set value to support the load, so pressure rise, not just transfer, is the purpose.
In a circulating system such as a heating loop, why is a pump needed even though the fluid returns to where it started?
Friction losses in pipes and components continuously dissipate energy, so the pump must add energy to keep the fluid moving around the loop.

notes.t: Machine elements required in pumps
pts: Pumps, like valves, are assemblies made up of smaller machine elements.
Shafts transmit rotational motion and torque between components within the pump.
Seals prevent leakage and come in two types: dynamic (between moving parts) and static (between stationary parts).
Gears and crankshafts are used to transmit and convert motion within pump mechanisms.
Bearings support rotating shafts and reduce friction.
tips: Distinguish clearly between dynamic seals (moving interfaces) and static seals (stationary interfaces) when naming seal types.
rq: Why are dynamic seals and static seals treated differently in pump design?
