Energy balance: \(Q=\dot m_h c_{p,h}(T_{h,in}-T_{h,out})=\dot m_c c_{p,c}(T_{c,out}-T_{c,in})\). Use it to find unknown temperatures or flow rates.
For the same four terminal temperatures, \(\Delta T_{lm,counter}\ge\Delta T_{lm,parallel}\), so counter-flow needs less area for the same duty \(Q\) (or gives more \(Q\) for the same \(A\)).
Only temperature differences matter, so use K or °C consistently in differences. Use absolute units only if a formula needs them.
If \(\Delta T_1=\Delta T_2\), the LMTD formula gives 0/0. In that case \(\Delta T_{lm}=\Delta T_1\).
Parallel flow does have a niche: it gives a more uniform wall temperature and is useful when the cold fluid must not be overheated. Its limit is that the cold outlet can never exceed the hot outlet.
conn: Energy balance with LMTD: the energy balance gives unknown outlet temperatures and \(Q\); LMTD then gives the required area \(A=Q/(U\Delta T_{lm})\).

Temperature profiles with effectiveness: the shape of the T–x plot (converging in parallel, roughly parallel lines in counter-flow) explains why the maximum effectiveness differs between the two arrangements.
Heat capacity rates: \(C=\dot m c_p\) determines which fluid has the larger temperature change, and so the slopes of the profiles and which fluid limits the duty.
Overall coefficient \(U\) with exchanger sizing: thermal resistances (convection and conduction) give \(U\), which then combines with LMTD in a design question.
exq: Hot oil enters at 120 °C and leaves at 70 °C. Water enters at 20 °C and leaves at 60 °C. Calculate \(\Delta T_{lm}\) for parallel and counter-flow, and state which needs the smaller area for a duty of 50 kW with \(U=300\ \mathrm{W/m^2K}\). Find that area.
Explain with sketched T–x profiles why the cold fluid outlet temperature can exceed the hot fluid outlet temperature in counter-flow but not in parallel flow.
For the same inlet temperatures and flow rates, determine whether parallel or counter-flow transfers more heat in an exchanger of fixed area. Justify using \(\Delta T_{lm}\) and energy balances.
A counter-flow exchanger has \(\Delta T_1=\Delta T_2=30\ \mathrm{K}\). Explain why the LMTD formula fails and give \(\Delta T_{lm}\). Describe what this implies about the heat capacity rates.

Given \(\dot m_c c_{p,c}\), the cold inlet and outlet temperatures and the hot inlet temperature, find the hot outlet temperature and then the area required in each configuration, stating the end definitions you use.

notes.t: Parallel vs counter-flow heat exchanger comparison (activity)
pts: Counter-flow lets the cold fluid leave near the hot inlet temperature, so it can be heated more closely to the hot fluid's inlet temperature.
In parallel flow both fluids exit at similar temperatures, limiting the achievable heat transfer.
Compare the given inlet and outlet temperatures to judge which flow arrangement transfers more heat for the same fluids.
Consider the flow directions of the two fluids when deciding which configuration is preferential.
tips: Keep consistent definitions of hot and cold ends when computing temperature differences for each configuration.
Temperatures must be in consistent units (K or °C differences); the temperature difference, not the absolute temperature, drives heat transfer.
rq: Why does the cold outlet temperature in a counter-flow exchanger can approach or even exceed the hot outlet temperature, which is impossible in parallel flow?

In counter-flow the fluids move in opposite directions, so the cold fluid exits next to the hot inlet, allowing its outlet temperature to be close to T_HI; in parallel flow the outlet temperatures converge toward a common value, so the cold outlet cannot exceed the hot outlet.
Using the given values, what is the temperature difference at the hot end and cold end of the exchanger?
Hot end: T_HI − T_CO = 90 − 50 = 40 °C; cold end: T_HO − T_CI = 55 − 20 = 35 °C, so the temperature differences are similar and large, favouring counter-flow.
Why is the cold outlet (50 °C) close to the hot inlet (90 °C) a sign of good performance?
It shows the cold fluid is heated to nearly the hot inlet temperature, meaning most of the available temperature difference is exploited, which is characteristic of counter-flow.

units.name: 5.9 Shell and tube heat exchanger construction and internals
units.ov: This module introduces the construction of shell and tube heat exchangers: a tube bundle inside a cylindrical shell, with one fluid inside the tubes and another outside. It covers the main components (shell, tubes, tube plates, headers, baffles, turbulators), pass arrangements, materials, and the logic for allocating fluids to the tube or shell side. Each component's function follows from the need to keep the fluids separate, enhance heat transfer, and allow cleaning and thermal movement.
must: Basic layout: tube bundle inside a shell; one fluid flows inside the tubes (tube side) and the other flows around them (shell side), with heat transferred through the tube walls, which are the heat-transfer surface
Tube plates (tube sheets) hold the tubes at each end and seal them, separating tube-side from shell-side fluid
Headers (end covers) enclose the tube plates and direct tube-side fluid into and out of the tubes; in multi-pass designs they reverse the flow
Baffles are perpendicular to the tubes; they support the tubes and force shell-side fluid to flow across the bundle, increasing turbulence and heat transfer, but they do not seal
The shell is a pressure vessel containing the shell-side fluid, typically cast iron or mild steel, as are the headers
Fluid allocation: the cleanest fluid goes on the shell side and the dirtiest goes through the tubes, where it is easier to access and clean
Single-pass means the tube fluid traverses the shell length once; double-pass means out and back, with the headers reversing the flow. Passes refer to the tube side, not to baffles or shells
Materials: tubes of brass, aluminium brass, titanium, stainless steel or Hastelloy (corrosion resistance and conductivity); tube plate of naval brass (resists seawater)
Turbulators inserted in tubes promote turbulence and raise the tube-side heat transfer rate
The diagram shows a fixed tube plate and an expansion tube plate, plus sea water and oil inlets and outlets; identify and label each component and say what it does
conn: Fluid allocation (dirty fluid in tubes) links to cleaning access, fouling, and the choice of tube material for corrosive fluids such as seawater
Baffles and turbulators both raise turbulence, so they increase heat transfer but also pressure drop and pumping power
Number of passes links header design to the tube-side flow path, velocity, and effective heat transfer area
Material choice per component (naval brass tube plate, steel shell, corrosion-resistant tubes) links to corrosion, cost, and the pressure-vessel function
exq: Sketch and label a double-pass shell and tube heat exchanger with sea water in the tubes and oil in the shell, and state the function of each labelled component.
Explain why the dirtier fluid is normally routed through the tubes and the cleaner fluid through the shell. What are the consequences for cleaning and maintenance?
Distinguish between single-pass and double-pass tube stacks. How do the headers produce a double pass, and what happens to the flow path and velocity?
Describe the role of baffles and turbulators in improving heat transfer. What is the penalty of using them?
State suitable materials for the tubes, tube plate, shell and end covers of a seawater-cooled oil cooler, and justify each choice.

notes.t: Shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: A shell and tube heat exchanger is built from a stack of tubes fitted inside an outer shell.
Two fluids are used: one flows inside the tubes and the other flows around the outside of the tubes, within the shell.
Tubes are sealed into tube plates at each end, which keeps the two fluids apart and gives the tubes a defined path for the cooling fluid.
Headers fit over the tube plates at each end, enclosing the shell and directing fluid into and out of the tubes.
defs: Shell and tube heat exchanger

A heat exchanger consisting of a bundle of tubes fitted inside an outer shell, in which one fluid flows through the tubes and a second fluid flows around the outside of the tubes so that heat is transferred between them.
Tube plate
A plate at each end of the tube bundle into which the tubes are sealed, separating the tube-side fluid from the shell-side fluid.
Header
A chamber fitted over each tube plate that encloses the end of the shell and distributes the tube-side fluid into and out of the tubes.
tips: Do not confuse the tube side with the shell side: the fluid inside the tubes and the fluid outside them are the two separate streams that exchange heat.
Describe the tube plates and headers as the components that seal and direct flow, not as the heat-transfer surface itself, which is the tube wall.
rq: Why must the tubes be sealed into the tube plates at both ends rather than simply left open?

Sealing prevents the two fluids from mixing, so the tube-side fluid stays inside the tubes and the shell-side fluid stays outside, while the tubes still provide a defined conduit for the cooling fluid.
What would happen to heat transfer if the two fluids were both passed through the tubes instead of one through the tubes and one around the outside?

Heat would not be transferred between the fluids in the intended way, because the shell-side fluid, which is the one that surrounds the tubes and exchanges heat through their walls, would be absent; the design depends on one fluid inside and one outside the tubes.

notes.t: Shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: A shell and tube heat exchanger is a common industrial design in which one fluid flows through a bundle of tubes while another fluid flows around them inside a cylindrical shell.
The image shows the external form: a cylindrical shell with inlet and outlet nozzles on each fluid side, flanged end covers, and support feet/brackets.
tips: Do not confuse the shell-side and tube-side fluids; state clearly which fluid is inside the tubes when calculating heat transfer or pressure drop.
The image is only a photograph of the external hardware; internal tube layout and baffles are not shown on this page.
rq: Why are the ends of a shell and tube heat exchanger flanged and bolted rather than welded?
Bolted flanged covers allow the tube bundle to be removed for inspection, cleaning and maintenance of the tubes and shell side.
Why do shell and tube exchangers use multiple nozzles on the shell, as seen in the image?
Separate nozzles allow the shell-side fluid to enter and leave the shell, and the nozzle positions set the fluid flow path around the tubes.

notes.t: Shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: The shell is a pressure vessel housing the tube bundle, pressurised to match the shell-side fluid.
Cold fluid flows through the tubes while hot fluid passes around them on the shell side.
Baffles support the tubes and force shell-side fluid to flow across the tubes, improving heat transfer.
Tube sheets fix the tubes at each end and seal them from the shell side.
Turbulators inserted in tubes increase turbulent flow and so raise the heat transfer rate.
defs: Shell
The outer housing of a shell and tube heat exchanger, acting as a pressure vessel that contains the shell-side fluid.
Baffles
Plates inside the shell that support the tubes and direct shell-side fluid across the tube bundle.
Tube sheet
A plate fixed at each end of the tube bundle that holds the tubes in position and seals them from the shell.
Turbulator
An insert placed inside tubes to induce turbulent flow and enhance convective heat transfer.
tips: Do not confuse the sides: the cold fluid is on the tube side and the hot fluid is on the shell side in this description.
Baffles improve heat transfer and support tubes; they do not seal the shell, which is the job of the tube sheets.
rq: Why are baffles needed on the shell side rather than letting the shell fluid flow straight along the tubes?
Baffles force the shell-side fluid to cross the tubes, increasing velocity and turbulence around them, which improves heat transfer; they also support the tubes against vibration and misalignment.
Why must the shell be designed as a pressure vessel?
The shell contains a fluid at pressure, so its walls must withstand that pressure; it is pressurised to match the shell-side fluid to avoid large stress or leakage between the two fluids.

notes.t: Internals of shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: In double-pass tube stacks, the end covers (headers) must route the liquid so it flows through the correct tubes on each pass.
Tubes are typically made from brass, aluminium brass, titanium, stainless steel or Hastelloy, chosen for corrosion resistance and heat transfer.
The tube plate is typically made of naval brass, which resists seawater corrosion.
End covers/headers and the shell are typically cast iron or mild steel, which are cheaper structural materials.
defs: Double-pass tube stack
A tube bundle in which the fluid travels along the tubes twice, out and back, with end covers reversing the flow between passes.
Single-pass tube stack
A tube bundle in which the fluid flows through the tubes once, from one end to the other, without reversal.
Tube plate
The perforated plate into which the ends of the heat exchanger tubes are fixed and sealed, separating the tube side from the shell side.
tips: Do not confuse the tube plate material (naval brass) with the shell/header material (cast iron or mild steel); the question may ask which material suits which part.
Remember that double-pass means two passes through the tubes, so the flow path is reversed by the end covers, not by the shell.
rq: Why must the end covers direct the flow correctly in a double-pass stack?
Without correct routing, fluid could bypass tubes or mix between passes, so the fluid would not follow the intended counter-/parallel-flow path, reducing heat transfer and performance.
Why is naval brass used for the tube plate while cast iron is used for the shell?
Naval brass resists corrosion from seawater at the tube joints, whereas the shell and headers carry structural loads cheaply and are not as exposed to the same corrosive attack.

notes.t: Internals of shell and tube heat exchangers
pts: Baffle plates are positioned perpendicular to the tubes and force the shell-side fluid to flow across all the tubes, improving heat transfer.
Cleanest fluid is routed around the outside of the tubes (shell side), while the dirtiest fluid is routed through the tubes so it can be cleaned.
Turbulence induced by baffles and tube flow aids cleaning and heat transfer; dirtier fluid inside tubes allows easier access for cleaning.
Double-pass and single-pass arrangements describe how many times the tube-side fluid passes along the shell length.
Labelled components in the diagram include shell, tubes, baffles, fixed tube plate, expansion tube plate, end covers, and inlets/outlets for sea water and oil.
defs: Baffle plate
A plate placed perpendicular to the tubes in a shell and tube heat exchanger that directs shell-side fluid across the tube bundle, increasing turbulence and heat transfer.
Shell side
The space outside the tubes inside the shell, through which the cleaner fluid flows in a shell and tube heat exchanger.
Tube side
The fluid path inside the tubes, typically used for the dirtier fluid so it can be cleaned and so fouling is easier to manage.
Double-pass
A shell and tube configuration in which the tube-side fluid makes two passes along the shell length, doubling the path and increasing heat transfer area use.
Single-pass
A shell and tube configuration in which the tube-side fluid flows once along the full length of the shell.
tips: Do not confuse the shell side and tube side: the cleaner fluid is normally on the shell side, the dirtier fluid inside the tubes.
Single-pass and double-pass refer to tube-side passes, not the number of baffles or shells.
rq: Why are baffle plates placed perpendicular to the tubes rather than parallel to them?

Perpendicular baffles force the shell-side fluid to cross the tube bundle repeatedly, creating turbulence and better heat transfer, whereas parallel flow would leave much of the tube surface poorly contacted.
Why is the dirtiest fluid usually sent through the tubes rather than around them?
Tube interiors are easier to clean (mechanically or chemically) and fouling is confined there, while the shell side is harder to access for cleaning.

units.name: 5.10 Tube pass configurations, erosion and S&T pros/cons
units.ov: This module covers the mechanical design features of shell-and-tube (S&T) heat exchangers: single-pass fixed/floating end plate and U-pass tube arrangements, how differential thermal expansion is accommodated, where erosion occurs, and the overall pros and cons of S&T units compared with plate exchangers. The ideas connect because tube layout determines how thermal expansion is handled, which joints and inlets are vulnerable, and what can be cleaned, repaired or expanded in service.
must: Differential thermal expansion: tubes and shell have different materials and temperatures (shell is cooler as it loses heat to atmosphere), so they expand unequally; if restrained, tubes buckle, fracture or pull out of the tube plate

Single pass end plate design: one end of the tube bundle is rigidly fixed to the shell, the other floats on two O-rings so the tube stack can slide axially; only the floating end accommodates movement
Leakage tell-tale: a connection between the two O-rings of the sliding joint that reveals leakage if one O-ring fails
Tube-to-tube-plate joints can be made by expanding the tubes, screwing and sealing, or explosion welding; the joint method affects leakage and erosion resistance
U-pass design: tube-side fluid enters and leaves at the same end, with U-shaped tubes (two tube passes) and no separate return header; the tubes are free at the bend end, which allows expansion
U-pass drawbacks: the U-bend makes the bundle hard to clean mechanically, and the shell-side flow is directed across the bundle by baffles
Baffles direct shell-side flow across the tubes, raising turbulence and heat transfer coefficient, and also support the tubes

Erosion hot spots: shell-side inlet (direct impingement on the bundle), tube-side inlet, and tube-to-sheet joints; risk is driven by high local velocity and impingement, not average flow; erosion (mechanical) is not corrosion (chemical)
S&T advantages: cheap materials, tube side cleaned easily and faster than plate units, cracked tubes easy to locate and plug, very long lifespan
S&T disadvantages: shell side hard to clean, lower heat transfer area than plate exchangers, size fixed at installation (plate units can add or remove plates)
conn: Differential expansion links to the tube arrangement: the floating O-ring end (with its tell-tale) and the U-bend both solve the same problem, but the U-pass sacrifices easy cleaning

Baffles raise shell-side heat transfer through higher velocity and turbulence, but the same high velocity at the shell inlet increases erosion risk, so there is a thermal versus mechanical durability trade-off
Joint type (expanded, screwed and sealed, explosion welded) ties together leakage, erosion at the tube sheet and the tube buckling or push-out failure under thermal stress
The pros and cons versus plate exchangers (cleaning, area, fixed size, lifespan, repair) are the context for choosing a tube configuration
exq: Explain why a fixed tube sheet at both ends would be unsuitable for a hot-tube, cooler-shell exchanger, and describe how the single pass end plate design with O-rings and a tell-tale overcomes this.
Describe a U-pass shell-and-tube exchanger with a sketch. State two advantages and two disadvantages relative to a single pass fixed/floating design, covering expansion and cleaning.
Identify the three locations most prone to erosion in a shell-and-tube exchanger, explain the mechanism, and suggest design measures to reduce it.
Compare shell-and-tube and plate heat exchangers for a fouling duty requiring a 30-year life: discuss cleaning, repair of leaks, lifespan, heat transfer area and flexibility to change capacity.
Distinguish erosion from corrosion, and explain why a high local velocity can cause failure even when average flow rate is acceptable.

notes.t: Single pass end plate configuration in heat exchangers
pts: One end of the tube bundle is rigidly fixed to the shell via the end plate, while the other end floats on two O-rings so the tube stack can expand and move within the shell.
Tubes and shell are made of different materials, so they expand at different rates; the shell is usually cooler than the tubes because it loses heat to the atmosphere.
If the tubes cannot expand freely they will buckle, fracture or push free of the tube plate, so differential thermal expansion must be allowed for in the design.
A leakage tell-tale connection is provided to reveal whether one of the O-rings in the sliding joint has failed.
Tubes can be secured to the tube plate by expanding them into position, by screwing and sealing, or by explosion welding.
defs: Single pass end plate configuration
A heat exchanger arrangement where tubes run once along the shell length, with one end fixed to the shell and the other end sealed by O-rings that permit axial thermal expansion of the tube stack.
Differential thermal expansion
Unequal expansion of components made of different materials or at different temperatures, which must be accommodated to avoid tube buckling, fracture or loss of seal.
Tell-tale (leakage tell-tale)
A small vent or drain connection between the two O-rings of the floating joint, used to detect failure of an O-ring by observing leakage.
tips: Do not forget differential expansion: materials differ, so the shell and tubes grow at different rates even at the same temperature rise.
Be clear which end is fixed and which end floats; only the floating end, sealed by O-rings, accommodates thermal movement.
rq: Why would the tubes be more likely to buckle than the shell if the free end could not move?
The tubes are hotter and expand more than the cooler shell, so the constrained tube stack is pushed into compression and buckles, fractures or pushes out of the tube plate.
What would a tell-tale reading of fluid flow indicate about the floating joint?
It indicates that one of the two O-rings has failed, so fluid is leaking past the seal and the sealing arrangement needs replacing.

notes.t: U-pass shell-and-tube heat exchanger configuration
pts: In a U-pass design the tube side fluid enters and leaves at the same end of the shell, so the tubes form a U-bend and no separate return header is needed.
The shell side (red) fluid is forced across the tube bundle by internal baffles, which increases turbulence and heat transfer coefficient.
The tube side (yellow) fluid travels through the tubes in two passes, entering at the bottom and exiting at the top on the same side.
Because the tubes are U-shaped, the bundle cannot be removed for cleaning in the usual way, which is a key mechanical design concern.
Differential thermal expansion between the shell and tubes must be accommodated, since the U-bend tubes are free at one end and the bundle is fixed at the other.
defs: U-pass configuration
A shell-and-tube heat exchanger arrangement in which the tube-side fluid makes a single U-shaped bend, returning through the same tube sheet end so both inlet and outlet are on one side.
Baffles
Plates placed inside the shell that direct the shell-side fluid across the tube bundle, increasing turbulence and heat transfer while supporting the tubes.
tips: Do not confuse the U-pass (single shell pass, tubes doubled back) with multi-pass designs using separate return headers; the flow arrangement and mechanical layout differ.
Remember that the mechanical concerns (thermal expansion, cleaning access, tube support) are separate from the thermal analysis of the flow.
rq: Why are baffles fitted on the shell side rather than the tube side?
Baffles force the shell-side fluid to flow across the tubes instead of along them, raising turbulence and the heat transfer coefficient, and they also support the tube bundle against vibration.
What would happen to the mechanical design if the tube bundle were rigidly fixed at both ends?

Differences in thermal expansion between tubes and shell would generate large thermal stresses, so the design would need expansion provision; the U-tube design avoids this because one end is free to expand.

notes.t: The erosion problem in shell-and-tube heat exchangers
pts: Erosion is most likely at the shell-side fluid inlet region, where the incoming fluid impinges directly on the tube bundle at high velocity.
The tube-side fluid inlet and tube sheet joints are also erosion-prone, since high-velocity flow enters the tubes and the tube-to-sheet connection is a weak point.
Tube-to-tube-sheet joints may be welded, expanded, or bolted and sealed; each method affects how well the joint resists leakage and erosion.
Seals at the tube-side inlet and outlet plenum connections prevent leakage between the tube-side and shell-side fluids.
tips: Erosion risk is driven by high local fluid velocity and impingement, not just by high average flow rate.
Do not confuse erosion (mechanical wear from flow) with corrosion (chemical attack) when describing these high-risk locations.
rq: Why is the shell-side fluid inlet region particularly prone to erosion?
The incoming fluid enters at high velocity and strikes the first tubes directly, causing localised wear on the tube surfaces (impingement).
What could be done to reduce erosion at the shell-side inlet?
Fit impingement plates or a sacrificial shield under the inlet nozzle, or use an inlet distributor to spread the flow and lower local velocity.

notes.t: Benefits and drawbacks of S&T heat exchangers
pts: Shell-and-tube exchangers use relatively cheap materials, keeping cost low.
The tube side can be cleaned without disturbing the shell side, and faster than for a plate exchanger.
A cracked tube is easy to locate and plug, so it can be taken out of service quickly.
Shell-and-tube units can be designed for a very long lifespan, far beyond plate exchangers.
Drawbacks: shell side is hard to clean, heat transfer area is lower than plate exchangers, and size is fixed at installation.
tips: Do not confuse ease of finding a cracked tube with ease of repairing it: plugging is quick, replacement is not.
Shell-and-tube size is fixed at installation; you cannot simply add area later, unlike a plate exchanger where plates can be added or removed.
rq: Why can the tube side of a shell-and-tube exchanger be cleaned without disturbing the shell side?
The tube bundle and shell are separate pressure-containing paths, so the tube interior can be accessed (e.g. via channel/header removal) independently of the shell-side fluid and surfaces.
Why is a plugged tube acceptable only up to a limit?
Plugging removes that tube's heat transfer area and flow; too many plugged tubes reduce performance excessively, so beyond a certain percentage the whole tube stack must be replaced.

units.name: 5.11 Design considerations and summary
units.ov: This material covers practical design and selection considerations for heat exchangers (fluid and coolant duty, venting, draining, filtration, corrosion protection) and summarises the two main types, plate and shell and tube, with their trade-offs. The ideas connect because the thermal duty determines the exchanger type and size, while material choice, maintenance and corrosion control determine lifespan, cost and reliability.
must: Selection inputs: process fluid type, temperature and flow rate; required heat dissipation (duty); coolant type, temperature and flow rate
Duty link: \(Q=\dot m c_p \Delta T\) for each stream, so the specified duty and the flow rates fix the temperature changes
Two major classes are plate and shell and tube, and hybrid designs also exist, so do not claim only two categories
Plate exchangers: more efficient and easier to clean, but more expensive, generally shorter-lived, and cleaning can sometimes take longer
Material properties, especially the heat transfer coefficient, are critical to performance (\(Q=UA\Delta T_{lm}\))
Air vents go at the highest points (usually two) to remove trapped air; drains go at the lowest points (usually at least two) to empty the system
Inlet filters are needed with seawater because meshes can still block, so debris must be kept out

Sacrificial anode: a metal more reactive to corrosion than the protected structure (e.g. zinc), which corrodes preferentially; a less reactive metal would not protect. Protective coatings such as rubberised paint also help
Heat exchangers need regular maintenance, temperature-based assessment (monitoring temperatures for fouling or degradation) and methodical cleaning
conn: Fouling and blockage (seawater, filters) reduce the effective heat transfer coefficient \(U\), which lowers \(Q\) and links to maintenance and cleaning schedules
Choosing plate or shell and tube trades efficiency against cost, lifespan and cleaning, and depends on fluid type, duty and temperatures
Corrosion protection (anodes, coatings) and material choice affect both thermal performance and lifespan, so they feed into the cost comparison
Air vents and drains affect performance and safety: trapped air reduces heat transfer area and flow, and drains enable maintenance and cleaning
exq: List the information needed to select a heat exchanger for cooling a process fluid, and explain how each item affects the design.
Compare plate and shell and tube exchangers in terms of efficiency, cost, lifespan and cleaning, and recommend a type for a seawater-cooled application with justification.
Explain where air vents and drains should be placed in a heat exchanger circuit, why at least two of each are normally provided, and what problems arise if they are misplaced.
Describe how a sacrificial anode works. Why must it be more reactive than the protected structure, and what other protective measures could be used?

A heat exchanger must dissipate a given duty, for example 50 kW, with water heating by 10 K. Calculate the required coolant mass flow rate and discuss how fouling would affect the outlet temperature and the maintenance required.

notes.t: General design considerations for heat exchangers
pts: Heat exchangers are designed or selected based on the fluid type (with its temperature and flow rate), the heat dissipation required, and the coolant fluid type (with its temperature and flow rate).
Air vents should be placed at the highest points of the system, usually two of them, so trapped air can be removed.
Drains are needed to empty the system, with usually at least two provided.
Inlet filters are important when using seawater, since meshes can still create blockages.
Sacrificial anodes are made of metals more reactive to corrosion than the structure they protect, such as zinc, or protective coatings like rubberised paint.
defs: Sacrificial anode
A metal more reactive to corrosion than the structure it protects, which corrodes preferentially so that the protected structure is preserved.
tips: Air vents go at the highest points and drains at the lowest, so do not place them arbitrarily; confusing their positions is a common error.
A sacrificial anode must be more reactive than the protected metal; a less reactive metal would not corrode preferentially and would fail to protect the structure.
rq: Why are two air vents usually fitted at the highest points of a heat exchanger rather than anywhere else?
Trapped air collects at high points and can block flow or reduce heat transfer, so vents there allow it to be removed.
Why might a mesh inlet filter still cause problems when using seawater?
Debris and organisms can accumulate on the mesh and create blockages, reducing flow through the exchanger.

notes.t: Heat Exchangers: Summary
pts: The two major classes of heat exchanger are plate type and shell and tube; hybrid designs also exist
Material properties, including the heat transfer coefficient, are critical to heat exchanger performance
Plate heat exchangers are more efficient and easier to clean, but are more expensive with a generally shorter lifespan and can take longer to clean
Heat exchangers need regular maintenance, temperature-based assessment, and methodical cleaning
tips: Do not assume plate exchangers are always better: they are more efficient and easier to clean but more expensive, shorter-lived, and can be more time-consuming to clean.
Note that hybrid designs exist, so do not state that every heat exchanger falls strictly into one of only two categories.
rq: Why might a plate heat exchanger be preferred despite its higher cost and shorter lifespan?
Its higher efficiency and ease of cleaning can outweigh the higher purchase cost and shorter life, depending on the application's performance and maintenance requirements.
Why does the heat transfer coefficient depend on material properties rather than only on geometry?

Thermal conductivity and surface properties govern how readily heat conducts through and across the exchanger walls, so the material choice directly sets how much heat can be transferred per unit area and temperature difference.

units.name: 5.12 Heat exchangers and coolers (summary notes)
units.ov: This module covers how heat exchangers transfer heat between two fluids across a conductive wall, comparing plate-type and shell-and-tube designs. It links the heat-transfer principles (area, path length, conductivity) to material choice, construction, maintenance and operational design such as venting, filtering and corrosion protection. Exam answers usually require justifying a design choice by trading off efficiency, cost, cleaning and fault-finding.
must: Definition: a heat exchanger transfers heat from one fluid to another through a separating plate or tube, with no mixing (works for liquids and gases)
Good design needs large surface area, short conduction path and high thermal conductivity \(k\) (W/m°C); \(k\) is a material property, whereas heat transfer rate also depends on area and thickness

Walls must be impermeable and thick enough to resist wear; metals are used for high heat transfer rates, polymers conduct poorly; cost and corrosion resistance also affect material choice (e.g. copper/silver vs titanium)

Plate exchanger construction: corrugated pressed plates (316/304 stainless, titanium, Hastelloy) with NBR/EPDM rubber seals, clamped in a frame, giving alternating hot/cold channels; corrugations add area, turbulence and stiffness

Plate exchanger pros and cons: large area in small volume, more efficient, size adjustable, easy plate replacement; but expensive plates, seals needing replacement, slow cleaning (disassemble and reassemble to original stack length), and leaks hard to locate

Shell and tube construction: one fluid in the tubes, the other around them in the shell; tubes sealed into tube plates (naval brass); baffles increase shell-side turbulence; shell is cast iron or mild steel
Thermal expansion: one tube-stack end is fixed and the other floats on two O-rings, otherwise tubes fracture from differential expansion

Shell and tube pros and cons: cheap, tube side easy to clean, a cracked tube is easy to find and plug (until the plugging limit is exceeded, then the stack is replaced); but shell side is hard to clean and it is less efficient than plate type
Operational design: vent valves at the highest points, inlet filters, temperature sensors for performance logging and control, sacrificial anodes against corrosion, especially in seawater
Tell-tale holes reveal seal leakage in tube-sheet joints; plate cleaning order is to close valves, drain, measure, loosen bolts, then flood, vent air and check for leaks
conn: Heat transfer principles (area, path length, conductivity) explain both why plates are compact and efficient and why metals are chosen over polymers
Material selection ties together conductivity, corrosion (seawater, anodes) and cost, and different components of the same exchanger (tubes, tube plate, shell, seals) use different materials

Maintenance and fault-finding drive the design choice: plate type gives easy size change and plate replacement but difficult leak location, while shell and tube allows easy leak location and plugging but hard shell-side cleaning
Differential thermal expansion links material choice to mechanical design (floating end with O-rings) and to the risk of tube fracture or leaks
exq: Compare plate-type and shell-and-tube heat exchangers for a marine engine cooling system, covering efficiency, size, cost, cleaning and fault-finding, and recommend one with justification.
Explain why differential thermal expansion is a problem in a shell and tube exchanger and describe how the tube stack is designed to accommodate it.
Describe the construction of a plate heat exchanger, stating the materials used for plates and seals and the function of the corrugations and seals.

List the design features needed to operate a seawater-cooled exchanger reliably (venting, filtration, temperature control, corrosion protection), explaining why each is needed and where vent valves should be placed.
A shell and tube cooler develops a leak. Explain how the faulty tube is found and dealt with, the limit of this remedy, and how the cleaning of tube side and shell side differs.

notes.t: Heat Exchangers
pts: A heat exchanger moves heat from one fluid to another, through a separating plate or tube, for liquids and gases.
Moving heat can be the purpose of a device (fridge) or needed to prevent overheating (engine).
Good design needs a large surface area, short heat flow path and high thermal conductivity.
Fluids must not mix, so walls must be impermeable and thick enough to survive wear over the lifespan.
Metals are used where high heat transfer rates are needed because they are good thermal conductors; polymers conduct heat poorly.
defs: Heat exchanger
A device that transfers heat from one fluid to another, typically two fluids separated by a plate or tube through which the heat is conducted.
tips: Conductivity values are in W/m°C; do not confuse conductivity (material property) with heat transfer rate (depends on area and path length too).
Choosing a material: silver and copper have the highest conductivities listed, but cost and corrosion resistance also matter in design.
rq: Why does a heat exchanger wall need high thermal conductivity rather than just a large thickness?
Heat flow through the wall is driven by conduction; high conductivity lets heat pass quickly, whereas thickness increases the heat flow path and reduces transfer rate.
Why are polymers unsuitable for high-rate heat transfer even though they are impermeable?
Polymers have low thermal conductivity, so heat transfer rate is low; they are only suited to low-rate applications like underfloor heating.

notes.t: Plate Type Heat Exchangers
pts: A plate heat exchanger is built from corrugated pressed plates separated by seals and clamped in a frame between end-plates.
Seals between plates create alternating passageways so the hot and cooling liquids flow in adjacent channels without mixing.
Corrugations aid heat transfer and support the large flat plate surface.
Plates are typically stainless steel (316, 304), titanium or Hastelloy; seals are usually NBR or EPDM rubber.
The flow pattern diagrams show M3 and M3-X plate arrangements, where the port arrangement determines how the two fluids route through the plate pack.
defs: Plate type heat exchanger
A heat exchanger made of corrugated pressed plates separated by gaskets and held in a frame, forming alternating channels for hot and cold fluids.
Corrugation
Pressed pattern on a plate that increases surface area and turbulence to improve heat transfer and add stiffness.
tips: Do not confuse the seal material (rubber gaskets) with the plate material when listing construction materials.
Remember the exchanger handles both liquids and gases, so do not restrict answers to liquid-only applications.
rq: Why must the seals between plates alternate the flow paths rather than allow both fluids into the same channel?
So each hot channel is bordered by cold channels, keeping the two liquids separated while allowing heat to conduct through the thin plate.
Why are titanium or Hastelloy plates used in some applications instead of stainless steel?
They resist corrosion from aggressive fluids (e.g. seawater or chlorides) better than standard stainless steel.

notes.t: Advantages, Disadvantages and Cleaning of Plate Type Heat Exchangers
pts: Plate heat exchangers offer a very large heat transfer surface in a small machine volume, and need less space than shell and tube coolers.
Both sides of the cooler are cleaned together and damaged plates can be replaced or removed easily, but the plates themselves are expensive.
Cooler size can be changed at any time in its lifespan, which is a key flexibility advantage.
Cleaning is slow and labour-intensive: the plates must be disassembled, cleaned, reassembled to the original stack length and re-tightened.
Seals have a finite lifespan and must be inspected and replaced regularly, so they are a maintenance cost.
defs: Plate type heat exchanger
A heat exchanger made of a stack of thin corrugated plates clamped together, with alternate channels carrying the two fluids, giving a large heat transfer area in a compact volume.
tips: Do not confuse the advantage of easy plate replacement with the disadvantage that finding a damaged plate is usually difficult; a leak is not easy to locate.
Cleaning procedure order matters: close valves and drain before measuring and loosening clamp bolts, and check for leaks only after flooding and venting air.
rq: Why must both sides of a plate cooler be drained and cleaned at the same time, and what does this imply for maintenance planning?

The plates form a sealed stack where each plate separates the two fluid streams, so the cooler cannot be opened on one side only; the whole stack must be taken down, making cleaning a full-shutdown, time-consuming job.
Why is it important to measure the plate stack length before disassembly and restore it when reassembling?

The compressed stack length sets the seal compression; if it is not restored by tightening evenly to the original length (or to a torque value), seals may leak or plates may be over- or under-compressed.

notes.t: Shell and Tube Type Heat Exchangers
pts: One fluid flows through the tubes while the other flows around the outside of the tubes inside the shell, transferring heat between them.
Tubes are sealed into tube plates at each end, providing a passageway for the cooling liquid; headers surround the plates and enclose the shell.

Materials are chosen per component: tubes depend on the fluids (e.g. aluminium brass, stainless steel, titanium, copper-nickel, Hastelloy), tube plates use naval brass, and shells and end covers use cast iron or mild steel.
Differential thermal expansion between tubes and shell (different materials and temperatures) must be accommodated or the tubes will fracture in service.
One end of the tube stack is fixed to the shell, while the other end uses two O-rings so the stack can expand and move within the shell.
defs: Shell and tube heat exchanger
A heat exchanger in which a bundle of tubes is fitted inside an outer shell; one fluid flows inside the tubes and the other flows around the outside of them.
Tube plate
A plate into which the ends of the tubes are sealed, forming the passageway for the fluid inside the tubes and separating it from the shell-side fluid.
Single- and double-pass arrangement
Configurations of the tube stack in which fluid makes one or two passes along the tube length, with the end covers directing flow through the correct tubes.
tips: Do not confuse the tube side and shell side: the tube-side fluid flows through the tubes, the shell-side fluid flows around the outside.
Remember thermal expansion differs between tubes and shell, so a rigid double-fixed design would cause fracture; always state the need for an expansion allowance.
rq: Why is one end of the tube stack fixed while the other end floats on O-rings?
To allow the tubes to expand and contract relative to the shell as temperatures change, preventing thermal stresses that would fracture the tubes.
Why might the tubes be made of a different material from the shell?
Tubes must resist corrosion from the specific fluids (e.g. seawater), so they are chosen for fluid compatibility, whereas the shell only needs structural strength at lower cost.

notes.t: Shell and Tube Heat Exchangers: Advantages and Disadvantages
pts: Shell and tube coolers are built from relatively cheap materials, making them cost-effective.
The tube side can be cleaned without disturbing the shell side, simplifying maintenance.
A cracked tube is easy to locate and can be plugged to isolate the leak.
Shell side of the tubes is difficult to clean, a key maintenance drawback.
Shell and tube coolers are less efficient than plate coolers.
defs: Baffles
Plates inside the shell that direct the shell-side fluid across the tube stack, increasing turbulence and heat transfer.
Tell-tale hole
A small drilled hole in a tube-sheet flange joint that reveals leakage of fluid past the neoprene seal rings, warning of seal failure.
Sacrificial anodes
Metal pieces fitted in the cooler that corrode preferentially, protecting the main structure from galvanic/electrolytic corrosion.
tips: Do not confuse which side is easy to clean: the tube side is easy, the shell side is difficult.
Plugging tubes is limited; state that the whole stack must be removed once the plugging limit is exceeded.
rq: Why can the tube side be cleaned without disturbing the shell side, and why does this not work the other way round?
The tube bundle is accessed from the end/header without opening the shell; the shell side is enclosed by the tube stack and baffles, so cleaning it requires removing the stack.
Why is a limited percentage of tubes allowed to be plugged?
Plugging reduces the heat transfer area and flow capacity; beyond a threshold the cooler performance falls too far and the whole stack must be replaced.

notes.t: Designing Coolers for Operation
pts: Vent valves should be placed at the highest points of the cooling system so trapped air can be released.
Temperature sensors can be used to log cooler performance over time, allowing its efficiency to be monitored.
Inlet filters protect the cooler from debris; in marine applications seawater makes this especially important.
Temperature control is needed so the cooled equipment operates within its safe temperature range.
Corrosion protection, such as sacrificial anodes, guards cooler metal parts against degradation, especially in seawater.
tips: Do not place vent valves at low points; trapped air collects at high points, so venting low will not remove the air lock.
Remember sea-water is a specific corrosion and blockage hazard in marine applications, so inlet filtering and corrosion protection are both needed.
rq: Why is seawater a particular problem for cooler inlets and metal parts?

Seawater carries sediment, marine debris and biological growth that can block inlet filters and tubes, and its high salt content is highly corrosive, accelerating galvanic and general corrosion of metals.
Why must vent valves be at the highest points rather than anywhere in the system?
Air and gases rise and collect at the highest points; if they are not vented there they form air locks that reduce coolant flow and heat transfer.

units.name: 6.1 Clutch purpose, requirements and design principles
units.ov: This material introduces the clutch as a non-permanent, controllable link between a drive side (attached to the prime mover) and a driven side. It covers the purposes and requirements of clutches, the main classes (positive contact, friction, overrunning, fluid coupling, magnetic) and the basic design logic of torque capacity versus applied torque with a safety factor. The ideas connect through the speed difference between the shafts: this determines which clutch type can engage, how much slip and heat occur, and how torque and power are transmitted.
must: Definition of a clutch: a device that smoothly and gradually connects two shafts rotating at different speeds, transmitting torque non-permanently (engaged or disengaged on demand); it is never a permanent connection
Safety factor: \( S.F. = T_{CAP}/T_{APP} \), dimensionless, usually > 2; capacity on top, applied torque below, both in N·m
Power-torque relation: \( P = T\omega \) with P in W, T in N·m and \( \omega \) in rad/s (convert rev/min using \( \omega = 2\pi N/60 \))
Positive contact clutches (square jaw, spiral jaw, toothed) transmit torque through interlocking jaws or teeth and cannot engage when there is a speed difference
Friction clutches (disc, drum, cone) can engage while slipping, so they connect shafts at different speeds; slip means output speed is below input speed, and with no slip they are equal

Overrunning clutches (roller, sprag, spring wound) transmit torque in one direction only, engage automatically by speed direction and freewheel when the driven member overtakes the driver; they stop reverse operation, not forward drive
Drive side vs driven side: the drive side is attached directly to the prime mover (engine or motor), and the driven side receives motion only through the clutch
Requirements of a clutch: low engagement force, constant friction (predictable torque), heat removal during slip, low wear for reasonable life
Design parameters: lining size and material, speed, torque, shock loading and operating temperature, all feeding into the safety factor; clutches are usually specialist-supplied designs

Other classes: fluid couplings (dry fluid, hydraulic) give variable speed hydrodynamically; magnetic clutches use magnetic particle, hysteresis or eddy current effects; actuation can be mechanical, pneumatic/hydraulic, electrical or magnetic
conn: Speed difference decides clutch choice: positive contact needs matched speeds, while friction clutches tolerate slip, which links to heat generation, wear and cooling requirements
Power-torque-speed: a power rating and shaft speed give the applied torque \( T = P/\omega \), which feeds into the safety factor calculation against \( T_{CAP} \)
Design factors such as shock loading, temperature and lining material change the effective torque capacity, so they link to the choice of S.F. and to the requirement for constant friction

Clutch versus overrunning clutch: on-demand engagement versus automatic engagement by direction of speed, which links to the drive/driven side definitions (freewheeling when the driven side overtakes the drive side)
exq: Define a clutch and state four requirements of a good clutch, explaining why constant friction and heat dissipation matter for a friction clutch
A motor delivers 15 kW at 1450 rev/min through a clutch with torque capacity 250 N·m. Calculate the applied torque and the safety factor, and state whether it meets S.F. > 2
Compare positive contact, friction and overrunning clutches by operating principle, ability to engage with a speed difference and direction of torque transmission, giving two examples of each
Explain the terms prime mover, drive side and driven side, and describe how a slipping clutch can control output speed with a fixed input speed
List the design parameters that affect clutch selection and explain how they combine in the safety factor; what would you do if the calculated S.F. were 1.4?

notes.t: Intended learning outcomes for clutches
pts: A clutch connects and disconnects power transmission between rotating shafts or components in a system.
Clutches are classified into major types and sub-types, which must be identified.
Positive contact, overrunning and friction clutches each have distinct basic operating principles.
Power and torque relationships govern how clutches transmit drive.
tips: Keep power and torque units consistent: power in W equals torque in N·m multiplied by angular velocity in rad/s, not rev/min.
Distinguish clutches (engaged and disengaged on demand) from overrunning clutches (engage automatically based on speed direction).
rq: Why must a friction clutch be able to slip, and what happens to the energy when it does?
Slipping allows smooth engagement while speeds equalise; the kinetic energy difference is dissipated as heat at the friction surfaces.
How does an overrunning clutch differ from a positive contact clutch in how it transmits torque?
An overrunning clutch transmits torque in one direction only and freewheels in the other, while a positive contact clutch locks via interlocking features in both directions when engaged.

notes.t: Purposes of clutches
pts: A clutch smoothly and gradually connects two shafts rotating at different speeds.
A clutch transmits torque from one shaft to another while connecting them non-permanently.
Engagement can be operator-controlled or automatic based on the driving shaft's speed.
A slipping clutch can control output shaft speed with a fixed input speed.
Clutches are found in cars, motorbikes and compressors, i.e. most engine or drive systems.
defs: Clutch
A device that allows the smooth and gradual connection of two shafts rotating at different speeds, transmitting torque between them in a non-permanent manner.
tips: Do not describe a clutch as a permanent connection; it is non-permanent and can be engaged or disengaged.
A slipping clutch relies on a speed difference between input and output; with no slip, output speed equals input speed.
rq: Why must a clutch connect the shafts gradually rather than instantly?
Connecting gradually lets the speeds of the two shafts equalise smoothly, avoiding shock loads, jerking and damage to the drivetrain.
What would happen to the output speed of a slipping clutch if the clutch were fully engaged?
The output shaft would turn at the same speed as the input, so no speed difference (slip) would remain and the output speed would simply equal the input speed.

notes.t: General design principles for clutches
pts: Clutches are rarely designed from scratch; specialist manufacturers supply existing designs that integrate with most systems
Key design parameters are the size and material of the clutch lining, speed, torque, loading (e.g. shock) and operating temperature
These factors combine into a safety factor ensuring the torque capacity is sufficient to operate safely; a common target is S.F. > 2
defs: Clutch lining
The friction part of a clutch that 'links' with another component to transmit torque.
Safety factor (S.F.)
The ratio of a clutch's torque capacity to the applied torque, used to ensure safe operation; usually greater than 2.
eqs: S.F. = safety factor (dimensionless); T_{CAP} = torque capacity (N·m); T_{APP} = applied torque (N·m)
tips: Keep S.F. dimensionless: torque capacity and applied torque must use the same units (N·m) before dividing.
Do not confuse torque capacity (T_CAP) with applied torque (T_APP); S.F. = T_CAP / T_APP, not the reverse.
rq: Why would a designer choose an existing specialist clutch rather than design one from scratch?
Specialist manufacturers offer proven designs that integrate with most systems, saving time and reducing risk.
What would happen to the safety factor if a shock load occurred that was not allowed for in the design?
The applied torque would rise above the design value, lowering S.F. and possibly making the torque capacity insufficient, risking slip or failure.

notes.t: Driving and driven sides of a clutch
pts: Every clutch has two sides: a drive side and a driven side.
The drive side is attached directly to the source of motion, the prime mover.
The driven side receives its turning motion through the clutch, not directly from the source.
defs: Prime mover
The source of motion (e.g. an engine or motor) to which the drive side of a clutch is attached directly.
Drive side
The side of a clutch attached directly to the prime mover, which supplies the turning motion.
Driven side
The side of a clutch that receives its turning motion through the clutch from the drive side.
tips: Do not confuse the drive side with the driven side: the drive side is connected directly to the prime mover, while the driven side only receives motion through the clutch.
The prime mover is the source of motion (e.g. engine), not the wheels or the gearbox.
rq: In a moving car, what is the prime mover and which side of the clutch is it attached to?
The engine is the prime mover; it is attached to the drive side of the clutch.
When a car is being started, what does the driven side do as the clutch is engaged?
It receives turning motion gradually through the clutch from the drive side (engine), accelerating the transmission and wheels until they match engine speed.

notes.t: Requirements of a clutch
pts: A clutch must not need excessive force to engage or disengage it.
Friction should stay constant so that torque transmission is predictable.
Heat generated during slipping must be carried away to avoid overheating.
Wear must be kept low so the clutch has a reasonable working life.
tips: Requirements are qualitative: state them in words, not as formulas, unless asked for a calculation.
Do not confuse the coefficient of friction (dimensionless) with the friction force (in newtons).
rq: Why does a constant coefficient of friction matter for a clutch?
If friction varies, the torque the clutch can transmit varies unpredictably, causing inconsistent engagement and drive behaviour.
Why is heat dissipation a requirement rather than just a side effect?
Kinetic energy lost while the clutch slips is converted to heat at the friction faces; if it is not removed, temperature rises, degrading friction and damaging components.

notes.t: Types of clutch
pts: Clutches are classified by method of engagement: mechanical, pneumatic/hydraulic, electrical or magnetic actuation.
Positive contact clutches (square jaw, spiral jaw, toothed) cannot connect when there is a speed difference between the two shafts.
Friction clutches (disc, drum, cone) can connect when there is a speed difference, so they allow slipping during engagement.
Overrunning clutches (roller, sprag, spring wound) stop reverse operation, transmitting torque in one direction only.
Fluid couplings (dry fluid, hydraulic) provide variable speed operation between input and output.
defs: Positive contact clutch
A clutch that transmits torque through interlocking jaws or teeth and therefore must be engaged at matching speeds.
Friction clutch
A clutch that transmits torque through frictional contact between surfaces (disc, drum or cone) and can engage while slipping.
Overrunning clutch
A clutch that transmits torque in one direction only, freewheeling when the driven member turns faster than the driver, with roller, sprag or spring-wound designs.
Magnetic clutch
A clutch that transmits torque by magnetic action, using magnetic particle, hysteresis or eddy current effects.
Fluid coupling
A clutch that transmits power hydrodynamically through a fluid (dry fluid or hydraulic), enabling variable speed operation.
tips: Do not confuse positive contact clutches (must engage at equal speeds) with friction clutches (can slip during engagement).
Overrunning clutches stop reverse operation; they do not stop forward torque transmission.
rq: Why can a friction clutch engage while a positive contact clutch cannot?
Friction clutches transmit torque through surface friction, which tolerates slip during engagement; positive contact clutches need interlocking jaws or teeth to line up, so the speeds must match.
Why would an overrunning clutch be used in a drive, such as a bicycle freewheel?
It transmits torque in one direction only and lets the driven part spin freely when it turns faster, so the drive does not reverse or drag the driver.

units.name: 6.2 Positive contact clutches: jaw and toothed types
units.ov: This material covers positive contact clutches, which transmit torque by mechanical interlock of jaws or teeth rather than friction. It looks at the square jaw (dog) clutch and the toothed (multiple serration) type, and at the need for alignment before engagement. It also covers backlash, the clearance that makes engagement possible but introduces play. The ideas connect through one trade-off: interlock gives non-slip, heat-free drive, but engagement is restricted and overload causes shear rather than slip.
must: Definition: a positive contact clutch transmits torque by direct mechanical interlocking of jaws or teeth, so driver and driven rotate at the same speed with no slip.
Positive contact clutches must be aligned before engagement, unlike friction clutches, which engage by slipping and then lock up.
Contact force acts at 90° to the contact faces, so torque is carried by bearing and shear on the jaws, not by friction (\(T = F r\)).
Square jaw (dog) clutch: square-profiled jaws, drives in either direction of rotation, suited to engagement when stationary or at low relative speed and not under load.
Engaging a jaw clutch at speed causes impact and wear. The notes also say the design must allow engagement at normal speed, so state the low relative speed caveat clearly.
The engaging member slides axially on a keyway or serrations, so it has axial movement only and is not free radially. Radial movement is a common mistake.
No friction means no slip losses and no unwanted heat. The drawback is that overload cannot be relieved by slipping, so parts shear.

Toothed (multiple serration) clutches have many fine radial serrations, so engagement is possible at small angular positions. They are often made with helical gears, which are kept in mesh because they are hard to shift in and out. The driven gear freewheels on its shaft when disengaged.
Backlash is clearance or play between mating parts. Some is needed to prevent jamming and to allow the parts to slot together, and zero backlash is only a theoretical ideal.
Backlash is not always bad. Judge it against the application: it helps engagement but gives lost motion on reversal and impact.
conn: Alignment and clearance: parts must be aligned to engage, and the clearance that lets them slot together is the backlash, so easy engagement is traded against play and shock on reversal.

Positive drive versus friction clutch: no slip means no heat and exact speed matching, but engagement must be at matched or low speed and overload leads to shear. Questions often ask for a comparison and a choice for a given duty.
Serrations, keyways and axial sliding: the same axial-only sliding feature links the square jaw clutch to the toothed type, and to gear and pulley layouts where one gear is engaged or freewheels.
Engagement speed and impact: engaging at speed causes impact, wear and backlash-related shock, linking operating conditions to failure modes.
exq: Define a positive contact clutch and explain, with a sketch, how a square jaw clutch transmits torque without friction. State why it can drive in either direction.
Compare a square jaw clutch with a friction clutch for a gearbox application. Cover engagement while running, heat generation, slip and overload behaviour, and recommend one with justification.
A square jaw clutch has jaws at mean radius 40 mm, with 4 jaws, transmitting 200 N·m. Find the force on each jaw, assuming equal load sharing, and state which failure mode applies on overload.
Explain backlash and why it is needed in a jaw or toothed clutch. Discuss one application where it is acceptable and one where it is undesirable.
Describe how a toothed (multiple serration) clutch differs from a square jaw clutch. Explain the role of the axial keyway or serration sliding and why the driven gear freewheels when disengaged.

notes.t: Positive contact clutches: square jaw (dog) clutch
pts: Positive contact clutches must be aligned before they can be engaged, unlike friction clutches.
Square jaw (dog) clutches suit applications where engagement and disengagement are not needed while in motion or under load.
Clearance between the jaws is required so the mating parts can slot together.
Engaging the clutch while running at normal speed is a key design requirement.
Square jaw clutches transmit power in either direction of rotation and are often used in gear and pulley systems.
defs: Positive contact clutch
A clutch that transmits torque through direct mechanical interlocking of jaws or teeth, requiring alignment before engagement.
Square jaw (dog) clutch
A positive contact clutch with square-profiled interlocking jaws on mating halves, used for non-slip torque transmission when stationary or only with limited relative motion.
tips: Do not confuse positive contact (dog/jaw) clutches, which transmit torque by mechanical interlock, with friction clutches, which rely on slip and friction.
Square jaw clutches should only be engaged at low relative speed; engaging at speed causes impact and wear, even though the page states they must engage at normal speed in design.
rq: Why can a square jaw clutch not be engaged freely while under load or in motion?
Its jaws must align and interlock mechanically; under load or relative motion the jaws would jam or collide rather than slide into place.
What would happen to a square jaw clutch if no clearance were provided between the jaws?
The jaws would not be able to slide into engagement and disengagement would be difficult or impossible, causing jamming or damage.

notes.t: Positive contact clutches – square jaw
pts: Square jaw clutch parts are shaped so one pushes the other, so both rotate at the same speed with no slip.
Torque is transmitted by positive mechanical engagement (interference/clearance fit), not by friction.
The engaging member slides axially along a keyway with serrations, so it moves axially only and is not connected radially.
Because no friction is involved, the square jaw clutch does not generate unwanted heat.
The drive gear is the grey part on the left and the driven gear is the gold part on the right.
defs: Positive contact clutch
A clutch that transmits torque through direct mechanical interlocking of jaws or teeth, so the driving and driven parts rotate at the same speed without slipping.
Square jaw clutch
A positive contact clutch whose interlocking square-profiled jaws on the two halves push one another to drive both at equal speed.
tips: Do not confuse positive contact (jaw) clutches with friction clutches: jaw clutches cannot slip and only engage when speeds are matched.
Remember that the connection permits axial movement only; mistakenly describing radial movement loses marks.
rq: Why does a square jaw clutch not generate unwanted heat, unlike a friction clutch?
It transmits torque by mechanical interlocking of jaws rather than by friction between sliding surfaces, so no slip energy is dissipated as heat.
Why must the square jaw clutch connection be axial rather than radial?
The keyway with serrations lets one part slide axially to engage and disengage while still rotating with the shaft; a radial connection would prevent this engagement movement.

notes.t: Positive contact clutches: toothed (multiple serration) type
pts: Positive contact clutches must be aligned before they can be engaged, unlike friction clutches.
Toothed clutches are often made with helical gears.
Helical gears are kept in mesh because they are hard to shift in and out of mesh.
The driven gear rotates freely on a shaft when no power is required, so it is disengaged from transmitting torque.
defs: Positive contact clutch
A clutch that transmits torque through direct mechanical interlocking of teeth or serrations, requiring alignment before engagement, rather than by friction.
Multiple serration clutch
A toothed clutch whose mating faces carry many fine radial serrations, allowing engagement at small angular positions.
tips: Do not confuse positive contact (interlocking, needs alignment) with friction clutches (slip-based engagement).
rq: Why are toothed clutches often kept permanently in mesh rather than engaged and disengaged each time?
Helical gear teeth are difficult to shift in and out of mesh, so the gears are left meshed and the clutch is controlled by letting the gear spin freely on its shaft when no power is needed.
What is the key practical difference between a positive contact clutch and a friction clutch?
A positive contact clutch needs alignment of its teeth before it can engage and transmits torque by interlocking, whereas a friction clutch can engage at any relative speed through slipping friction.

notes.t: Power transmission by direct mechanical contact and backlash
pts: Power and torque are transmitted through direct mechanical contact, not friction.
Force/torque acts at 90° to the contact faces, so the drive is a positive (non-slipping) mechanical coupling.
This coupling is explicitly not a friction-type clutch, so it does not slip under load but can shear if overloaded.
Backlash is the clearance between mating parts caused by gaps; it may or may not be desirable depending on the application.
Zero backlash is the theoretical ideal, but some backlash must be allowed in practice to prevent system jamming.
defs: Backlash
The clearance or play between mating parts of a mechanism, caused by gaps between them, which allows a small amount of movement before the drive is engaged in the reverse direction.
tips: Do not confuse this positive mechanical coupling with a friction clutch: it cannot slip, so overload causes shearing rather than slipping.
Backlash is not always bad; state whether it is desirable for the specific application before judging its effect.
rq: Why must some backlash be allowed in a reversing gear train even though zero backlash is the theoretical ideal?
Without clearance, the parts would bind or jam due to thermal expansion, manufacturing tolerances and lubrication needs, so some gap is required for smooth operation.
Why is a direct mechanical coupling like this not suitable as a friction clutch for overload protection?
Because it transmits torque by hard contact rather than friction, it does not slip when overloaded; instead the drive members are liable to shear.

units.name: 6.3 Friction clutches: drum (centrifugal) type
units.ov: This material introduces friction clutches, focusing on the drum (centrifugal) type, in which flyweights carrying friction linings are thrown outward against a cylindrical drum above a critical speed. It covers the components, automatic engagement and disengagement, the dependence of torque capacity on friction and normal force, wear effects, and externally actuated drum clutches. The ideas link as follows: speed sets the centrifugal force, the force sets the normal force, and the normal force together with \(\mu\) sets the transmissible torque.
must: Centrifugal clutch principle: flyweights/shoes move radially outward and press linings on the inner surface of the drum; engagement is automatic once speed exceeds a critical value.
Engagement depends on speed, not torque: below the critical speed the clutch does not engage regardless of load.
Torque capacity depends on both friction coefficient and normal force (pad mass, speed, spring force), never on \(\mu\) alone: \(T=\mu N r\) per shoe, summed over the shoes.

Normal force on a shoe: \(N = m\omega^2 r_g - F_s\), where \(F_s\) is the spring force. Engagement begins when \(m\omega^2 r_g = F_s\), which gives the engagement speed \(\omega_1=\sqrt{F_s/(m r_g)}\).
Components: hub (inner, on the drive shaft), flyweights, pins, tension springs, friction linings, drum (outer, driven). The drive side is the inner part; do not confuse hub and drum.

Functions: lets the prime mover start and run up with minimal load (lower motor start currents and engine stress), disengages automatically as speed falls, and the driven shaft can stop while the driver keeps running.
Springs and masses set the engagement speed and the smoothness of engagement, and absorb RPM fluctuations; slipping during engagement generates heat.
Wear (glazing, polishing, material degradation from repeated cycles) lowers \(\mu\), so the clutch eventually slips; this is the standard explanation for slip.
Externally engaged drum clutches use the same design but are actuated pneumatically, hydraulically, magnetically or by mechanical linkage. They are fully controllable and independent of shaft speed.
Drum clutch (outward-pressing shoes on a cylinder) versus disc clutch (flat friction faces pressed together); applications of centrifugal clutches include chainsaws, go-karts and overload releases.
conn: Centrifugal force \(m\omega^2 r\) minus spring force gives the normal force, which with \(\mu\) gives the friction force, torque and transmitted power \(P=T\omega\).
Spring stiffness and pre-tension set the engagement speed, which also sets how much slip and heat is generated during run-up and how smooth the engagement is.
Wear reduces \(\mu\), which reduces torque capacity, so the clutch slips at the same speed; this links maintenance and material choice to design torque.
Centrifugal (speed-triggered, automatic) versus externally actuated (controlled, speed-independent) clutches are often compared in selection questions.
exq: A centrifugal clutch has 4 shoes, each of mass 1.5 kg, with centre of gravity at 80 mm radius at engagement and drum inner radius 100 mm. The springs exert 800 N on each shoe and \(\mu=0.3\). Find the engagement speed in rpm and the torque transmitted at 1500 rpm.
Explain how a centrifugal drum clutch works, naming its main components, and state why it suits starting an electric motor under load.
Why does a centrifugal clutch slip after prolonged use? Discuss glazing, polishing and the effect on torque capacity, and suggest design changes to compensate.
List four methods of engaging an externally actuated drum clutch and compare this type with a centrifugal clutch.

Derive an expression for the power transmitted by a centrifugal clutch at speed \(\omega\) in terms of shoe mass, spring force, \(\mu\), number of shoes and the radii. State how the power changes if the spring force is increased.

notes.t: Friction clutches
pts: Friction clutches use friction as their fundamental mechanism to transmit torque between shafts.
A centrifugal drum clutch connects or disconnects two shafts depending on the speed of the driving shaft.
Centrifugal clutches engage and disengage automatically, with no operator input, once shaft speed passes a critical value.
Key elements are forced radially outwards by centrifugal action and press against the inner radius of a mating cylindrical drum.
The two main key types of friction clutch covered are the drum type and the disc type.
defs: Centrifugal clutch

A friction clutch that engages or disengages automatically when the driving shaft speed exceeds a critical value, using centrifugal force acting on radially moving elements to press them against a drum.
tips: Do not confuse the drum and disc types: a drum clutch uses outward-pressing keys against a cylindrical drum, while disc clutches press flat friction faces together.
Centrifugal clutches depend on speed, not torque, for engagement, so a low-speed shaft will not engage regardless of load.
rq: Why does a centrifugal clutch need no operator input to engage, and what determines when it engages?

Centrifugal force on the key elements increases with shaft speed; once it pushes them outward enough to contact the drum, friction transmits torque. Engagement occurs when speed exceeds a critical value.
What would happen to a centrifugal clutch if the driving shaft speed stayed below the critical value?
The key elements would not be forced outward strongly enough to contact the drum, so the clutch remains disengaged and no torque is transmitted.

notes.t: Friction clutches: drum (centrifugal) clutches
pts: Friction clutches use friction as their fundamental mechanism to connect and disconnect a driving and driven member.
A drum clutch makes a radial connection for movement only; in a centrifugal operation only the inner part of the clutch can be the drive side.
Engaging a friction clutch can generate unwanted heat from the slipping friction surfaces.
Centrifugal clutches are used in chainsaws, overload releases and go-karts.
defs: Clutch
A machine member used to connect a driving shaft to a driven shaft so the driven shaft can be started or stopped at will without stopping the driving shaft.
Centrifugal clutch
A clutch in which the engaging force is generated by centrifugal action of shoes or masses as the drive speed rises, so it engages automatically with rotational speed.
tips: Do not confuse the clutch's role: it disconnects the driven shaft while the driving shaft keeps running, not the reverse.
For centrifugal clutches, remember the drive side is the inner part, a condition of validity for the radial operation.
rq: Why must the drive side of a centrifugal drum clutch be the inner part?
Because the radial centrifugal action pushes the shoes outward against the inner surface of the drum, so the drum (outer part) becomes the driven side and only the inner assembly can be driven.
Why does a clutch generate heat when engaging, and why does this matter?
Heat arises from slip between friction surfaces before they lock together; excessive heat wears the lining and reduces efficiency, so it is an unwanted effect to be minimised.

notes.t: Friction clutches: drum (centrifugal) clutch
pts: A drum clutch uses friction as its fundamental mechanism to connect and disconnect the prime mover from the load.
It lets the prime mover start and run up to operating speed with minimal load, reducing start currents in electric motors and stresses in engines.
It engages automatically: once the drive shaft spins fast enough, the clutch starts to engage (centrifugal flyweights press the linings against the drum).
It disengages automatically when the prime mover slows down, which also stops an electric motor being turned by the load.
Main components: hub, flyweights, cylindrical pins, tension springs, friction linings and the clutch drum.
defs: Drum clutch

A centrifugal friction clutch in which flyweights driven by shaft rotation press friction linings outward against a clutch drum, engaging automatically above a set speed and disengaging when speed falls.
tips: Engagement is speed-dependent: the clutch engages above a set speed, not at a fixed position; state the trigger clearly in answers.
Do not confuse the drum (outer rotating part) with the hub (inner part attached to the shaft).
rq: Why does a drum clutch reduce the starting current of an electric motor?
Because the motor starts unloaded: the clutch is disengaged at low speed, so the motor accelerates without driving the load, avoiding the large inrush torque demand.
What would happen if the drum clutch did not disengage when the prime mover slowed?
The load would keep the motor turning, so an electric motor would be driven as a generator/load-driven machine and could be damaged or fail to stop safely.

notes.t: Friction clutches: drum (centrifugal radial) clutches
pts: Friction is the fundamental mechanism; pads need high friction coefficient and mass or the clutch slips
Pad material degrades with repeated engage/disengage cycles, so the clutch eventually slips
Pad and drum wear (glazing and polishing) reduces the friction coefficient over time
Pad mass and friction coefficient set the maximum torque the clutch can transmit
Springs and masses control engagement speed and smooth engagement, absorbing engine RPM fluctuations
defs: Friction clutch
